en: A Brief Commentary on the Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Original Life and the Mind-Ground Contemplation, Scroll Four.
Annotated by the Śramaṇa Lai Zhou of Chantansi Temple outside the Capital of Qing.

△ Second, the section on Zhiguang’s resolve for enlightenment, leaving home, requesting the Buddha to dispel doubts, and the preaching of the Dharma (this section contains the major themes of three scrolls).

(That is, the first, second, third, fourth, fifth, and sixth fascicles. First, the formal entry into the monastic life, describing doubts and requesting the Dharma; second, the title of the first chapter. Chapter Three: On Renunciation (*Nirveda*) and Abandonment (*Tyāga*).

"Renunciation" (*nirveda*) means loathing and aversion; "abandonment" (*tyāga*) means liberation and detachment. Regarding the title "The Light of Wisdom": it is named because he heard that the mind has nothing to be attained.

To repay his debt of gratitude, he reflected upon the profusion and turmoil of worldly affairs; his mind could not find stillness, and out of weariness and a desire for liberation, he renounced secular life to enter the monastic order.
This is why it is called "wearied renunciation. △ Second, the main text has four sections. First, the formal presentation of the inquiry has four parts.
First, the sūtra narrator describes the ritual setting:
At that time, the elder Jñānaprabha, sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet,
joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power" means that through the light of the Buddha’s vision and wisdom, and by virtue of having heard the preceding chapter, he gave rise to a great resolve;
therefore, the Buddha bestowed his supernatural power upon him, causing him to transcend his doubts and present his request. The narrator attributes this grace to the Buddha and thus records it.
△ Second, expressing gratitude and describing one's own state of mind.
“World-Honored One, having now heard from the Buddha this profound and wondrous Dharma of repaying kindness, my heart leaps with joy at what I have never before experienced.
Like a person suffering from hunger and thirst who encounters ambrosial food, I now desire to repay the four debts of gratitude by taking refuge in the Buddha,
the Dharma, and the Sangha, leaving the household life to cultivate the Way, constantly exerting diligent effort in the hope of realizing Bodhi.”
Regarding the two phrases beginning with "the mind harbors [equanimity]," there are two interpretations: the general and the specific.

The general interpretation holds that upon hearing the Buddha’s verses, which once again demonstrate the four debts of gratitude and further clarify them through the subtle elucidation of precepts and repentance, he hears for the first time what he had never heard before;

thus, he leaps for joy and offers praise such as has never been known. The specific interpretation holds that the single phrase "the mind has nothing to be attained" is the point of intimate realization.

Because he attained awakening from this, it is said that "he attained what he had never before. Yet, "what has never before been attained" is precisely non-attainment; this refers to the emptiness of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*). By wondrously penetrating the Buddha’s intent, one must necessarily realize the threefold emptiness within all matters of self-benefit and benefit for others, as well as within both phenomena and principle. Only then is it a practice that truly accords with the Way. Upon hearing [this], joy filled his heart so completely that he could not contain it; thus it is called "leaping for joy. He presented his understanding to the Buddha, hence the phrase "never before had [such a thing occurred].

Taking awakening as attainment, he attained the truly non-outflowing (*anāsrava*) Dharma of non-attainment. The two lines beginning with "Like one who is hungry" mean that in the past he did not obtain the flavor of the Single Vehicle Dharma, which was like hunger;
he had not yet obtained the water of wisdom to quench his thirst, which was like parchedness. Now, having heard the sublime...
The Dharma has opened my breast and fulfilled my original aspiration, like drinking nectar that eliminates both hunger and thirst.
All of the above constitutes my expression of gratitude. I shall now describe my inner thoughts: having attained realization of the Dharma, I ought to recognize and repay this kindness;

therefore, I have entrusted myself to the Triple Gem, leaving the household life to practice and realize the Way. Now, as for why one must necessarily leave the household life to repay this kindness, it is based on...

The Buddha said: "It is only with a mind of non-attainment that one can truly repay [the Buddha's] kindness. If one remains at home, one will be distracted by worldly affairs and unable to attain purity of mind;

therefore, one seeks to leave the household life to distance oneself from the dust of the world. Thus, the three emptinesses (trīṇi śūnyatāni) become easy to realize, and it is said that one 'rarely attains Bodhi.
△ Third, citing the past to address doubts, in two parts. First, praising the householder and raising doubts, in three parts. First, preaching the Dharma.
Mind-only. Out of great compassion, at one time the Buddha was in the city of Vaiśālī and taught the profound Dharma for the sake of Vimalakīrti.
You, Vimalakīrti, take the pure mind as the root of wholesome karma, and the unwholesome mind as the root of unwholesome karma.
Roots. Because the mind is pure, the world is pure; because the mind is defiled, the world is defiled.
In my Buddha-dharma, the mind is sovereign; there are no phenomena that do not arise from the mind.
Vaiśālī is here translated as "Extensive Purity" (Guǎngyán). Vimalakīrti is "Stainless Renown" (Jìngmíng);
since "stainless" (*vimala*) is equivalent to "pure" (*viśuddha*) and "renown" (*kīrti*) is equivalent to "name" (*nāman*), this is the literal rendering of the term *Vimalakīrti*.

The "profound Dharma" refers to the Dharma of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*). By stating "because it is pure," the text formally indicates Mind-Only; for the pure mind is precisely the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*).
Both are quiescent. When the unwholesome mind arises, evil thoughts run rampant. Because the mind is the root from which karma is generated and retribution is summoned, it is called the "root.
This will be explained in the following text. It is like a straight form casting a straight shadow, or a beautiful countenance reflecting a lovely image.
Thus, when the mind is pure, it is tranquil and luminous, non-active, and unattached to all phenomena; this is the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*). From this pure mind...
The manifested world has a ground of natural lapis lazuli, adorned with the seven treasures, such that there is nothing impure;
hence it is said, "Because the mind is pure, the world is pure. The following two lines are the opposite of this: because the mind is already defiled and turbid.
Because they manifest from a defiled mind, one perceives excrement, impurities, rubble, and thorns; there is nothing that is not defiled. Therefore it is said:

"Because the mind is defiled, the world is defiled. (The mind encompasses both the holy and the ordinary; the world encompasses both the sentient and the insentient. My Buddha concludes [the section] below.
All dharmas encompass the entirety of the ten dharma-realms, including both the environment and its inhabitants. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "One should contemplate the nature of the dharma-realm:
all things are created solely by the mind. This sutra says: "The mind is sovereign; there is nothing that does not proceed from the mind.
Therefore, Master Tianru composed the "Diagram of the Ten Dharma-Realms as Solely Mind," which is based upon this principle. △ Second, praising the householder.
You now dwell at home with great merit and virtue; you possess every kind of precious necklace and ornament in abundance. Your children and kinsmen live in peace and happiness.
You have perfected right view and do not slander the Triple Gem. With a heart of filial piety, you revere and support your elders and kin.

He gives rise to great compassion and bestows gifts upon the solitary and destitute; he does not inflict harm even upon ants and termites. He takes patience as his garment and compassion as his dwelling;
he honors those of virtue with a mind free from arrogance, regarding all beings with pity as if they were his own infants.
They do not covet wealth or profit, but constantly cultivate the virtue of renunciation and make offerings to the Triple Gem with a heart that never knows satiety.

For the sake of the Dharma, they would sacrifice their bodies without any sense of stinginess. Laypeople who act in this way, though they have not left the household life, have already perfected immeasurable and boundless merit.
Since it is stated that he is "a householder," it is clear that Vimalakīrti is a layman (*gṛhapati*). The passage beginning with "possessing great" is a general praise of his virtues;

the three characters "great merit and virtue" (*mahāpuṇya*) serve as the general title, while the subsequent sections specifically manifest these qualities. The section beginning with "with various jewels" manifests the fruits of worldly merit in the present life.
The section beginning with "sons and daughters" manifests the manifestations of his worldly virtue. Not slandering the Triple Gem is precisely right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*). Regarding... [text ends]
Regarding the teaching on the Three Jewels as one essence: through right view, one realizes that the self-nature’s awakening is the Buddha Jewel;
the self-nature’s preservation of the path is the Dharma Jewel; and the self-nature’s harmony is the Sangha Jewel. To fail to realize this self-nature is slander;
to be able to realize this self-nature is non-slander. However, slander necessarily entails lack of faith, and lack of faith leads to a failure to awaken. This...

Thus, through faith one attains awakening; this constitutes right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*). From "By means of filial piety" (*yǐ xiào xià*) onwards, it praises filial care for one's honored parents as the foundation of all virtues.
This is a mark of merit in the present life and also a cause for merit in future lives.
Furthermore, from "Giving rise to the great" (*qǐ dà xià*) onwards, it again praises the benefit of others (*parārtha*), meaning that one is able to provide for those who are solitary and destitute.
"Refraining from harming even ants and the like" constitutes the marks of virtue in the present life and serves as the cause for virtue in future lives.
Regarding "patience": just as clothing can cover the body so that its unseemly form is not revealed, patience can cover resentment so that the form of anger is not revealed.
Furthermore, just as clothing can protect the body so that cold cannot enter, patience can protect the Path so that calamities cannot enter.

Forbearance is, in truth, the fundamental basis for entering the Way. Regarding the passage "benevolence and compassion": just as a room can contain one's body, so too can benevolence contain all things.

Furthermore, the room serves as a metaphor for the profound and subtle realm realized by the sages; since the sage’s learning culminates in this profound subtlety, it must necessarily be manifested through benevolence and compassion.
Benevolence and compassion are identical to humaneness (*ren*). Suppose there were even a single thing that was not encompassed by them...
Zé: This does not fully capture the measure of the Way of Benevolence (*ren*). A Bodhisattva who can give rise to this mind has no birth that is not saved and no thing that is not accepted.
Furthermore, the meaning also contains the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) as the seat; it is merely a textual omission.

If it were not for the emptiness of phenomena, all would be conditioned functions (*saṃskṛta-kriyā*); how then could there be the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhivyākaraṇa*) in the subsequent text? One should revere those of virtuous merit.
Furthermore, to see one's own virtues is to possess the virtue of having the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) as one’s seat. How is this known?

It is because there are eight kinds of arrogance (*māna*) and seven kinds of pride (*abhimāna*); without relying on the dual emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*), these are difficult to subdue.
To feel compassion for all beings as if they were one's own infants is the chamber of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā*).

This refers to virtue, such as non-attachment and so forth, culminating in the perfection of the *dānapāramitā* by relinquishing one's body without stinginess. These two characters refer to Vimalakīrti;
although he is not an ordained monk, the term "although" is used as a living expression to indicate that while he currently manifests in the body of a layman (*gṛhapati*).

"Rather, one proceeds backward on the bodhisattva path. Therefore, it says "already complete," etc.; this refers to the previous perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) encompassing the simultaneous cultivation of sixty thousand practices, hence the phrase "immeasurable merit.

(Regarding the eight kinds of *mada*: namely, pride of physical vigor, pride of nature, pride of wealth and status, pride of sovereignty, pride of longevity, pride of intelligence, pride of conduct, and pride of beauty.

Regarding the seven kinds of *māna*: namely, pride, pride of self, pride of superiority, pride beyond pride, pride of overestimation, pride of inferiority, and false pride. To look down upon others is called *māna*; to rely on oneself is *mada*. △ Three.
Furthermore, I grant you this prophecy:
in a future age, when your myriad practices are perfected, you shall transcend the three realms and realize great bodhi. This is the mind you have cultivated.
Such a person is truly a śramaṇa, and also a brāhmaṇa; they are a true bhikṣu and a true renunciant.
A person such as this is what is called one who is both a householder and a renunciant.
The cause is fully perfected through the completion of the myriad practices; the fruit of great bodhi is fully realized.

One who transcends the three realms must necessarily be free from the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*). This meaning encompasses not only the transcendence of the three realms, but also the transcendence of the three vehicles (*tri-yāna*), as well as freedom from the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-maraṇa*).
The above constitutes the bestowal of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) to those who come. As for what you have written below, it is a praise of the present.
In the world, one practices cultivation; ordinary persons cultivate the body, while Bodhisattvas cultivate the mind.
A true śramaṇa does not take the body to be the śramaṇa, but takes the mind to be the śramaṇa. Suppose one’s body is clad in the dharma-robes, yet the mind does not enter the Way;
such a person is merely a bhikṣu in name. Even if one’s body is in white robes, if the mind can enter the Way, that person is a true [śramaṇa].
"A bhikṣu is one who, though having a wife and children, has a mind that has transcended the three realms; such a person is truly a renunciant.
All of the above are the words of the Buddha, as recorded by Jñānaprabha. This was intended for those who harbor doubts. Part Two: Refuting Doubts Regarding Renunciation, in three sections.
First: Directly refuting the group of six monks (*ṣaḍvargika*).

"World-Honored One, there was once a time when, at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove Monastery, you were teaching the Dharma of exhortation to the six groups of monks of evil character, and you addressed them, saying:
'You bhikṣus, listen closely, listen closely! Faith is the root for entering the ocean of the Buddha-dharma;
the precepts are the raft for crossing the river of birth and death. If a person has gone forth from the household life and does not protect [the precepts]...'"
Regarding the prohibitive precepts: they are greedily attached to worldly pleasures and destroy the jewel of the Buddha’s precepts.

Or, having lost right view, they enter the forest of false views and lead immeasurable people to fall into a great, deep pit. Such bhikṣus are not called renunciants; they are not śramaṇas, nor are they brāhmaṇas.
Their forms resemble those of śramaṇas, but their minds always dwell at home. Such śramaṇas lack the practice of detachment.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Veṇuvana Monastery was located on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
Its grounds were level, majestic, and pure, surpassing all other places. Because the Buddha had previously preached the Dharma therein, a monastery (vihāra) was established there.
'Kalandaka' has no equivalent translation; it is the name of a grove. 'Vihāra' refers to a refined and elegant hall, namely a Dharma-hall. As for the 'Six Groups'..."
During the time of the Buddha, they gathered in groups and engaged in various improper acts; because they went out and entered in large parties, they were called the "Six Groups.
The first was Upananda, who was Chandaka and of the Śākya clan. The second was Kālodāyin, which means "Black Light.
These two men were characterized by much greed and delusion and would not accept the advice of others; they resided in the village of Kālācala in the country of Kāśī.

They committed various acts contrary to the rules of decorum. At that time, the upāsakas of the village of Kālapavana came and informed the Buddha, saying, "The group of six bhikṣus are performing various illegal acts in that village.
The Buddha ordered Ānanda, together with sixty bhikṣus, to go there and carry out the formal act of expulsion (*pravāsanīya-karman*). The two of them, knowing this, went out one yojana to meet them.
He requested Ānanda to seek his confession on his behalf, saying: "What I have done was not good; from this day forward, I dare not do it again.
He then returned with Ānanda to the place where the Buddha was. Third was Sandhāna; fourth was Mahāśanava;
fifth was Aśvajit—these three men were of many delusions and would not accept the words of others; sixth was Pūrṇa.

They were by nature prone to anger. These four men were all of the Śākya clan; they constantly engaged in improper conduct and would not accept the advice of others, hence they were called "the ill-natured ones.
As for the six groups, each gathered a following and acted unlawfully, hence they were called "the group of six.
When the Buddha spoke the Dharma of instruction and admonition to them, it was to teach and warn them, desiring that they reform their faults and become virtuous. You all...
Below follows the formal instruction: "The Buddha-dharma is like a great ocean; faith is that which enables one to enter it, serving as its very foundation.
Among the eleven wholesome dharmas, faith is the foremost; it is the source for entering the Path.
These two preceding lines urge one toward faith, making it clear that the aforementioned lack of faith was a deficiency. "To cross the river of birth and death, precepts serve as the boat and raft."

Exhortation and admonition: one should fully recognize one’s previous lack of restraint. The passage beginning with “If a person” and following consists entirely of reproaches and insults, which are easy to understand.

The term “deep pit” refers to the hells. The passage beginning with “In this way” names and personally rebukes him, stating that while he outwardly resembles a son of the Buddha, his mind is not that of a son of the Buddha;
therefore, it is said he cannot be called a renunciant. Because he possesses the physical form of a monk while his mind is not stained by the Path, it is said...
He is not a śramaṇa; because his body dwells in a village while his mind lacks pure conduct, he is said to be "not a brāhmaṇa.

Because worldly sentiments have not yet receded and liberation has not been achieved, it is said that he "lacks the practice of detachment" (only when one can transcend the dust of the world and leave behind false views is it the true practice of detachment;
the group of six [monks] has not attained this, and thus they are so rebuked). △ Second, the teaching on the practice of detachment.
There are two kinds of practice for seclusion: first, physical seclusion; second, mental seclusion. Regarding physical seclusion:
if a person has gone forth and dwells in a solitary place, remaining untainted by the objects of desire, this is called physical seclusion.
However, if one’s body is indeed secluded while the mind still craves the objects of desire, such a person is not said to be secluded. This applies to both faithful laymen and faithful laywomen.
Dwelling in a village, one generates the unsurpassed mind and benefits all beings through great compassion; practicing in this manner is called true seclusion.

"Secluded from the inferior" introduces and enumerates the names; "physically distant from the inferior" explains the meaning. As for "one who has left the home life," they have abandoned their ancestral inheritance.
Renouncing what one holds dear and bidding farewell to kin, one leaves the mundane household for the sake of the self.

As for "solitude," it refers to dwelling in deep mountains and remote valleys, or in serene and elegant gardens, to settle in peace and advance upon the Path, remaining unconfused by sounds and sights; hence it is said that one is "unstained by the realm of desire.
Because the body is at ease and the Path exists, this is "physical distancing. Although the body [remains], the following four phrases are...
This is countered and severely rebuked. "If pure" and below clarifies that true practice of detachment does not fall into outward traces;
thus it says, "whether man or woman. Just as one dwells in the dust of the world without being stained, and follows the Way without doubt, it is called "pure faith.
A "village" refers to a place of worldly splendor and the five desires. "The unsurpassed mind" means to give rise to the Buddha-mind from within the ordinary mind.

The mind of great compassion acts as a Buddha even amidst the defilements of worldly toil; because it possesses the merit of raining down benefits upon both self and others, it is said to "benefit all.
Thus concludes the praise below. For the single matter of cultivation does not originally depend on whether one is a layperson or a monastic;
its essence lies in severing delusion to clarify the truth. Only those who transcend the mundane and enter the sacred can uphold this.
Indeed, if one’s deluded mind has not yet ceased and continues to pursue objects and conditions, then even while dwelling in deep mountains, one’s thoughts remain tethered to the mundane world.

For such a class of people—whether monastics or laypeople—the roots of karma for birth and death persist; thus, it is right that the Buddha censured them as those who have not distanced themselves from worldly attachments, and it is likewise right that practitioners should censure them.
There are others whose bodies, though they remain at home, have their minds roaming the ocean of enlightenment, such that the five sensory dusts are dissolved [into wisdom].

This constitutes their intrinsic nature. The six recollections are integrated into Bodhi; furthermore, they flow forth from the heart of great compassion as wondrous practices to benefit sentient beings.
Such a person is both bound by and liberated from the fetters; therefore, the Tathāgata extolled this "True Far-Going" with the utmost praise.
△ Third, the Six Groups Obtain Benefit.

Thereupon, the six groups of ill-natured bhikṣus, upon hearing this sound of the Dharma, attained the patience of compliance (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). Generally, those of an evil nature are mostly rigid; those who are rigid are mostly rebellious. Now, having heard the Buddha’s censure, they gave rise to great shame and remorse; their evil natures were instantly released, and they became directly compliant. This is what is meant by "the place where the wild mind ceases is itself bodhi. Nevertheless, [The text continues: ...it is like a person who has been struck by a poisoned arrow and is suffering from the pain. At that time, there is no other way but to extract the arrow. If one does not extract the arrow, the poison will spread throughout the body. If the poison spreads throughout the body, the person will surely die. Therefore, one must extract the arrow. Once the arrow is extracted, the poison will not spread. Because the poison does not spread, the person will not die. For this reason, one must extract the arrow. Thus we know that at the assembly of Vimalakīrti, the disparagement of the partial and the small, and the praise of the Great and the Perfect, were precisely of this nature. △ Fourth, seeking the Buddha’s definitive answer, in four parts: first, recounting the doubt, offering praise, and making the request.
Nevertheless, although we now have faith in the Buddha’s teaching, each of us harbors doubts and our minds have not yet reached certainty. How excellent, World-Honored One!
You are the one who can sever all the doubts of the world, the one who has attained mastery over all dharmas, and the speaker of truth.
One who speaks without duality is a knower of the path and an opener of the path.
We pray that the Tathāgata, for our sake and for all sentient beings of future ages, will set aside expedient means and proclaim the true Dharma, so that we may forever be free from doubt and regret.
"Causing them to enter the Buddha-way.

However, these are words used for the purpose of rephrasing the text; although they are incomplete statements, because the Buddha has already passed away, they are all words of truth, and I dare not fail to believe them.
Yet, as my mind does not understand them, I cannot avoid harboring doubts. Thus it is said: "Though one believes, one still doubts."

It is said "each and every one" because it does not refer to a single person. His intention was to leave the household life, yet due to the censure of the group of six (ṣaḍvargika), he had not yet reached a firm decision.
The preceding passage expresses his doubts; "Excellent! and what follows is praise of the Buddha, intended to seek the truth, as the Buddha’s words were not yet definitive.

Faced with the difficulty of both accepting and rejecting, one first exclaims "Excellent! in order to request the Buddha’s true teaching; this constitutes the general praise. What follows is the specific praise:
"One who can sever doubt" praises the Buddha’s wisdom for its profound penetration; "one who possesses mastery over the Dharma" praises the unity of the provisional and the ultimate;
"one who speaks words of truth" praises speech that accords with reality; and "one who speaks words without duality" refers to—
"Deciding" refers to the Buddha's ability to personally realize [the truth]. "Opening the Way" refers to the Buddha's ability to provide instruction.
Having offered such praise above, the intention is to seek a definitive resolution; therefore, the subsequent text expresses a fervent plea, saying, "I only pray," and so forth.
"We" refers to the present assembly, while "future" refers to sentient beings of later generations. Just as...
This would then belong to the provisional; yet, while clearly knowing that suppression and exaltation are provisional, one cannot help but harbor doubts.
Therefore, I hope the Buddha will set this aside and speak only of the ultimate truth—this is my earnest plea for intimacy. May you resolve it with a single word, so that I may no longer hesitate.
Therefore, it is said that one is "permanently free from doubt and regret. Turning directly beneath [the feet], one immediately hastens toward the ocean of enlightenment;
thus, it is said that one is "caused to enter the Buddha-way. △ Second, restating his own view.
In this assembly there are two bodhisattvas: one is a renunciant and the other is a householder.

These two bodhisattvas are well able to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings without ceasing. As I consider it, the renunciant bodhisattva does not equal the householder in practicing the bodhisattva path.
There are two kinds of bodhisattvas; both are those who practice the bodhisattva path. The "renunciant" refers to one who has abandoned their six kin and shaved off their hair and beard;
the "householder" refers to one who remains amidst their six kin, dwelling in the dust of the world without being defiled by it.

These two "lows" refer to the distinction of form while the path remains the same. Those who are skillful adapt with subtle ingenuity to the needs of beings; those who bring benefit and joy have attained the meaning and transcend words.

When it says "all sentient beings," it means one does not discriminate according to their capacities. "Without rest" means that one never tires of instructing others. "Only conjecturing" refers to measuring things through one's own subjective mind.
As for the statement that "leaving home is not as good as staying at home," [it is said from the perspective of those who have not yet realized the truth].
This is because he has abandoned his parents and lacks the way to nourish them. △ Third, the interrogation and explanation of the reason:
Why is this so? Formerly, there was a Golden Wheel-turning King who gave rise to the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Disgusted with and detached from the impermanence, suffering, and emptiness of the world, he renounced the rank of wheel-turning king as if discarding mucus or spittle, remaining pure.

He renounced the household life and entered the path of the Buddha. At that time, the eighty-four thousand ladies of the inner palace and court attendants, seeing the king’s renunciation, each harbored deep longing and affection;
their hearts broke into wailing and lamentation, giving rise to great distress. They experienced the suffering of separation from those they loved, as agonizing as the torments of hell.
This included the precious women who had appeared when the Golden Wheel-turning Sage King first ascended the throne, as well as the king’s thousand sons and his ministers.
The retinue, together grieving over this separation and his renunciation of the throne, filled the four quarters of the world with their wailing cries.
These kinsmen each spoke these words: "Our King’s merit and wisdom were immeasurable and boundless; how could he abandon us to go forth?
Alas, what misery! The world is now empty and void; from this day forward, we shall have no refuge and no protector."
The first phrase poses a question: Why is it that those who have left the household life do not, in fact, practice as well as those who remain at home?

The passage beginning with "In the past... provides the explanation. A Golden Wheel-turning King (Cakravartin) appears during the period of increase (*utsarpiṇī-kalpa*), whereas Śākyamuni appeared during the period of decrease (*avasarpinī-kalpa*);

thus, he has never personally seen such a king, but may have heard of him through successive transmission, hence the expression "In the past there was. The explanation of the Golden Wheel-turning King is found in the first fascicle. [He] gave rise to the aspiration for... [the Mahāyāna].
The "equal" refers to the very mind that can give rise [to the resolve]. Disenchantment and so forth are the foundation for giving rise to this mind.
"Impermanence" means that the world undergoes flux, the realms experience formation and destruction, humans face birth and death, and things undergo transformation;

because all are oppressed by impermanence, they are called "suffering. Because they ultimately end in extinction, they are called "empty. Due to the disenchantment with suffering and emptiness, he renounced the kingship.
As for the stage [of renunciation]: because one casts off everything without looking back, it is said that it is like discarding mucus and spittle;

because not even a speck of dust can defile it, it is called "purely leaving the household life"; and because one realizes the fruit through practice without failing one's resolve, it is called "entering the Buddha-way."
At that time, the attendants of the inner palace wailed and lamented; their grief and longing were like those of a person mourning their father or mother, or like the suffering of those in hell.
Just as those in hell are oppressed by the fires of karma, they too were oppressed by the fire of sorrow due to the pain of separation from what they love.
This is comparable to hell, yet it is not a true hell. Thus it was previously described.

The queen, the court ladies, and the others were filled with such grief and longing. Furthermore, beneath the passage concerning the golden wheel, the circumstances of the separation from the thousand sons, the precious women, the ministers, and the common people are described in this manner. Regarding the passage beginning with "wailing and weeping":
since all within the four seas are the King’s subjects and the sovereign is the lord of his ministers and people, once the sovereign has left the household life, the people have no one to rely upon.
Where, then, is there no one who does not know? Who is there who does not feel pain? Thus, the sound of wailing fills the four continents under heaven.
To say that the world is empty and void is merely an expression of grief and a lack of reliance; one should know that this is merely an intellectual speculation.
While leaving the household life is indeed sublime, this [attitude] harms compassion. How can such a heart be so hard? △ Fourth, shifting to address the doubt.
It is difficult.
If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, resolve upon Bodhicitta,
and leave their parents behind to renounce the world and enter the Path, their parents— out of deep compassion and profound affection— will be moved by the sorrow of separation.
Heaven and earth are like a fish in a dried-up rut, writhing upon the ground; the suffering of separation from those one loves is likewise so.

Just as the mind of a universal monarch’s retinue [is devoted], how can a renunciant bodhisattva who benefits sentient beings bring harm to his parents, wife, and children, causing immeasurable people to undergo great anguish? For these reasons, the renunciant bodhisattva lacks compassion.

They lack compassion and do not benefit sentient beings; therefore, they are not like the householder bodhisattva, who possesses great loving-kindness and compassion, feels pity for sentient beings, and benefits all.
This further cites the case of men and women of pure faith who, mindful of birth and death and seeking liberation, have never failed to hold their aspirations in high esteem.
That their parents wail and lament, unable to let them go, is likewise the common sentiment of worldly people; this is illustrated by the analogy of drawing water from a parched well.
A "rut" (*cheda*) is the track left by the wheels of a carriage. "Dried up" (*kha*) means parched. When a fish enters a parched rut and writhes about, it will inevitably die;

this is no different from the parents' weeping for their child, where their gallbladders and livers shatter. Therefore, it is said that the suffering of separation from those one loves is likewise so.
As in the passage below, this is consistent with the preceding metaphor. One should know that the preceding metaphor is used [to illustrate this].
The lower [section] concerns compassion for those above. This analogy uses a father’s compassion for his son; although the upper and lower [positions] differ, their sorrowful grief is the same.
Indeed, the two preceding cases are merely illustrative instances. The section on "leaving home" below is the point of doubt and difficulty:
it means that the reason a Bodhisattva leaves home is fundamentally to benefit sentient beings. If it were as in the two preceding cases, not only...
It is of no benefit to one's parents and others, and instead results in harm; because one cannot help but harbor suspicion, it is asked: "How is this?
This follows upon the preceding text to censure their great transgression. Not remembering the kindness of one's parents in nurturing and raising them is a lack of *maitrī* (loving-kindness);
not remembering the affectionate bonds of one's wife and children is a lack of *karuṇā* (compassion). As for those who are most intimate...
If one cannot even look after those they love, how much less so for sentient beings? Therefore, it is said that "one does not benefit sentient beings.

The two characters "is" (是) and "therefore" (故) here follow from what precedes; they do not function as a concluding summary as they do below. This means that a lay bodhisattva, above, does not abandon their parents, and below, does not abandon their wife and children;
since they possess both compassion and pity, is this not indeed pitying and benefiting sentient beings?
Is it not so? Truly, phenomena do not arise in isolation; teachings emerge by relying upon conditions.

Were it not for the presence of doubt and inquiry, how could the great benefit of leaving the household life (renunciation) ever flourish? Yet, the vision of Zhiguang has not yet transcended the mundane;

he draws from the very root of birth and death to claim it as a benefit for saving sentient beings—is this not tragic? (The "root of birth and death" refers to affectionate attachment. As long as affectionate attachment is not severed, one is never free from birth and death.)
...therefore it is called a "root. △ Second, the Buddha resolves the doubts in three parts. First, praising and censuring what is improper:

At that time, the Buddha addressed the Elder Jñānaprabha: "Excellent, excellent! You possess great compassion, for you have exhorted me to speak of the relative superiority and inferiority of the two types of practitioners:
the renunciant and the householder. Regarding your current question, the renunciant bodhisattva is not superior to the householder."
This interpretation is not correct.

"Excellent" (*sādhu*) is a praise for his request; it signifies that he intends for the Buddha to distinguish between the superior and the inferior, and that his purpose possesses the beauty of benefiting others—hence the term "excellent.
To repeat it twice indicates the height of excellence. His intention is such that he cannot proceed with this proposal until [the Buddha] has first granted permission.
Having heard of the excellence of leaving the household life, you now further criticize it as being improper because you do not understand its profound depths.
△ Second, the inquiry and explanation of the reason.
Why is this so? Because a bodhisattva who has gone forth is infinitely and boundlessly superior to one who remains at home, beyond all comparison.
Why? Because by the power of right wisdom, the bodhisattva who has gone forth minutely observes the various faults inherent in the household life.
Why is it that, although the words of the Buddha are cited, one still censures them as being incorrect?
This refers to the fact that those who have left the household life possess the power of wisdom (*prajñā*). Now, the term "wisdom" in its correct sense carries the connotation of discernment.

This is because a bodhisattva who has left the household life holds their aspirations in high esteem; they seek out spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), hear the true Dharma, and thereby give rise to right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). Furthermore, by means of...
Wisdom enters into principle and investigates it deeply; hence it is said that one "subtly observes. Not falling into absurdity is called "subtle" (*miao*);

not being coarse or superficial is called "fine" (*xi*). Initial awakening shining inward is called "observation" (*guan*); harmonizing phenomena and returning them to principle is called "investigation" (*cha*).
This is the excellence of the renunciant life. All readers should, regarding this subtle observation, make a definitive severance [of delusions] while remaining at home.
To cite another example: as for those who live as householders, although they may possess the aspiration for transcendence, they cannot avoid the burdens of worldly toil.
Unable to consult spiritual friends extensively, and lacking the leisure to study the holy teachings broadly, right wisdom has no means by which it can arise.

Furthermore, their minds are turbid with the five desires; they are bound by greedy seeking and preoccupied with thoughts, chasing after objects and grasping at conditions. Therefore, it is said that [they plant] seeds.

Regarding these faults (here, Jñānaprabha should pose a question: "As the Buddha has taught that those who have left the home life are superior, and as Vimalakīrti was formerly praised as a true renunciant, how can this not contradict the Buddha’s words?

The World-Honored One should answer: "Vimalakīrti is the manifestation of the Tathāgata Suvarṇapuṣpa. For the sake of those householders who ultimately cannot leave the home life, he manifested as a layman to practice the bodhisattva path;

therefore, I praised his virtues as a skillful means to attract householders to the path. As for entering the path in its true sense, one must truly yield to those who have left the home life. Thus, the preceding and following passages correspond, and the meaning of the text is coherent). △ Third.
The nine extensive explanations of various metaphors begin with six metaphors for craving, the first of which establishes the basis of the analogy:
"All the houses and dwellings in the world are accumulated therein without ever knowing satisfaction, just like the great ocean."
It receives all rivers, great and small, yet it is never filled.
"The world" refers to that which is within the three realms; "the house" refers to the body composed of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

The *ālaya-vijñāna* is like the master of the house—that is, the master who is the nature of sentient beings' consciousness—dwelling in reliance upon the five aggregates. Therefore, [it takes] the body of the five aggregates...
"Call it a dwelling. All subsequent instances are modeled after this. Furthermore, a dwelling can contain things; this is a metaphor for a person's greedy mind.
The following line explicitly clarifies that greed: regarding all desirable objects of the five sensory realms (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*), although one may accumulate them, one still knows no satisfaction.
Yet, it is like the great ocean swallowing all rivers without distinction; what was previously called "various faults" is one such instance.
△ Second, the illustration of swallowing the flow.
"Good son, to the south of Mount Gandhamādana and to the north of the Snowy Mountains lies Lake Anavatapta. There dwell four great nāga kings, each occupying one corner.
The nāga king in the southeast has the head of a white elephant; the nāga king in the southwest has the head of a water buffalo; the nāga king in the northwest has the head of a lion;
and the nāga king in the northeast has the head of a great horse. From each of these four corners, a great river surges forth."
The Gaṅgā River: wherever its waters reach, white elephants emerge following them. Second, the Śiṃśumāra River:
wherever its waters reach, water buffaloes emerge following them. Third, the Vakṣu River: wherever its waters reach, lions emerge following them.
Fourth, the Sītā River: wherever its waters reach, great horses emerge following them. Of such great rivers, each one has five hundred medium-sized rivers.
Within the central river, there are immeasurable smaller rivers; all these waters—great, medium, and small—flow into the great ocean.
Yet this great ocean is never filled to satiety.
Lake Anavatapta. The *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions) states: "In the center of Jambudvīpa lies Lake Anavatapta; in the language of China, it means 'Free from the Torment of Heat.
It is also called Lake Anavatapta (some say that 'Anavatapta' is a corruption of the Sanskrit term; this is because the Sanskrit nomenclature varies across the five regions of India.
In my view, however, it is not an absolute corruption). It is situated south of Mount Gandhamādana and north of the Great Snow Mountains, with a circumference of eight hundred [yojanas]."

[It is] one *li* [in circumference]. Adorned with gold, silver, copper, iron, lapis lazuli, and crystal, its banks are embellished. Golden sand covers the bottom, and the clear waves are as bright as a mirror.
Great Earth Bodhisattvas, by the power of their vows, manifest as dragon kings and dwell therein in concealment, producing pure, cool water.
Thus, from the golden ox-mouth on the eastern side of the pool, the Gaṅgā River flows out, encircling the pool once.
It encircles [the lake] and enters the southeastern sea. From the golden elephant’s mouth on the southern side of the lake flows the Sindhu River;
it circles the lake once and flows into the southwestern sea. From the lapis lazuli horse’s mouth on the western side flows the Vakṣu River;
it circles the lake once and flows into the northwestern sea. From the crystal lion’s mouth on the northern side of the lake flows the Sītā...
The Gaṅgā river encircles the lake once and flows into the eastern sea;

some say it flows underground and emerges from Mount Jīvaśaila (Ji-shí-shān), becoming the source of the Sindhu River and thus the source of the rivers of the Middle Kingdom. (Gaṅgā means "coming from heaven," as it is seen to come from a high place;
Sītā means "river of faith" or "verified river"; Vakṣu means "blue river"; Sindhu means "cold river"—all of which flow out from within the lake. However, this original sūtra and that...
Regarding the slight differences: that [text] states that the dragon kings are manifestations of bodhisattvas, whereas this sutra does not yet say so.

This sutra clearly explains the distinctions in the physical forms of the dragon kings, stating they have the heads of white elephants, water buffaloes, and so forth; those [distinctions] were not yet set forth there.
Furthermore, it is said that from the four sides of the lake, there are river mouths flowing out, such as the "mouth of the golden ox" and the "mouth of the golden elephant.
This sutra does not provide names for these river mouths; rather, it simply states that the rivers flow out from the four corners.
While it may be acceptable for these accounts to differ in what they emphasize or omit, the contradiction between "sides" (*mukha*) and "corners" (*koṇa*) lacks any standard basis. Or...
That "corner" (jiǎo) refers to the ocean into which rivers flow is beyond doubt.
However, since the sutra clearly states that "great rivers surge forth from each of the four corners," it may be that the translator erroneously rendered "face" (miàn) as "corner.
Alternatively, it may be that the *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) erroneously rendered "corner" as "face. Whichever it may be, this remains uncertain. Even so...
The present sutra employs an analogy; the matter arises from a hypothetical construction. Nevertheless, the doubts regarding names and characteristics must be resolved.

The remaining text is easy to understand and need not be explained (the *siddha* of this sutra is the same as the *siddha* of that [other text]). △ Third, the application of the Dharma to the analogy.
It is the same for all the dwellings and houses of the sentient beings in the world:
various treasures come from the four directions and enter entirely into the houses, yet they are never satisfied; they seek much and accumulate, thereby committing all manner of evils.
Impermanence arrives suddenly, and one must abandon one's former dwelling. At that time, the master of the house undergoes retribution according to his karma;
for immeasurable eons, he has no place of ultimate return.
Among the beings of the world, those who are capable of greed amass various precious treasures—these being the very objects of their craving—and thus they dwell in this "house."
The "dwelling" is the body; thus it is said, "it is also like this. This corresponds to the previous image of the great ocean swallowing all streams.

"Gathering all" [refers to] the four directions corresponding to the four great rivers above; "all precious treasures" corresponds to the medium and small rivers and the immeasurable tributaries mentioned above.
"All enter" corresponds to the previous description of the various streams returning to the sea and so forth. "Those who seek much and accumulate" refers to those who obtain one [thing].

Hoping for two; obtaining little while hoping for much; even to the point where the more one obtains, the more one feels insufficient—this is the common sentiment of sentient beings, no different from that great ocean which is never satisfied. Regarding "seeking much" below, this clarifies those who create karma out of greed:
for by seeking much, one inevitably loses what is correct; either one plots for wealth at the expense of virtue, or one covets form and...
They deceive their own hearts, performing all manner of improper acts by force. As for "planning to seize, wounding, or killing," this is called creating various kinds of offenses.
"When impermanence suddenly arrives" means that at the time of death, one cannot preserve even morning or evening. "Abandoning the old residence" refers to [the body].
The corpse has already been discarded. The master of the house is the *ālaya-vijñāna*. "Following karma" means that consciousness is led away by karma;
"karma" refers to the projecting karma (*ākṣepaka-karman*), namely the good and evil deeds performed during one's lifetime, which perfume and form karmic seeds.
Drawn by karma and receiving retribution according to that karma, sentient beings possess no autonomy. Alas!

Were one not to encounter the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, or great spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), who reveal the path and inspire the resolve to cultivate the Way, then not only in this present life could one escape impermanence;
even until the end of the future, there would ultimately be nowhere to turn for refuge.
By contrast, this reveals that seeing the Buddha-nature and realizing Bodhi is that toward which one should turn for refuge. △ Fourth, the explanation of the meaning of the "house":
"Good son, that which is called the house is the body of the five aggregates; the master of that house is your fundamental consciousness."
The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are namely form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Although the aggregate of form is broad, for now, we shall define the phenomena of form (*rūpa-dharma*) by way of the differences in physical appearance—such as height, shortness, fatness, leanness, and facial features—of one’s own parents’ biological offspring.

The latter four are collectively mental phenomena (*citta-dharma*). Feeling refers to the experiencing of an external object; it is that which perceives what is disagreeable or agreeable. Perception, with respect to...
The object of perception (*ālambana*) is that which is remembered without being forgotten. The practitioner refers to that which flows and shifts from moment to moment, never remaining new or stable.

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) is that which discerns the preceding object and contains seeds. Regarding the five factors, "aggregate" (*skandha*) carries the meaning of "to store," because it stores the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*);
thus, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*), while the preceding five aggregates are...
To explain it generally: the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) specifically manifests this, which is the Buddha-nature of sentient beings as they carry along their afflictions (*kleśa*).
However, the Buddha-nature resides within the body of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), just as a person dwells within a house. △ Fifth, the wise do not accept [this].

Who among the wise would delight in the house of the conditioned? Only the Bodhisattvas dwell in the precious palace of peace and bliss, free from old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.

If there are sons of good family with sharp faculties and profound, pure faith who wish to deliver their parents, wives, children, and kinsmen, leading them into the unconditioned palace of ambrosia, they must take refuge in the Triple Gem, leave the household life, and study the Path.
"Conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) refers to the karma created by sentient beings, because there is active conditioning. The two phrases beginning with "Who... are words of exhortation;

they mean that those who possess wisdom will certainly not delight in or cling to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as a basis, nor will they greedily cling to the five sense objects (*pañcaviṣaya*) to create karma.
Only the lower-grade bodhisattvas—namely, the wise—rely upon the "jeweled palace," which is a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*. Thus, the bodhisattva relies [upon it].
It is like dwelling in a palace. Nirvāṇa is the virtue of cessation; therein all afflictions are exhausted and birth-and-death are forever extinguished.
Hence it is said that one is "free from old age, illness, and so forth. The following section encourages practice: hearing once and awakening in a thousand ways constitutes sharp faculties;
resolving the will without doubt constitutes pure faith; the sincerity and firmness of that faith constitute its depth. O sons of good family!
Those who possess pure faith and wish to deliver their parents are encouraged by our World-Honored One to fulfill the way of a filial son, just as Maudgalyāyana saved his mother.
Those who wish to deliver their wives are to fulfill the way of a devoted husband, just as the Buddha delivered Yaśodharā.
Those who wish to deliver their kinsmen and relatives are to fulfill the way of a father and elder brother, just as the Buddha delivered Rāhula and others.

Nanda and others: the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is *nirvāṇa*, and ambrosia (*amṛta*) is a metaphor for *bodhi*. A "dwelling" (*gṛha*) refers to that which is relied upon. Ordinary beings dwell relying on a house;
noble ones (*ārya*) dwell relying on *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. Because wisdom and principle must be brought into accord, it says "causing them to enter.

"Must" (*xu*) means necessarily employing; "returning" (*gui*) means relying upon and turning toward. This is the formal exhortation below. [The character] "with" (*yi*)... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragmentary commentary on a Buddhist scripture, likely the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, discussing the transition from worldly existence to the goal of enlightenment.)

The Three Jewels serve as one’s reliance; this is how one finds a true teacher. There are two kinds of renunciation (*pravrajyā*): that which involves shaving off the beard and hair, whereby one first leaves the secular household;
and that which transcends birth and death, whereby one further leaves the household of the triple world (*tridhātu*).

The two characters for "studying the Way" (*xué dào*) refer to cessation (*śamatha*) and contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), or meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). One who is capable of both awakening to and practicing these is a true seeker. This was because Zhiguang had [already] renounced the world.
Because his resolve was hesitant and undecided, the Tathāgata specifically employed metaphors through alternating suppression and encouragement;
this too is a potent medicine that accords with the timing and addresses the specific ailment. △ Sixth, the verse is repeated as a summary.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again in verse.
This serves as the introduction. There are two types of verse: first, *geya* (repeated verse), and second, *gāthā* (isolated verse).

*Geya* refers to repeated verse, which is a restatement in verse of the preceding prose (*prose-sūtra*). *Gāthā* is called "isolated" because it does not restate prose; it is a verse composed independently.
The renunciant bodhisattva is superior to the householder; no calculation or analogy can compare them. This is the formal verse.
The first two lines of the verse provide the basis for the analogy. "Calculation" (*suan*) refers to reckoning with counting sticks;

it means to know their relative proportions by means of numerical comparison. "Proportion" (*fen*) refers to a fractional part; it means to measure the renunciant by comparing them to the householder. [This comparison] is exhaustive.

The ultimate limit of such calculation still does not equal even one part of leaving the household life. Regarding the "analogy" (dṛṣṭānta), it means that even when employing metaphors and comparisons to their absolute limit, they still do not equal one part of leaving the household life; therefore, it is said that nothing can compare to it.
This merely establishes the point, which is then explained through the following analogy.
Living at home is as oppressive as a prison; seeking liberation from it is exceedingly difficult.

Leaving the home life is as vast and open as space—free, unconditioned, and detached from all bonds. Contemplate carefully that living at home is full of many faults; one commits boundless sinful deeds therein.
This verse does not follow the prose; it appears abruptly as an *udāna* (isolated verse).
Like one in prison, it merely speaks of being constrained and lacking autonomy, hence the term "oppression. As the worldly saying goes: "Children are golden shackles;
wife and children are jade fetters. Being pressed by the conditions of emotion and entangled by affection, one seeks liberation; this is like awakening from a dream.
It is difficult [to understand]. Therefore, it is compared to a prison, which does not refer to the person being reviled.

Those who have left the household life and dwell in leisure and vastness mean that above they are not bound by the constraints of royal service, and below they are not entangled by wives and children; like solitary clouds and wild cranes, they are free from all obstructions. Thus, they are likened to empty space.
"Sovereign and unconditioned" (svatantra-niṣkṛta) is a metaphor for the fruit of the path attained, namely, the fruit of disjunction (visamyoga-phala). This is the Truth.
The two lines beginning with "Contemplating" [and so forth] contrast the faults of householders against the leisure and seclusion of those who have left the home life.

This is because the worldly prison does not restrain those who are without fault; rather, it is precisely the faults of householders that are revealed. Sentient beings themselves create these [faults]:

their activity consists of pursuing sensory objects, and the completion of such evil karma constitutes transgression. The multiplicity of such transgressions is described as "boundless. Thus say the ancient masters.

It is said: "The ten entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) and the ten proclivities (*anuśaya*) accumulate to form the causes of outflows (*sāsrava*). The six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) falsely produce boundless transgressions.
Seeking gain in one's livelihood, one is constantly insatiable, just as the great ocean is difficult to fill—like the Dragon King of Lake Anavatapta."

From its four corners, four great rivers surge forth; all the waters of the large, medium, and small rivers flow day and night without ceasing for even a moment, yet that great ocean is never filled. The houses one craves are likewise like this.
This verse correctly illustrates the metaphor for greed (*lobha*). The first line represents the Dharma; all subsequent lines are metaphors.
To manage one's livelihood is called "engaging in business" (*yingsheng*); to hope for and seek to acquire is called "greed" (*tānqiu*); to seek more as one obtains more is called "insatiability.

Thus, Master Sishi Chan said: "I laugh coldly at the wealthy householder: his business is as frantic as a speeding arrow; while moths breed in the rice within his granaries, [his treasures fill] his storehouses..."
The coins in the middle are worn and tangled; by day one weighs them on a scale, and at night one lights a lamp to count them.
Their forms are as startling as puppets; do not let the cords snap. How excellent these words! For the most part, wealthy men of this world are like this.

The second line uses the great ocean as a metaphor for greed, with the four rivers serving as the whole. The "small" and "medium" [oceans] are the streams resulting from the division of those four rivers.
"Send forth the ears. This refers collectively to all rivers, canals, and streams that flow day and night without ceasing for even a moment, all of which return to the ocean;
yet that great ocean is never filled. This is merely a metaphor; the final line applies it to the Dharma.
That which is craved as a "dwelling" is the body possessed of craving. This corresponds to the aforementioned great ocean; therefore, it is said:
It is just so. Those living at home give rise to many evil karmas, yet they never wash them away through repentance to extinguish them.

They vainly know how to cherish their fragile bodies, yet fail to realize that their lives will end like morning dew. The messengers of Yama press them with urgency; wives, children, and houses—none can follow.
Followed [by the results of karma] through the long night of profound darkness and obscurity, one proceeds alone toward the gate of death to experience [retribution] according to one's deeds.
When the Buddhas appear in the world, they give rise to compassion, desiring to cause sentient beings to grow weary of the mundane world. You have now obtained this body so difficult to find;

you should exert yourself with diligence and not be negligent. The household life and its dwellings are deeply loathsome; the precious abode of empty tranquility is inconceivable. Forever free from...
"Sickness, suffering, and distress"—this section stands alone as an exhortation to make people take heed. The first phrase clarifies karma:

that is to say, for those living at home who have wives, children, and property, the five desires intermingle with the mind; as the mind moves in accordance with its objects, the body and speech follow the mind. Thus...
What karma has not been created? Yet, among those who are not sages or worthies, who is able to be without transgression?

If there are those possessed of a sense of shame and remorse, they may cleanse their hearts and seek repentance, whereby [the transgressions] can be eliminated. It is like a body that is turbid and impure; if it is washed, it becomes clean.

As for the claim that [transgressions] have "never occurred," this likely refers to laypeople for whom the five desires are a constant occurrence, and who thus proceed according to their impulses without restraint.
Knowing this, how can one seek repentance? If these long-accumulated habits remain firm, they will become the very conditions for falling [into suffering]. How lamentable!

From "In vain one knows" (*kōchi*) below, the text extensively clarifies the swiftness of birth and death to serve as a warning. Furthermore, although worldly people clearly know that the physical body is precarious and fragile, who among them does not try to preserve it?
Yet, that which is precarious cannot remain secure for long, and that which is fragile is known to be destined for death.
Therefore, they love and cherish them, providing them with abundant clothing and sufficient food; they treat their illnesses and administer medicine, desiring for them long life.
Yet, they are unwilling to cleanse their minds through repentance, nor to cultivate the mind through precepts and meditative concentration. Hence it is said that they "know in vain.

Thus, as days pass and months come, the time of death approaches, yet they remain without understanding. Therefore, it is called "unawareness. As for "dew on the morning grass," this refers to the early dawn.
Dew vanishes at sunrise; with a single breath not returning—alas, one is dead! *Yama* is the Lord of Death (*Yamen-jun*). His messengers are the ghost-sentinels.
Those who urge one on allow no extension of time. Upon reaching this point, nothing of the myriad things can be taken along;
only one’s karma follows the body. Thus it is said: "Wife and children, etc. The dark gloom of the netherworld is the earth.
Regarding "Hell": The Sūtra states that the dark and gloomy space between the two Iron Ring Mountains (Cakravāḍa) is called hell.
When a person dies with transgressions, they must enter therein. "Going alone" means that even one's closest kin cannot accompany them, nor can power and influence provide rescue;
only the solitary soul departs, entering the gate of death. "Receiving according to karma"—here, "karma" refers to [the actions] prior to birth.
This is the cause of what has been created. One undergoes this experience of suffering in hell; for the soul is led by karma, and suffering is experienced according to karma.
It is like a shadow following a form—it cannot be escaped. From the words "The Buddhas" onwards, the Buddha’s original intent is revealed:
that the reason the Buddhas appear in the world is out of compassion and pity, to preach impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, and how birth and death are swift.

It causes people to weary of the suffering of birth and death, to resolve upon the Bodhi-mind, and to realize the Unsurpassed Way (the meaning of "resolving upon the mind" and "realizing the Way" is implicitly contained within the verse).
There are two kinds of worlds: first, the insentient container-world (*bhājana-loka*), which undergoes the cycles of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness;
second, the sentient world of living beings (*sattva-loka*), which experiences birth, aging, sickness, and death. Since both are impermanent, they cause one to feel weary of them.
The desire to seek liberation through weariness [with saṃsāra] is precisely the compassion of the Buddha. "You now" refers to the subsequent admonition and entrustment.

"A body difficult to obtain" refers specifically to a human body, for among the six realms of existence, only the human body is difficult to obtain. As Prime Minister Pei stated in his preface to the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*:
"Ghosts and spirits suffer the bitterness of being submerged in the darkness; birds and beasts harbor the sorrow of frantic flight. Asura... [text continues].
Anger. While the various devas enjoy their pleasures, it is only through the human realm that one can rectify the mind and incline toward Bodhi;
thus, it may be said that among the six realms of existence, the human body alone is difficult to obtain. The following line exhorts practice:
having obtained this human body, one must not let it pass in vain, but must arouse a diligent mind, initiate vigorous effort, and never be negligent. Below...

The phrases clearly express what is to be loathed. As the preceding text states: "Oppressive as a prison; craving and longing like the great ocean," and so forth. The intent is to cause one to renounce them.
Regarding "empty stillness" (*śūnyatā-vyupaśama*), it is also as in the preceding text: "Leaving the household life is vast and open, like empty space.
Regarding the "jeweled house," this refers to the monastic who stores the aggregates of morality, concentration, and wisdom within their own person, just as...
It is called a "jewel-house" because it contains abundant jewels. Regarding the phrase "inconceivable," it is also as explained in the preceding text:

that the bodhisattva who has left the household life is infinitely and boundlessly superior to one who remains at home, beyond all comparison. The intent is to exhort people to certainly practice [the path].
The meaning of "permanently free from the suffering of illness and so forth" is exceedingly profound. This refers to both physical and mental illnesses.

"Mental afflictions" (*daurmanasya*) refer to the mental illnesses of the five abodes of affliction (*pañca-vāsa-kleśa*). "Suffering of illness" refers to the physical illnesses of the two kinds of birth-and-death (*dvividha-jāti-maraṇa*).
Because one leaves the household life, attains the Way, and is never born again, it is said that one is "permanently free."

May all those who possess wisdom observe this well: they should seek out faithful sons and daughters of good family who wish to deliver their parents and kinsmen, leading them into the city of unconditioned nectar.
May they aspire to leave the household life to cultivate the wondrous path, gradually practicing until they achieve perfect enlightenment and turn the unsurpassed, great wheel of Dharma.

This verse concerns how the wise do not undergo birth and death. Having already clarified above the faults of the householder’s life and the merits of renunciation, the wise must therefore carefully examine this. "One should seek" refers to those sons of good family with profound pure faith mentioned in the prose section. As for the meaning of the two characters "should seek" (dāng qiú): [The commentary continues: "Seeking" means to pursue and investigate. Because one has heard that the suffering of birth and death is immeasurable, one seeks to transcend it; because one has heard that the bliss of nirvana is boundless, one seeks to attain it. Furthermore, "seeking" means to practice diligently. Because one fears the suffering of birth and death, one practices the path of liberation; because one desires the bliss of nirvana, one practices the path of cultivation. Moreover, "seeking" means to apply oneself with resolve. Because one knows that the nature of birth and death is impermanent, one resolves to abandon it; because one knows that the nature of nirvana is eternal, one resolves to realize it. Furthermore, "seeking" means to cultivate with vigor. Because one perceives the faults of birth and death, one cultivates the power of diligence to escape them; because one perceives the virtues of nirvana, one cultivates the power of diligence to enter it. Moreover, "seeking" means to maintain mindfulness.

Because one remembers the suffering of birth and death, one maintains mindfulness to leave it behind; because one remembers the bliss of nirvana, one maintains mindfulness to attain it. Furthermore, "seeking" means to practice with wisdom. Because one understands the emptiness of birth and death, one practices wisdom to transcend it; because one understands the reality of nirvana, one practices wisdom to realize it. Thus, "should seek" means that one must, by means of these various modes of seeking, diligently strive toward the goal of liberation. This is the essential meaning of the two characters "should seek."
This is not appropriate; it would be better to use the two characters "ruò yǒu" (若有). This would then correspond with the prose section.

However, the phrase "rén zhě yī jù" (然諸有智者) is a verse summarizing the prose passage beginning with "shuí yǒu zhì zhě" (誰有智者). Thus, one knows that the two characters "ruò yǒu" are consistent throughout both the preceding and following sections.
If one were to use the two characters "dāng qiú" (當求), it would be utterly tasteless; even if one were to follow the error with further error, it would still be so.
The explanation ultimately does not accord with the meaning. It may be an error by the translator, or a corruption during transcription.
If one must insist on seeking an explanation, one should act as a Buddha commanding a wise person to observe and seek the capacity of the listener before speaking.
If there is one who possesses pure faith and wishes to deliver their parents, aspiring to leave the household life and practice the wondrous Way, they must certainly cultivate it gradually.
"Go! You who have attained perfect enlightenment should turn the unsurpassed Great Dharma for others. Why?
Since he has left the household life to practice the wondrous Way and gradually attained perfect enlightenment, there is no unsurpassed Great Dharma that would not be suited to his capacity."
One should know that this interpretation is acceptable regarding the meaning, but it is not acceptable regarding the prose commentary. Reflect on this.
△ Second, the analogy of a spark from a flint burning wood, in four parts. First, the actual presentation of the metaphor.
Furthermore, son of good family, a renunciant bodhisattva contemplates worldly dwellings as being like sparks from a stone, giving rise to a profound sense of weary aversion.
Why is this? It is because, for example, even a tiny spark can burn all manner of grasses, woods, and the like.
As for "stone-fire," it is like a single spark produced when striking stones. One who feels deep revulsion and anxiety thinks:
although this single spark is minute, if left unchecked, it can burn across ten thousand acres of wilderness; therefore, it is to be feared and loathed.
For example, the two characters "lei" (雷同) mean "similar to. One should change "shíhuǒ" (石火) to "suīwēi" (雖微); in both the heading and the explanation, this is consistent.
Second, the application of the dharma to the analogy:
The houses and dwellings of the world are also like this. With a greedy mind seeking after them, one rushes about in the four directions; yet, even if something is obtained...
Their enjoyments are insufficient; at all times they pursue them without satiety. If they obtain nothing, their minds become tormented with feverish distress as they pursue them day and night.
Therefore, all dwellings in the world can give rise to the fire of immeasurable afflictions.

To give rise to a greedy mind, one is constantly without contentment. Worldly wealth and treasures are like grass and trees; the greedy mind is like a worldly house, and the house is the body of sentient beings.
Hereafter, all [analogies] follow this pattern, further aligning the lower part of the metaphor by equating the body with the house.
Greed is like a spark struck from stone; the greedy mind’s seeking and so forth are described as "hopeful and insatiable.
Just as a spark from stone burning wood never knows satiety, so too does the act of seeking inevitably cause one to run hither and thither—this is the manifestation of greed.
It means that thought arises in the mind and movement is stirred in the body, depriving one of freedom, much like the spreading of a stone-spark.
Every place of contact is ablaze and cannot be extinguished by itself. "If there is the inferior" refers to seeking that which accords with one's heart and enjoying it;
the more one obtains, the more one lacks. Yet the Sage views this as a fire to be feared, while sentient beings pursue it even further, exhausting all their time without ever reaching satiety.
This means that what accords with one's desires nourishes greed; if there were not...
Below. Furthermore, because one cannot obtain what is desired due to craving, distress gives rise to anger. Using anger to fuel craving causes that craving to become even more urgent;
hence it is said, "pursuing day and night. To "pursue" means to crave forcefully what should not be craved, which inevitably exhausts both body and mind.
This, moreover, shows how delusion arises from craving. Therefore, the following section follows upon the previous to reveal the harm it can cause. It is able to...
"Those who give rise to the immeasurable fires of affliction" refers to those whose root- and subsidiary-delusions arise all at once; furthermore, they do not stop at the three types mentioned above.
Because they give rise to the lower [afflictions], when one traces back the cause of their harm, it is entirely due to the arising of a single thought of greed, which constantly lacks contentment.
The phrase "the world below" connects this to the preceding metaphor, meaning that wealth and treasures are like...
Regarding "grass and trees": the subsequent phrase should have stated that "desire is like a spark from stone. Yet, instead of saying "spark from stone," it says "house.

This is because the house represents sentient beings; the house is itself the fire. This is truly because grass and trees are consumed by a spark from stone, while wealth and treasures are exhausted by being seized by a greedy mind. △ Third, the conclusion of the metaphor of the burning house.
For this reason, all Buddhas declare that the three realms are called a burning house.
Good son, when a renunciant bodhisattva can contemplate in this way and feel weary detachment toward the world, they are said to be a true renunciant.
The first phrase refers back to what preceded: because a single mind of craving draws forth all afflictions, one is oppressed day and night, with body and mind exhausted by suffering.
It is due to such causes and conditions that all Buddhas have taught that the three realms offer no peace, being like a burning house;
this is precisely intended to cause people to feel weary of and seek detachment from them. Furthermore, there are two interpretations of these causes and conditions. First, it is general...
It is said: For example, by means of conditions, a single momentary arousal of greed gives rise to immeasurable afflictions (*kleśa*).

This is because it acts as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for their arising. Second, in a specific sense, that which directly produces them may also be considered the cause; namely, the greedy mind itself.

The supporting factors serve as conditions; that is, the desire for wealth. Due to the various afflictions such as worldly desire for wealth, which act as inciting conditions, the mind of greed first arises.
Through the convergence of causes and conditions, immeasurable suffering is produced and one is oppressed in manifold ways. How could this be anything other than a house on fire?
[This concludes] the exhortation at the end of the section for the virtuous sons. △ Fourth, the verse restatement.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again in verse:
"The renunciant bodhisattva contemplates the household life as being like a small spark in the human world; it can gradually burn away all grasses and trees.
Know that the household life is likewise: the various wealth and treasures possessed by sentient beings are constantly pursued one after another."
There is never enough; the suffering of not obtaining what one seeks constantly dwells in the mind. The fires of old age, sickness, and death are never extinguished.

For these reasons, the World-Honored Ones have described the three realms as a house on fire. If you wish to transcend the suffering of the three realms, you should practice the holy life as a śramaṇa.
When samādhi and supernormal powers are manifested before you, the benefit of self and others will be fully perfected.
The first line establishes the subject. The following two lines provide the simile. "The worldly house" and below provide the application to the dharma.
"Beings" clarifies that the greedy mind becomes increasingly intense. "Mutually" means it is not just one person, but is so throughout the world. "Seeking" refers to the state of mental exhaustion.
"Constantly insufficient" means that even when seeking what accords with one's heart, one still feels inadequate; thus, greed becomes ever more intense.
