Buddhism does not betray one's own spirit; it may truly be called the repayment of the four debts of gratitude. △ Eighth:
The Parable of the Young Girl’s Dream. First, the presentation of the dharma and the analogy.
Furthermore, son of good family, a renunciant bodhisattva contemplates all dwellings in the world as being like a great dream.
△ Second, the entire family rejoices together.
For example, suppose there was an elder’s daughter who was fifteen years of age, beautiful and exceptionally lovely.

At that time, her parents were staying on a three-storied mansion, and they took their beloved daughter to enjoy various pleasures. During the middle of the night, the mother and daughter lay down together to sleep.
They lie together in repose upon a single precious bed.

The mention of "elders" and so forth is a provisional designation for the sake of illustration; it merely serves as a metaphor for ordinary worldlings who indulge in the pleasures of the three realms.
Such, in general, is the delight of the five desires and the joy of the entire family; there is no need to further employ the analogy of the elder representing the Buddha.
△ Third, the dream of being betrothed and giving birth to a son.

Thereupon, the young girl dreamed that her parents betrothed her to a husband’s family. After many years had passed, she gave birth to a son who was handsome and extraordinary, possessing the marks of intelligence.
As he grew day by day under their loving care, he became able to walk on his own and resided in a high tower.
Although the matter of dreams is an illusory realm, it is nevertheless an image manifested by the independent mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which lacks any reality in its own essence;

yet one falsely gives rise to conceptual discrimination. This is truly because the maiden’s dream of marrying a husband and bearing a son serves as a metaphor for the entirety of the worldly path of human relations.
Furthermore, the son possesses extraordinary and wondrous features and the capacity for intelligence; his mother—
"Must love. This further illustrates the exhaustion of all worldly affection and attachment (*sneha*).

"Able to walk by oneself, yet standing atop a high tower" further illustrates those who have attained fame, eminence, and success throughout the world. △ Fourth: The Child Falls and Is Eaten by a Tiger.
As she was about to fall from a precarious height before reaching the ground, she saw a starving tiger catch her and devour her.
At that moment, the young girl was seized with redoubled terror and raised her voice in a loud wail. Thereupon, she awoke from her dream.

Regarding "falling due to danger": "danger" refers to peril. This is a metaphor for how, although one may be noble in the human realm or occupy a high station in the heavens, once one's karmic retribution is exhausted, one returns to fall back into the various realms of existence (*gati*). The starving tiger is a metaphor for King Yama;

it should be understood that all tainted merit (*sāsrava-puṇya*), even if it reaches the meditative absorption of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), cannot escape the hands of the "Iron-Faced Old Man."
Furthermore, his startled terror and wailing in the dream serve as a metaphor for the suffering of parting from those one loves throughout the entire world.
"Awakening from the dream" serves as a metaphor for a person of great wisdom who suddenly attains profound realization, only then perceiving that all phenomena are but the mind alone.
Life and death are an illusion. △ Fifth, the awareness of shame upon waking from a dream.
At that time, her parents asked their daughter, "By what cause and condition have you suddenly become so terrified? Then the daughter, out of shame, refused to speak of it.
Her mother, with great persistence, secretly questioned her as to the reason. Thereupon, the daughter privately recounted the matter to her mother as described above.
When her parents asked about the matter of her dream, it was like an unenlightened person of the world questioning one who has already attained enlightenment.
How could she have attained such realization so easily? Yet that enlightened person did not utter a word; why was this? It is because this single point is like a person drinking water.
Water—its coldness or warmth is known by oneself. An ancient worthy said: "When one arrives here, the mouths of all Buddhas of the three periods of time hang upon the wall;
the patriarchs of successive generations hold their tongues in awe of the wind.

As for what is spoken in secret—whether it be the words and phrases of a spiritual friend according to specific conditions, or the use of the staff or the shout—it is a single point of vital message that, in the end, cannot be fully disclosed to others.
This is precisely how the Tathāgata uses causes, conditions, parables, and skillful means to provide instruction.
Even his own self-realized noble wisdom cannot be fully expressed in words, just as that young girl, though she may describe her dream in secret, can never truly convey the events within the dream.
This is because dream-events are illusory; upon waking, one feels shame for them. This serves as a metaphor for the delusions of birth-and-death, which vanish upon awakening.
Later, it will result in nothing but great laughter. △ Sixth, the application of the Dharma to the metaphor.
"Good son, the conditioned house of worldly birth and death involves dwelling long in saṃsāra without yet attaining true awakening;
for all those stages, one constantly remains within a dream. Birth, old age, sickness, and death within the house of the triple world are like that young girl dwelling [there]."

In a dream, false conceptualization is likewise. The yakṣas and messengers of Yama suddenly arrive, like that hungry tiger, seizing the infant from mid-air and devouring him. All sentient beings are impermanent from moment to moment;
the sufferings of old age, sickness, and death are just so.

"World" (*loka*) refers exhaustively to the three realms of the dependent retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*). "Birth and death" (*saṃsāra*) concerns, for the time being, the segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*) of the six classes of ordinary beings.

"Conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) refers to sentient beings. "Dwelling" (*layana*) refers to the bodies of those beings. "Abiding therein" (*tatra-stha*) means not departing from them. "Cyclic wandering" (*saṃsaraṇa*) is birth and death.

"True awakening" (*bhūta-bodhi*) is original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*). "Not yet having attained" it refers to delusion. "To such an extent" (*iyat*) is a demonstrative term used to distinguish [the scope].
The "stages" refer to the retributive fruits of the six realms. Just as humans have their own human status, so it is with the devas and others.

Their constant dwelling within these stages is like being in a dream. This is because the True Suchness of the original enlightenment of sentient beings never departs from them for even a moment, whether in motion or stillness;
yet, drifting along in non-awakening, they undergo birth and death in vain—this is truly the world.
The Venerable One’s great compassion is such that He instructs people through various parables.
From "birth and old age" downward, this precisely corresponds to the maiden within the parable; therefore, it is said that "false conceptualization is likewise so.
This above section generally corresponds to the matters of marrying a husband in a dream, giving birth to a son, and experiencing joy. From "Yama" downward, it corresponds to [the realm of] hunger.
The tiger devours its own offspring. Yama is precisely Yanluo. The ghost messengers are those who pursue the soul and seize the life-force.

Since one cannot guarantee survival from morning until evening, it is said that [death] arrives suddenly. "As in that [example]" below provides the analogy; "Furthermore, all" below applies the Dharma to the analogy.
That every thought-moment is impermanent is precisely the shifting flow of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). It urges [one on].
One is driven by forces beyond one's own control. Then the demon of impermanence suddenly arrives;
it disregards human sentiment, fears neither power nor influence, accepts no bribes, and cannot be evaded. Alas! One can only follow it away.
At this point, neither loving parents nor filial children can provide rescue; fame, achievement, wealth, and honor are all no longer one’s own. It may truly be said:
"Of all things one cannot take with them, only karma follows the person. How is this different from a starving tiger devouring its own offspring? Therefore it is said:
"The sufferings of old age, sickness, and death are likewise thus. △ Seventh, the exhortation to practice the Way.
What person of wisdom would cherish this body? For this reason, one should contemplate birth and death as being like a long night of dreams;
thus, by giving rise to the bodhicitta and becoming weary of and detached from the world, one shall attain the Tathāgata’s wondrous fruit of eternal abiding.
Whoever possesses these two statements has a resolute intention regarding life. This clearly reveals that the fool loves the body, whereas the wise person loathes the body.
One who loathes the body will certainly seek liberation; one who loves the body will certainly undergo entanglement.

Those who are entangled fall forever into the cycle of birth and death, while those who have attained liberation will surely realize the Buddha-way. For this reason, the wise do not love the causes and conditions [of existence], and thus they contemplate.
Contemplate that ignorance regarding birth and death is like a long night; that all phenomena are impermanent, just as in a dream.
Below this, the section on "Arousing the Bodhicitta" concludes with an exhortation to practice the Path. △ Eighth: Reiteration by Verse.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again in verse: "O Son of the Buddha, seeking the unsurpassed path, You should contemplate your home as being like a dream.
It is like a wealthy and noble elder Who has a young daughter of exquisite beauty;
Following her parents up to a high tower, She gazes upon their travels and delights immensely."

The first two lines present the dharma and its analogy. The subsequent four lines eulogize the joy of the entire family, which serves as an analogy for the affection between father and son throughout the world;
the happiness of wealth and nobility does not exceed this.
The woman had such a dream while in her chamber; she clearly dreamed that she had recently taken another man as her lover. Later, at her husband’s house, she gave birth to a son.
Her mother, out of love and compassionate concern for him, [said]:

This verse concerns dreaming of marrying and giving birth to a son. "Suitable" (*shì*) means to marry; "born" (*dàn*) means to give birth. The remainder is to be understood according to the prose (*chángxíng*).

The son ascends a high tower, indulging in joy and pleasure; due to the danger, he falls into the mouth of a tiger. Thereupon, losing his voice, he awakens from the dream, only then realizing that the dream-visions were fundamentally not real.
The obscuration of ignorance (*avidyā*) is like a long night; until one attains perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one does not know [the truth].
Within the dream-like cycle of birth and death, the world is eternally unreal; deluded conceptualization and discrimination are likewise so.

Only the four wisdoms, the Great Perfect Radiance, destroy darkness and are called true, wondrous enlightenment. Impermanence changes moment by moment like a starving tiger; conditioned phenomena are false and cannot endure long.
As birds that roost together part ways at dawn, so too is the separation when life ends. Thus do beings come and go.

Subject to karma, one receives various retributions; the kindness of parents is not recognized. Alas! The ordinary person’s body of birth and death revolves through the three miserable realms, suffering long-lasting pain.
The first two lines of the verse describe the son falling into the tiger’s mouth; the next two lines describe awakening from the dream and feeling shame.

The section beginning with "ignorance" (*avidyā*) provides the textual application (*dharmasaṃgraha*). The three lines beginning with "not yet accomplished" indicate that not only is the birth-and-death of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) unreal like a dream, but even the fruits of the provisional teachings of the Two Vehicles are like the conjured city (*nirmita-pura*). As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "There is no..."
The other vehicles, whether two or three, are all like dreams. There are only the latter two lines [of the verse], for which an external inquiry is added to the text as follows:
"If the provisional fruits of the two vehicles are still dreams and not yet real, then who is it that truly realizes them? It is said:
"Only the four wisdoms (catur-jñāna) and so forth. As for these four wisdoms, they are those produced by the transformation of the eight consciousnesses and their mental factors (citta-caitta).
As explained in the second fascicle, "Great Perfect Brightness" (*mahā-vimala-āloka*) is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). "Darkness" (*tamas*) refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).
"Shattering" (*bhedana*) encompasses both the subject and the object; that is, wisdom is the shatterer and darkness is that which is shattered.

Thus, once ignorance is shattered, birth and death are entirely empty, and delusive thoughts and worldly afflictions are transformed in an instant into true awakening and wondrous clarity. [The section on] Impermanence follows.
The Dharma and its analogy are easy to understand. The two lines concerning the birds roosting overnight clarify this through a specific metaphor:

birds roosting in a forest sleep together for one night, yet at dawn they each fly away in different directions. This is a metaphor for the separation from all worldly loved ones; therefore, it says, "it is also like this.
"Coming and going" refers to the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). "Subject to karma" means that the soul follows the turning of karma. The deceased has no self-...

Regarding the various retributions received according to one's lot: for the time being, this refers to ordinary beings within the five destinies who each receive their specific retributions in accordance with their own past karma.
Yet, there is the delusion of falling into the womb, whereby one’s head and face are changed; even the kindness of one’s parents or the affection of one’s kin—who could recognize them?
Thus it is said, "they do not know one another. This is an expression of lamentation, referring to what are called "delusion and karma."

Through habitual practice, the cycles of retribution revolve like a wheel; through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they cannot be halted or severed. Thus it is said that they "revolve" and so forth.
If one knows that good and evil follow the inducement of karma, one should practice repentance to cause them to be extinguished.

All the wondrous fruits of bliss for humans and devas have shame (*hrī*) and remorse (*apatrāpya*), as well as right view, as their causes. One should resolve to generate the firm bodhicitta and don the armor of diligence to exert oneself.
"Cultivation and study.

This verse concludes by exhorting one to cultivate the Path. Good and evil karmas are unequal in their gravity; among evil karmas, the most grave are the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and the ten non-virtuous actions (*daśākuśala*).
At the time of death, a person is drawn away by their primary karma, or they may be seized by executioner-demons (*yamadūta*). Directly...
They fall into the Avīci Great Hell, where they undergo every form of suffering of the five *ānantarya* (uninterrupted) karmas.

If one commits the five *ānantarya* or ten evil deeds but not all of them, one falls into the hell of interruptions, where the experience of suffering is intermittent. If the offenses are further light, the retribution received is likewise light.

As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Light [offenses] lead to birth in the hell of interruptions; heavy [offenses] lead to birth in the uninterrupted [hell]," and the same applies to the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Those who, like those who slander the Triple Gem, are extreme in their stinginess and further hindered by jealousy and envy—such heavy offenders fall among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).

Their throats are as narrow as needles and their mouths are like flaming torches, with fire burning upon their limbs and joints. Those whose offenses are slightly lighter carry sand and shoulder stones.
Filling rivers and blocking seas; furthermore, those who are light in transgression—such as those who consume human impurities and so forth—and those whose karma belongs to the animal realm:

if they violate the principles of human relations, corrupt social customs, practice deception and theft, or borrow goods and fail to repay them, they will immediately fall into those [animal] categories.
They become heavy as the fur-bearing beasts or light as the winged tribes, repaying past debts to humans or perhaps debts for their lives.

When they have exhausted their retribution in the three miserable realms and first emerge as humans, they will inevitably be dull-witted, ignorant, and debased; their six sense organs will be incomplete, and they will be poor, lowly, and subject to the commands of others.
As it is with evil karma, so it is with good karma. If, through the practice of the Three... [text truncated]

Those who come from among the treasures must possess the capacity for intelligence. Furthermore, their status as wealthy, noble, or honorable varies according to the gravity of their original karma, resulting in different retributions.
If one possesses superior-grade outflowing (sāsrava) precepts and wholesome deeds, they will lead to rebirth in the various heavens; these too vary in degree.

If one merely practices precepts and wholesome deeds, one is born in the six heavens of the desire realm (kāmadhātu). If this is further augmented by outflowing meditative concentration (dhyāna), it brings about rebirth in the dhyāna realms.

O Deva, if one cultivates the meditative concentration on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), one will be reborn in the four heavens of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). If, despite practicing the precepts and wholesome deeds, one is moved by anger and resentment, one will be reborn as an asura.
Indeed, because of the causal conditions of good and evil karma, one receives retributions that are either auspicious or inauspicious;

who would dare not believe this? "If you know" [the following]—this follows the previous exhortation to renounce [worldly life]. It means that although the various devas are superior, they still possess birth and death; therefore, it is logically appropriate to seek liberation from them.
If one wishes to escape suffering and seek liberation from this class of beings, one must seek repentance to eliminate all obstacles;

if one does not repent, one will certainly be unable to leave it behind. Yet, the merit of repentance is inconceivable; therefore, the Buddha urgently exhorts that one "should [practice] equally," and so forth.
Regarding the subsequent detailed clarification of the wholesome paths: inferring the cause from the result, the upper line indicates the result and the lower line indicates the cause.

Since it has been stated that shame, remorse, and right view are the causes for rebirth as humans or devas, this conversely reveals that a lack of shame and remorse is the cause for rebirth among animals, while wrong view is the cause for rebirth as malevolent spirits and the like. One should now conclude with an exhortation to generate [the resolve for enlightenment].

This is because, although the fruits of human and celestial realms are subtle and pleasant, the Buddha’s exhortations have never taught the generation of a mundane, out-flowing (sāsrava) mind directed toward those states. And...
The World-Honored One is greatly compassionate. Those whom he frequently exhorts to arouse are all urged toward the bodhicitta, and it is essential that this be firm and stable.

Now, it is not that the Buddha does not exhort [beings] toward the precepts and wholesome deeds of humans and devas; rather, such outflowing causes and effects are insufficient grounds for exhortation.

Thus we know that the arousal of the bodhicitta is especially difficult. Those whom he exhorts to arouse do so fundamentally for the sake of spiritual practice, and therein they are further encouraged to increase their refinement.
Furthermore, advancing is likened to one donning armor. Fearing that the path of the Buddha is long and distant, if one should retreat for even a single thought, laziness will arise;
thus, one will end up merely displaying empty fame without attaining any real fruit. Is this not to be lamented?
Therefore, the Tathāgata exhorts them, saying that diligence must rely upon firmness, just as a great general dons armor and mail. Not...

This is out of fear of powerful adversaries; it is simply because the intention lies in attaining realization. One should know that within the verses and the prose commentary, the two matters of cultivation and realization are respectively hidden and manifest.
This is because the prose merely states that one "shall attain the Tathāgata’s wondrous fruit of eternal abiding."
It does not mention "cultivating and learning" [in the prose], yet the verse only says "arousing the mind to cultivate and learn," without mentioning the realization of the fruit.
This is likely due to the skill of the translator; the intent is that the fruit must be accomplished through causes, and that the cause ultimately realizes the fruit. △ Ninth:
The Parable of the Multitude Trading for Jewels (8). First: Stating the Dharma and the Analogy.
Furthermore, son of good family, a renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his house as being like the Mare’s Mouth Ocean,
which emits fierce flames that swallow and consume the four great rivers and all the myriad streams and currents, leaving nothing unburnt.
This fascicle contains nine parables in total. The first eight all serve as metaphors for the various distinctions between afflictions (*kleśa*) and the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Through various exhortations and various encouragements, they insist that one must resolve to leave the household life and seek the unsurpassed fruit; only then can one be liberated.
Now, the ninth is specifically intended as an exhortation regarding matters pertaining to the practice after one has already resolved to leave the household life; one must seek what is wholesome.

Wisdom guides; one must cherish this so as not to encounter downfall. One should know that although the "house" is used as a metaphor for the human body, its meaning encompasses both the general and the specific.
Generally, it metaphorically represents all ordinary beings within the three realms; specifically, it represents one's own single body.
"Good sons," and so forth, means that once a renunciant bodhisattva has left the household life, they ought to reflect upon their state...
At the time of the house, the abode of the five aggregates possesses both the true mind and the deluded mind. The true mind is buddha-nature; the deluded mind is affliction.
The true mind is like the great ocean, vast and boundless, fully endowed with the treasures of the Dharma.
The deluded mind is like the Mare’s Mouth Sea, which issues forth from fierce flames. Nevertheless, this Mare’s Mouth Sea has two functions. First, [it...]

[The fire] is able to receive the flowing [waters]. Second, it is able to burn them away entirely. (The retributions of the three miserable paths, the evil karma of body and speech, and the afflictions of the five abodes can all be metaphorically likened to fire.

As for the "four great rivers," they are the Yangtze, the Yellow River, the Huai, and the Ji; as for the "hundred streams," this is a general designation for various currents, which metaphorically represent all objects of the five desires within the realm.
Greed is likened to receiving the flow, and anger is likened to fierce flames. Thus, these serve as the primary metaphors to indicate their respective abodes. △ Second, the assembly.
Seeking a teacher:
For example, in the past, in the kingdom of Rādha, there was a bodhisattva named Supāraga.

This bodhisattva possessed a heart of compassion and always harbored a desire to benefit others. There were some merchants who entered the sea to gather treasures, and they took this bodhisattva with them.
[Sa]. They were all aboard the same ship and reached the Isle of Jewels together, crossing over perils and difficulties without any hindrance, arriving at the other shore.
As for "Rāḍha," its meaning in the vernacular (Chinese) is not detailed; since it refers to the past and specifies both the name of a country and the name of a bodhisattva.
This must surely be a factual event from a previous age; it is now borrowed here as a metaphor.
A "Bodhisattva" is a general term for one who possesses the aspiration for the Way (bodhicitta); he is the guiding teacher.

He is named "One Who Has Attained the Other Shore" because, through his compassionate mind that leads the multitude, his words of truth, and the protection and assistance of benevolent deities, his journey encounters no perils and he knows the way.
The paths are perilous or level; the mind reaches the other shore. Thus, based on actual virtue, his name is manifested.

He is likened to the Buddhas and spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), who, out of compassion, benefit sentient beings and act as guides pointing out the way. This is a lower praise of virtue. The various merchants represent those who have left the household life;
they raise their minds to practice and seek to realize *bodhi*, like entering the sea to gather treasures. The leader is one who raises his mind [to guide them].
"Those who share the same carriage" refers to those wishing to travel together on the same ship. An "island" (*dvīpa*) is a piece of land that emerges from the midst of the ocean;

because treasures emerge from within the island, it is called a "Treasure Island," which is a metaphor for the fruit of Buddhahood. A large ship upon the great ocean is called a "vessel" (*pota*); avoiding the perils and traveling along level ground is called "crossing.
Not encountering danger or hardship is called "being without obstruction"; fulfilling one's aspirations and reaching the destination is called "arriving."

"The other shore" refers to reaching the shore of the precious island. However, just as there are many treasures on the island in the analogy, yet one cannot reach it without a guide, so too the Dharma-treasures are inherently complete within the nature of phenomena, yet they cannot be realized without the Buddha as the guide. △ Third, the subsequent plea of the merchants.
Later, as the Bodhisattva grew old and his years advanced until he was already a hundred years of age, he required support to rise and sit, and lacked the strength to move forward.
A certain merchant leader came to the Bodhisattva’s dwelling, paid him homage and made offerings, and said to him: "I wish to enter the sea."
Seeking various precious jewels, they may forever leave poverty behind and attain great wealth and nobility. I now request that the Bodhisattva go with me.
At that time, the Bodhisattva said to the merchant leader: "I am now old and decrepit; my strength is feeble, and I cannot enter the sea."
The merchant leader spoke again: "I pray that the Great Being, not forsaking his compassion, will graciously accept my invitation and simply remain seated within my ship; this is my earnest wish."
One should understand that the preceding section was taught by way of analogy concerning the Buddha while he was practicing the bodhisattva path as a cause.
This present section is taught by way of analogy concerning the Buddha having reached the state of fruition (*phala*). "Gradually growing old" refers to advanced age and the completion of learning;

this is an analogy for the Buddha’s quality of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*). "Decaying" refers to the full maturation of the faculties and resolve; this is an analogy for the Buddha’s quality of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*). "A hundred years" refers to the full measure of a lifespan; this is an analogy for...
The Buddha has realized the Dharma-body, which is fully endowed with myriad virtues. [The phrase] "rising from his seat" serves as a metaphor:

once the Buddha has realized the Dharma-body, it is appropriate that he should eternally abide within the Light of Quiescence (prabhāsvara) and enjoy the bliss of the Dharma. [The phrase] "there was one person below" refers to the merchant leader, who represents the capacity of later students seeking the Buddha;
for although the Buddha enjoys the bliss of the Dharma, he will surely respond whenever there is a cause for doing so. Thus, the merchant leader went to pay his respects.
"Et cetera. This metaphor signifies being moved by sincere devotion. "I wish to describe my resolve below" is a metaphor for requesting the Buddha to provide instruction.
"Leaving poverty behind" is a metaphor for abandoning birth and death; "attaining wealth and nobility" is a metaphor for seeking the fruit of Buddhahood. "Now, I request...

and so forth refers to the desire for the Buddha to certainly respond by providing instruction and guidance. "At that time... and so forth, regarding those who push back and refuse to go, is a metaphor for the Buddha’s examination and testing.

Regarding this "capacity" (*ki*): if it were not the capacity, he would not have been willing to transmit the mind-dharma. The section beginning with "The Merchant Leader" describes his vow to manifest the height of sincerity;
it serves as a metaphor for the great capacity of sentient beings' true mind being activated. This is because, within the metaphor, even a guide cannot be moved unless there is sincerity;
how much more so for the Buddha-dharma, which is profound and mysterious—how could it respond unless there is ultimate sincerity? △
Fourth, accepting the invitation and leading [the way]:
At that time, the Bodhisattva accepted the merchants' invitation and, boarding a great ship, entered the vast ocean, heading toward the southeast corner.
"Proceeding to that place of jewels" is most clearly illustrated by the preceding analogy. To apply this to the Dharma: the great ship is a metaphor for the Mahāyāna’s true teaching;

the great ocean is a metaphor for the mind-dharma of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). Regarding "proceeding toward the southeast corner to reach that place of jewels": in the system of the eight trigrams, the southeast corresponds to Xun.

The ground possesses the virtue of pliancy, which serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s provisional teachings (*upāya-dharma*). Because these provisional teachings can accord with the capacities of sentient beings, the "jeweled place" serves as a metaphor for the fruit of Buddhahood (*buddhatva-phala*).

The meaning is that by riding upon the Great Teaching and entering the Great Principle, one accords with the provisional to reach the ultimate reality, thereby attaining the final fruit of Buddhahood.
△ Fifth, the violent wind shifts the location.
At that time, they encountered a north wind and were driven into the South Sea. The fierce wind was so swift that it did not cease day or night.
As for the "north wind": in the system of the trigrams, the north corresponds to Kan (Kǎn), which is a place of peril and entrapment; when the wind arises from within it, it is a perilous wind.
The south is the region of detachment (*viveka*), a land of emptiness and luminosity. Thus, the perilous winds are a metaphor for the pressing urgency of birth and death (*saṃsāra*);

emptiness and luminosity are metaphors for the śrāvaka’s samādhi of mere emptiness. One should understand this metaphor: first, raising the mind to seek the treasure is like a person resolving to attain Buddhahood;
the guide leading them toward the southeast is a metaphor for the Buddha observing that the faculties of sentient beings are not particularly sharp.
Furthermore, let us allow them to follow provisional means and enter through the gradual teachings; yet they will inevitably have to undergo a long period of time.
Their mental faculties are fearful, believing that the Buddha-way is so remote that it cannot be accomplished in the near term.

Desiring instead a minor fruit that is easily attained, their initial thought arises like a fierce wind, and every moment they wish to advance like a fierce wind that never ceases, directing their aspirations toward the *nirvāṇa* with remainder.

"Pan. It is like being adrift and falling into the Southern Sea. Furthermore, the fierce wind that rushes on without ceasing is a metaphor for the desire to realize *nirvāṇa* while it has not yet been realized;
one increases one's efforts and practice, just as the fierce wind does not cease. One should know that this fierce wind possesses two meanings:
first, it is a metaphor for the pressing urgency of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); second, it is a metaphor for the practitioner’s resolve. However, ordinary beings—
Birth and death are indeed likened to a violent wind. Yet, one still does not understand the aspirations of those of the Two Vehicles;

even if they realize *nirvāṇa*, they have not yet escaped *pariṇāmika-jarāmaraṇa* (the death of transformation). Although there is a difference between the noble and the ordinary, their birth and death are no different;

therefore, both are likened to a violent wind. [Question: This sutra is a teaching of the sudden [vehicle]; why then does it follow expedient means? [Answer: This is because Jñānaprabha wished to leave the household life but held doubts and could not decide. Fearing that he might fall back, the Buddha entered [the discourse] by following expedient means. [However, this] does not mean that [the listeners] were not startled.

The wind and waves have been experienced for a long time, yet it is not equal to the certainty of a single thought that enters directly into Bodhi; this is called "sudden entry. One should know that the Buddha employs this metaphor because there is a profound meaning contained within it).
△ Sixth, the dual presentation of benefit and harm (three parts). First, seeing the benefit by following the wind (four parts). First, seeing gold by following the wind.
After seven days had passed, he saw that the waters of the great ocean had turned golden, like molten gold.
At that time, the merchants said to the Bodhisattva, "By what cause and condition have the waters turned golden, manifesting such a sign? The Bodhisattva replied:
"You all should know: I have now entered the great ocean of gold. It is filled with immeasurable and boundless purple-golden *jāmbūnada* gold;
the precious metals reflect one another, and such is its appearance. Since you are able to transcend the right path,"
Having fallen into this sea, each diligently sought means by which to return to the north;
this matter is clearly evident. However, Dharmodgata wishes to realize unsurpassed bodhi and must therefore pass through the realms of humans and devas.

Thus, one surpasses humans and devas and transcends the small fruits [of the śrāvaka]; the precious throne is thereby attained. Now, arriving at the Sea of Golden Color is a metaphor for the human realm.

From this passage onward, the journey through the various seas generally serves as a metaphor for the six realms of existence; these are to be assigned according to the opening and closing of the categories of good and evil.
As for the human realm being metaphorically represented by gold here: gold is the foremost among all treasures, and thus it serves as a metaphor for all the worthy sages.
It is accomplished within the human realm; that is to say, to uplift the mind and incline it toward Bodhi, only the human realm is capable of doing so.

In the parable, the merchant leader addresses the Bodhisattva, which is a metaphor for the practitioner who, having entrusted himself to a teacher and followed their instruction, must inquire whenever doubt arises.
The Bodhisattva’s response represents the opening of instruction in accordance with the inquiry. The passage beginning with "I now" is a metaphor for the Buddha.
He reveals that human birth is difficult to obtain and entrusts them with the meaning of not falling back or degenerating; he instructs them to cherish this. "You all, below...
is a metaphor for the Buddha’s profound exhortation. "The right path" is a metaphor for the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground (*cittabhūmi*).

The two characters "to exceed" (*chāoguò*) should be read as "to miss" (*cuòguò*). This means that while raising the mind was originally intended to follow the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground to seek the fruit of Bodhi, now...
Although a human body is difficult to obtain, one has nevertheless missed this opportunity. Each person should, below [this teaching], exhort themselves to practice;

as for the "skillful means," it consists of maintaining the mind and focusing the attention. Regarding "returning to the north": the north represents this shore, which is a metaphor for birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Just as a traveler practices and realizes the path, having already obtained a human body, one must not forget birth and death. "Returning" refers to the arising of the thought of returning.
Death. This refers to what is called "indulgence" (the preceding passage on the various seas was a metaphor for the opening and closing of the good and evil of the six realms;

it stated that the six realms constitute the two types of good and evil as "closing," and then further dividing those two types of good and evil into humans, devas, and so forth constitutes "opening"). △ Second, again seeing pearls.
After several more days had passed, they saw that the waters of the great ocean had turned white, like jade or snow. The Bodhisattva addressed them, saying, "You should know this:
I have now entered the great ocean of pearls; white jade and pearls fill the sea."
The jewel reflects the color of the water with such characteristics. You should exert all your strength and employ various skillful means to return to the north.
[The phrase "the merchant leader did not ask" is a textual omission. The Bodhisattva spoke these words as an instruction to enlighten him.

Within the Dharma, the "White Sea" is a metaphor for the heavenly realms of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). It is like a practitioner who, proceeding from the human realm, diligently cultivates the virtues of precepts and goodness.
Having reached that heaven, the white jade, pearls, and so forth serve as metaphors for the blissful realms of the heavens where one may look east and forget the west.
You must descend; this is the compassionate exhortation of the Buddha. Although celestial blessings are pleasant, they will inevitably perish after a long time.
Do not linger here; you must exert all your strength to advance and contemplate the suffering of birth and death, as if returning to the north. △
Third, they saw a crystal jewel.
After several more days had passed, the waters of the great ocean turned blue, like blue lapis lazuli. The Bodhisattva said:
I and you have already entered the sea of blue beryl; immeasurable and boundless blue beryl jewels fill this great ocean, and the colors of the beryl reflect one another in this manner.
This is a metaphor for the fruit-stage of the various devas in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).

Just as a practitioner, on the basis of virtuous precepts, further cultivates contaminated meditative concentration (*sāsrava-dhyāna*) to reach those heavens; the blue lapis lazuli and so forth metaphorize the bliss of those dhyāna-heavens.

Within this [metaphor], there is no mention of anyone returning to the north, yet logically such a case ought to exist; it is merely an omission in the text. The underlying meaning also serves as a warning, as explained previously.
△ Fourth, he saw a red jewel.
After several more days had passed, the waters of the great ocean turned red, appearing just like blood. The Bodhisattva said:
I and you have already entered the sea of red beryl; immeasurable and boundless red beryl jewels fill this great ocean.
Their jewel-colored crimson hues intermingle and reflect one another in this manner.
This metaphor represents the devas of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). The red glass and so forth represent the blissful states of their meditative absorptions (*śūnyatā-samādhi*).

The exhortations and encouragement are the same as in the previous two cases. [Question: If the meaning of exhortation and so forth must necessarily exist, what does this mean? [Answer: Even the various devas of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) still possess pleasures such as forgetting what is to the west while looking toward the east;

how much more so for the two classes of devas in the dhyāna and formless realms! Were it not for the reminders and exhortations of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—and were one not to mistake the fruition for the fruition itself, taking it to be *nirvāṇa*—by what means could the state of a Tathāgata be attained? [Question: Regarding the metaphor, who is the guide, the Bodhisattva?

If one travels on the same ship as the multitude of merchants, it is convenient for providing admonition. But in the Dharma, do Buddhas and Bodhisattvas follow along with them? Answer: The scriptures state that the Heavenly Kings of the Three Realms are all manifestations of inconceivable Bodhisattvas appearing to engage in the same activities as others in order to gather and transform them, causing them to transcend their worldly conditions;
this is precisely the meaning of being a "Guide" (Śāstṛ). II. Falling into Suffering Due to the Wind. (Seven parts) 1. Fire Appears Within the Water.

After several more days had passed, the water turned black, like ink. From afar, the sound of fierce explosions was heard, like that of a great fire burning a grove of bamboo or the blazing flare of a beacon fire; it was truly terrifying. Such were the omens.
Never before have I seen or heard of such a thing. Furthermore, I saw a great fire arise from the south, resembling a cluster of mountain peaks, rising over a hundred *zhang* in height.
Its flames surged into the air, sometimes merging and sometimes dispersing; its radiance flashed like lightning. Such a phenomenon as this has never been seen or heard of before.
"Our own bodies and lives are indeed difficult to preserve;

this is a metaphor for the distinctions among the realms of the three miserable paths. The aforementioned four sections are metaphors for the wholesome fruits of humans and devas, reaching as far as the four formless absorptions and the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-perception.
Yet when their retribution is exhausted, they fall and cannot avoid the three miserable paths. One should know this."

The following metaphors serve as a powerful exhortation for practitioners. Specifically, the transformation of water into blackness is a metaphor for the four signs of decay in the human realm and the five signs of decline in the celestial realms;
it refers to the manifestation of these signs of senescence, indicating that death will soon be imminent.
The sound of a violent fire exploding is particularly used as a metaphor for the sign of death: the separation of the four great elements and the snapping of the sinews.
The bones separate, and the spirit-consciousness is filled with terror; the sound of suffering is one of bitter lamentation—this is the sign of being scorched by the fire of death.
Furthermore, "hearing from afar" is a metaphor for those who have not yet fallen into that state but already exhibit signs of decay, just as if they were hearing it from a distance.

These preceding points are partial metaphors for the signs of death, intended to stir the human heart. If these are taken as comprehensive metaphors for the three miserable realms, then for the hells, there is fire.
This constitutes their essence. There is nothing that does not burn: the limbs and joints of hungry ghosts (*preta*) are ablaze with fire;
and though there is no burning by fire in the realm of animals (*tiryagyoni*), they cannot escape being consumed by the fire of ignorance.

"Blazing" describes the intensity of the flames; "thick smoke" describes the density of the fumes. "Extremely terrifying" is a metaphor for the three miserable destinies (*durgati*). Upon hearing this, one’s heart is struck with dread.

Cold! Who would not be struck with terror? The general characteristics of suffering in the aforementioned three miserable realms are roughly as described above. Furthermore, regarding the sight of a great fire arising from the south:
the south was previously used as a metaphor for the *śūnyatā-samādhi* (emptiness samādhi) of the two vehicles—that is, the *nirvāṇa* of the small fruit.

How can it be said that this is "fire"? The meaning is as explained by Tiantai in his commentary on the *Pumenpin* (Universal Gate Chapter): there is the fire of karmic retribution (*vipāka*). Evil... [text ends]
The fire of karma, the fire of afflictions (*kleśa*), and the fire of retribution—the latter being the experience of suffering in the three miserable realms—are fires of burning.
The fire of evil karma pervades the three realms; for example, the four signs of decay in the human world and the five signs of decline in the heavens are all transformations of karma.

They possess only the sense of "burning" and are not actual fires. The fire of afflictions pervades the three vehicles, as is currently being discussed; even those who have attained the lesser fruits [of the Śrāvakas] still...
There are dust-like and river-sand-like *avidyās*; how much more so for the various devas? Yet it is not only those of the Lesser Vehicle;
even Bodhisattvas still possess fundamental *avidyā* and the death-and-rebirth of transformation (*pariṇāmika-jarāmaraṇa*).

The metaphors used, such as "peaks clustered together, exceeding a hundred fathoms in height," all serve to manifest their intensity. However, the power of fire causes harm through burning; those of the Two Vehicles are attached to *nirvāṇa*.
They are submerged in darkness and stagnate in stillness; their passions are extinguished like ashes and they are entangled in emptiness.
Failing to give rise to the bodhicitta and failing to practice the path of the bodhisattva, they view the three realms as a house on fire; yet for the Buddha’s bodhi, this harm is no small matter.
Therefore, it is metaphorically described using a blazing, fierce fire. Because it harms bodhi, it is called "fire," though it is not a literal fire. Its flames surge through the air.

The phrases "converging and dispersing" and "flashing like lightning" describe the characteristics of fire; in the Dharma, one need not force a literal correspondence for every phrase, but should instead harmonize them according to the general meaning.
From "never yet" onwards, it is merely a hypothetical assumption intended to inspire awe. As for those who have attained the fruits of the Two Vehicles:
To be addicted to such pleasures, how could one know they are like fire? Only a Buddha perceives that they harm the Dharma-body; out of compassion, it is as if there is a sense of dread.
Therefore, within the Bodhisattva precepts, it is said that if one gives rise to the mind of a Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha, [one commits a transgression].

For those who have violated the Bodhisattva precepts and must resolve to attain Bodhicitta, as well as for disciples of the Buddha— although the meaning of "kindling the lamp" applies generally to all three vehicles—
it shall here be explained primarily in terms of the Three Realms, while also encompassing the provisional meanings of the Two Vehicles. △ Second, the Bodhisattva’s exhortation to the assembly.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva addressed the multitude, saying: "Why do you now feel such great fear? For what reason?
We have already entered the Sea of the Mare’s Mouth and shall all be consumed by fire. Why is this?
By the sovereign power of the karma of sentient beings, the natural fires of heaven are able to burn the waters of the sea. If these celestial fires did not burn the waters of the sea, [then...]"
Day and night, all the dry land has been transformed into a great ocean, and all sentient beings have been submerged and swept away.
Now we have encountered a great black wind and are being carried along by this Sea of the Mare’s Mouth. We who are here now have but little life remaining.
In the analogy, the Bodhisattva addresses the assembly; internally, this corresponds to the Tathāgata preaching the Dharma. Why should there be any fear?
This precisely illustrates how the Buddha uses the four marks of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, as well as the five signs of decay, to provide awakening.

Why [is it so]? This interrogatively introduces and explains the meaning of "fearfulness": it means that a person’s deluded mind possesses all afflictions (*kleśa*), which can produce evil karma and bring about rebirth.
Death is like entering the mouth of the Mare’s Head Ocean (*Vaḍavāmukha*). All the Dharma-wealth and merits inherent in one's nature and disposition are utterly consumed by the fire of deluded karma.
For this reason, the text provides a further inquiry and re-explanation through a metaphor:
due to the sovereign karmic power of sentient beings, a natural celestial fire burns the seawater, whereby the lands of the world become level and secure. This is what worldly people [perceive].
It serves as a dwelling place; it is that by which the five grains, grasses, and trees are brought forth.

Had the celestial fire not burned them, within a single day and night, all people and things upon the great earth would have been submerged. Yet, what follows below is intended precisely to warn the multitude.
It is said that although the fires of heaven burning the sea are beneficial to the world, people must not violate them;
for if one touches them, they will burn, and if one enters them, death is certain. Therefore, it concludes by saying, "one's remaining life is but little" (meaning one will not live long).
The analogy above is thus easy to understand. In terms of the Dharma, water corresponds to birth and fire corresponds to death. Suppose there were birth without death—
If that were so, the world of sentient beings would have no room to contain them; how would this differ from the great earth being submerged by water?

The force of superior karma (*adhipati-karma*) serves as a metaphor for the shifting flow of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); thus there is birth and there is death. The black wind serves as a metaphor for ignorance (*avidyā*).

Now, the reason the former metaphor refers to birth and death while this metaphor refers to ignorance is because definitions are established according to the specific textual passage; yet, in the case of dharmas and their metaphors, there is much mutual interchangeability.
Regarding "transformation," one should rely on the meaning rather than being constrained by the literal phrasing. The Buddha’s meaning is lively and active;
do not use metaphors to challenge the Dharma. This is because, in the metaphor, the boat is blown by the wind and thus flows into the Mare’s Mouth Sea;

whereas in the Dharma, due to the permeation of ignorance upon True Suchness, one falls into the deluded mind. From "I now" onwards, the metaphor illustrates the Buddha’s teaching as a warning to the world.

The Dharma is thus: as the matter of birth and death is of great importance and impermanence is swift, it is further illustrated by how the merchants wailed in grief because they were exhorted by their leader;
so too, practitioners arouse their minds because they are enlightened by the Buddha.
△ Third, the multitude seeks salvation through lamentation.
At that time, there were more than a thousand people on the ship who simultaneously raised their voices, wailing and weeping in grief. Some tore out their own hair;
others threw themselves down, speaking these words: "We have now entered the great ocean for the sake of seeking precious treasures."
Encountering this perilous difficulty, they cried out, "Alas! What suffering! By what means might we escape this calamity?

At that time, the thousand people took refuge with utmost sincerity; some invoked the Compassionate Mother, some the Benevolent Father, some Brahmā, some the Heavenly King Maheśvara, and others the Greatly Powerful Nārāyaṇa.

"The thousand people wailing" implies that they believe there is death but no rebirth. As for their plucking out their hair and casting themselves [down], this further manifests the height of their grief.
It is like when a person dies—whom does it not terrify? To speak in such terms as these...
He immediately confessed his own transgressions, saying that he had originally acted out of greed and did not expect to encounter such suffering. "Kua! is an exclamation of lamentation.
"By what means? asks how one might seek liberation. He offered a sincere prayer below to entreat the deity.
Maheśvara—also known as Akaniṣṭha—is the celestial realm at the summit of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). He has three eyes and eight arms, rides a white ox, and holds a white fly-whisk.
He is the Honored One of the three realms, possessing mastery over supernatural powers; therefore, one seeks him. Nārāyaṇa, the celestial being of great physical strength, can likewise save people.

This analogy is easy to understand. Applied to the Dharma, it corresponds to a practitioner who, whether having violated the essence of the precepts or lacking firmness in meditative concentration, experiences signs of decline.
At such a time, the meaning of feeling shame, repenting one’s transgressions, and offering prayers is as follows:
Seeking deities is a metaphor for abandoning the root to pursue the branches and racing outward in search.

Even if one aspires to the realms of humans or devas, one cannot achieve liberation from birth and death. This is no different from seeking deities to no avail. △ Fourth, seeking a teacher face-to-face.
Some take refuge in the Bodhisattva Attaining the Shore and pay homage to the Great Being, saying: "We pray only that the Bodhisattva will deliver us.
This is a metaphor for all practitioners of the path: although their desire to seek liberation is the same, their knowledge and views differ. Some...

Those who run outward in pursuit also have those who maintain their attention on the original inquiry; thus we know that those who seek elsewhere labor in vain, while those who look back to the source obtain benefit.
However, the Bodhisattva Attaining the Shore has two metaphors: one internal and one external.

The first metaphor illustrates the bodhisattva who possesses within himself the investigation of his own mind, yet rescues his own mind from suffering and distress. The second metaphor illustrates the external...
Seeking the Buddha, the Sage; take refuge in him to save me, that I may escape birth and death. △ Fifth, the Bodhisattva’s consolation:
At that time, the Bodhisattva, in order to free these people from all terrors, spoke these verses:
"The Great Man, supreme in the world, enters the gateway of death yet feels no fear. If you lose your wisdom through grief and sorrow, you should [unify your mind]..."
The mind should establish skillful means. If one attains the gateway of skillful means, one will leave behind all eight difficulties and transcend to the other shore.
Therefore, settle the mind and do not harbor anxiety or fear; you should earnestly contemplate the Great Compassionate Honored One.
In the analogy, the bodhisattva may represent the Buddha, or he may represent all those who possess knowledge; there must certainly be wise maxims to instruct him.
The words "in this world" and so forth are words of consolation, such as a great man regarding death as returning home.
If one applies this to Dharmodgata’s case, it is like saying that birth and death are like an illusion and one should not grieve excessively; for if one grieves too much, wisdom will not [arise].
It can be aroused, yet death cannot separate one from it; therefore, one should dwell single-mindedly.

Even if one cultivates various skillful means (*upāya-dvāra*), if one encounters the skillful gate of "mind-only" (*cittamātra*), and if one truly awakens to mind-only, then one will transcend all eight difficulties.

The World-Honored One of Compassion (*Maitreya*) is none other than the Buddha of one’s own mind. (The eight difficulties are: hell, animals, hungry ghosts, blindness, deafness, and muteness, as well as worldly cleverness and intellectual sharpness.)

Before a Buddha or after a Buddha, in Uttarakuru, or among the long-lived gods—if a person falls into these eight difficulties (āpatti), they cannot see the Buddha or hear the Dharma, and thus cannot achieve liberation from birth and death; therefore, these are called "difficulties.
△ Sixth, making vows to rescue the multitudes.
Thereupon, having spoken these verses, the Bodhisattva burned various famous incenses and paid homage and made offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
He made this vow, saying: "Namo to the Buddhas of the ten directions! Namo to the Buddhas of the ten directions! To the assembly of all Great Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas;
to all the worthy and holy ones of the four stages and four fruits; to those who possess the divine eye; and to those who possess the divine ear."

One who knows the minds of others and possesses mastery over the multitude, I, for the sake of sentient beings, have exercised a heart of great compassion to sacrifice my own body and life to rescue them from all suffering and hardship.
Now, within this body of mine, there remains one root of goodness: that I have upheld the Tathāgata’s precept against false speech.
Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, I have never failed or transgressed [this precept]. If I have uttered a single word of falsehood in this present life, may this fierce wind now intensify further;
yet, if such virtuous discipline is not in vain, I pray that by means of this merit, it may be dedicated to all beings.
"I and all sentient beings shall attain the Buddha-way. If this is true and not false, may these evil winds cease immediately;
may favorable winds arrive according to our thoughts as we wish. For all sentient beings are my own body; sentient beings and I are one."
They are equal and without distinction.

Although the metaphor is provisional, it also expresses sincerity. If a practitioner deeply contemplates that the matter of birth and death is great and that impermanence is swift, and washes their heart to seek repentance, there will naturally be a spiritual response; this is no different from the metaphor. Burning incense represents...

Faith. Prostration expresses sincerity. However, in the analogy, the Bodhisattva’s sincere prayers are fundamentally for the purpose of saving sentient beings from suffering and enabling them to attain happiness.
If one aligns this with the Dharma, the Bodhisattva possesses two meanings: first, he is a metaphor for the Buddhas and spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).

Through the spiritual power and might [of the Buddhas], they bestow grace and protection, causing one to leave suffering behind and attain happiness. (The phrase "spiritual power and might," etc., is combined with the preceding metaphors of burning incense and offering prayers.

First, the Bodhisattva is a metaphor for the compassion of one’s own mind. One should give rise to sincere faith from within one's own mind, seek the Buddhas within one's own mind, and rescue oneself from the hardships within one's own mind.
As it is said: "One should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm; all..."

This is precisely what is meant by "all is created by mind alone. This is because the four stages and four fruits of the śrāvakas, as well as the three insights and six supernormal powers of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, are all inherently possessed within one's own mind. If one gives rise to the Buddha-mind, one can become a Buddha; the same applies to Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas.
To seek the Dharma outside of the mind is impossible. Now, the following section clarifies that precepts are the cause for such realization.
This is the fundamental principle. Although the categories of precepts are numerous, speech is paramount.
For false speech arises from a deluded mind, while truthful speech arises from a true mind. Now, by invoking the response through truthful speech, the evil winds have ceased.
The wind will surely follow and arrive. Thus, for all those below, it is clarified that the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings are non-differentiated in these three respects.

This is because, just as it was with the metaphors above, so it is with the Dharma. When an ordained Bodhisattva employs truthful speech and maintains firm precepts, their roots become deeply established;
then, the branches and leaves of all meditative concentration and wisdom will naturally sprout, leading to unsurpassed Bodhi.

It may be hoped that [this goal] will be attained. (All sages and saints encompass both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles. In the Mahāyāna, the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*), the ten practices (*daśacaryā*), and the ten stages of dedication (*daśapariṇāmanā*) constitute the Three Worthies (*trividha-ārya*). From the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the tenth stage, as well as the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and the Subtle Enlightenment (*pratyakṣa-bodhi*), are all considered Saints.

In the Hīnayāna, the five stages of settling the mind (*pañca-citta-viśrāma*), the mindfulness of specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa-smṛti*), the mindfulness of general characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa-smṛti*), the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*), Peak (*mūrdhan*), Patience (*kṣānti*), and the Supreme Worldly Dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*) constitute the Seven Worthies.

The four fruits (*catur-phala*) and the four approaches (*catur-pratipannaka*) constitute the Saints. Regarding the four fruits: the *Srotāpanna* is the first fruit; the *Sakṛdāgāmin* is the second fruit; the *Anāgāmin* is the third fruit; and the *Arhat* is the fourth fruit. Regarding the four approaches: this refers to the meaning of being on the verge of reaching the fruit before long, having not yet arrived at it. As for the severing of delusions, there are eight...)

The complete severance of the eighteen latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the delusions of view constitutes the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). If these have not been fully severed and a small remainder still persists, one is merely termed a candidate for the first fruit (*srotāpattipratipannaka*). If one further severs a portion of the delusions of conduct (*bhāvanā-heya*), which are divided across the nine stages (*bhūmi*) of the three realms, with each stage containing nine grades (*prakāra*), [one becomes a candidate for the second fruit].

This refers to the superior, middling, and inferior grades. If one has completely severed the first six grades of the afflictions of volition (*cetanā-kleśa*) within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it is called the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returner). If one has severed up to five grades, one is merely called a candidate for the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*. If one further severs the remaining three grades and exhausts all residual afflictions of volition, it is called the fruit of *anāgāmin* (Non-returner);

such a person will not return to the desire realm to undergo rebirth. If one has severed three grades but not yet exhausted them, or even up to two grades, one is merely called a candidate for the fruit of *anāgāmin*. Furthermore, by severing and exhausting the seventy-two grades of afflictions of volition across the eight stages of the two upper realms, it is called the fruit of *arhat* (Worthy One).

If one has severed them but not yet exhausted them, up to the seventy-first grade, one is merely called a candidate for the fruit of *arhat*. △ Seventh: Liberation from Suffering according to One’s Vow.
Once this great bodhisattva had generated such great compassion of identical essence and unimpeded vows, within the span of a single thought-moment,
the violent winds ceased, he obtained a favorable wind, and was liberated from all hardships.
In the parable, the Bodhisattva, through his compassion of shared essence, his words of truth, and his unimpeded vows, was able to liberate the multitude from their hardships;
yet he did not fail the request of the merchants. Truly, he could serve as a teacher.

As for Dharmodgata, it goes without saying that the great compassion and truthful speech of the Buddhas are inherently effective. (In the parable, the Bodhisattva, by virtue of his moral discipline and truthful speech, was certainly able to move...)

The difficulty of liberation is thus. Within the Dharma, it is only logical that all the Buddha’s teachings should be followed by sentient beings; by doing so, one may escape the hardships of the three miserable realms, transcend the ranks of humans and devas, forever leave birth and death behind, and ascend high to the other shore.

Even if the Buddha provides excellent instruction, it is not necessarily the case that sentient beings will fail to practice it. One should know that this present discussion is based on the premise of such practice. Alas! A teacher who is enlightened and a student who is compliant are the means by which suffering is escaped.
If one possesses only the name of a "knower" while lacking actual virtue, one cannot even liberate oneself from hardship and distress.
It is impossible for one who has not distanced themselves from their own faults to liberate others from suffering and hardship.
Therefore, one who acts as a teacher must first benefit themselves before benefiting others, and first achieve self-realization before leading others to realization.
As for those who remain mired in their own ignorance while wishing to make others enlightened—such shameless individuals should they not feel ashamed even unto death? Thus it was said by Zeng Shen.
Those who study the Way as disciples may possess a heart that yearns for the Way, yet they do not undergo genuine suffering;

they merely parade about with empty reputations, claiming that their practice is ineffective. Such individuals not only fail to achieve the Way, but they also incur the transgression of slandering the Dharma.
Are they not ashamed even unto death? △ Third: Turning the Head to Reach the Shore.
Having reached the place of treasures, they obtained various precious gems. At that time, the Bodhisattva addressed the merchants, saying:

"Such precious gems are difficult to encounter and difficult to find. It is because you practiced the giving of *dāna* extensively in previous lives that you have now encountered these many wonderful and precious gems."
In the past, when you practiced giving, your mind harbored stinginess. Due to these causes and conditions, you have encountered this malignant wind.
You merchants must know the limits of the precious treasures you have obtained; do not take more than necessary, lest you indulge your greed and subsequently invite great calamity.
"You all should know that among all treasures, the treasure of life is supreme. If one preserves their life, it is a priceless treasure.
At that time, the merchants, having received the Bodhisattva’s instruction, gave rise to a mind of contentment and did not dare to take more than they needed. Then, the multitude of people...
They escape calamity and obtain great treasures; they leave poverty far behind and reach the other shore.

Just as in the parable, having escaped danger and reached the place of treasure, the teacher further warns that such treasures are difficult to encounter, and demonstrates this through the matter of cause and effect:
namely, that the extensive giving of past lives serves as the cause for obtaining these treasures in the present.
This is the retribution for the stinginess of his previous life, which served as the cause; that he now encounters a foul wind is likewise retribution.
Furthermore, he was cautioned not to take too much, lest he indulge his greed and subsequently invite great calamity. Moreover, he was warned that life and treasure are of the utmost importance.
This is indeed the essential precept for Bodhisattvas. When the merchants disembarked, the Venerable Teacher measured out [the goods]; this was also the contentment of the multitude of merchants.
At that time, the concluding verse reached the other shore. However, the analogy is certainly like this; as for its application to the internal reality:

once the practitioner has reached the place of jewels, they are immediately in accord with the state of Buddhahood, and there is no dharma-wealth that accords with their nature which is not fully possessed.
The Bodhisattva warns the assembly that they must harmonize with the witnessing of all Buddhas, or the certification of spiritual friends and seals, and so forth.
One must know the limits of the precepts and not take too much; this accords with the Middle Way and equanimity. To let the mind run wild and invite calamities does not accord with the Middle Way:
to lean toward emptiness invites the calamity of the Two Vehicles’ sinking into obscurity, while to lean toward the provisional invites [the calamity of] existence.
This constitutes the difficulty of bondage. Because one falls into the two extremes and turns one's back on Bodhi, it is a great hardship.

That which is called "not clinging to emptiness or existence, dwelling the spirit in the Middle Way, and wondrously realizing the True Constant" is what constitutes direct realization through immediate perception (*pratyakṣa*).
When life is regarded as a treasure, it should be united with the wisdom-life; yet this wisdom-life is truly priceless. [The character] "time" (時) follows "merchant" (商). Combined.

That the Honored One’s teaching is perfectly centered and that one returns thanks to the Buddha—such that one may escape calamities and remain far removed from poverty—is equivalent to exhausting the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*) and forever extinguishing the two deaths (*dvividha-mṛtyu*).
That one obtains great treasures and reaches the other shore is equivalent to personally realizing *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. △ Seventh: Applying the Dharma to the Parable.
"O sons of good family, it is likewise for the renunciant bodhisattva who draws near to the Buddhas and virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Just as that merchant encountered the bodhisattva, he will forever leave birth and death behind and reach the other shore;
just as the caravan leader attains great wealth and nobility. All conditioned dwellings in the world are like the Mare’s Mouth Sea, which can consume all things."
Flow. It is the same for the renunciant bodhisattva as well. They carefully and thoroughly observe the faults of the household life.

O son of good family, you shall not be stained by the five worldly sensual pleasures; having developed weary detachment from the suffering and hardship of birth and death within the triple world, you will enter the great city of coolness and peace.
The first two lines synthesize the preceding metaphors as a whole; "approaching" (*upasaṃkramaṇa*) and the following lines provide the specific synthesis of the distinctions.
The renunciant bodhisattva corresponds to the merchant, while the Buddhas, spiritual friends, and teachers correspond to the bodhisattvas who have skillfully reached the other shore.
This means that when a renunciant approaches true spiritual friends, it is like the merchant obtaining those bodhisattvas. Thus, the Dharma and the metaphor are clearly correlated.

The meaning of this passage is most clearly expressed. That which constitutes a dwelling is simply the body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which possesses birth, old age, sickness, death, the eight sufferings, and the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
This is comparable to the ocean of the Mare’s Mouth (*vaḍavāmukha*) being able to consume all other streams; it serves as a metaphor for fire within the midst of water being able to burn the water.
If one dies according to the Dharma, one can overcome rebirth. The faults of household life do not exceed those of the five desires;

for fear that there may be negligence, I further exhort you to examine them with careful discernment. The five worldly desires correspond to the golden ocean of jewels and so forth in the preceding parable.
Through non-attachment and weary detachment, one combines with the previous practice of diligently seeking various skillful means for each person to bring an end to birth within the three realms.
The suffering of death is difficult; it corresponds to being burned by fierce fire and drowning in water, which aligns with the two preceding phrases.
Reaching the shore through the preceding cessation of the winds corresponds to "coolness. Birth and death are like a great blazing torch, while nirvana is like a pool of coolness.

The body of suffering is like the ocean of the Mare's Mouth, while nirvana is like the Great City of Peace and Bliss. This is the text that provides the correct correspondence, whereas the previous metaphors were...

Regarding the sections within the main body where there are combined explanations (*he-shi*): because the metaphors (*yu*) are expansive and the text is lengthy, while the corresponding textual passages (*he-wen*) remain distant, the connections are sparse and lack a clear point of return;
thus, one cannot help but provide these combinations. Nevertheless, this follows the ancient masters and is not a fabrication (*du-zuan*). As for "following the ancients" (*fa-gu*):

it is like Tiantai’s explanation of the parables in the *Fire House* chapter of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Since the corresponding textual passages were extremely remote, he provided a section-by-section correlation between the metaphors and their meanings, enabling students to understand the Dharma through the metaphors. The present work does likewise; therefore, it is said to "follow the ancients. As for "fabrication" (*du-zuan*): in ancient times... [text truncated]

There was Du Guangting, who composed Daoist scriptures himself and claimed they were spoken by the Celestial Honored One; this is what is meant by "Du-zhuan" (meaning he acted on his own authority). △ Eighth, the method of praising through metaphors.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke again in verse: "When a renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his home, it is like a mare in the ocean consuming all the streams.
For example, in the past, in the kingdom of Ratha, there was a bodhisattva named Prāptatīra.
Possessing great wealth, wisdom, and skillful means, he gathered sentient beings through unconditional compassion. This bodhisattva boarded a ship, and the merchants gained their reward."
Ratnottara had already crossed to the other shore. However, this Great Being was advanced in years and, taking no pleasure in benefiting others, was devoted to meditative stillness.
There was a merchant leader who invited the Bodhisattva, wishing to enter the great ocean to seek precious jewels.
The first two lines set forth the Dharma and the analogy. The subsequent ten lines eulogize the assembly’s collective search for a teacher.

The character "fu" (富) in the phrase "endowed with great wealth and wisdom" is likely a scribal error for "fu" (福); because one possesses merit (*puṇya*), one reaches the place of jewels; because one possesses wisdom (*jñāna*), one discerns the treacherous from the level.
This serves as a metaphor for the Buddha’s perfection in both merit and wisdom. The remaining text follows the same principle as before.
"I only pray that the Great Being will accept my invitation, so that I may be wealthy and free from want.
This verse expresses the merchant leader’s piteous plea; it is a metaphor for a practitioner who, with a sincere heart, moves the Buddha, or one who aspires to seek a teacher.
The first phrase consists of words of compassionate entreaty; the second phrase conveys the intent of that entreaty.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva, moved by great compassion, accepted the invitation and boarded a ship. Then, with the sails fully unfurled and meeting a favorable wind, he proceeded directly toward the southeast to reach the place of treasures.
This verse describes the acceptance of the invitation and the guidance [of beings]. It is like the Tathāgata responding to conditions and manifesting his response to deliver various capacities.

Here, the Bodhisattva is a metaphor for the Buddha; the boat is a metaphor for the teaching; the wind is a metaphor for roots of goodness; and the southeast is a metaphor for provisional teachings. The "place of jewels" is a metaphor for the ultimate fruit.
This means that one first uses provisional vehicles to guide [beings], and subsequently realizes the fruit through the One Vehicle, as explained in the prose commentary.
"Suddenly encountering a violent wind that blows the ship, it is driven adrift into the Southern Sea, lost as to its destination.
This verse refers to the shifting of a fierce wind; in the analogy, it represents how, due to the frequent arising of avarice, one is struck by a violent wind that causes one to lose one's way.
In the dharma, it represents how, when a practitioner suddenly gives rise to cowardice and retreat due to ignorance perfuming the *tathatā* (Suchness), they become fearful.
The path of the Buddha is long and distant; because they wish to attain only the minor fruits, they are deluded regarding the Buddha’s bodhi.

The analogy of the South Sea represents the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who dwell in the samādhi of mere emptiness; having regressed from the Great Mind, they harbor an inclination toward the Lesser Vehicle, and thus they are like a fierce wind that easily shifts its direction.
After seven days, the waters of the great ocean all turned into a golden hue; the purple-golden *jāmbūnada* gold filled the sea, and the radiance of the jewels manifested as a true golden color.
After several more days, the waters of the great ocean changed to a white color like that of jade or snow;
pearls and precious gems filled the sea, which was why the seawater became white. After yet another several days...
The waters of the great ocean transformed into a deep azure like lapis lazuli; blue beryl beads filled the great ocean, which was why the water took on that deep azure hue.
After several more days, the waters of the great ocean all turned into a crimson red;
red beryl beads filled the midst of the sea, and thus the color of the water changed to match them.
From this point downward, all verses present both benefit and harm together. First, the verses praise seeing profit by following the wind;
