"Sustaining the Three Jewels" means settling the mind in the Buddha-way; awakening and illuminating one's own mind is what constitutes sustaining the Buddha.

The Jewel of the Dharma: To practice in accordance with the teachings and maintain the precepts without fail is to uphold the Jewel of the Dharma. To dwell together with the assembly in harmony and without anger is to uphold the Jewel of the Sangha.
Thus, one ensures the Three Jewels flourish and remain forever in the world, serving as a model for gods and humans and acting as a compassionate vessel for transcending the world;
hence, it is said that this brings great benefit. △ The Eight Precepts bring benefit without expectation of reward.
Eighth, when begging for alms, one must not give rise to a mind of longing by praising all men and women in order to seek food and drink.
The dharma of begging for alms consists in being content with whatever conditions arise; therefore, one must not give rise to a mind of longing. Even if...
To seek food by falsely offering praise is flattery and deceit. Because one respects the sons of the Buddha, one should not act in this way;
rather, the benefit lies in the cessation of greed. △ Ninth, the practice of impartial compassion for the benefit of others.
Ninth, when practicing alms-gathering, one must follow the proper sequence; one should not discriminate between poor and wealthy households.
This non-discrimination is the practice of equality, meaning that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is equal and fundamentally devoid of high or low.

One should beg in accordance with this nature, remaining free from emotional attachments and biased views. This may be called the supreme benefit of universally launching the compassionate vessel. △ Tenth, the Buddha.
Joy is a beneficial condition.
Tenth, one should constantly practice begging for food. This brings joy to all Buddhas and is the most excellent condition for attaining all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Following the teaching, one should practice accordingly; by taking begging for food as a condition, one attains all-knowledge. For this reason, the Buddha rejoices; [it leads to] all-knowledge.
This is because alms-seeking provides the sustenance for life; life being preserved, one may cultivate the Path;
the Path being perfected, wisdom arises; and wisdom knows all phenomena (*dharmas*). It is by way of the phenomena known that this name is obtained, and thus it is called "Omniscience" (*sarvajñā*).
Furthermore, both this Path and this wisdom arise from the life sustained by alms-seeking. Therefore, alms-seeking is the means by which wisdom is attained.
This is a most excellent cause and condition. △ Third, concluding the summary while encompassing the detailed exposition:
"O Bodhisattva Jñānaprabha, I have briefly explained these ten kinds of benefits for you all. If they were to be analyzed in detail..."
It is immeasurable and boundless. You bhikṣus, as well as those in future ages who seek the Buddha-way, should train yourselves in this manner.
△ Second, the verse summary.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse: “Jñānaprabha Bodhisattva, listen attentively!
A great being who has left the household life should abandon greed and give rise to a mind for supramundane practice. To subsist on alms and to practice the dhūta austerities is the foundation.

Ordinary people dwell upon tainted food; noble ones rely entirely upon untainted food. For all noble ones and ordinary people—whether they partake of the tainted or the untainted—all [such distinctions] are ultimately non-existent.”
Not dwelling in dependence on food, I, for you sons of the Buddhas, shall expound the three supramundane beneficial practices praised by the Tathāgatas of the three times.
There are ten benefits in the merit of begging for alms.

This verse admonishes the listener and indicates the benefits [of the practice]. "Mahāsattva" is a designation for a Bodhisattva. "One should be free from greed" means that those who have left the household life rely on food to assist their path;
they should use whatever is obtained as it comes and must not harbor expectations for fine food—this is what it means to be free from greed.
Although there are twelve types of *dhūta* (ascetic practices), taking alms-seeking (*piṇḍapātika*) as the foundation, an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) refers to one of common, everyday character.

Now, they merely know how to wear clothes and eat food, eating when hungry and drinking when thirsty. "To dwell" means to rely upon; one can only abide in the world by relying on the nourishment of food and drink.

"With outflows" (sāsrava) refers to the fact that because humans possess the grasping of a self (*ātman*), their food is subject to arising and ceasing—namely, the four kinds of nutriment mentioned later in the text:
contact, volition, consciousness, and edible food. This is because they have not yet attained the true and eternal.
Because they fall [into cyclic existence], they are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*). Those "without outflows" (*anāsrava*) take the joy of dhyāna and the delight in the Dharma as their sustenance.

Below, the terms "with outflows" and "without outflows" serve as a double conclusion regarding the noble and the ordinary. This means that although the categories of the noble and the ordinary differ, there are none who do not abide by means of sustenance.

(Sustenance is fundamentally both with and without outflows; however, whether one has outflows or is without them depends solely on the person. For instance, ordinary beings within the realms have not extinguished the grasping at a self and do not transcend the three realms; they fall into the states of humans, devas, and so forth. Therefore, they are called "with outflows.")

"Outflow-free" (*anāsrava*): The noble ones of the Three Vehicles have exhausted their grasping at a self and do not fall back into taking birth within the three realms; therefore, it is called "outflow-free. Regarding the "two benefits," these are self-benefit and benefiting others.

For example, when begging for food to sustain the body and using the body to cultivate the Path, this constitutes self-benefit; causing the person who gives the food to obtain merit through their offering constitutes benefiting others.
Although food comprises four types, here we refer specifically to "edible food" (*kavadīkāra-āhāra*). The final two phrases of the third verse conclude [the section].
This reveals the benefit of the designation.
It is specifically said that this practice is the most supreme. Entering and exiting with mastery, one is free from bondage. First, one causes the donor to generate the initial resolve;
only after causing them to incline toward Bodhi does one eat. To eliminate stinginess and greed, one preaches the sublime Dharma, enabling them to proceed toward great renunciation.
With a mind of measure, relying on the Great Master’s teaching, he practiced begging for food and increased immeasurable pure conducts (*brahmacarya*).
The seven and nine types of pride were extinguished of their own accord, and he was revered by all humans and devas. The Tathāgata’s cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) is invisible;
he turned the wondrous wheel of Dharma to transform the ten directions. Until the end of the future, may this Dharma be transmitted so that the lineage of the Triple Gem is never severed. If for...

Food and drink give rise to deluded thoughts; one should not praise men or women. One should give rise to great compassion and an impartial mind, not generating discrimination between the poor and the wealthy.
Pure alms-seeking is praised by the Buddha; from this, all-knowledge is born.
This verse summarizes ten benefits. The first two lines summarize the first benefit of the prose section.
This practice refers to the practice of begging for food mentioned in the prose; it is the most excellent benefit because it abandons greed and aids the path. Regarding "being without fetters":
since one constantly practices begging for food, one stands alone and attains self-mastery, remaining unobstructed and unhindered; this corresponds to the prose statement on "not being attached."
Regarding the meaning of "therefore": first, the latter two lines of the verse [correspond to] the second section.

"Causing those who have not yet resolved their minds to resolve them" means teaching the Dharma and providing instruction to cause those who have not yet generated the aspiration for enlightenment (bodhicitta) to do so; hence it is called "the initial mind.

"Causing them to incline toward Bodhi" refers to the "wholesome mind" mentioned in the preceding prose; while the prose version speaks only of a "wholesome mind," the verse specifies "causing them to incline toward Bodhi. So it is said.
This refers to the virtuous mind that enables the donor to proceed toward Bodhi. "Proceeding" means to head toward;
it refers to the initial aspiration directed toward the fruit [of enlightenment]. As for "then eating," this refers to the vow and practice of the one who begs for food.
Just as they have not yet received the food, they first raise their intention, wishing that the person who gives the food may first realize Bodhi. Following this prayerful wish:
Only then does one eat it. It is not that the donor truly eats only after having attained the Way and the beggar only then eats;

this is to eliminate the latter two lines [of the verse]. The verse summarizes the third long passage [of the prose], which was intended to eliminate stinginess and greed—that is, for those who do not practice giving.
Because they were stingy and greedy and would not practice giving, the sublime Dharma was taught; the merits of generosity were extensively praised to suit the disposition of those who were miserly.

Thus it is called the "sublime Dharma. Because the Dharma suited their disposition, it caused those who were miserly to attain great awakening, enabling them to incline toward great relinquishment—namely, to break open the bag of stinginess and bring forth the treasury of jewels. Therefore, it is called the "immeasurable mind."
[This] is also [the case]. Based on the two lines following "依大" (relying on the Great), the verse summarizes the fourth [section]. "The Great Master" refers to the Buddha;

"Brahmacarya" refers to the preceding Chapter on Precepts (*śīla-varga*), the meaning of which encompasses both merit (*puṇya*) and wisdom (*jñāna*). The two lines beginning with "Seven, Nine" summarize the fifth [section].
The two lines beginning with "Tathāgata" summarize the sixth [section]. The prose states that he "should receive vast offerings from the world," while the verse says "turning the wondrous Dharma."

Regarding the wheel [of Dharma] that transforms the ten directions: there is mutual concealment and manifestation. Since the prose section only mentions receiving offerings and does not mention preaching the Dharma, it is the reception of offerings that is manifest and the preaching of the Dharma that is concealed. In the verse, this is reversed.

If the preceding and following sections correspond, then because the turning of the wheel of Dharma teaches and transforms the ten directions, the full meaning of the resulting offerings from devas and humans is entirely realized. This is not yet finished.

The second couplet praises the seventh [section] above. One who transmits this Dharma—that is, the method for begging for food while eliminating greed—transmits it to others in succession, thereby enabling the Three Jewels to abide eternally;
hence it is said that they shall not be interrupted. If these are taken as the following two couplets, they praise the eighth [section] above.
The long prose states: "One must not give rise to a heart of longing in order to seek food and drink. The verse says: "If..."
Regarding the phrase "giving rise to deluded thoughts for the sake of food and drink": if the characters do not flow smoothly, it is best simply to use the character "not" (不).

One should not place [the character] below; rather, one should add the two characters "for food" (為食), so that it reads "one should not praise men or women for the sake of food," which accords with the long prose version.
The two lines following "giving rise to the great... are a verse summarizing the ninth section. The previous text stated that one must follow the proper sequence, and the verse says "level" (平).
"Et cetera. This refers to the practice of universal compassion through successive stages. The two lines following "pure" eulogize the tenth [point] mentioned previously.
The previous text says, "The Buddha rejoices," while the eulogy says, "Praised by the Buddha"; this is because he praises him due to his joy.
"All-knowledge" (*sarvajñā*) is the wisdom of the Buddha. "Arising from this" means that tracing back against the current to its source, all originates from begging.
This refers to the arising of food. Indeed, begging for alms is the departure from greed; it is itself the stainless nature (*vimala-dhātu*).

Within this stainless nature, one gives rise to untainted conduct (*anāsrava-caryā*), which possesses immeasurable virtues and ultimately realizes the Buddha-wisdom. What worldly benefit could surpass this?
Therefore, it is entirely appropriate to designate these as "superior benefits."
The Tathāgatas of the three periods appear in the world to teach the four kinds of nutriment for the sake of all sentient beings. These four are: edible food, contact, volition, and consciousness;
all of these are tainted, worldly nutriments. Only the nutriment of the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna is that which is consumed by the noble sages.
You should cultivate weariness and detachment toward worldly flavors and seek instead the untainted nutriment that transcends the world.
This verse concludes by manifesting the supreme benefits. The Buddha taught that all sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment (*āhāra*), and there are four kinds of nutriment.

Here, the first two lines establish the framework, while the third line enumerates their names. "Edible food" (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) refers to that which is taken in mouthfuls or portions (it carries the sense of being "divided").

It has the nature of the three objects—odor, flavor, and tangible—and functions to sustain the sense faculties once it has entered the stomach and been transformed; thus it is called "edible food. In ancient translations of the sūtras and vinayas, this was rendered as "lump-food" (*piṇḍa-āhāra*), because it is taken up with the hand in a lump. Later translations [reverted to the standard term].

It is said that liquids and drinks cannot be taken as "lumps"; therefore, they are translated as "edible morsels" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*). Next is "contact-food" (*sparśāhāra*): "contact" (*sparśa*) means "object" (*viṣaya*). This refers to the various objects such as forms (*rūpa*) and so forth, which are the objects of the six consciousnesses;

through softness, smoothness, cold, warmth, and other tactile sensations, joy and pleasure arise, thereby nourishing and benefiting the sense faculties. Thus, it is called contact-food. Furthermore, all ghosts and spirits feed by contacting their breath; hence it is named contact-food. Next is "volition-food" (*manahsaṃcetanāhāra*):

"volition" (*saṃcetanā*) refers to the sixth consciousness contemplating a desirable object and giving rise to a mind of longing, which can moisten and benefit the sense faculties. It is like a person suffering from hunger or thirst who reaches a place where food and drink are available; by the mere hope of obtaining them, the body does not perish. Therefore, it is called volition-food. Next is "consciousness-food" (*vijñānāhāra*).

Food. (Consciousness has "sustaining" as its meaning; it refers to the eighth consciousness. Because it is supported by the power and portions of the first three foods, this consciousness is able to increase and excel, sustaining all the sense faculties; therefore, it is called the "consciousness-food. Furthermore, regarding the gods of the formless realm...)

As for the sentient beings in the various hells, they do not require food or drink; they possess only the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) which sustains their long lifespans, and thus they have the sense of "nourishment.

These four types of nutriment are all categorized within the realm of outflows (*sāsrava*), which is why it says "all are," etc. Only the final two lines refer to the nutriments that are without outflows (*anāsrava*).

"Joy in the Dharma" refers to the delight experienced upon hearing the Dharma, which is able to satisfy hunger; thus, it possesses the sense of "nourishment. "Delight in meditation" refers to untainted meditation (*anāsrava-dhyāna*).

In meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is tranquil and at ease; the mind is joyful and able to be fully satisfied. Thus, it possesses the meaning of "food. It does not employ the four worldly foods;
this is the food of the noble sages (*ārya*). As the *Lotus Sūtra* says: "The food of the joy of Dharma and the delight of dhyāna—there is no thought of any other food.
Your [text’s] final two lines provide a concluding exhortation. Now, although worldly food comprises four types, [the noble food is distinct].
Regarding the types [of food], that which the Buddha prescribed for begging is *kavaḍīkāra-āhāra* (edible food).

Now, as for the exhortation to renounce it, this refers to the Buddha’s instruction for newly ordained śramaṇas to renounce the four wrong means of livelihood (*mithyājīva*), to constantly practice begging for alms, and to eliminate greed and pride while sustaining the sense faculties;
these are nothing other than conditions that assist the Path. However, even after practicing this for a long time, one must not become attached to it; the intention is as follows:
If one seeks the path that transcends the world, one must seek food that transcends the world; this necessitates investigating the Buddha-dharma and rejoicing upon seeing the Way.
Furthermore, by using meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to soothe the spirit, one may sustain the life of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*). This constitutes the "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*).

This is also what is meant by "returning from the provisional to enter the real. Moreover, when begging for food in ordinary circumstances, one does not form the notion of food, nor does one perceive a self.
Subject and object are both forgotten; the three spheres are simultaneously stilled. Thus, even solid food becomes untainted (*anāsrava*).
△ Third, the ten benefits of constantly taking discarded medicine, in two parts. First, the prose section, in three parts. First, pointing out the heading and posing the inquiry.
Furthermore, Jñānaprabha Bodhisattva, as a renunciant son of the Buddha, should not be attached to various medicines.
If he falls ill, he should take whatever medicinal decoctions others have prepared and discarded—such as harītakī, vibhītaka, and āmalaka—and consume them.
Even throughout his entire life, he should consume such discarded medicines, always maintaining [this attitude] toward all medicines.
Contentment. One who is thus is called a true śramaṇa, a son of the Buddha who has gone forth.
Constantly taking discarded medicine, such a person attains ten kinds of benefits. What are these ten?

This refers to the stainless nature within these medicines. Regarding "discarded medicine": this refers to the dregs remaining after others have boiled and drunk them, which are discarded and no longer used.
This is because when the four great elements are unbalanced or the five viscera are disharmonious, it is said that one has an illness;
medicine must then be used to treat it, and recovery can be achieved by administering what is appropriate for the specific condition.
I have never heard of others taking discarded dregs as medicine once they have already been used. According to medical treatises, such things are utterly devoid of flavor.
That the Buddha now employs them has two excellent reasons: one of fact (*vastu*) and one of principle (*nyāya*).

As for the fact, it is like discarded medicine that, having lost its potency, has never even been administered to a patient; yet one still desires its efficacy—this refers to the three fruits (*triphala*).
It is power. By employing the fruit as an inducement, there is no ailment that cannot be cured. This is the knowledge of the Tathāgata’s direct perception (*pratyakṣa*);
do not challenge it with worldly arguments. As for the three fruits: the first is *harītakī*, which in Chinese is called "that which the Deva holds."
This fruit is used as medicine; its efficacy is vast, penetrating everywhere and proving effective in all cases.
Second is *vīrī* (fully called *vīrya*), which means "the fruit of diligence. If this fruit is used, it possesses the power to track down the root of a disease.
Third is *āmalaka*; its leaves resemble those of the jujube tree, its flowers are white and small, and its fruit is like [the *āmalaka*].
Walnuts: their flavor is sweet and sour; they may be used for medicinal purposes. These three fruits are to be discarded along with the medicinal decoction, or made into pills or powders;
the method is not fixed. The above is explained according to the general principle; in actual practice, one uses discarded medicine. The three fruits are not included in this [Chinese] formula;
if it were in the Western Regions (Xiyu), it would be acceptable, but here in this land, it is not yet appropriate. One must not be dogmatic.
Pillar. Second, the exposition according to principle: phenomenal medicine treats the body; principled medicine treats the mind.
This is because although mental illnesses are many, when summarized they do not exceed six types. First is the illness of greed: one craves the five worldly desires without satiety.
For an ordained bhikṣu, the medicine of giving is used to cure it by generating the mind of liberation. Second is the illness of negligence and committing evil.
One should treat it with the medicine of ethical discipline (*śīla*). Third, the disease of anger should be treated with the medicine of patience and joy (*kṣānti*).

Fourth, the disease of indolence should be treated with the medicine of diligence (*vīrya*). Fifth, the disease of dullness and delusive thoughts should be treated with the medicine of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Sixth, the disease of ignorance should be treated with the medicine of wisdom (*prajñā*). Extending broadly, the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) are all diseases; one should...
He treated them using eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* medicines. Question: The Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) inherently possess the meaning of medicine, yet they have never been discarded.
Why, then, do you employ this as a metaphor for discarding medicine? What principle does this follow? Answer:

The Dharma of the Six Perfections is truly a wondrous elixir for transcending the mundane and a divine prescription for entering the state of a Sage (*ārya*). The Buddhas employ it to treat the five [aggregates].
Abiding amidst the various maladies of affliction, they remain far from the calamities of the two deaths and have not yet realized the wondrous realm of the One Vehicle;

yet, never having abandoned them, [the Buddha observes] that ordinary beings do not believe in cause and effect, do not reflect upon sin and merit, and through heedlessness create karma, willingly entering the realms of suffering and placing their hands in submission at the gate of death.
Although there exists the excellent medicine of the Six Perfections, they turn away and pay it no heed.
How could it not be a rejection? Now, the Buddha employs phenomena to manifest principle. One who should wear [the robes] wears them;
one who is satisfied in every matter and attains the truth in every place is called a true śramaṇa, a disciple of the Buddha.

Constantly wearing the lower [robes], he demonstrates ten benefits and the names of the three fruits, or manifests precept, concentration, and wisdom (*śīla-samādhi-prajñā*). (From the *Huashan Zhizhi Huiji*, citing the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-ekottara-karman*: "There are five kinds of fruits.")

Whether it be at the improper time or during illness or health, one may eat these as one pleases: first, *āmalaka*, which is called "brought by the Lord of Heaven" (devadāru); second, *vibhītaka*; and third, *āmalaka* (the *yeganzi* of Lingnan), which resembles the *pūga* fruit in shape.

Eating it dispels wind. "Four ends of millet" refers to black pepper. "Five *juli*" refers to *kǔjiàng* (the sound of *kǔ* is *jǔ*; it may also be used as medicine). △ Second, the explicit explanation of the ten benefits, in ten parts.
First, the benefit of quelling greed through right mindfulness.
First, for the sake of seeking medicinal herbs, one does not associate with others, forever ceasing greedy pursuit and abiding securely in right mindfulness.
Since these are medicinal herbs discarded by others that exist everywhere, one takes them as they are found and uses them.
"Not associating with others" means not rushing outward in search. "Forever ceasing greedy pursuit" means not giving rise to deluded thoughts.
One who abides in right mindfulness does not regress from the mind of the Path. △ Second, the benefit of accomplishing the gate of contemplation:
second is the gate of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). It is easy to accomplish, and one can attain firmness in the supramundane mind.
The Buddha instructed those of initial resolve who possess many desires to practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).

This means to clarify the mind and settle it in meditative reflection upon the thirty-six kinds of impurity throughout the interior and exterior of the entire body, which constantly flow from the nine orifices, thereby engendering a profound sense of revulsion so that the desire-mind does not arise.
This is one of the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-vinodana-citta-sthāpana*). That [contemplation] is the correct observation; this [practice] employs discarded medicine as an aid.
That which is easily accomplished refers to things that have been discarded, which are turbid and loathsome.

When these are combined with contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), and when the primary and auxiliary practices are integrated, one’s efforts will gain strength, the aspiration for the Way will naturally become firm, and the method of contemplation can be perfected.
△ Third, the benefit of swiftly realizing the joy of dhyāna.
Third, one is constantly free from attachment to various delicacies and flavors, swiftly realizes right knowledge, and partakes in the flavor of the joy of dhyāna.
"Always being without greedy attachment" means that when encountering circumstances, one follows conditions as they arise; when faults occur, one does not engage in false conceptualization.

Where the greedy mind ceases, right wisdom manifests. Because mindfulness and wisdom are unified, it is called "realized wisdom. Meditation is the essence of concentration; wisdom emerges from meditation.
Furthermore, one can awaken to dhyāna, just as the tongue experiences flavor when eating. △ Fourth, the benefit of liberation through contentment:
Fourth, regarding all worldly wealth and possessions, one is always able to be content and thus attains liberation early.
The ancients said: "One who knows contentment finds honor; one who knows sufficiency finds wealth. This is true even in worldly truth, let alone for a śramaṇa.
Having donned the robes and discarded [worldly] medicine, the three poisons are all eliminated. To not give rise to a single thought regarding any material goods is itself liberation.
△ Fifth, the benefit of associating with virtuous friends.
Fifth, do not associate with any worldly ordinary persons, but associate with supramundane, pure spiritual friends.
By taking this "medicine of abandonment," one is forever free from greedy seeking; the mind becomes like clear water or snow, and conduct like ice or frost.
Therefore, by not associating with ordinary persons, the five desires cannot defile one; by associating with spiritual friends, the aspiration for the Way will surely increase.
△ Sixth, knowing the benefit of liberation through shame (*hrī*).
Sixth, by not loathing discarded medicines and the like, one attains liberation even regarding coarse food and drink.
Affection arises in the mind; karma issues from affection. When affection assails the heart, craving (*rāga*) blazes forth, and one takes delight in what is beautiful.

To loathe what is coarse is the common sentiment of humanity. For this reason, the Buddha instructed the bhikṣus that by discarding both food and medicine, they would sever both attachment and aversion, thereby accomplishing the path of liberation. △ Seventh: The Benefit of Worldly Veneration.
Seventh, regarding those things held in high esteem, one never harbors expectations, for there is nothing in all the world that is not honored.
"Those things held in high esteem" refers to what the people of the world value most. "Never harboring expectations" means that a renunciant disciple of the Buddha has only the Path to cultivate;
though the body may be afflicted by illness, since they possess no private hoard, how could they falsely [seek worldly gain] for the sake of this wretched frame?
Having ascended the gate of the donor’s residence, one should understand that what the Buddha prohibits is that which is improper to do yet is done by force;

it does not prohibit that which is proper but is not so performed. Suppose a donor were to offer medicine of great value with sincere devotion—if one ultimately refuses to accept it, this would be even more improper. Why? Because the donor’s offering...
To nourish one's vital essence for the sake of seeking blessings is already a pursuit; how much more so for a śramaṇa, for whom benefiting others is paramount?
If you do not accept [the offerings], the other’s wish will not be fulfilled, and you yourself will wound compassion. How could this be right?

It is simply that what the Buddha prohibited was the expectation of receiving offerings from those who do not provide them. Naturally, one’s virtue will evoke respect and spirits and ghosts will provide protection; thus it is said:
"Equal to all worlds," etc. △ Eighth, the benefit of attaining the Dharma-body:
eighth, one is swiftly able to subdue the diseases of all afflictions and realize the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharma-body.

The afflictions encompass the five abodes; the illnesses likewise encompass the two deaths. Subduing them refers to the effort of cultivation and realization. "Swiftly" carries the meaning of suddenness:
it means that once the afflictions have perished, birth and death are also exhausted, and one realizes the Dharma-body, which is eternally abiding and indestructible.
△ Ninth, the benefit of the permanent eradication of afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Ninth" refers to the permanent eradication of all afflictions within the three realms (*tridhātu*). This is capable of curing the grave illnesses of body and mind of sentient beings.
This follows from the preceding benefits. Since all afflictions have already been permanently eradicated, the very root of the disease of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) has likewise [been removed].

Excluding [self-interest], they give rise to practices for the benefit of others through a mind of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), and are further able to subdue the physical and mental illnesses of sentient beings;
thus, the merit of benefiting both oneself and others becomes even more apparent. △ Tenth, attaining the benefit of Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
Tenth, one is able to accord with the Buddha’s teachings, cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva, perfect merit and wisdom, and attain great enlightenment.
To "accord" means to follow and practice the Buddha’s teachings; it is like taking medicine that cures illness, which is the stainless nature.

To "cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva" means not to depart from the six perfections. In their meaning, these encompass both self-benefit and benefiting others: by benefiting others, merit is perfected; by cultivating for oneself, wisdom is perfected.
Fulfilled. With the perfection of merit and wisdom, one ultimately attains Buddhahood; therefore, it is said that "great bodhi is attained" (great bodhi being the fruit of the Buddha’s wisdom).
△ Third, the conclusion and entrustment for dissemination.
Jñānaprabha, you should know that for your sake I have briefly explained these ten kinds of benefits of abandoning medicine.
Such sublime practices are cultivated and studied together by all bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present.

You should expound and disseminate them for the sake of all sentient beings so that they shall not be interrupted; this is itself a vast offering made to the Tathāgata, surpassing anything found in the world.
Such offerings of wealth and respect cannot equal it. Regarding the bodhisattva practices, one shall no longer regress and will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
One who practices such wondrous conduct takes even discarded medicine, as well as clothing, food, and drink; this is the practice of the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

This is the practice cultivated together by the Bodhisattvas. Your instruction to "transmit and circulate [this teaching] below" so that it shall not be severed means to continue the life-force of the Buddha's wisdom.
This constitutes the comparison of superiority [of the recipient] below. However, the character "wei" (為) has two pronunciations and two interpretations.
One pronunciation is "wei" (唯), meaning that "wei" signifies "appropriate" or "correct. It is appropriate that the Tathāgata offers this Dharma-offering with his stainless nature.

Sentient beings: because the Buddha perceives that sentient beings possess the Buddha-nature but lack the practice [to realize it], he preaches this for them so that they may cultivate and realize it.
This is the Buddha’s offering of the Dharma to sentient beings. Because there are various kinds of benefits, it is said that "he extensively provides" [it]. One should understand this interpretation.
Regarding the phrase "lest what is non-existent be cut off," this is a brief statement of a single negation; although it is expressed thus...
"You all should expound and disseminate this sutra; for this sutra is spoken by the Buddha, and it is itself an offering to the Tathāgata.
This is one interpretation. Second, the phrase "for" (*wei*) means "to bestow upon" (*yu*).

This refers to Jñānaprabha and others, meaning that if you expound and disseminate [this teaching] for the sake of all sentient beings, it is equivalent to making extensive offerings to the Tathāgata. Thus.
To expound the teachings on behalf of the Buddha and not to contravene the Buddha’s commands is itself to make offerings to the Buddha.
Regarding the comparison with those of inferior worldly status, this also refers to Jñānaprabha and others; both interpretations are valid as they speak of the benefits obtained through cultivation.
△ Second, the verse in praise.

At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse: "O Bhikṣu Jñānaprabha, listen well! The stainless medicine worn by those who have left the home-life— This is the foremost of the Bodhisattva’s sublime practices.
Regarding the illnesses of sentient beings as one's own, One rescues them from all sufferings through the grace of great compassion;
Furthermore, employing a heart of loving-kindness, one bestows peace and joy, Giving this most supreme and wondrous medicine to others."
The main verse says that "excellent medicine saves people. Since it speaks of discarding the medicine, how can one remain free from defilement?
Generally speaking, defilement and purity originate from the mind. If the mind is free from craving and seeking, then one's own mind is pure;

as things follow the movement of the mind, even if discarded medicine were to enter the mouth, would it not be clean? Furthermore, if this is supplemented by the three fruits, what illness would not be cured? However—
The first three phrases concern self-benefit. "Sublime practice" is a general term for all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); this specific term refers to the abandonment of medicine.
Thus, he praises the extraordinariness of the Dharma and speaks of it as primary. The fourth phrase concerns the benefit of others:
it states that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, which they share equally with oneself; therefore, their illness is like one's own illness. By means of this...

The first line, "Great Benevolence" (Dàbié), implies that since there is great compassion, there must be the grace of benefiting all beings and saving the world; hence it is called "Saving from Suffering.

Furthermore, the second line, "Again Using [the Power]" (Fù yòng xià), implies that since one can save others from suffering, they will surely attain peace and security; thus there is the kindness of vast benevolence and virtuous grace, hence it is called "Peace and Joy.
The third and final line steps upon the preceding points of saving from suffering and bestowing joy, signifying that these are all sublime medicines bestowed upon others.
Furthermore, as previously stated, "medicine" possesses both the meanings of phenomenon (*dharma*) and principle (*li*). If explained from the perspective of phenomena:

when sentient beings suffer from physical illness, they experience pain and lack joy; now, by administering medicine suited to their ailments, they are restored to health and naturally attain peace and happiness—this is the wondrous medicine that rescues the body from disease.
If explained from the perspective of principle: "medicine" is the Dharma. To skillfully employ it...
The method of seizing the opportune moment can cure the mental illnesses of sentient beings. Because sentient beings possess afflictions and the cycle of birth and death, they suffer and find no joy.
Now, by preaching the Dharma for them and causing them to practice according to the teachings, it is as if they have taken medicine;
they sever the root of affliction, transcend the suffering of birth and death, and naturally come to enjoy the bliss of the Dharma.
Taking what was discarded by others for one’s own use, the Bodhisattva does not discriminate between noble and base medicines; he merely treats all ailments to bring peace and security.

By taking the leftover medicines discarded by others and using food and drink to cure his illnesses, he gains ten benefits from taking such discarded medicines, which are praised together by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time.
This verse concerns the discarding of medicine for one's own consumption. Now, a bodhisattva is not only able to perform deeds that others cannot perform;
they are also able to take medicines that others do not wish to take.
Yet, while good medicine benefits others, the act of discarding it to consume it oneself is precisely what defines a bodhisattva as a bodhisattva, distinguishing them from ordinary people.
This is beyond their reach.
Though they seek medicine, they do not approach others; they forever cease all pursuit and abide in right mindfulness.

The gateway of the contemplation of impurity easily reaches maturity, and they are able to create the distant cause for Bodhi. Without attachment to sweet flavors and free from all greed, they should seek the joy of the Dharma and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Delighting in the food [of Dharma], one is able to find contentment with worldly wealth and treasures, attaining the seven noble riches that are free from outflows (*anāsrava*).

Abandoning those foolish commoners, one does not dwell with them; instead, one draws near to the noble and holy as virtuous friends. By this means, one does not disdain the medicine that rejects the multitude, nor does one sever the craving for food and drink.
One harbors no desire for rare delicacies or exquisite medicines, yet respects all that exists in the world, being able to heal [all beings].
Having awakened to the body of the *tathatā*-dharma-nature, one eternally severs all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the triple world and realizes unsurpassed, true liberation.
Able to follow the Buddha’s teachings toward *bodhi*, one perfectly accomplishes the fruit of the *saṃbhogakāya* through the perfection of merit and wisdom.
This verse praises the ten benefits of discarding medicine. The first two lines praise the first part of the prose commentary;
the latter two lines, beginning with "impure," praise the second part of the prose commentary. "The cause of Bodhi" refers to the supramundane mind mentioned in the prose.

As for the phrase "being able to act as a distant [cause]," it means that [the impure object] serves as a proximate auxiliary condition for the contemplation of impurity, while acting as a distant auxiliary for the fruit of Bodhi.

This refers to the cause. The first two lines praise the third [section] mentioned previously; the second two lines beginning with "In the world" praise the fourth. Regarding the seven noble riches (*saptāryadhanāni*):

first is the wealth of faith (*śraddhā-dhana*). (Faith is the faculty of conviction; it means believing that one can resolutely receive and uphold the True Dharma as the requisite for attaining Buddhahood.

Since faith is the root of the Path, it is called the wealth of faith. Second is the wealth of diligence (*vīrya-dhana*). (Diligence is *vīrya*; it means that before one has attained the vision of the Truths, one single-mindedly exerts diligence to seek the path of liberation as the requisite for attaining Buddhahood. Therefore, it is called the wealth of diligence.)

1. The wealth of the precepts (*śīla-vitta*). (The precepts refer to the *vinaya*. This means that the precepts are the foundation of liberation; they can prevent the transgressions of the three karmas and cease the evils of the three karmas, serving as the requisite for attaining Buddhahood.

Therefore, they are called the wealth of the precepts. 2. The wealth of shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya-vitta*). (Shame (*hrī*) is shame before Heaven; remorse (*apatrāpya*) is shame before men. This means that if one possesses both shame and remorse, one will not create various karmas, thereby serving as the requisite for attaining Buddhahood.

Hence, it is named the wealth of shame and remorse. 3. The wealth of hearing (*śruta-vitta*). (Hearing is the foremost of the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*). Hearing necessarily leads to reflection (*cintā*), and reflection necessarily leads to cultivation (*bhāvanā*). This means that if one hears the Buddha’s teachings, one will develop subtle understanding and practice according to what has been taught.)

These are considered the requisites for attaining Buddhahood; hence they are called "wealth of renown. Sixth is the wealth of relinquishment (*tyāga*). "Relinquishment" means giving. This refers to being able to exercise a mind of equanimity, free from both hatred and attachment, and to bestow one's life, body, and material possessions upon those who seek them, without any stinginess.

Because this serves as a requisite for attaining Buddhahood, it is called the wealth of relinquishment. Seventh is the wealth of concentration and wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*). Concentration and wisdom refer to *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight).

Concentration gathers the mind so that it does not scatter and ceases all deluded thoughts. Wisdom illuminates and understands all phenomena, thereby destroying all false views. Once false views are destroyed, no further views arise. As these serve as requisites for attaining Buddhahood, they are likewise considered "wealth. Now, since it has already been stated that [these belong to] the sages...
Thus one knows that material wealth fosters greed, whereas the noble wealth (ārya-dhana) aids the Path. The latter two lines [of the preceding verse] comment on the fifth point;
the subsequent two lines comment on the sixth point, wherein the severance of greedy seeking corresponds to the meaning of attaining liberation in the preceding text.
The latter two lines beginning with "precious food" comment on the seventh point; the latter two lines beginning with "able to heal" comment on the eighth point.

One realizes unsurpassed, true liberation. This is urgent from the perspective of one's own benefit; yet, by first benefiting oneself and subsequently benefiting others, both aims are not lost.
This can accord with the following two lines, which recapitulate the tenth verse. The previous verse stated: "Attaining great bodhi."
The verse says: "It accomplishes the fruit of the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya). Now, bodhi is precisely the bodhi of the fruit of reward.
You, sons of the Buddha, shall all practice and study it; you shall sit within the true adamantine site of enlightenment."

This verse concludes by exhorting one to practice. The two terms "practice" (xiū) and "study" (xué) encompass both *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, as well as meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), along with the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).

All of these take the fourfold stainless nature (*catur-vimala-dhātu*) as their fundamental basis. As for the "Vajra True Dharma-Assembly," this refers to the Vajra-mind of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*).
Prior to the Path of Liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), it is the immediate, supreme effort—extremely firm and extremely sharp—which is capable of severing [all obstacles].
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the characteristic of arising; as it is the essence of subtle delusion, it is metaphorically likened to a diamond (*vajra*).

The "true site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) refers to the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), serving as a site of practice that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

The two characters for "should sit" signify the union of wisdom and principle, just as a body sits upon a seat. One should know that at this stage, if one practices gradually, one will vertically traverse fifty-five stages.

This is the true path to Bodhi; only by reaching this point can one attain it. For those of sharp faculties who practice through sudden cultivation, within a single kṣaṇa, they correspond with wondrous contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), exhaust fundamental ignorance (*mūlavidyā*), and immediately enter wondrous enlightenment, ultimately achieving Buddhahood.

This sutra is a teaching of sudden realization and should be explained according to the sudden method. Thus concludes the preceding detailed explanation of the four categories of nature. To answer the previous question, one should say:

This is the question regarding "abiding. As for the term "subsequent explanation" (*paścād-vyākhyāna*), it refers to the fact that the headings are presented first and the detailed explanations follow later;

since the section on "subduing" (*vinaya*) intervenes between them, the explanation occurs after that section, hence it is called a "subsequent explanation. This is because one knows that the Buddha’s speech is sovereign.
Nevertheless, these three meanings intersect with one another; for now, the topical outline is established based on the predominant meaning. △ Third, the Explanation.
Cultivation. How does one cultivate stainless karma? This answer is divided into three parts: first, training the mind through the authentic teachings of the Tathāgata;
second, [the long prose section], which is divided into five parts; first, the instruction to dwell in an araṇya (forest hermitage).
Furthermore, Jñānaprabha, a renunciant bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, far removed from clamor and bustle,
cultivating and collecting the mind for immeasurable thousands of years in order to seek the Buddha-way.
The Sanskrit term *araṇya* is translated as "a place of tranquility. One who stays far removed from clamor and bustle is not deluded by the five desires.
To dwell in an *araṇya* is to observe the summer retreat (*vassa*) in a quiet location—whether among the mountains or beneath the trees—in any place where one is not distracted by sounds or sights;
such places are all called *araṇya*. They serve as the environment upon which practitioners of the path rely.
Cultivating and gathering the mind constitutes the path to be practiced; the renunciant bodhisattva is the person capable of such cultivation.
This is because the deluded mind is as unrestrained as a wild horse or a mad monkey, galloping without rest due to the provocations of the mundane world.
For this reason, the Buddha commanded those who have left the household life to distance themselves from all worldly dust, thereby naturally entering the state of the ultimate realm.
With a mind tranquil and at ease, it is easy to practice. Even if there are already perfumed seeds [of affliction], one should subdue and sever them by means of precept, concentration, and wisdom;
this is called "cultivating the gathering of the mind. The passage beginning with "Immeasurable" (無量) correctly demonstrates the non-obstruction between the long and the short.
This means that in such a secluded and tranquil place, one utterly forgets worldly affairs; unaware of the existence of the body, one is also unconscious of the passage of time.
A single thought lasts ten thousand years, and ten thousand years are but a single thought. Though it may be said to be immeasurable thousands of years, the meaning of suddenness (*tun*) is not lost.
△ Second, citing the testimony of the noble ones to establish the point:

The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, having distanced themselves from all clamor and bustle, dwelt in tranquil seclusion; by cultivating the myriad practices, they realized the fruit of Bodhi.
The Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas—all worthy sages who have realized the fruits of holiness—are likewise so.

The Tathāgata is the fruit already accomplished; the myriad practices are the causes preceding the Way. To speak of the cause by relying upon the fruit is intended to exhort people to cultivate and realize it.
Since this is true for one Buddha, it is so for all Buddhas; hence, they are called those of the "Three Times. All...
The clamorous and noisy are sounds that delude the mind; therefore, one distances oneself from them. The tranquil and still are profound serenity and non-action; therefore, one dwells therein.
When this is so, the mind is empty and the environment is still; person and phenomena both vanish. Thus it is called "dwelling in leisure.

Because one practices without practicing, it is called the "ten thousand practices. By accomplishing a single practice, all practices are fully perfected; by realizing a single stage, [all stages are realized].

All stages are manifested simultaneously; therefore, it is called "further cultivation" (*zengxiu*). However, since it speaks of the "ten thousand practices" (*wanxing*), one must necessarily pass through the successive stages;

these are precisely the ten thousand practices cultivated sequentially throughout those stages. Furthermore, "cultivation" refers to the effort of gradual progression, while "realization" (*zheng*) refers to the actual fruit personally attained.
Because the Way is accomplished based upon cultivation, it is said that "one realizes the fruit of Bodhi. This explanation applies exclusively to the Buddha Vehicle.
It is said: below, the two vehicles are specifically mentioned. Those who attain the Way through the twelve links of dependent origination are the *śrāvakas*.

Those who realize the fruit by hearing the Buddha’s teaching on the four noble truths are the [bodhisattvas]. "All worthy sages" refers collectively to those of the three vehicles, each having different stages of worthiness (*bhadra*) and sagehood (*ārya*).
These are all those who, proceeding from the state of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) into sagehood, have personally realized and reached the truth.

Because it is accomplished through cultivation in a quiet hermitage (*araṇya*), it is said, "it is likewise so. Now, benefiting others must take place within the secular world, while one's own cultivation truly belongs to the mountain forests.
It may be said: "Cultivating in stillness brings joy to the dragons and devas; dwelling in the dust causes concern for the Buddhas and Patriarchs."
If one dwells amidst the dust of the world without being stained by it, this is impossible unless one possesses the highest faculties.

Nevertheless, discussing the practice of cultivation in general, it must necessarily proceed from stillness and tranquility. △ Third, the heading and inquiry regarding the ten virtues, in two parts: first, the heading and inquiry.
That araṇya possesses ten kinds of virtues that enable one to realize the fruit of *sambodhi*.
What are these ten kinds of supreme virtues?
Part Two: Explaining the Ten. First, the virtue of mastery over deportment.
First, one dwells in an araṇya to attain mastery, because within the four modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), one is not dependent on others.
The original purpose of leaving home is to distance oneself from worldly dust; if one does not follow stillness, how would it differ from secular life?

Furthermore, mastery is not for the sake of seeking ease; the intention is for cultivation and realization. It is precisely for the sake of cultivation that one dwells in an araṇya; thus, the four modes of conduct can be understood.

"Not belonging to others" is, in this single phrase alone, a supreme virtue. "Others" refers to worldly affairs. If one dwells amidst the dust of the world, one is led astray by the circumstances and objects of one's six relations;
there are things that do not depend on oneself. Now, dwelling in an araṇya (hermitage), one does not belong to the distractions of external conditions.
Being secluded, tranquil, and autonomous, the realization of the Way will surely be easy. How could this not be a supreme virtue? △
Second is the quality of being free from "I" and "mine.
Second, that which is free from "I" and "mine" is called an araṇya (forest hermitage). This is because when staying under a tree, there is no attachment.

"I" refers to the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), because one falsely clings to the idea that there is a sovereign master within the body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). "Mine" refers to what belongs to that self.
There are [objects of attachment], such as wife, children, and kinsmen, or fame, achievements, wealth, property, fields, and so forth.
To grasp at these as truly existing externally is the grasping at phenomena (*dharmagrāha*). Now, dwelling in an araṇya, one is not disturbed by external objects and the self-mind remains unmoving.
Whether the two types of grasping—at self and at phenomena—are suppressed or severed, since neither arises, the single nature is profound and still; this is the very state of the self-mind.
"Āraṇya. This is explained in terms of principle (*li*). If one stays beneath a tree and so forth, saying "under a tree" is synonymous with "āraṇya";

this is explained in terms of phenomena (*shi*). The Buddha prescribed eating once a day and staying overnight under a tree; thus, all external conditions are suddenly severed, and one practices pure cultivation for a single thought-moment.
Realizing that the myriad dharmas are but mind alone, there is no attachment—is this not supreme virtue? △ Three: Non-attachment.
The virtue of fearlessness regarding affection.
Third, one has no attachment to bedding and such. By means of this, one shall lie upon the bed of the four fearlessnesses.
"Bedding" refers to the implements for reclining the body. For householders, these may be carved beds and silk pillows, which give rise to attachment.
Attachment may arise from craving, which indulges the passions and obstructs one's nature. A renunciant bhikṣu takes caves and trees as his dwelling and spreads grass for his seat;
through shame, remorse, and contentment, he has nothing to which he is attached. From this point downward, virtue is brought forth through diligent effort.

"Si" means "this. That is to say, because there is no attachment due to causes and conditions, the power of the Way increases day by day, and one cultivates until attaining the Tathāgata’s great state of rest.
Therefore it says, "one should lie down," and so forth. Fearlessness represents the bed; fearlessness itself is not the bed.
These are all the virtues of the Buddha, which the practitioner possesses in part. Being at ease and fearless, the Way is contained therein, just as the body lies upon a bed. Thus it is said.

It is said: the throne of the four fearlessnesses (the four fearlessnesses are: fearlessness regarding all-knowledge, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows, fearlessness regarding the teaching of the dharmas that obstruct the path, and fearlessness regarding the teaching of the path that exhausts suffering).
△ Fourth, the virtue of being far removed from the three poisons.
Fourth is the forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*). Here, the three poisons are attenuated because one is free from the objects that give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion.
The "three poisons" refers to greed, hatred, and delusion. "Attenuated" does not mean they are entirely absent;

rather, because the mountain retreats are secluded and quiet, and there are no external objects to serve as conditions, the three poisons do not manifest in active operation. Therefore, they are said to be attenuated. However, after a long time, they will inevitably...
Both the seeds and the manifestations are extinguished. By relying on an araṇya, one obtains this benefit. △ Fifth, the virtue of not seeking the five desires:
fifth, one delights in the araṇya and practices the conduct of seclusion because one does not seek the pleasures of the five desires of humans and devas.
There are two kinds of the five desires (*pañca-kāma*). First, wealth, beauty, fame, food, and sleep; because these are the objects desired by sentient beings, they are called the five desires.
Alternatively, visible forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles; because these are the objects of the five sense faculties (*pañcendriya*), they are also called the five desires.
The first character, "joy" (*le*), expresses the practitioner’s heart of yearning and aspiration. "Cultivation" refers to the spiritual practice performed within the *araṇya* (hermitage).
"Seclusion" refers to the profound meditative concentration in which the mind does not engage with objects and remains unattached to anything.
As for the latter two lines: since it is said that one does not seek the five desires but sets one's will upon unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*, this constitutes excellence.
Virtue. △ Sixth, practicing the Buddha-way virtue.
Sixth, being able to abandon clamor and bustle, dwelling in a secluded and quiet place to practice the Buddha-way, not begrudging one's body or life.
It is for the sake of cultivating the Buddha-way that one abandons clamor to follow stillness. To "not spare one's body or life" means that a great man values only the Way;

he does not begrudge his toil and is unaware of the existence of a physical body. If one were to cherish and protect one's body and life, one could not avoid being weary of labor and fearful of suffering.
With even a slight sense of self-preservation, the will becomes indolent and practice becomes lax. Now, it is said—
Regrettable! This is what constitutes a virtuous quality. △ Seventh, the quality of easily accomplishing worldly activities:
seventh, one delights in tranquility; thus, all worldly activities are easily accomplished because they are free from obstacles.
Quiescence is the araṇya (hermitage). All activities—namely morality, meditative concentration, and wisdom—are the deeds for attaining Buddhahood;
these untainted karmas all arise from within quiescence. Therefore, it is said that accomplishment is easily attained.
If the mind harbors delusions or one’s practice encounters obstructions, these constitute hindrances. Now, with the mind in quiescence and the environment empty, there are no such hindrances.
Furthermore: △ Eighth, easily accomplishing supramundane virtues.
"Eighth" means that all worldly and supramundane undertakings are easily accomplished because they are free from obstacles.

Although the preceding section spoke of the matters of attaining Buddhahood through precepts, concentration, and wisdom, it did so from the perspective of practice during the causal stage (*hetu-bhūmi*).

This present section speaks from the perspective of realizing the fruit (*phala*). Regarding "the mundane and supramundane": this means that without departing from the mundane fruit, one achieves the supramundane fruit.
The activities within the state of fruition include such things as supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*), wondrous functions, and meditative absorptions (*samādhi*).
Liberation. The remainder is as previously explained. △ Ninth: The virtue of nine hundred thousand samādhis.
Ninth: The forest hermitage (āraṇya) is the emptiness of this samādhi, for it can attain one hundred thousand great samādhis.
In Sanskrit, this is *samādhi*; here it is translated as "right reception" (*samyak-samāpatti*). It is an alternative designation for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

However, afflictions arise from movement, whereas *samādhi* is accomplished through stillness. Once a single concentration is achieved, all concentrations become applicable. Regarding the "emptiness of *samādhi*":

it means that within the state of concentration, one does not grasp at any phenomena; thus it is called the "emptiness *samādhi*" (*śūnyatā-samādhi*). Furthermore, regarding the phrase "capable of attaining five thousand": it refers to the essence of concentration.
There is no duality. Although phenomena differ in a thousand ways, responding to myriad affairs while the single mind remains unmoved is precisely the hundred-thousand samādhis.
△ Tenth, the virtue of unimpeded great wisdom.
Tenth, it is pure like space, serving as one's dwelling. Because one attains great wisdom, the mind is free from obstruction.
Since there are no worldly disturbances within the *āraṇya*, it is called "pure. Because it is vast and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is said to be "like space.
Practitioners rely upon it just as they would a house. As for "the mind being without obstruction," this refers to the true mind.

Regarding the essence: because the delusions of the five stages have been exhausted and the causal practices are already fulfilled, one attains "Great Wisdom," which is the wisdom of the Buddha, as the fruit of Bodhi has been realized.
△ Fourth, exhorting one to abide and not depart.
Jñānaprabha, you should know that there are such immeasurable merits in forest hermitages (araṇya).
For this reason, a bodhisattva who has gone forth should vow to sacrifice body and life rather than leave the mountain forests.

Even if one must leave the araṇya to listen to the Dharma, to provide for the sick, or to attend to teachers, monks, parents, or elders within a village, one should quickly return to the forest hermitage.
The vow to sacrifice body and life rather than leave the mountain forests is intended as a formal exhortation to resolve one's will.
Indeed, it is not that people do not love their own lives; however, when weighed against the Way, the two cannot be preserved simultaneously.

Therefore, those who desire to achieve the Way swiftly become unaware of the existence of the body. Even when faced with moments of extreme peril or adversity, they would rather sacrifice their bodies than depart from the mountains.
In mountain forests, if one were even momentarily separated from [the community], the mind would be led away by external objects and become deluded by them, making it difficult to regain composure.
If, however, one must leave for purposes such as hearing the Dharma, then leaving is permitted; yet this is granted only as a temporary concession.
Furthermore, since a village is a place where the Dharma is taught, there will inevitably be teachers, monks, and the sick who require one’s presence to visit.
One may visit one's parents, or make offerings to teachers and monks, or go to visit the sick; nevertheless, one must not follow after external objects and drift with the current.
Therefore, it is said: "It is appropriate to return quickly. △ Five: Contemplation When Encountering Obstacles.
If there are causes and conditions such that one has not yet attained refuge, one should form this thought: "This village is like a mountain forest;
the wealth and goods obtained therein are as empty and false as a dream. Whatever is acquired should not be clung to with greed.
Such a son of the Buddha is a mahāsattva.
The first two lines refer to those who cannot arrive because the road is too distant; those who cannot reach their destination because it is late at night;
or those who are detained by others due to urgent matters. In all such cases of obstructing conditions, although the body has not yet returned, the mind does not abandon its resolve.
Therefore, the Buddha taught that one should contemplate the village as being the mountain forest. What is obtained...
"Regarding 'wealth and goods' below: these are the material offerings provided by donors, such as alms and provisions.
Even when receiving them, one must not allow the mind to become defiled. To fulfill the vows of the donor, one must accept these things;

yet, because one has thereby realized that the three spheres (trimaṇḍala) are empty in essence, it is said that they are like illusions or dreams. Thus, through such contemplation, one may enter the marketplace and respond [to worldly affairs]."
The conditions are such that they benefit sentient beings by following the winds and waves; there is nowhere they go that is not an araṇya (a forest hermitage).
The final two lines conclude: "Such a Buddha-son is a mahāsattva. *Mahā* means "great.
This indicates that these individuals are not merely bodhisattvas, but indeed great bodhisattvas. △ Second, the verse in praise.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse: "Distant from clamor and noise, a place of tranquility—this is the dwelling place of the ṛṣis.
This correctly praises the instruction to dwell in an araṇya. Regarding the residence of the ṛṣis, there is no text in the prose section; one should know that it is to be understood by implication.
The analogy of the immortal (śramaṇa) does not value the person, but values the place. For famous mountains and grottoes are regarded as the hidden abodes of immortals;
they are secluded and free from the dust of the world, and thus resemble an araṇya. It is only the sense of stillness that is taken up, not the conduct of an immortal.
Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time seek enlightenment and attain perfect awakening within the araṇya.

The noble assemblies of pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas likewise realize bodhi in this very place. By dwelling in an araṇya, one obtains ten benefits and is able to realize the fruits of the Three Vehicles.
This verse cites the teachings of the Sage to exhort practice. While the prose says "Tathāgata," the verse says "Bodhisattva.
This is because the Tathāgata is the fruit that follows the path of the Bodhisattva, whereas the Bodhisattva is the cause that precedes the path of the Tathāgata.
Thus, the preceding fruit and the subsequent cause are not of different categories. The remaining five lines are identical to the prose, with the sole exception that one obtains ten benefits.
A verse: Taking his stand within it, he roams with sovereign ease like a lion;
among the four modes of conduct, he is without bondage. The mountain forests and beneath trees are what the noble ones delight in;
being free from "self" and "mine," this is called an araṇya (hermitage). Having no attachment to robes or bedding, he sits as a teacher possessed of the four fearlessnesses.
This is the seat of the Son. To be free from all afflictions is called an araṇya. Having no attachment to any craving or love, one constantly dwells beyond material things, weary of worldly toil.
Not delighting in the pleasures of the five desires of the world, one remains far removed from clamor and dwells in tranquility. Casting aside body and life, one seeks the Buddha-way;
able to abide in silence where there is no sound of human voices, one does not give rise to a distracted mind regarding worldly or supramundane matters.
All virtuous deeds in the world are accomplished without mental obstruction; thus, the araṇya is the root from which hundreds of thousands of samādhis arise.
Taking great emptiness and stillness as its void, the practitioner’s body and mind are free from hindrance.
This verse praises ten kinds of supreme virtues. The first two lines praise the first [virtue]:
the lion is the king among beasts; wherever it goes, it has no fear or dread. A bhikṣu dwelling in an araṇya is likewise: his mind is free and at ease, without any fetters.
The second couplet concerning the mountain forests praises the second [virtue]. Regarding clothing... [and so forth].

The two lines [of the verse] correspond to the third point of the preceding prose. The two lines on "being free from all duality" correspond to the fourth point of the preceding prose. "Defilements" refers to the aforementioned three poisons.
The prose states "free from the objects of perception," while the verse says "all craving and attachment have no place of clinging.
Logically, the word "objects" (*viṣaya*) should be added beneath "craving and attachment," meaning that one has no clinging toward the objects of all craving and attachment.

The first line indicates the subject, while the second line provides the explanation. The two lines beginning with "Constantly dwelling" (*chángjū*) eulogize the fifth [point] above. "Beyond worldly things" (*wùwài*) refers to the *āraṇya*;
"disliking the toil of defilements and not delighting in the five desires" corresponds to the practice of "cultivating seclusion" (*xiū yuǎnlí xíng*) in the prose section.

The two lines beginning with "Secluded from" (*yuǎnlí*) eulogize the sixth [point] above. Following "turmoil" (*kuìniào*), the character "dwelling" (*zhù*) is omitted; it should read "secluded from turmoil" (*yuǎnlí kuìniào*).
Regarding "dwelling amidst bustle while remaining in tranquility": the latter lines mean that one does not ultimately abandon the body nor ultimately relinquish life.

This is said only because, in seeking the Buddha-way, one practices with such fierce diligence that one cannot afford to cherish body or life to the point of giving rise to indolence; thus, one is able to abide in the following four lines.

These verses correspond to the preceding [lines] seven and eight. The first two lines of this verse correspond to the preceding [line] on "delighting in dwelling in tranquility," as there are no people [to disturb it].

The three characters "sound" (*śabda*) explain the meaning of "tranquility" (*śānti*). For where there is sound, there is movement; where there is no sound, there is stillness. Regarding the phrase "among all [others]":
it means that distraction arises from clamor, whereas concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are perfected in profound stillness. Now, since there is no human voice...
A distracted mind has no basis from which to arise. The latter two lines of the verse praise the eighth [point]: that all undertakings are easily accomplished, and so forth.

The preceding statement that "undertakings" (karmānta) belong to the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is here distinguished as the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) by dividing them into mundane and supramundane.
That is to say, the mundane refers to contaminated wholesome karma, which is the seventh [point]. The supramundane refers to...
Untainted wholesome karma is the eighth. Regarding "the mind being without obstruction": this builds upon the preceding seventh and eighth [stages].
Because the mind is not distracted, there is no afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which brings worldly wholesome matters to fulfillment.

Because of tranquility and the absence of sound, reaching the ultimate point where both mind and dharmas have perished, the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is likewise absent, and all supramundane wholesome karma is accomplished.

Therefore, by means of the following two lines, the preceding seventh and eighth [verses] are taken up; the ninth verse is summarized by the two lines beginning with "By means of the Great" (*mahā-*) below.
"Great emptiness and quiescence" (*mahā-śūnyatā-śānti*) does not refer to an emptiness of annihilation, but rather to the wondrous essence of true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*).
This serves as the basis for the preceding hundred thousand samādhis, because true emptiness constitutes the essence (*svabhāva*) and samādhi constitutes the function (*vṛtti*). Thus it is said:
The character "empty space" (*ākāśa*) here is likely incorrect; logically, it should be the character "suchness" (*tathatā*).
This refers to the wondrous principle of true emptiness, which is all-pervasive, perfectly interfused, and profoundly encompassing—just like empty space.

Alternatively, it is possible that the two characters "empty space" are an error by the scribe for the preceding two characters "abode. As for the "practitioner," this refers to the person who is capable of cultivation. [He] desires...
Having realized the Dharma-body and attained accord with the true mind, one is entirely liberated; therefore, there is no obstruction.

This is because the "long practice" refers to the attainment of great wisdom, which is explained in terms of Bodhi. The "body and mind" mentioned in the verse refer precisely to the Dharma-body and the true mind.
Speaking in terms of *nirvāṇa*, these are all the specific characteristics of the fruit of Buddhahood.
Because it is fully endowed with these ten benefits, the noble ones (*ārya*) constantly dwell therein.

It is because of these benefits that the noble ones reside there. The preceding verse concludes by manifesting this and exhorting one to abide [therein]. "The noble ones" refers generally to the three [vehicles].

The "person who rides upon the fruit" (chengguo ren) also refers to inferring the cause from the fruit. This means that prior to attaining the fruit of sainthood (*āryaphala*), while practicing the path (*mārga-bhāvanā*), one constantly dwells in an araṇya;
it does not mean that one dwells there constantly after having attained the Way.
Jñānaprabha and you, sons of the Buddha, if you wish to swiftly accomplish all-knowledge, do not abandon the path of enlightenment in the forest hermitage even in your dreams.
Those who resolve their minds after my parinirvāṇa and are able to dwell in forest hermitages shall,
before long, sit upon the king of jewel-flowers and realize the fruit of the eternal bliss of the Dharmakāya.
This verse demonstrates the realization of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). "Omniscience" (*sarvajñatā*) refers to "knowledge of all aspects" (*sarvākārajñatā*).

Because the seven characters [of *sarvajñatā*] form a complete phrase, one aspect is abbreviated. (As for "knowledge of all aspects": by means of a single type of knowledge, one knows all paths and knows all aspects; this is called "knowledge of all aspects," which is the wisdom of the Buddha.)
"Aranya" (below) means that bodhi is itself the path; because it is cultivated and perfected by relying on an araṇya, the place is referred to as the "path.
"When I have passed away" (below): "I" refers to the Tathāgata’s self-designation, which is also a conventional designation of a self following worldly usage.
"Nirvāṇa" has two meanings: first, speaking in terms of principle, it means that the Buddha is able to extinguish the afflictions of the five abodes and cross over the two kinds [of birth].
Regarding birth and death: because one realizes the fruit of the path of true permanence, it is called "extinction" (nirvāṇa). Second, speaking in terms of phenomena:

this refers to manifesting the concealment of one's traces and returning to the truth, which is what is meant by "after extinction. As for "sentient beings": this refers to all beings throughout the limits of the future. As for "those who resolve their minds [for enlightenment]":...

This refers to those who have resolved their minds for enlightenment in future lives. "Able to descend" refers to the place of reliance; "not long" indicates that they will achieve it instantaneously.
"Sitting upon jewels" clarifies the ritual appearance of attaining Buddhahood. "Jewel-flower king" refers to the lotus flower upon which the Buddha sits;
because of its veneration, it is called a "jewel" and a "king. "To realize" [the phrase] "below" means to perfect the four virtues of the Dharma-body: permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

The fruit is one of the two [aspects] of the four virtues; its meaning also encompasses all four. Collectively, these are called *bodhi* (enlightenment) and *nirvāṇa*, both of which emerge from the *araṇya* (hermitage).

Regarding those who conventionally employ the designation "self," there are four types of self: first, the self of the ordinary person’s pervasive conceptual attachment, which refers to the notion that there is a sovereign master within the body of the five aggregates; second, the *ātman* of the non-Buddhists;

third, the provisional self of the followers of the Two Vehicles, whose grasping at a self has been severed and who ought not to be called "self," yet are provisionally termed "self" to conform with worldly conventions and to distinguish between host and guest; fourth, the true self of the Tathāgata’s *dharmakāya*, which is realized solely by the Buddha. Now, as for this true self of the *dharmakāya*:

Fundamentally, there is neither arising nor ceasing. What is now called "after my parinirvāṇa" is spoken of merely in terms of the conventional, provisional self that accords with worldly convention. Since it is improper to refer to this as "I," it is termed the "provisional self.
(The above, the first major section on the Tathāgata’s extensive exposition, is hereby concluded. △ Second, the benefits obtained by those who hear [this teaching].

At that time, when the World-Honored One was preaching this Dharma, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of those who had first resolved their minds attained non-retrogression from the unsurpassed path.
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattvas, including Jñānaprabha and others, attained dhāraṇīs and were endowed with great supernormal powers.
A million beings, both gods and humans, gave rise to the bodhicitta and realized the three gates of liberation.
As for those who had first resolved their minds [on enlightenment], they were people who had only recently entered the path of hearing the Dharma;
by hearing about the four kinds of stainless nature and their respective ten benefits, as well as the ten [virtues] of dwelling in an araṇya, they attained non-retrogression in the unsurpassed path.

They cultivate supreme virtues; thus, upon seeing the worthy, they aspire to equal them.
