Having first resolved upon the Great Mind, they attain non-retrogression in the unsurpassed Buddha-way, with their intent fixed on definitive cultivation and realization—this is also the superior mind that cultivates the cause in anticipation of the fruit.
Zhiguang and others attained *dhāraṇī*, which here is translated as "total retention" (*zongchi*); it is the essential substance of the true mind, which universally encompasses all virtues.
Yuanwu is the wondrous essence. "Possessing great spiritual powers" refers to the great function within that essence.
It was because he had heard from afar of the Buddha’s teaching on the Dharma for repaying the four debts of gratitude that he, though a son of unworthy conduct, desired to transform his own mind.
He did not decline the vast distance of the journey, nor did he shrink from the hardships of travel; thus, leading a multitude, he came to seek the Buddha’s instruction.
Having heard the Dharma, they further sought to practice acts of gratitude and resolved to leave the household life.
Since they themselves had left the household life, their sons likewise left the household life; thus, the entire community under their leadership united in leaving the household life.

Now, having heard the "Chapter on the Stainless Nature" from beginning to end, they have all attained sudden and perfect awakening, acquiring the virtue of *dhāraṇī*. This may truly be called not passing through [the stages].
The *Saṃghāṭa* [Sūtra] attains the Dharma-body. Indeed, such Bodhisattvas not only do not fail their own spirits, but they also do not fail the Buddha’s grace.

However, the original intent of his coming was to instruct his son; now that both father and son have attained awakening, the debt of natural affection and the way of father and son can go no further. As for the son, it is not merely the Buddha...

The kindness [of one's parents] is difficult to repay; even were one to shatter their body and sacrifice their life, they could not repay even a ten-thousandth part of what their parents have done for them.

Alas, how ultimate! Among the millions of people under heaven, there are those who, having heard the Buddha-dharma, realize that the tainted cycle of birth and death within the realms of humans and devas cannot be escaped.
They consequently give rise to the Great Mind and awaken to the three gates of liberation. Such individuals are truly sublime men.

Ah! (There are three liberations. First is liberation through intrinsic purity: because one realizes that the self-nature is fundamentally pure and unstained by any defilements, it is liberation in its very essence. Second is liberation through realization achieved through cultivation: although the self-nature is pure, it is currently obstructed by the delusions of views and thoughts;

if one does not practice, it is difficult to realize this proof. Third is liberation through the purity of skillful means: one subsequently gives rise to contemplative practice and employs skillful means to arouse true wisdom, thereby being able to manifest function from the essence—like a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru).
△ Third, the benefits following the Buddha’s explanation, which has two parts. First, the exhortation to uphold and disseminate [the teaching].

At that time, the Tathāgata addressed the great assembly: "If there are sons or daughters of good family with pure faith who hear this profound Dharma-gate of the four kinds of stainless nature, and receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and transcribe it."
The preceding section was arranged by the compilers of the sutras; this section consists of the Tathāgata’s own words. The phrase "If there be... identifies those who hear and uphold [the teaching];
it does not refer specifically to those present here, but speaks generally of those with a karmic affinity in future generations.

"Pure" means being unstained by mundane affairs; "faithful" means having a resolute mind that does not waver. Such men and women will certainly serve as the requisite conditions for receiving the Way. They shall attain...

"Upon hearing" below indicates the dharma-gate that is to be heard, namely, the fourfold nature of purity (*catur-vimala-svabhāva*). "Profoundly deep" below explains the meaning: it is called "deep" because one realizes the principle through phenomena;
it is called "profoundly deep" because one swiftly attains the Buddha-way. A dharma possesses the quality of maintaining its track (*dhṛti*), while a gate possesses the sense of passage;
that is to say, by means of this dharma-gate, one reaches and enters the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Regarding "receiving and upholding," there are two meanings: first, the literal matter...

To uphold [the teachings]: to hold them in one’s hands and observe them with the eyes, ensuring that mind and speech do not deviate from them; to uphold them through both principle and practice, so that wisdom merges with the principle and one maintains it without loss.
To read means to become thoroughly familiar with the text and understand its meaning. To recite means to repeat it from memory without forgetting.

To explain means to analyze the structure of the text and comment upon its meaning. To lecture means to expound and differentiate the details. To transcribe means to apply the brush to produce a formal composition. To copy means to carve, engrave, or print.

These acts of giving are all for the purpose of circulating the transformative teachings of the Dharma and continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom. △ Second, the explicit explanation of the subsequent benefits, in four parts:
1. Benefits regarding the place of rebirth.
Wherever such persons as these are born, they shall encounter spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), cultivate the bodhisattva practices, and never fall back;
they shall not be disturbed or confused by any karma or afflictions (kleśa).
The first phrase refers to those who previously received and upheld the teachings. The second phrase clarifies the place of rebirth in future lives.

"Encountering the good" and so forth constitute the superior conditions (*pratyaya*). Due to having received and upheld [the teachings] in this life, they perfume the seeds of the noble ones (*ārya-bīja*) to serve as the proximate cause (*hetu*).
Encountering a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) necessarily provides instruction, serving as the external condition; this draws forth the seeds to initiate their actual manifestation (*samudācāra*).
Therefore, it is said that one "cultivates the bodhisattva practices. Because one has resolved with determination to achieve [enlightenment], it is said that one "never regresses.
As for "not being [disturbed] by the lower": since one has cultivated pure seeds from the stainless nature, one naturally possesses a pure endowment;
thus, one is not disturbed by various delusions. △ Second, obtaining benefits in the present life.
In this present life, one obtains great merit and wisdom, sustains the Three Jewels, attains the power of mastery, and succeeds to the lineage of the Buddhas so that it remains uninterrupted.
"The present life" refers to this very birth. To be able to hear the Great Teaching is itself the attainment of merit; furthermore, being able to read and study it, and so forth [is likewise].
One will inevitably attain wisdom. To settle the mind and establish practice constitutes the upholding of the Triple Gem.
Indeed, the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are all called "gems" because they can deliver people from birth and death, shatter the darkness of ignorance, and give rise to wisdom.
Their sacred function is divine and wondrous; therefore, they are all called gems. Those who have attained the power of mastery do so through every thought-moment.
One causes the spirit to dwell within the Three Jewels. Wisdom issues forth from such practices as receiving and upholding [the teachings];

because it does not involve forced effort, it is called "sovereign. Power (*bala*) is the function of wisdom; its capacity to destroy the heterodox and manifest the orthodox constitutes its functional power.

Because these are transmitted and passed down in succession, enabling the Three Jewels to abide eternally, it is said that one "succeeds to the lineage of the Buddhas," and so forth. (Attaining Buddhahood by relying on the Dharma; the Dharma is...)
The Buddha-seed shall be transmitted and circulated from one to another, thereby ensuring its succession.

△ Third, after birth in Tuṣita, at the end of life they will certainly be reborn in the palace of the Heaven of Satisfaction (Tuṣita), where they will attend upon Maitreya and realize the stage of non-retrogression. At the first assembly under the Dragon Flower Tree, they shall attain enlightenment.
One shall hear the True Dharma, receive the prediction of enlightenment (*bodhi-vyākaraṇa*), and swiftly attain the Buddha-way.
"Contentment" (*tuṣita*) is the Chinese translation for Tuṣita; "celestial palace" (*deva-loka*) refers to the Inner Court. "To pay homage and behold" means to serve and attend upon [Maitreya].
Because one pays homage and beholds him, one will certainly study the Way, taking Maitreya as one's teacher. This refers to attaining the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
Having already been born in Tuṣita, there is a fixed time for the realization of the Holy Path; therefore, it is called "non-retrogression.

Upon reaching the time when Maitreya attains Buddhahood and delivers the Dharma in three assemblies, those who hear the prediction at the first assembly will immediately attain Buddhahood. This is because by continuing the lineage of the Buddhas, one obtains this supreme benefit.

(According to the Separate Teaching [biejiao], Bodhisattvas sever the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the stage of the First Abode (*prathama-vihāra*), and sever the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) from the Second through the Seventh Abodes. Because they never again fall back and transcend the rank of ordinary beings, it is called the Stage of Non-Retrogression.)
△ Fourth, rebirth according to one’s vow:
If one wishes to be born in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, one will attain rebirth in accordance with that vow, seeing the Buddhas and hearing the Dharma.
One shall ultimately never regress from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

With the prior practice of upholding, reciting, and studying as the cause, and the making of vows as the auxiliary condition, one is impelled by these causes and conditions to be reborn according to one's wishes.
Having attained such rebirth, one will see the Buddhas and hear the Dharma, and regarding *anuttara*...
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. It is naturally ultimate and non-retrogressive. The major section on cultivating and collecting the mind according to the True Teaching of the Tathāgata is hereby concluded.
II. The Great Being’s Inquiry Regarding Cultivation and Realization in the Araṇya (The Hermitage). Part Three. 1. Title of the Chapter.
The Title of the Chapter: The title of this chapter is established based on the title of the sutra; it is called "The Aranya Chapter of the *Mahāyāna-mūla-janma-citta-bhūmi-darśana-sūtra*.

This is an *adhikaraṇa-samāsa* (dependent compound), as the chapter contains a discussion of the matters concerning the cultivation and realization of the *āraṇya* (wilderness retreat) through a series of questions and answers. It is named according to that which is questioned and answered.
Establishing the Title. △ Second, the Sūtra Text. Part One: The Prose Exposition, Section Six. First, the Narrator’s Account of the Ritual Setting:
At that time, there was in the assembly a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva named Constant Diligence (*Sadāparibhūta*).

Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
One who is constantly diligent gives rise to three internal states of mind and externally cultivates the myriad practices.

Finding insufficiency in themselves yet never wearying toward others, they establish this auspicious name based upon their own vows and conduct. Furthermore, this chapter must necessarily rely on one who is constantly diligent to initiate it;
for although one may dwell in an araṇya, that is merely the stillness of the environment. If one’s mind is not refined and free from distraction, there will be no progress on the Path.
I am weary; fearing that there may be a beginning but no end, I have made this effort for two purposes: first, to resolve doubts, and second, to serve as a warning and an exhortation.

Regarding those who "rely upon the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power," this refers to the matters of cultivation and realization within the *araṇya*. This is the site of practice cultivated by all Buddhas;

therein, the appearances of favorable and adverse conditions are known only to the Buddhas themselves. Without the need for questions and answers, it is difficult to resolve the doubts of the multitude.
This is indeed a momentous matter. Were it not for the empowerment of the Buddha’s power, even one who is constantly diligent would be unable to inquire into it.
For this reason, the compiler of the sutra discerned its significance and recorded it here. △ Second, the statement of the intent and the posing of questions.
World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, the forest hermitage (āraṇya) is the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).

Those who resolve to seek enlightenment should not abandon the forest hermitage. Within these hermitages there are many sentient beings—tigers, leopards, jackals, wolves, venomous insects, and malevolent beasts, even down to birds and hunters—who do not recognize the Tathāgata. They do not...
They have heard the True Dharma, yet they do not revere the Saṅgha. These sentient beings possess no further roots of goodness and are far removed from liberation.
For what reason does the Tathāgata cause those who practice and study to go to the araṇya so that they may swiftly attain Buddhahood?
From "As the Buddha said" down to "one should not abandon the *āraṇya* (forest hermitage) location," all is the teaching of the Buddha;
now the Bodhisattva recounts it. From "This *āraṇya*" onwards, he raises an example to express a doubt. His intention is this:

the Buddha stated that through cultivation and realization in an *āraṇya*, one quickly attains Buddhahood. Currently, the mountain forests are secluded, tranquil, and spacious; these are precisely the *āraṇyas*. As for their...
Within it appear many kinds of sentient beings, such as tigers, leopards, and so forth, up to flying birds;
this is a general reference to all beasts and fowl. As for the "hunters," these are those who capture animals in the mountains;

this specifically refers to one type among the human race who are fond of killing, of whom there are many varieties, though here only a few are mentioned. The Bodhisattva’s thought was that the Buddha’s words applied to all [beings].
All sentient beings possess Buddha-nature. Those who possess Buddha-nature shall all attain Buddhahood.
Since these sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, and furthermore dwell in forest hermitages (araṇya), they are neither deluded by the five desires nor entangled by human affections.
This is precisely the time for practice; all may thereby achieve the Way. Only then will one see the efficacy of dwelling in an araṇya.

"Not knowing" and so forth clearly demonstrates that dwelling there in vain is of no benefit. Since they do not recognize the Tathāgata, nor hear the True Dharma, and furthermore do not respect the Saṃgha, they possess no roots of goodness and remain far removed from liberation; this clearly shows that there is harm and no benefit. For what reason?

This follows the previous inquiry regarding doubt and strangeness: if such a state is of no benefit, yet the Buddha causes people to cultivate it, claiming that Buddhahood will be swiftly attained, what benefit is there in the fruit? △ Third, the earnest plea to resolve the doubt.

I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for the sake of all sentient beings, analyze and explain this in detail, resolving their doubts and causing them joy, so that they may give rise to the bodhicitta and never regress.
This means that the Tathāgata resolves their doubts so that those who have resolved their minds shall not retreat from their aspiration. △ Fourth, the Tathāgata’s praise and approval:
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Constant Diligence, saying, "Excellent, excellent! Son of good family, you possess great compassion."
Question: Regarding the Tathāgata’s pure liberation, which benefits all future practitioners, its merit is immeasurable.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well. I shall now, for your sake, analyze and expound the various merits of the araṇya dwelling.
"Excellent" (*sādhu*) is a term of praise; it carries the meaning of the Buddha’s joy. "Praising again" signifies the height of this joy.
It means that the teaching does not arise in isolation but must emerge in dependence upon conditions. Because he spoke in response to a question, he has explained the matter with exhaustive detail.

This serves not only to resolve the doubts of the assembly, but truly to further increase their benefit. From the words "You, with great compassion... onwards, the Buddha recounts [the Bodhisattva's] constant diligence.
The intention behind Jin’s question was not that he truly did not know; rather, he asked deliberately for the sake of the great assembly, in order to manifest true compassion.
This is why the Buddha praised him as one of "pure liberation," which refers precisely to the supreme benefits of the tranquil virtues found within the *araṇya*.
"Benefiting those of lower capacity" below describes the great benefit within that question. "Listen attentively" below is an admonition to listen and a permission to speak.
△ Fifth, the appropriate response of the audience:
"So be it, World-Honored One; we wish and desire to hear."
△ Sixth, the Tathāgata’s direct response in four parts. First, a direct rebuke that [the former position] is not appropriate.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Constant Diligence: "As you have said, one may become a sage in a forest hermitage (araṇya).
Yet, there are many sentient beings within the mountains and forests; for what reason do they not attain Buddhahood? This meaning is not so."
"However.
As for what you have said, it is precisely based on what you have said. [The passage] from 'A-lan' (Aranya) downward is the Buddha’s restatement of the Bodhisattva’s question;
only the final phrase directly rebukes his error, hence he says, 'It is not so. △ Second, the interrogation and explanation."
This is why. Why is this? Those sentient beings do not recognize the Three Jewels; they do not know contentment; they do not distinguish between good and evil.
Although there are various worldly treasures within the mountain forests, they are unable to know the location of the hidden hoards.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is not like this.
Why is it that [the Buddha] directly refutes [this view] as being not so? It is because those sentient beings you have cited do not recognize the Three Jewels;
they are the height of ignorance and folly. How could they be compared to practitioners who cultivate the Way, such that one would doubt them?

Those sentient beings—namely, tigers, leopards, birds, beasts, and various hunters—are such that the birds and beasts are ignorant and devoid of knowledge, while the hunters are evil by nature and fond of killing. Because of their folly, they do not recognize the existence of the Three Jewels;

because of their evil nature, they do not know contentment for themselves, acting according to their own whims and failing to understand the causes and effects of good and evil. Such are these types of beings.

"Can they be vessels for the Way? Beneath the mountain, he separately raised the distinction between the enlightened and the ignorant, saying that within the mountains and forests there are all hidden treasures of precious gems; yet due to their folly, they do not even know their location.
If they do not even know the location of worldly treasures, how much less could they realize the great treasure of the Dharma-King that transcends the world? Therefore,"
The wise person is not the same as birds and beasts; therefore, the text concludes by stating that a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is not like this.
To examine the Buddha’s words closely, there is indeed a subtle point of transformation: those who dwell in the mountains yet do not enter the Way are no different from birds and beasts;
those who greedily seek after things and thereby harm the Way are no different from hunters. Alas! Even the blind cultivation of aged monks may fall into such a state.
Startling! △ Third, the explicit clarification of the intent of abiding.
Good son, a bodhisattva is able to know that the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha is the supramundane treasure, while the seven precious hidden treasures are mundane treasures.
He is fully able to discern their various characteristics and colors and knows where they are located, yet he does not greedily seek them after them. Nor...
One does not even wish to see them, much less take them. When a bodhisattva leaves the household life, they give rise to a firm resolve;
disregarding their own body and life, they abandon their parents and six kinds of kinsmen and relatives, delighting in dwelling among the mountains and forests.
The Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha represents ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); therefore, it is called the supramundane gem.

This means that by being able to penetrate ultimate truth, one transcends the three realms; truly, it is a treasure. The seven precious treasures hidden as a storehouse represent conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*); they are called mundane gems.

If one penetrates the conventional, it is itself the ultimate, and one likewise transcends the three realms. Thus, the ultimate and the conventional are of one essence, yet the ultimate and the conventional remain distinct. Therefore, it is said that [the Bodhisattva] is fully capable of...
"Discerning their various colors, forms, and so forth" means that although one expresses them, one does not cling to them; thus, both mind and objects are empty.
"Nor delighting in seeing them and so forth" means severing all deluded thoughts. [The section] beginning with "The Bodhisattva leaves the household life... [follows].

The conclusion summarizes and exhorts one to abide [in the Dharma]. (Regarding the two characters "fu-zang" [hidden treasure], they are open to doubt and require clarification. For the Sūtra states that birds, beasts, and the like do not know the location of hidden treasures because they are hindered by ignorance. Now, as for a "hidden treasure" (*nidhāna*):

it refers to gold, silver, or precious jewels that an ancient person buried in the earth because they could not carry them with them when fleeing from war or seeking refuge; at that time, only the person who buried them knew its location. Later, once that person had passed away, others were unaware of it. Such things exist everywhere and are common occurrences.

However, the current claim that birds, beasts, and the like do not know [the treasure] because they are obstructed by ignorance is questionable. If one argues that while birds and beasts do not know it, those in the world who are intelligent...)

This principle ought to be understood. In the present world, it is not that treasure-troves do not exist; yet who is able to recognize them? Even those of keen intelligence may fail to perceive them, let alone birds and beasts. Furthermore, it is said that Bodhisattvas can know the hidden stores of the seven treasures.

This goes without saying for Bodhisattvas of deep rank who possess the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), as they would naturally see them. However, when the sutras speak of this, they refer to beginners learning the Path who are designated as "Bodhisattvas" but have not yet attained a deep stage of realization;

how could such individuals know of these treasures? Nevertheless, there are two interpretations regarding what is being discussed here: first, that the matter may be used metaphorically to represent a Dharma principle, as explained in the commentary; second, that "hidden store" (*nidhāna*) does not necessarily mean a buried hoard, but may instead refer to a mineral deposit—such as gold ore or silver ore, both of which exist [within the earth].

In the mountains, birds and beasts do not know [this], yet the wise can know it. It is simply because the scriptural text lacks clarity that this explanation is provided (one cannot help but speak at length). △ Fourth, maintaining visualization to fortify the will:
A single thought [reveals] that the environmental retribution is impermanent.
He constantly reflects thus: "Suppose that at the end of the kalpa of this trichiliocosm, seven suns appear simultaneously;
the calamity of fire blazes forth, incinerating all things—the sun, moon, and stars, Sumeru, the king of mountains, and the seven golden mountain ranges."
The Iron Ring Mountains and the like all disperse when their time comes;

one should constantly practice the contemplation of downward observation. By means of this contemplative visualization, when the kalpa is destroyed and the seven suns appear simultaneously (as explained in the first fascicle), the trichiliocosm is utterly ruined.
Thus, the conditioned environment is impermanent; one should know that this contemplation is fundamentally intended to make the mind firm and steadfast.
That is to say, even the great trichiliocosm is subject to destruction; how much more so this body? Second, reflecting on the impermanence of the retributive reward:

even at the summit of the three realms, the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception, when eighty thousand kalpas have ended, one returns to the lower planes. This is also true for the Universal Monarch (Cakravartin).

Surrounded by a thousand sons and accompanied by the retinue of the seven treasures, he brings the four continents under his sway. Yet when his lifespan and karmic retribution are exhausted, not even a moment remains.

Even the Heaven of Neither Perception Nor Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), the highest among all heavens, uses impure meditative concentration (*sāsrava-samādhi*) to suppress and dwell within deluded thoughts so that they do not manifest;
yet although the seeds remain, it further takes half of the arising aspect (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) from within the seeds as they arise and perish moment by moment.
These are likewise suppressed and do not function; only the characteristic of extinction remains in the seeds, which they take to be the ultimate fruit of *dharmatā-nirvāṇa*.
However, within eighty thousand kalpas, when the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is superior, both the seeds and their manifestations are suppressed.

Once the eighty thousand kalpas have passed and the power of concentration declines, the generative potential of the seeds is activated, and deluded thoughts gradually arise in unspeakable suffering. After a long time, then—
They fall, or are born among humans and so forth; thus it is said that when eighty thousand kalpas have ended, they return to birth on the lower planes.
This refers to the highest heaven, yet even there one cannot escape falling; the same can be known for the other heavens.
Even a Cakravartin King, the most honored among men, has a thousand sons—such a multitude of sons as these is not found among humans—and he is fully endowed with the seven treasures and his retinue.
He is protected by his followers; moreover, he surpasses all people of the world. His wealth is ultimate and his nobility is supreme.
With his majesty he subdues the four continents, such that there are none who do not submit. His honor is ultimate and his power is supreme. The final two lines speak of the time when his life ends:
as soon as the summons arrives, it must be acted upon without even a moment's delay; thus it is said, "not pausing for a single instant. This refers to the human realm.

Even the Most Honored One cannot escape impermanence; of others, it may be known by extension. The above constitutes the observation of the signs of impermanence from the external perspective of the body.
△ Third, reflecting on the impermanence of one's own body.

I am just the same now. Even if one were to live a full hundred years, possessing all seven treasures and experiencing every pleasure, when the messengers of Yama arrive, one cannot escape impermanence.
The first phrase uses oneself as an analogy for others, hence it says "it is likewise. Among humans, those with a lifespan of a hundred years are rare;
the poor are many while the wealthy are few, let alone those who possess all seven treasures. This is the practitioner’s pure mental observation, thinking:

"Even if my life were to last a hundred years and my wealth reached the extent of the seven treasures, and I were to experience every kind of pleasure, none would be anything other than a candle before the wind or grass [blown by the wind]."
The frost upon one's head cannot be maintained forever; when the messengers of Yama arrive at times, one cannot avoid following them away.
Thus it is said that one cannot escape impermanence. Now, all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas were originally ordinary beings who achieved their realization through cultivation;
had they not relied on such antidotes, how could they have given rise to the mind of weary detachment and accomplished the path to Bodhi? May those with the karmic affinity and wisdom [apply this].
People, let them take this as a mirror for themselves. △ Fourth, receiving the resolve and making vows, in two parts. First, making the vow in general:
He reflects thus: "I do not yet know how to act on behalf of my parents and all sentient beings to cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva."
One shall attain the indestructible body of vajra. Returning to the triple world, one shall rescue and deliver one's parents.
Having made this vow, one dwells in an araṇya and gives rise to great aspirational vows for the sake of all sentient beings.
"I do not now know [the truth]," and so forth, expresses the arising of shame and remorse. To say, "I lack the sagely and divine brilliance and the penetrating illumination of a saint;
I am barely able to look after myself, so how could I replace my parents and all sentient beings to cultivate the bodhisattva practices?"—this is the generation of the vow.
"Unbreakable like a vajra" refers to the Dharma-body and Reward-body (*dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya*).
The two bodies are those to be attained upon becoming a Buddha. "Returning to descend" means that once Buddhahood has been attained, one turns the vessel of compassion back toward the triple world;
relying on supernatural powers and wisdom, one rescues and delivers one's parents and all sentient beings. This concludes the preceding section.
As for "relying on vows to dwell in stillness," it means to store up and nourish one’s practice deeply, resolving with determination to cultivate and realize the Way. This...
To still not forget the kindness of one's parents and the suffering of sentient beings may be called the vow of a Bodhisattva.
△ Second, the detailed classification of grades has four parts. First, the generation of vows by those of the three faculties.
The bodhisattvas of superior capacity make this vow, saying: "May I, until I have attained Buddhahood, always sit in the open air and never lie down.
The bodhisattvas of middling capacity make this vow, saying: "May I, until I have attained Buddhahood..."
Amidst the leaves of trees, he sat constantly without reclining. A bodhisattva of inferior capacity made this vow, saying:
"May I, until I attain Buddhahood, sit constantly without reclining within a stone cave."

The Way is fundamentally called the "root. There are differences in superiority and inferiority, and distinctions between sharp and dull faculties. This reveals that although they dwell together in an araṇya (hermitage), their aspirations are not uniform;
therefore, they are divided into three grades: superior, middle, and inferior. Regarding the superior root, the section on "descending" precisely clarifies the making of the vow.
"Not yet attained" refers to the period after the mind has been resolved toward enlightenment and before the fruition of Buddhahood is reached. The intervening stages are passed through.

The time limit is indefinite; one constantly sits and never lies down, and must do so in an open space. Such a person is judged to possess superior faculties (*agradhātu*), for their resolve is firm and their practice is austere;
they do not dread wind or rain, nor do they fear cold or heat. Seeking the Way that can be attained, they are unaware of their own physical body.
Since sleep and mental obscurity cause the loss of wisdom and lead to a state of non-defined nature (*avyākṛta*), the wise do not desire them; thus, they resolutely determine their will.
Do not lie down; constantly sit and investigate, taking the realization of the Way as your goal.
This may be called the "superior grade" for one whom a thousand sages could not call back from their path. Regarding the "intermediate grade among those under trees," there are two explanations.

First, the character "middle" (中) may be an error for the character "lower" (下), because while the former person was in the open air, this person is under a tree where branches and leaves provide shade.
[The first type] merely covers [the body] to ward off frost and dew. The second type uses tree leaves spread out as a seat;
sitting within them, they use this to block the cold air. Their resolve is the same as the former, but their mode of dwelling differs; thus they are judged to be of middling capacity.
As for the stone chamber: it is either beneath a mountain crag or within a mountain cave; all such places constitute stone chambers.
One does not maintain a fire or smoke, nor does one store any other belongings. When going out, one begs for food; when returning, one sits in quietude.

Their determination to achieve Buddhahood is identical to the two previous cases; they differ only in that they dwell in stone chambers to avoid wind and rain, and to provide a slight defense against cold and heat.
His ascetic practices were somewhat inferior, and he was thus judged to be of dull faculties.
Now, to dwell alone in a stone chamber and devote one’s whole heart to the Way is something that even ordinary people in the world cannot do;

yet he was still judged to be of dull faculties when compared to people today who reside in high halls and grand mansions, enjoy the warmth of red stoves and heated rooms, wear silks and satins as clothing, eat fine flour and oils for food, and receive offerings from donors.
Faith is the lard and fat [that sustains the body]; it is the blood and sweat of those who labor on the path.

Yet, those who are frequently turned by worldly conditions and bound by greed and hatred—what root can they possibly be said to possess? One ought to feel shame and remorse. △ Second, the conclusion revealing the merit.
Thus, these three types of root bodhisattvas who have gone forth sit upon three kinds of seats, each forming this thought:
"The bodhisattvas of the past sat upon this seat and were able to realize the gateways of dhāraṇī and attain mastery over merit.
All bodhisattvas of the past, present, and future likewise attained the dhāraṇīs upon this seat and realized mastery in cultivation. I, too, am like this."
Sitting here now, you shall certainly achieve mastery over the dhāraṇī.

"Dhāraṇī" means "total retention" (saṃgraha-dhāraṇa), signifying that it encompasses all phenomena and upholds immeasurable meanings. Furthermore, it is called "total retention" because it protects the good and obstructs the evil.
It is able to maintain the myriad virtues and immeasurable treasures of the Dharma without loss, and it is able to protect [the practitioner].
It never fails to preserve all untainted (anāsrava) wholesome dharmas; it is able to obstruct all tainted (sāsrava) evil karma so that it does not enter.
Because its name is established based on its function, it is called *dhāraṇī*. It is precisely the *nirvāṇa* realized by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
"Gate" (*mukha*) has the meaning of "passage. This means that one exits through this gate when function arises from the essence, and enters through this gate when the false reveals the true.

The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "The Unsurpassed Dharma King possesses the Great Dhāraṇī Gate, from which flow forth all true suchness (*tathatā*), Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), bodhi, nirvāṇa, and the pāramitās, thereby instructing bodhisattvas. This is named according to its manifest function.
Regarding "sovereignty over merit": cultivation of the cause is termed "merit" (*guṇa*), while the realization of the fruit is termed "virtue" (*guṇa*). It transcends birth...

Upon death, one will enjoy the bliss of the Dharma; therefore, it is called "sovereignty. This refers exclusively to the past. From "past and present" onwards, it refers generally to the three periods of time.
From "I too" onwards, one uses others to verify oneself and uses oneself as an example for others; therefore, it says, "I too am thus.
Those who now sit upon this seat—whether on open ground or elsewhere—will certainly achieve accomplishment; this is what is meant by "valiance."
With a mind that upholds the resolve of a man of integrity, he takes realization as his goal and does not retreat even unto death. △ Third, regarding the failure to fulfill his vow:
if he has not yet achieved mastery, he shall never abandon his dwelling in the *āraṇya*.

One should know that from this section onward, up until the later passage on "sitting constantly without rising," these are called the twenty-six types of *bodhi-araṇya-pratipatti* (forest-dwelling practices for awakening).
It is stated in all cases that one shall never abandon the forest hermitage (*araṇya-sthāna*). Although they belong to the same category, the textual meanings differ;
this will be understood from the subsequent text. Within this context, there are two kinds of mastery: first, contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

Mastery over objects (*viṣaya-vaśitā*). (This means that a bodhisattva, through correct wisdom, illuminates and realizes the realm of true knowledge and is able to penetrate all phenomena with perfect, harmonious mastery; for this reason, the name is established. Second, mastery over function (*karma-vaśitā*).

(This means that a bodhisattva, by illuminating the realm of *tathatā* with correct wisdom, is immediately able to give rise to function from its essence, manifesting bodies and preaching the Dharma to transform all sentient beings, thereby attaining mastery.
If one can achieve this, then one manifests bodies and preaches the Dharma everywhere; if one has not yet achieved it, then [one remains] constantly...

While seated, he constantly practiced; he never abandoned the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka). He thought to himself, "The Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time all realized enlightenment from this place.
What kind of person am I that I would seek elsewhere apart from this? It must never be so."
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have attained perfection in the four immeasurable minds, never abandon their dwelling in the araṇya.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have attained perfection in the five supernormal powers, never abandon their dwelling in the araṇya.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have fully perfected the six pāramitās, will never abandon the aranya.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have fully perfected skillful means (upāyakauśalya), will never abandon the aranya.

The four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) are the four types of altruistic intentions: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). As for the five supernormal powers (*pañca-abhijñā*):

the power of the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) allows one to observe from afar, such that mountains and walls do not obstruct vision; the power of the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) allows one to hear from afar, such that the myriad sounds of nature do not cause confusion;

the power of the transformation of the physical body is subtle and wondrous beyond measure; the power of knowing the minds of others allows one to know their thoughts without them being spoken; and the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrva-nivāsānusmṛti*) [reveals] the cycle of birth and death.
From beginning to end, it illuminates all-pervasively. These five aspects are all "spiritual" (*shen*) because they are numinous, wondrous, and unfathomable;

they are "penetrating" (*tong*) because they are sovereign and unimpeded. "Power" (*li*) refers to the meaning of practical application. The six *pāramitās*—the six perfections—are explained and illustrated in the first fascicle.

"Skillful means" (*upāya-kauśalya*) refers to provisional wisdom; by employing provisional methods, one adapts to the capacities of others and responds to the timing, thereby enabling them to follow the transformation.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have been able to subdue all sentient beings, will never abandon their dwelling in an araṇya.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have been able to perfect the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), will never abandon their dwelling in an araṇya.
There may be bodhisattvas who, though they have not yet been able to cultivate the practice of the six recollections, never abandon their dwelling in an araṇya.
There may be bodhisattvas who, though they have not yet achieved the wisdom of extensive learning, never abandon their dwelling in an araṇya.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have achieved the power of firm faith, shall never abandon the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka).
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have severed the sixty-two views, shall never abandon the forest hermitage.
"Sattva" (sentient being) refers to that which possesses consciousness and discrimination; it is a specific designation for living beings.

Because their mental states (*citta*) may be wholesome or unwholesome, and their discriminations may be deviant or correct, this term encompasses all beings born from the womb, from eggs, from moisture, or through transformation; thus they are called "all.

To "tame" (*vinaya*) is the Bodhisattva’s activity for benefiting sentient beings, comprising both the two gates of subduing (*nigraha*) and gathering (*anugraha*). "Taming" means to regulate and harmonize; "gathering" means to receive and sustain them in goodness.
"Person. "To subdue" means to humiliate and bring low those wicked types, causing those sentient beings to know that there are the Three Jewels and to turn their minds toward the Path.
As for the four methods of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), they are: giving (*dāna*), pleasant speech (*priyavāditā*), beneficial conduct (*arthacaryā*), and cooperation (*samānārthatā*).
A Bodhisattva, in order to transform and guide sentient beings, employs these four methods to gather them in, causing them to rely [on the teaching], and thereafter...
He guides them by means of the true path of the Mahāyāna. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* says: "First, one entices them with the hook of desire;

subsequently, one causes them to enter the Buddha-wisdom. First is the gathering through giving (*dāna-saṃgraha*). This means that a bodhisattva gathers sentient beings through two kinds of giving: material and Dharma. If sentient beings delight in material things, he gathers them by bestowing material gifts.

If they delight in hearing the Dharma, he provides them with the teaching, gathering them through the Dharma. Once sentient beings have received the benefit of these two types of giving, they consequently develop feelings of affection and intimacy; they rely upon him to receive the Path and attain abiding in the True Principle. Therefore, it is called the gathering through giving.

2. *Priyavāditā-saṃgraha* (Gathering through affectionate speech): This means that when a bodhisattva accords with the faculties and dispositions of sentient beings and comforts them with kind words, all sentient beings delight in hearing such kind speech. Because they hear it, they give rise to feelings of affection and love; they rely upon [the bodhisattva] to receive the Path and abide in the True Dharma.

Therefore, it is called gathering through affectionate speech. 3. *Arthacaryā-saṃgraha* (Gathering through beneficial conduct): This means that when a bodhisattva initiates wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind to benefit all sentient beings, because of this, they give rise to feelings of affection and love;

they rely upon [the bodhisattva] to receive the Path and abide in the True Dharma. Therefore, it is called gathering through beneficial conduct. 4. *Samānārthatā-saṃgraha* (Gathering through common purpose): This means that a bodhisattva, by means of the Dharma-eye, clearly perceives sentient beings...

Regarding the faculty of nature (*indriya-gotra*): according to what each being delights in, one immediately manifests various forms and appears in their likeness, performing the same activities so that each may receive benefit. Because of this, they give rise to affection and love, relying [on the teacher] to receive the Way and attain abiding in the True Principle;

therefore, it is called "gathering through common purpose" (*samānārthatā*). As for the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), "recollection" means to keep in mind clearly without forgetting. There are six such recollections. The first is the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).

This means to recollect the Buddha as complete in the ten titles, possessing great kindness and great compassion, the radiance of wisdom, and immeasurable supernatural powers, capable of uprooting the sufferings of all beings. With a pure and upright heart, I draw near to the Buddha; my heart gives rise to joy, and because of this joy, the body attains... [benefit].

Joy. Because of joy, the mind attains concentration (*samādhi*). Because of attaining concentration, the mind becomes equanimous. By practicing the contemplation of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), one will certainly proceed toward *nirvāṇa*. This is called "recollection of the Buddha. 2. Recollection of the Dharma (*dharmānusmṛti*):

(This means that the Dharma consists of all the virtues possessed by the Tathāgata, namely the ten powers (*daśabala*), the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*), and so forth. With a pure and upright mind, I draw near to the Dharma; joy arises in my heart. Thus, up to the point of practicing the contemplation of the Dharma, one will certainly proceed toward *nirvāṇa*). 3. Recollection of the Saṃgha (*saṃghānusmṛti*):

(This means that the Saṃgha are the disciples of the Tathāgata who have attained the untainted Dharma (*anāsravadharma*), are endowed with morality, concentration, and wisdom, and are able to serve as a fertile field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for the world. They should be revered. With a pure and upright...)

With a mind of straightforwardness, one draws near to the Sangha. Joy arises in the heart, and by practicing the contemplation of the Sangha, one will surely proceed toward Nirvana. Fourth is the mindfulness of precepts (*śīla-smṛti*). This means reflecting on how the various prohibitions and precepts can restrain all evil afflictions (*kleśa*).

This means reflecting on the wholesome benefits obtained through one's own acts of giving. "While all the world is shrouded by stinginess and envy, I have now attained freedom from such stains of greed and have come to abide in a mind of relinquishment (*tyāga*). Regarding a single...

To cut things [for others], with a heart free from stinginess, one should practice giving. Having given, my mind should be joyful; because of this joyful mind, the body attains happiness. When the mind reaches equanimity, one cultivates the perception of giving (*dānasaṃjñā*) and will certainly proceed toward *nirvāṇa*.

This is called "recollection of giving" (*dānānusmṛti*). Sixth, recollection of the devas (*devatānusmṛti*): This refers to recollecting that the various heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are all attained through the roots of merit from past discipline and giving, whereby one experiences celestial bliss there.

I too currently possess such merits of discipline and giving; at the time of death, I shall certainly be reborn in those heavens. Because of this recollection of the devas, one leaves behind unwholesome states and the mind gives rise to joy. One cultivates the perception of the devas and will certainly proceed toward the heavenly path. This is called "recollection of the devas. Much learning (*bahuśruta*).

"Attaining" means that what reaches the ears is not forgotten; this constitutes "hearing. "Much" refers to those such as the Venerable Ānanda, who heard the Buddha’s teachings on the provisional and the real, the sudden and the gradual, and all their various distinctions, just as one pours water from a vessel without a single drop leaking out; thus, he is called "one of great learning.

"Wisdom" means that by virtue of hearing the Buddha’s words, one awakens to and realizes the Middle Way, remaining far removed from the two extremes, and attaining a perfection that is utterly free from error; therefore, it is so named.
"Extensive learning is wisdom. Firm power of faith is decisive knowledge and vision.

Whenever one hears the Buddha’s teachings on all the causes and effects of defilement and purity pertaining to both the noble and the ordinary, one deeply endures, delights in, and desires them, remaining resolute and free from doubt.

To be firm means to possess eternal faith without doubt; this is what constitutes firm faith. From the arousal of faith, the myriad practices are cultivated to perfection;

Regarding the five aggregates (*skandhas*)—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—one gives rise to four kinds of conceptualization for each aggregate (as it is said, by means of conceptualization...).
When these [four] views are combined with the twenty views, they constitute twenty views. When analyzed according to the three periods of past, present, and future, they become sixty views.
With the two views of annihilationism and eternalism as their root, they collectively form the sixty-two views. Regarding the four types of views:

within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), first, one calculates that the self is large and matter is small, and that the self resides within matter; this is the first view. Second, one calculates that the self is large and matter is small, and that matter resides within the self; this is the second view. Third, one calculates that matter itself is the self; this is the third view. Furthermore, one calculates... [the fourth view].

To hold that "the self is apart from form" constitutes four views. These four views arise with respect to the aggregate of form; likewise, there are four views for each of the remaining aggregates—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—all of which are false views.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have cultivated the eightfold noble path, will never abandon the forest hermitage (āraṇya).
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have eternally severed the habitual tendencies (vāsanā) of the two obscurations, will never abandon the forest hermitage.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have perfected the subtle wisdom of administering medicine according to the illness, shall never abandon the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka).
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have perfected the great bodhicitta, shall never abandon the forest hermitage.
There may be bodhisattvas who, until they have perfected samādhis as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, shall never abandon [the forest hermitage].
In a forest hermitage (āraṇya), there may be a bodhisattva who, though not yet having perfected immeasurable supernormal powers (abhijñā), never abandons the forest hermitage.

Regarding the Eightfold Noble Path (aṣṭāṅgamārga): it consists of eight factors; because they do not rely on partiality or deviation, they are called "noble" (samyak); because they lead directly to nirvāṇa, they are called the "path."

The Path: 1. Right View (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*). (This refers to cultivating the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) and clearly perceiving the Four Truths. It destroys the various false views of non-Buddhists, such as those concerning existence and non-existence; this is right view. 2. Right Intention (*samyak-saṃkalpa*).

(This refers to, at the time of seeing the Four Truths, correctly recollecting and reflecting, observing and deliberating so that contemplation may increase; this is right intention. 3. Right Speech (*samyag-vāc*). (This refers to constantly restraining verbal karma through untainted wisdom and remaining far removed from all speech that is false and unreal;

this is right speech. 4. Right Action (*samyak-karmānta*). (This refers to, by means of untainted wisdom, cultivating and gathering the mind to abide in pure and right action, thereby severing [unwholesome deeds].)

All actions that are deviant and false constitute right action. Fifth is right livelihood (meaning that those who have left the household life should abandon the four types of wrong livelihood for gain and sustenance, and instead always sustain their lives by begging for alms;

this is called right livelihood). Sixth is right effort (purity is "effort" (*pra*) and continuity is "exertion" (*vī*); it means diligently cultivating the path of morality, concentration, and wisdom with single-minded devotion and without interruption, taking the realization of the Way as one's goal; this is called right effort).

Seventh is right mindfulness (meaning to keep in mind the right path of morality, concentration, and wisdom, as well as the five methods of mental abiding that assist the path, thereby being capable of advancing toward *nirvāṇa*; this is called right mindfulness).

**Right Concentration (Sammā-samādhi):** This refers to gathering all scattered thoughts so that body and mind are tranquil and still, abiding correctly in the principle of true emptiness without wavering. Alertness and stillness mutually guide one another; this is called right concentration. **The Habitual Tendencies of the Two Obstructions:** 1.

**The Obstruction of Principle (Li-zhang):** This refers to the source of the fundamentally enlightened mind (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), which is profoundly serene and pure. Due to the delusive defilement of ignorance (*avidyā*), it is obstructed from correct knowledge and vision, preventing one from attaining the principle of True Suchness (*tathatā*); this is called the obstruction of principle. 2.

**The Obstruction of Phenomena (Shi-zhang):** This refers to sentient beings being shrouded by the obstruction of ignorance, such that birth and death continue in succession with no way to escape. Encountering every path, they encounter stagnation; this is called the obstruction of phenomena. **Habitual Tendencies (*vāsanā*):** That is to say...

The seeds of the two obstacles (arise from afflictions of beginningless ignorance, which perfume and form the seeds of the two obstacles; they are submerged, subtle, and profound, making them difficult to eliminate. Only upon reaching the final thought-moment of Equal Enlightenment can one begin to sever them through a single moment of correspondence).
When the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the two obstacles are exhausted, one enters Wondrous Enlightenment and becomes a Buddha.

Regarding "subtle wisdom that administers medicine according to the illness," this refers to the wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-prajñā*). For example, [the Buddha] may deliver beings by means of the Śrāvaka Dharma as appropriate.

This refers to the teaching of the Dharma corresponding to the Four Noble Truths and so forth; it is collectively termed "teaching according to the capacity" (投機之教), named after the metaphor of medicine prescribed according to the illness.
The Great Bodhicitta consists of the three minds, the four vows, and so forth. As for the "samādhis as numerous as the sands of the Ganges":

Their functions differ, and their names vary according to those functions; they are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Briefly stated, the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are of six kinds, namely:
the divine eye, the divine ear, and so forth up to the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Extensively, they are also immeasurable, for they are fully perfected only at the stage of Buddhahood.

Or, there may be a bodhisattva who, until they have perfected the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) and the ten thousand practices (*daśasahasra-caryā*), shall never abandon the forest hermitage. Or, there may be a bodhisattva who, regarding...
Throughout a hundred kalpas, they have been unable to cultivate the karma for the marks and signs [of a Buddha]. They never abandon the *āraṇya* (forest hermitage) dwelling.

"Concentration" (*samādhi*) refers to meditative absorption; "penetration" (*abhijñā*) refers to thorough mastery. For a Bodhisattva at the stage of profound rank, within the clarity and perfection of concentration, all mental phenomena are empty.

Their very substance is pure, and they penetrate and illuminate all things without obstruction. This is the power of concentration and penetration, through which they perceive the eighteen kinds of emptiness.
This "seeing" is not seeing with the eyes, nor is it a clear, distinct perception; rather, it is seeing through the constant illumination inherent in stillness.
Nevertheless, although it is able to illuminate and perceive—just as a mirror reflects objects—it is entirely devoid of conceptualization; therefore, the mind is not startled.

Regarding the eighteen kinds of emptiness: first is internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*). (The "internal" refers to within the body. There are thirty-six kinds of impurity;

the nine orifices constantly flow [with secretions], and thus a pure characteristic cannot be found. Therefore, this is called internal emptiness. Second is external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*). (The "external" refers to external forms. That is to say, for the foolish...)

Because of the defilement of desire, one contemplates the forms to which one is attached and falsely deems them pure. Yet when seeking their pure characteristics, they are found to be like one's own body; pure characteristics cannot be obtained. They are illusory and lack reality.

This is called "emptiness of the external" (bāhya-śūnyatā). Third, emptiness of the internal and external (adhyātma-bahirdhā-śūnyatā): This means that just as one's own body is impure, so too are external objects; and just as external bodies are impure, so too is one's own self. They are equal and without distinction, like illusions or transformations.

Since pure characteristics cannot be obtained, it is called "emptiness of the internal and external. Fourth, emptiness of emptiness (śūnyatā-śūnyatā): This means that the internal body, the external body, and both the internal and external bodies are all empty. Yet, one still clings to this emptiness and it becomes a sickness. Therefore, one further employs the dharma of emptiness to dismantle these three types of emptiness. This is called "emptiness of emptiness. Fifth, great emptiness (mahā-śūnyatā).

(That is to say, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, these are the derivative forms produced by the four great elements. Conventionally, the place where the sun rises is designated as the eastern direction, and the place where the sun sets is designated as the western direction.

Such directional characteristics exist only because of worldly convention. If within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), not a single dharma can be apprehended; this is called "Great Emptiness" [1]. Six, "Ultimate Emptiness": Among all dharmas, the foremost dharma is named *nirvāṇa*. The dharma of *nirvāṇa* is empty and devoid of characteristics; this is called "Ultimate Emptiness" [2]. Seven, "Emptiness of the Conditioned":

Within the dharmas such as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), neither self nor what belongs to a self (*ātman-ātmīya*), nor any characteristic of permanence, can be apprehended; this is called "Emptiness of the Conditioned" [3]. Eight.

The emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). (Since there is no purposeful activity, it does not possess the characteristic of existence. Now, in contrast to the conditioned, the unconditioned is spoken of. If conditioned phenomena are already unapprehendable, then what could one be attached to regarding unconditioned phenomena?)

This is called the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). Ninth is ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*): this means that by means of the preceding eight kinds of emptiness, all phenomena are dismantled until nothing remains; since no phenomena exist, there is also no emptiness to which one could become attached.

This is called ultimate emptiness. Tenth is beginningless emptiness (*anavarāgra-śūnyatā*): this means that worldly sentient beings have no mark of a beginning. Just as the present life exists due to causes and conditions from a previous life, and that previous life in turn existed due to a life prior to it—thus revolving in succession, a beginning cannot be found.

This is called beginningless emptiness. Eleventh is dispersal emptiness (*anavakāra-śūnyatā*): this means that because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are combined, the appearance of a person arises; if wisdom analyzes and disperses them, [the person is no longer found].

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the person are empty and non-existent. It is like a chariot, which is formed by the combination of spokes, rim, shaft, and hub; if these are dispersed and each remains in a separate place, the name "chariot" is lost. This is called the emptiness of dispersion (*vibhava-śūnyatā*). Twelfth is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*):

this means that the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*dharma*) is fundamentally empty. All arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions; if they do not so conjoin, such phenomena do not exist. Thus, the nature of these phenomena cannot be apprehended, and is therefore called the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

Thirteenth is the emptiness of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*): this means that all phenomena have two kinds of characteristics. First is the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), and second is the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*). The general characteristic involves arising and ceasing without abiding; it was originally non-existent and now exists, and having existed...
14. The emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*): This refers to the phenomena of the five aggregates, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements.

They possess no real characteristic; all are empty, without grasping or abandoning, and far removed from all views. This is called the emptiness of all phenomena. 15. The emptiness of the unapprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*):
This refers to the fact that all phenomena and their causes and conditions are ultimately empty and entirely unapprehendable. This is called the emptiness of the unapprehendable.

16. Emptiness of Non-existent Dharmas (*abhāva-śūnyatā*). (This refers to the fact that when all dharmas have ceased, even that cessation itself does not exist; this is called the emptiness of non-existent dharmas. Furthermore, past and future dharmas are called unconditioned dharmas (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*);

(This refers to the fact that all dharmas exist through the combination of various causes and conditions, yet the essence of these dharmas is fundamentally unreal;

There is the emptiness of non-existence and existence (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*). The four foundations of mindfulness (the contemplation that all phenomena arise from conditions and are all devoid of self). II. The four right efforts (*samyak-prahāṇa*). "Right" means not being deviant; "effort" means not being indolent. 1.

To cause evil that has already arisen to be permanently severed. (This means that if any unwholesome dharmas have already arisen, one should apply diligent effort with a single mind to decisively eliminate them so that they are forever severed.

2. To prevent evil that has not yet arisen from arising. (This means that if any unwholesome dharmas have not yet arisen, one should apply diligent effort with a single mind to restrain them so that they do not sprout again.)

Third, causing unarisen wholesome states to arise (meaning that when various wholesome dharmas have not yet arisen, one should apply oneself with diligence, single-mindedness, and vigor so that they may be brought forth). Fourth, causing arisen wholesome states to increase.
