Furthermore, a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya should, day and night in continuous succession, contemplate in this manner.
This constitutes one general section, which is divided into twenty-one segments for the sake of explanation. The first provides a general indication of the characteristics of contemplation;
the preceding sections have repeatedly elucidated how, by dwelling in an araṇya, one becomes free from all terrors and accomplishes all [virtues].
Regarding the merit: this final summary concludes that one ultimately attains Buddhahood.
This extensively clarifies that the myriad virtues and the wealth of the Buddhadharma—the ultimate, supreme fruit—all have the araṇya as their source. This marks the conclusion of this section.
This teaching and its practice value uninterrupted continuity; therefore, it is called "successive" (*saṃtati*). The two characters "thus" (*evaṃ*) are terms that point to the dharma;
the subsequent sections constitute the actual contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
This is the araṇya, where one can skillfully cultivate the four stainless natures; it is a place of peace and happiness.
This is the araṇya, where one can skillfully cultivate contentment.
This refers to those of stainless nature who are born among the gods of the Heaven of Satisfaction (*Tuṣita*) after emerging from the *araṇya*. The first phrase establishes the definition;
one should know that the three characters for *araṇya* encompass both the phenomenal and the principial dimensions.

If explained in terms of the phenomenal, it means being removed from human settlements and dwelling in seclusion within deep mountains and secluded valleys—a place free from all clamor and distraction, untainted by the realms of the five desires.
This is the araṇya of phenomena (*vastu-araṇya*). However, once the environment has become tranquil, the mind also becomes at ease;

delusive thoughts do not arise, and alertness and stillness mutually guide one another, like the bright moon in a clear pool. This is the araṇya of principle (*tattva-araṇya*). Therefore, principle lacks the assistance of phenomena and is difficult to perfect;
phenomena lack the completion of principle and are of no benefit. When principle and phenomena support each other, the mind and its objects are both tranquil. This is...

This is the true *araṇya*. The following sections are all modeled after this. One who is "skillfully able to practice" is so called because they are both "skillful" (*kuśala*) and "capable" (*śakya*), being fully equipped with both the phenomenal facts and their underlying principles.
Regarding the "fourfold absence of... and below: because both mind and objects are quiescent, this is truly stainless; this is truly peace and bliss.
"Contentment" (*saṃtuṣṭi*) is a flowery expression for Tuṣita. It refers to the state where both mind and objects are empty;

this is contentment (one should know that the Buddha-dharma consists of living words, and thus there is nothing that cannot be used even through inverted or unconventional means). If one says, "It is an araṇya, well-suited for cultivation," these words function as terms pointing toward the Dharma, spoken in reference to the physical *araṇya*.

Whether it be among mountains or beneath trees—any place of profound stillness is an *araṇya*. If one says, "A place of peace and bliss is an *araṇya*," this is spoken according to principle. This means that because one is able to cultivate the four stainless natures (*catur-vimala-dhātu*), greed and defilement come to rest, and thus the single nature becomes peaceful.

"Leisurely. Nature itself is the *araṇya*. This term should be viewed as it stands. Whenever reading the works of the high sages, one must not allow the literal phrasing to obstruct the underlying meaning. These [sections] comprise twenty-one parts in total. As this section is thus, so it is with all the others.
This is an araṇya, a place where one attains liberation from all afflictions (*kleśa*). This is an araṇya, a place endowed with extensive learning and wisdom.
This refers to attaining liberation by being free from afflictions; both extensive learning and wisdom arise from the state where both mind and objects are simultaneously stilled.
It is attained.
This is an araṇya, the place for subduing and severing the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations. This is an araṇya, the place where one can enter the three gates of liberation.
This refers to the fact that severing afflictions and entering liberation both arise from the *araṇya* (hermitage). The two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) are to be understood as before.

"Subduing" (*vinaya*) means restraining and halting the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) so that it does not proceed; "severing" (*prahāṇa*) means the eternal extinction of the seeds of the two types of grasping (*dvaya-grāha*).

The three liberations (*vimokṣa*) are also to be understood as explained previously. Because both mind and objects are tranquil, liberation is easily attained; therefore, it is said that one "is able to enter."
This is an araṇya, where one is well able to realize the eight liberations. This is an araṇya, where one is well able to contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination.
This is an araṇya, where one is well able to sever the obstacles of karma.

This refers to the cultivation of the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*); that which is attained is called the eight emancipations (*aṣṭa-vimukti*). The twelve links of dependent origination are the same as before.
The karma produced by the seven branches of body and speech is called an "obstruction of karma" (*karmāvaraṇa*) because it can hinder pure conduct.

These three matters above are all attained through the emptiness and stillness of mind and境 (object). Therefore, it is said that one is "skillful. Since all [these qualities] emerge from this, it is said:
This is a dwelling place;
this is an araṇya. This is an araṇya where one can attain the first fruit, the stage of stream-entry.
This is an araṇya where one can attain the second fruit, the stage of once-returning. This is an araṇya where one can attain the third fruit, the stage of non-returning. This is an araṇya.
The place where one attains the fourth fruit, Arhatship, is an araṇya. The place where one realizes the fruit of a Pratyekabuddha is also an araṇya.
This refers to the fact that those who attain the four fruits as well as the Pratyekabuddhas all emerge from within the araṇya.

The first fruit is called *srotāpanna* in Sanskrit; in the Han language, it is called "entering the stream" (*yuliu*). "Entering" (*yu*) means to participate; "stream" (*liu*) refers to the category or flow. This refers to the first [fruit] of the two vehicles.
By severing the delusions of views, one enters the stream of the noble ones; all of this is realized through practice within the *araṇya* (forest hermitage).

Therefore, the *araṇya* is pointed out as the place where the fruits [of the path] are attained. Regarding the second fruit, called "Once-returner" (*sakṛdāgāmin*): in Sanskrit it is *srotāpanna*, and in Chinese it is translated as "once-returner.
This means that having severed the delusions among humans, one returns only once more. This is because the delusions of views were already eliminated at the first fruit.

It has already been severed. The afflictions of thought (*cintā-kleśa*) are innate, subtle afflictions that are severed during the stage of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*); they are also called "afflictions of cultivation" (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).

However, because these afflictions are most subtle, they cannot be severed all at once in a single lifetime; therefore, they are divided into nine grades each according to the nine levels (*navabhūmi*) of the three realms (*tridhātu*), and are severed sequentially.
Only the nine grades of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are most powerful and difficult to sever, as each successive higher grade...

The superior grade of the superior class (adhimātra-adhimātra) moistens two births alone; therefore, it can only be severed after two rounds of coming and going between the heavens and the human realm.
The superior-middle and superior-inferior grades together moisten two births, and likewise require two rounds of coming and going before they can be severed.
The middle-superior grade moistens one birth alone, and is severed by a single round of coming and going. The middle-middle and middle-inferior grades together moisten one [birth].

Furthermore, one must undergo one more birth and one more round of coming and going before being able to sever it. When the severance reaches five grades, one is called a candidate for the second fruit (*dvitīyaphala-pratipannaka*).

When all six grades are severed, this is named the second fruit, the *Sakṛdāgāmi-phala*. Generally speaking, after completing six rounds in the heavens and six rounds among humans, and having exhausted the first six grades of the afflictions of thought (*kāmāsrava*), the second fruit is finally accomplished. This is because, having already realized the second fruit, and furthermore—
One is called a "Once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin) because the final three grades of afflictions of the desire realm still remain.

Since one grade of the upper level alone moistens half a lifetime, while the middle and lower grades of the lower level together moisten the other half, one returns once more to the human realm to sever them;
thus, one is named a Once-returner. The third is the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi); in Sanskrit, it is *anāgāmin*.

"Anāgāmin" (含). In the Han language, this means "Non-returner. Because one was previously at the stage of the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*), having severed the final three grades of afflictions but not yet exhausted all residual *saṃskāra*-afflictions, one is termed a "candidate for the third fruit" (*trtīyaphalapratipannaka*).
Only when these three grades are completely exhausted does one realize the third fruit; thus, one is named a "Non-returner" (*anāgāmin*).

This is because, after the previous seven rounds of coming and going, one has completely severed the nine grades of *saṃskāra*-afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); since the causes of the desire realm have perished, one will no longer [return].
Because they do not return to take birth in the desire realm, they are called "Non-returners" (Anāgāmin).

Residing in the four dhyānas among the five classes of Non-returner heavens, they sever the seventy-two grades of afflictions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) pertaining to the upper realms—the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya*).

If they have severed up to seventy-one grades, they are designated as "Arhat-candidates" (Arhattva-pratipannaka); when the seventy-two grades are completely exhausted, they realize the fruit of Arhatship.

This refers to the fruit. As for the Pratyekabuddha fruit, having already severed both *darśana-heya* (afflictions of views) and *bhāvanā-heya* (afflictions of thought), they further erode the residual habits (*vāsanā*).
Compared to Bodhisattvas, they fall short; compared to Arhats, their faculties are sharp. This is because Arhats still possess residual habits, whereas Pratyekabuddhas do not, and are thus sharp.
These four fruits and the state of a Pratyekabuddha, though realized through human effort, are not easily attained except in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*).

Thus, the *araṇya* (hermitage) is the place from which they emerge. Question: If those who have attained the second fruit still return once more to the human realm to sever their afflictions (*kleśa*), it is appropriate for them to reside in an *araṇya*.
However, as for those who have attained the third fruit, they abide in the fourth dhyāna and do not return to the human realm;

how then can one speak of an *araṇya* for them? Answer: There are two meanings. First, regarding the tracing of the current back to its source: although they dwell in the heavens of dhyāna, [they remain connected to the source].
First, it is because one sets out from the *araṇya* (hermitage). Second, *araṇya* is translated as "place of tranquility.

Once one has entered the four dhyānas, where both suffering and pleasure have vanished, that is truly a place of tranquility. According to the former interpretation, it possesses both the principle (*li*) and phenomena (*shi*).
The emptiness-principle realized by those on the four paths and four fruits, as well as by the *pratyekabuddhas*, serves as the basis for wisdom.

All are called *araṇya*. (The above seven rounds of coming and going for severing delusions is explained according to those of ordinary, dull faculties. If one were a great *āyuṣmat* during the Buddha’s lifetime who suddenly realized the fruit of *arhatship* in a single lifetime, they would not fall under this category.

Furthermore, the reason there must be seven rounds between the heavens and the human realm is that the suffering in the human world is heavy and cannot be severed all at once in a single round; because the heavens serve as a place of rest, one severs [delusions] gradually through these comings and goings.

Such is the dullness of the faculty of vision. (Question: This sutra is a teaching of sudden enlightenment (*tun-jiao*). Why does it clarify this gradual cultivation? Answer: This does not discuss sudden versus gradual; it simply states that the *āraṇya* is the source from which the realization of the Way emerges.)
This is the araṇya, the place where what was to be done has been accomplished and mastery is attained. This is the araṇya, the place where all heavy burdens are cast off and lightness is attained.
This is the araṇya, the place where the suchness of the two kinds of emptiness is realized.
These three kinds of merit all arise from the *araṇya* (forest hermitage). First, when the four fruits have not yet been attained, one has "not yet accomplished what was to be done" (*akṛtakṛtya*).
When the four fruits are achieved, truth is exhausted and delusions are ended; this is called "having already accomplished what was to be done" (*kṛtakṛtya*).

One who has attained mastery is one for whom view-delusions and thought-delusions (*dṛṣṭi- and kleśa-saṃyojana*) are already empty, who has already departed from birth and death (*saṃsāra*), and who will not undergo further existence. Furthermore, [the text continues with] the three...
He clarifies the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Mountains and walls do not obstruct him; wherever he goes follows his will, and thus he is said to be "sovereign" (*vaśitā*).

Next, what is called the "heavy burden" is precisely birth and death (*saṃsāra*). "Various" means not only the *pariccheda* (segmented) form of existence, but also includes the *pariṇāma* (transformative) form.

"Light ease" is *nirvāṇa*. This means that because the heavy burden has already been cast off, it is called "light"; because one no longer undergoes oppression, it is called "ease. Furthermore, next it says:

The "two emptinesses" refer to the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena (*pudgala-śūnyatā* and *dharma-śūnyatā*). Since the two attachments to persons and phenomena are empty, the principle realized is non-deceptive and unchanging;
therefore, it is called *tathatā* (suchness). Regarding these three types [of practice], the *araṇya* (hermitage) is likewise the place where they are accomplished, attained, and realized.
This is an araṇya, a place where one can cultivate immeasurable great loving-kindness. This is an araṇya, a place where one cultivates and realizes immeasurable great compassion.

They are well able to cultivate the immeasurable state of equanimity (*upekṣā*).
The explanation and vision are as in the preceding text; the locations are also the same as before.
This is an araṇya, a place capable of giving rise to the bodhicitta. This is an araṇya where Bodhisattvas practice until they reach the tenth [stage].
The stage of faith is an araṇya. Furthermore, progressing and practicing until reaching the stage of the ten abodes (daśabhūmi) is an araṇya.
Progressively cultivating further until reaching the stage of the ten practices (daśacaryā) is an araṇya. Progressively practicing the ten dedications (daśapariṇāmanā) is an araṇya.
This section, from the arousal of the bodhicitta to the dedication of merit, consists of five stages of meritorious practice, all of which emerge from the *araṇya* (hermitage).
When a Bodhisattva’s cultivation reaches the stage of the Ten Faiths, it is because the Bodhisattva is a recipient of the Mahāyāna.
One practices the conduct of the Mahāyāna. Faith and the other [virtues] constitute the stages of the Mahāyāna.

"Faith" refers to hearing the teaching that the mind itself is the Buddha, and then deeply accepting it with joyful aspiration, resolving one's will without doubt. It is the foremost of the three levels of the Ordinary Beings (*pṛthagjana*) and the precursor to all practices;
therefore, it is explained first. However, those who wish to proceed from the stream of ordinary beings and enter the stages of the sages must rely upon faith.

It serves as the precursor, beginning with the mind of faith and culminating in the mind of aspiration; these collectively constitute the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), acting as the skillful means for the true cultivation of a Bodhisattva.

As for advancing in cultivation to reach the stage of the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*): previously there was only faith without yet having entered [the stages], whereas here, one cultivates based on faith and enters based on that cultivation.
This "abiding" (*vihāra*) refers to the realization of the principle through its differentiation; it is the wisdom that relies upon the principle.
It is like a person’s residence. "Advancing" (*jin*) refers to the diligence of augmentation; "cultivation" (*xiu*) refers to the practice of traversing the objective realm;

"reaching" (*dao*) refers to the attainment resulting from such effort. The "ten" refers to the Bodhisattva’s progressive cultivation according to the stages (*bhūmi*), taking initial awakening (*ādikṣānti*) as the foundation.

Entering by way of faith, one is then able to abide therein. Beginning from the first arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*) and culminating in the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), this constitutes the sequential order.

The ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). Each subsequent stage is superior to the preceding one; collectively, they constitute the Ten Abodes (*daśavihāra*). Regarding "progressively cultivating and increasing" (*krama-vṛddhi*): "progressing" (*krama*) refers to moving from the former to the latter;
"advancing" (*vṛtti*) refers to proceeding in successive order; "cultivating and increasing" (*vṛddhi*) refers to practicing again and again. As for the "ten practices" (*daśacaryā*):
because the merit of the progressive cultivation following the ten abodes has reached fulfillment, one becomes a child of the Buddha, attains one's own benefit, and [benefits others].
His practice was not yet perfected; therefore, he has reached this stage where he extensively performs acts of benefit, acting in accordance with sentient beings to cause them joy.
Because it consists purely of benefiting others, it is called the "stage of practice" (caryā-bhūmi). However, practice has degrees of depth, beginning from the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).

Ultimately reaching the ultimate reality. There are ten types of dharmas for benefiting others; therefore, they are called the "Ten Practices" (*daśa-caryā*). Regarding the "Ten Dedications" (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*):

"dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*) means turning back and directing toward. Arousing the mind of great compassion to rescue and deliver sentient beings, one turns the merit of the Ten Practices and directs it toward three points:
first, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), which is that which is realized; second, unsurpassed enlightenment...

This is what is sought. Third, all sentient beings are those to be delivered. By means of the mind that can dedicate and the virtuous deeds to be dedicated, one directs them toward those myriad classes of beings, fulfilling the Brahma-conduct and entering equally into the Dharma-realm.

Because of these ten successive stages, they are called the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*). Thus, from the initial generation of the bodhicitta at the beginning up to the dedication at the end, all are attributed to this merit.
It is within the araṇya that one cultivates and realizes what is to be attained. Nevertheless, one’s own mind reflects and responds, never losing sight of the two aspects of principle and phenomena.
This araṇya is a place where one can skillfully cultivate the four roots of goodness; this araṇya is where one practices the six perfections.
The place of the pāramitās is an araṇya. The place for practicing from the first bhūmi to the tenth bhūmi is an araṇya.
The place where one realizes the purification of the six sense faculties is an araṇya.
These four kinds of merit all arise from the *araṇya*. The "four roots of goodness" (*catur-kuśalamūla*) refer to the four stages of application (*catasraḥ prayogabhūmayaḥ*);

that is to say, the goodness of the stage of application serves as the root for entering the [bodhisattva] grounds (*bhūmi*). The six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) and so forth may be understood accordingly. Regarding "from the first ground to the tenth ground":
this refers to the single moment of mental correspondence (*ekakṣaṇa-samprayukta*) at the very first stage prior to the grounds, wherein [all afflictions] are completely severed.
By discerning the two obstacles and attaining the realization of the all-pervading *tathatā* (suchness), one enters the first stage (*bhūmi*).
That which is called a "stage" is so named because all Buddha-dharmas arise in dependence upon the principle realized by the Bodhisattva, just as the earth produces all things.

Furthermore, there are gradations of depth, beginning with the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā*) and culminating in the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), collectively constituting the ten stages. [The six faculties...]
"Purity" refers to the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind, each being free from false seeing, false hearing, and so forth, and thus not defiled by delusive taints.
That is to say, with the very eyes born of one's parents, one perceives clearly all forms within the trichiliocosm;
the ears can universally hear all sounds within the trichiliocosm; and even the mind can pervasively [cognize all objects].
One knows the dharmas of the trichiliocosm; being without defilement and without obstruction, it is called "pure.
This is also because it is accomplished within the *araṇya* of both principle and phenomena.
This is an araṇya, a place well-suited for realizing the supernormal power of the divine eye.

This is an araṇya, where one attains the supernormal power of the divine ear, the knowledge of past lives, the clear vision of birth and death, the supernormal power of miraculous transformations, and the knowledge of others' minds—such are the places of supernormal powers found in this araṇya.
Regarding the section on "possessing shame and remorse":

these six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the merit of shame and remorse all arise from the forest hermitage (*araṇya*). The explanation of the six supernormal powers is found in the preceding text.

The knowledge of past abodes (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*) is the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtyabhijñā*). The clear knowledge of birth and death (*cyutyupapādajñāna*) is the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayābhijñā*).

It refers to the clear knowledge attained when the outflows (*āsrava*) of birth and death have been exhausted; this is the "clear knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows" (*āsravakṣaya-vidyā*), which is like the "knowledge of non-arising.

The "supernormal power of the physical realm" (*ṛddhi-viṣaya*) refers to skillful arts, such as water emerging from the upper part of the body and fire from the lower part, and the mastery of the eighteen kinds of supernatural transformations.
The "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracitta-jñāna*) refers to perceiving the intentions and thoughts of others without the need for verbal communication.
To litigate means to be able to discern clearly. Shame and remorse are as previously described. Such merits likewise arise from the araṇya;
this araṇya is the place of non-negligence; this araṇya is the place for cultivating the five faculties.

These two types of merit are likewise not outside of this. Non-heedlessness (*apramāda*) has the nature of diligence in the three types of action, consisting of the prevention of evil and the cultivation of good regarding what is to be practiced and abandoned;
its function is to counteract heedlessness and to bring to completion all mundane and supramundane wholesome deeds.
The five faculties (*pañcendriya*) are the five factors of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom; they serve as the entry point to the Path.
Because they are the root, they are called the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).

This is the araṇya, the place where one realizes immeasurable and boundless samādhis. This is the araṇya, the place where one can attain the gates of dhāraṇī as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and realize mastery.
These two kinds of merit also arise from this. The essence of samādhi is the same, yet its applications differ;
thus, its designations are manifold and infinite. Regarding the term "dhāraṇī" as a "gate," it has a pervasive meaning:
because it can both retain and release. To retain it is for the myriad dharmas to become one; to release it is for the one to become the myriad dharmas. Thus, essence and function are both present.
Practice. Because phenomena and principle are unimpeded, it is called "sovereign freedom.
This is araṇya. To realize the patience of non-arising—this is araṇya. It is the place where one forever transcends the triple world and severs birth and death.
This is the araṇya. One attains non-retrogression;

these three kinds of merit all arise from the araṇya. Regarding the dharma that is without birth and without cessation, to perceive the nature of mind through a single moment of serene awakening is called "enlightenment.
Like a person drinking water, knowing for oneself whether it is cold or warm is called "patience" (kṣānti). This is non-retrogression.
This refers to advancing upon the Path with such vigor and tirelessness that even if a thousand sages called for one’s return, one would not turn back;
it is the resolve that shall certainly never waver. If interpreted as the three types of non-retrogression, they are also explained as before.
This is an araṇya: where all maras and enemies are subdued, karmic obstructions are eliminated, and one beholds the Buddha and hears the Dharma—such a place is an araṇya;
where one attains the supreme, unshared dharma-gate of the Buddhas.
This section concerns the subduing of Māra and the attainment of the supreme dharma, all of which occurs within the *araṇya* (hermitage). An ancient master said:
"When the Way is one chi high, Māra is ten chi high. The Sanskrit term *māra* translates here as "the slayer," meaning that which injures and kills the *dharmakāya*.

It is that which harms the life-force of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*). "All" refers to the demon of afflictions (*kleśamāra*), the demon of death (*mṛtyumāra*), the celestial demon (*devaputramāra*), and the demon of the five aggregates (*skandhamāra*).
These various demons have been fundamental enemies since beginningless time; however, it is the celestial demon alone that specifically harms those who cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Whether entering the heart and viscera or attaching itself to others, it disturbs and confuses the practitioner. This is stated because of its great [power].

To eliminate [obstacles] through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-jñāna-bala*) is called "subduing. The seven branches of body and speech consist of outflow-tainted (*sāsrava*) karma that can obstruct the Noble Path;

therefore, they are called "karmic obstacles" (*karmāvaraṇa*). Now that these have been dissolved and eliminated, there is no longer any obstruction, and thus one is able to personally behold the Buddhas and hear their teachings.
Mount Lanruo is the place where this occurs. Regarding the term "unshared" (*asādhāraṇa*), it means not being common [to others].
This is shared by the two vehicles, yet it is realized solely by the Buddha; this is the supreme dharma-gate.
This is because, were it not for the physical *araṇya*, one would be disturbed by the five desires and unable to subdue Māra or eliminate hindrances.
That which can subdue and eliminate is precisely the power of concentration, wisdom, and knowledge; furthermore, this constitutes the *araṇya* of principle.
This is an araṇya, a place for cultivating the purity of the aggregate of ethical discipline.
This is an araṇya, a place for giving birth to untainted samādhi. This is an araṇya, a place capable of generating wisdom that realizes liberation. This is an araṇya.
This is the place where the knowledge and vision of liberation can arise.

This section clarifies the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcāṅga-dharmakāya*), which likewise emerges from the forest hermitage (*araṇya*). The aggregate of ethical discipline (*śīlaskandha*) is the body of morality (*śīlakāya*).

"Aggregate" (*skandha*) has the meaning of accumulation; it refers to the accumulation of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, which constitute the body of a sentient being.
When a person is able to maintain the precepts, this is itself cultivation. Because body and mind are free from transgression, it is called "purity.
Samādhi is an alternative name for meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Not clinging to the marks of concentration is termed "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*); this is the "body of concentration.
It is accomplished in a secluded and tranquil place, hence it is said to be "born. Prajñā refers to wisdom; this is the "body of wisdom. Liberation depends upon—
Precepts, concentration, and wisdom—being free from all fetters and embodying sovereignty—is the body of liberation (*vimukti-kāya*).

As for the "knowledge and vision of liberation" (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*), it means that through the attainment of liberation, all delusive thoughts are empty; therein, the true illumination of fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is able to know and see.
This is the body of knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-kāya*). These fivefold dharma-bodies (*pañca-dharma-kāya*) are the transformation of the five [aggregates].

One who studies that which is constituted by the aggregates (*skandha*) should understand this: for while the five aggregates certainly carry the meaning of "accumulation," the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*) likewise carries the meaning of "accumulation.

That is to say, it is the body formed by the coalescence of these five: ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*prajñā*), liberation (*vimukti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana*).
This means that if sentient beings can maintain ethical discipline, cultivate concentration and wisdom, and practice all forms of purity...
Karma can thus transform this five-aggregate physical body (*pañca-skandha-rūpa-kāya*) into the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharma-kāya*).
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "By the cessation of this form (*rūpa*), one attains the eternal form; and so it is for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

First, the aggregate of form is transformed into the aggregate of morality (*śīla-skandha*). (The aggregate of form refers to the name for the accumulation of the various faculties: the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body. Morality is able to prevent misconduct of the three [doors of body, speech, and mind]...)

The four dharmas: First, if sentient beings can maintain the precepts with firm resolve, they attain purity of body and the essence of the precepts (*śīla-skandha*) is perfected; being without "holding" or "violating," this is the transformation of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) into the body of precepts.

Second, the transformation of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) into the body of concentration (*samādhi-skandha*). As for the aggregate of sensation, it is the name for the accumulation of the six consciousnesses as they experience the six sense objects. Concentration refers to right concentration;

that is, if sentient beings can cultivate untainted meditative absorption (*anāsrava-dhyāna*), then the faculties and objects will be extinguished and purified, and one will be free from all distraction. This is the transformation of the aggregate of sensation into the body of concentration. Third, the transformation of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) into the body of wisdom (*prajñā-skandha*). [As for the aggregate of perception...]

"Zhe" (the one who) refers to the name for the accumulation of the six sense objects through the conceptualization of the mental consciousness. "Hui" (wisdom) refers to transcendent wisdom (*prajñā*). This means that if sentient beings can awaken to the fact that all deluded thoughts are merely false and subject to arising and ceasing, then the ground of the mind will become clear and pure, perceiving all things with unobstructed illumination.

This is the transformation of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) into the body of wisdom (*prajñā-kāya*). Fourth, the transformation of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) into the body of liberation (*vimukti-kāya*).

(The aggregate of formations is a name for the accumulation of various karmic actions. Because of these formative actions, there is bondage. Liberation has the meaning of sovereignty; it means that if sentient beings do not perform various karmas, they will be freed from their bondage and attain sovereignty. This is called the transformation of the aggregate of formations into the body of liberation.

Fifth, the transformation of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) into the body of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-kāya*). (The aggregate of consciousness is a name for the harmonious accumulation [of cognitions]. Liberation...)

Regarding "knowledge and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*): "knowledge" refers to knowing through wisdom; "vision" refers to seeing with the eye. This is the eye of the wisdom of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*), which illuminates with sovereign clarity. That is to say, if sentient beings can clearly illuminate and understand that the mind of consciousness is entirely false and discriminative, then the eye of the wisdom of non-arising will be clearly manifest with sovereign mastery.

This is because the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) has been transformed into the body of liberation-knowledge and vision. This explanation is from the *Daming sanzang fashu* (The Three Storehouses of Dharma Numbers of the Great Illumination).

Herein, the definition of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) differs from other sutras; other sutras all state that the aggregate of formations consists of the flux of arising and ceasing.
"Meaning" (*artha*). This is designated by the term "activity" (*abhisamskāra*). For "transmigration" (*saṃsāra*) carries the sense of movement, and "activity" likewise carries the sense of movement.
Furthermore, transmigration pertains to the internal functioning [of consciousness], whereas activity pertains to external operation.
This is araṇya; therein one attains the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment. This is araṇya; therein one is able to attain liberation from the twelve bases of cognition (*āyatana*).
This is araṇya; therein one is forever detached from the eighteen realms of existence (*dhātu*) that are subject to outflows (*sāsrava*).
This section concerns the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) and the merits of the three categories; it likewise emerges from the midst of the concise and the detailed.
Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, their explanation may be found in the preceding text. As for "liberation through the twelve bases" (*dvādaśāyatana-vimukti*):

the "twelve" refers to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) and the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*). They are called "bases" (*āyatana*) because each has its own location. "Bases" (*āyatana*) means that the sense organs can enter into the sense objects and proceed toward them.

"Object" (*viṣaya*) means that which serves as the condition for consciousness. "Dust" (*rajas*) also refers to entering the sense-faculties; it carries the meaning of drawing forth consciousness. Regarding "liberation":

this is said in contrast to sentient beings who are bound by entanglements. It means that if sentient beings can forget objects and exhaust the faculties—such that objects are no longer engaged and the faculties have nothing with which to pair—then both are liberated.
As for the "eighteen realms" (*dhātu*): a "realm" (*dhātu*) signifies a distinct boundary or limit. This is because of sentient beings...

Because both mind and form are deluded, form is opened into ten realms and mind is opened into eight realms, so that one may contemplate these two dharmas—form and mind—and see that they both arise from false causes and conditions.
These cause sentient beings to give rise to afflictions and create karma, revolving through birth and death.
If one realizes that these false conditions have no substantial reality and are devoid of names and characteristics, then...

One is not deluded by the defilements of affliction, nor is one bound by birth and death; all this is attributed to the power of the *araṇya* (hermitage), for it is the place where such attainments are possible.

(Regarding the classification of form into ten realms: this refers to the five faculties—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and body—and the five objects—form, sound, odor, taste, and touch—all of which belong to the category of form-dharmas.)

Therefore, they are opened up to make ten. To "open the mind" to make eight refers to eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the mind-faculty (*manas*), and mental objects (*dharmadhātu*); as these all belong to the mind, the mind is opened up to constitute the eight elements (*dhātus*).

Some say that mental objects belong to form (*rūpa*), asserting that they are the falling-away of the five sensory objects, appearing as reflected images that serve as the objects of mental consciousness; because they are invisible yet possess resistance (*sapratigha*), they belong to the category of form-dharmas. Others say that mental objects have no substantial reality and their essence is itself the mind;

therefore, they belong to the category of mind-dharmas. Still others say that half belong to form and half belong to the mind; one should rather say that ten parts are half-form and seven and a half parts are half-mind, for only then would the meaning be fully exhausted. Generally speaking, the three—the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses—total eighteen when combined in sets of six, each having its own distinct boundary.
This is merely because the functions of the various realms are not the same. As for what is called "outflow" (*āsrava*): it refers to the deluded state of ordinary beings.
Being constantly partitioned, they are unable to achieve integration; thus, they encounter obstructions at every turn and fall into the cycle of birth and death. Therefore, it is named "with outflow.

If a person turns back from delusion to return to the truth, their thoughts will instantly transform into supreme awakening. Hence, it is said that they are "permanently free from outflows. This concludes the summary.
As before, this is an araṇya, a place for the subtle observation of the eighteen kinds of emptiness. This is an araṇya, a place that accommodates the emptiness of all dharmas.
This is an araṇya, a place where the ten wholesome dharmas increase and arise.
This clarifies that the ten wholesome paths of action are all empty, and they likewise arise from the *araṇya* (hermitage). The explanation of the eighteen emptinesses is found in the preceding text.
"Observation" (*vipaśyanā*) refers to the wisdom of clear illumination; "subtle and wondrous" (*sūkṣma-adbhuta*) is a designation for the ultimate.

If it were not for subtle and wondrous observation, how could one thoroughly awaken to the principle of emptiness? Regarding "to contain and receive": the emptiness of all phenomena is precisely the eighteen emptinesses. However...
The two characters "accepting and containing" (*rongshou*) differ from those mentioned previously. The former, "observation," refers to the wisdom of *ādikṣānti* (initial awakening);
these, "accepting and containing," refer to the principle of *mūlapratyavekṣā* (fundamental awakening).

Because the measure of fundamental awakening is all-pervasive and its essence is universally omnipresent, all principles of emptiness return to fundamental awakening—like water merging with water, or space merging with space. As the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* says: "Observe..."

Phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are fundamentally illusory; they are the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). Observing their nature (*svabhāva*) as fundamentally real is the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Therefore, original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*) embraces them, unifying them into a single principle. Regarding the ten wholesome dharmas (*daśakuśala-dharma*): "wholesome" (*kuśala*) carries the meaning of being in accord with principle.

This means that practicing these ten dharmas all accords with principle, and thus they are called "wholesome. Furthermore, there are two types: first, cessation (*saṃvara*); second, cultivation (*caryā*). Cessation...
Ceasing one’s own evil, not afflicting others, practicing superior virtues, and benefiting all beings.

The ten [precepts] are: first, refraining from killing (not harming any living being; this is the virtue of abstaining from killing. Since one does not kill, one should practice the virtue of releasing captive creatures; this is the foremost virtue). Second, refraining from stealing (meaning not to pilfer the property of others;

this is the virtue of abstaining from theft. Since one does not steal, one should practice the virtue of giving). Third, refraining from sexual misconduct (meaning that sexual desire is an improper action; if one does not engage in it...)

1. Abstinence from sexual misconduct: This is the virtue of ceasing sexual misconduct. Since one does not engage in illicit sex, one should practice the virtue of pure *brahmacarya*. (2. Abstinence from false speech: This means not uttering empty words to deceive and delude others; it is the virtue of ceasing false speech.

Since one does not speak falsely, one should practice the virtue of truthful speech, which is the foremost virtue among the actions of speech. 3. Abstinence from divisive speech: This means not speaking of this person’s virtues and that person’s faults to both sides to incite strife;

it is the virtue of ceasing divisive speech. Since one does not engage in divisive speech, one should practice the virtue of speech that promotes harmony. 4. Abstinence from harsh speech: This means not uttering coarse or wicked...

1. To refrain from reviling others is the virtue of ceasing harsh speech (*pāruṣya*). Since one does not engage in harsh speech, one should practice the virtue of gentle and soft words. 2. To refrain from frivolous chatter (*saṃbhinnapralāpa*) means not to adorn speech with flowery rhetoric merely to please others;

this is the virtue of ceasing frivolous chatter. Since one does not engage in frivolous chatter, one should practice the virtue of straightforward and truthful speech. 3. To refrain from covetousness (*abhidhyā*) means not to be greedily attached to sensual desires and external objects;

this is the virtue of ceasing covetousness. Since one does not harbor covetous desires, one should practice the virtue of pure celibacy (*brahmacarya*). 4. To refrain from malice (*vyāpāda*) means not to give rise to a mind of anger or resentment.

To feel resentment toward others is precisely the opposite of the virtue of ceasing anger; since one does not harbor malice, one should practice the virtues of loving-kindness and patience. Tenth is the absence of wrong views (mithyādṛṣṭi): this means not holding biased or heterodox views, nor persisting in taking what is false to be true.

This is precisely the goodness of ceasing wrong views. Since one no longer holds wrong views, one should practice the goodness of right faith and right view. Regarding these three matters, the conclusion is the same as before.
This is an araṇya, a place where the bodhicitta increases and becomes firm. This is an araṇya, a place praised by the Buddhas of the three times.
This is an araṇya, a place thus revered and praised by all Bodhisattvas.
This possesses three kinds of merit, which likewise arise from it. Regarding the term "firm" (*dṛḍha*) for the bodhicitta:
it refers to the resolve to attain Buddhahood being non-retrogressive. Regarding "increasing" (*vṛddhi*): it means becoming ever more excellent as time passes.

Because of this, one does not become discouraged over long periods, and even when encountering adverse conditions, one becomes ever more renewed. Once the mind is firm, enlightenment is easily attained. (3)
In this world below, it is only in the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka) that one can sever all evils and attain all virtues from cause to fruition;
thus, the merit is attributed to the dwelling place. This is why all Buddhas praise it and Bodhisattvas revere it.
This is an araṇya where Vipaśyin Buddha attained enlightenment beneath a nyagrodha tree.
This is an araṇya where Śikhin Tathāgata attained enlightenment beneath a śirīṣa tree. This is an araṇya where Viśvabhū Tathāgata...
The place where he attained enlightenment under the Aśvattha tree is an araṇya. The place where Krakucchanda Buddha attained perfect enlightenment under the Aśoka tree is an araṇya.
The place where the Tathāgata Kanakamuni attained perfect enlightenment under the Udumbara tree is an araṇya.
The place where the Tathāgata Kāśyapa attained perfect enlightenment under the Sāla tree is an araṇya.

The Aranya. At the place where Śākyamuni Tathāgata attained enlightenment beneath the Pippala tree—this clarifies that the enlightenment of the seven Buddhas all emerged from within the aranya (wilderness/forest hermitage).

These comprise the final three Buddhas of the past *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa* (Adorned Aeon) and the first four Buddhas of the present *Bhadrakalpa* (Fortunate Aeon), totaling seven Buddhas. The first is Vipaśyin. Furthermore...
His name was Vipaśyin, which in this language means "Victorious Vision. This is a title for one who has attained true perfection and exhausted all afflictions (*kleśa*). The *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"At the completion of three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*), one encounters Vipaśyin, Dīpaṃkara, Ratnaśikhin, and finally Śākyamuni in reverse order.

Thus, at the very beginning, Śākyamuni first cultivated the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) under the Buddha Vipaśyin; therefore, Vipaśyin is honored as the foremost of the seven Buddhas. Nigrodha... [text continues].
*Tā* (or *Nyagrodha*). This is translated as "knotless tree" (*wújié shù*); in meaning, it corresponds to willow.
Although the names differ, the substance of the tree is one and the same. It was beneath this tree that the Buddha attained enlightenment. *Śikhin* means "fire. Fire can burn objects;
this serves as a metaphor for how wisdom can sever delusions. He is named after this wisdom. Furthermore, he is called "Uṣṇīṣa-dhara" (Holder of the Topknot). "Dhara" means to uphold or maintain.
"Ji" (髻) refers to the topknot (*uṣṇīṣa*). Because he holds the heart and crown of the Buddha by means of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), it is so called.
"Śirīṣa" is the *móuhūn* tree (Pterocarpus indicus) of this region; there are two varieties.

That which is named *śirīṣa* has both leaves and fruit that are large, while that named *śirī-kṣetra* has both leaves and fruit that are small. Although they differ in size, they belong to the same species. The Buddha was beneath this tree.
Because he attained the Way, he is called Viśvabhū. In full, it is Viśvabhū; in the language of China, it means "Pervasive Sovereignty over All.
This refers to the fact that his afflictions (*kleśa*) have been completely severed, such that there is nowhere he does not possess mastery. Aśibatu has not yet been translated;
however, there is *Śitavana*, or perhaps this is a different transliteration of the same Sanskrit term. This translates as "Cold Forest" (*śītavana*), referring to a cemetery. People...

Because he feared the cold, the Buddha sat beneath it and attained enlightenment. K Krakucchanda (translated as "That Which Should Be Severed") refers to one who is able to sever all afflictions (*kleśa*) so that they are forever exhausted without remainder.
This occurred during the ninth *apakarṣa-kalpa* (decreasing eon) within the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Eon).
When the human lifespan had decreased to sixty thousand years, he appeared in the world and attained Buddhahood, becoming the foremost of the thousand Buddhas.
As for the *aśoka* tree—its Sanskrit name is *aśoka*, and its Chinese name is "Sorrowless Flower Tree"—it is because the Buddha sat beneath it when he realized the Way.
Kunālamuni is translated in the language of China as "Golden Silence" (Jinjì). This means that "gold" signifies luminous manifestation, while "silence" signifies the absence of obstruction.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* also names him Kanakamuni, which in Chinese is "Golden Immortal" (Jinxian), meaning his body was golden in color.
When the human lifespan had decreased to forty thousand years, he appeared in Jambudvīpa and attained Buddhahood beneath a tree.
The one named Udumbara is here translated as "Auspicious Omen. When a Buddha is about to appear in the world, this tree first blooms;

thus one knows that a Buddha is appearing, and the Buddha responds by sitting beneath it to attain enlightenment. Kāśyapa means "Drinking Light" in the language of India, signifying that his bodily radiance is so brilliant it eclipses all other lights.
He appeared in the world and attained Buddhahood when the human lifespan had decreased to twenty thousand years.
The *śāla* tree—its Sanskrit name and its Chinese translation are both uncertain. It was beneath this tree that the Buddha sat and attained Perfect Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Śākyamuni:
in the language of India, this means "Able Benevolent One" (*nengren*) and "Tranquil Silence" (*jimo*). "Able Benevolent One" is his clan name; "Tranquil Silence" is his personal title.

Because he is tranquil and silent, he does not undergo birth and death; because he is able and benevolent, he does not abide in nirvana. With compassion and wisdom operating in tandem, he benefits sentient beings without end.
Therefore, this title was established. He appeared in the world when the human lifespan had decreased to one hundred years;
he is the fourth Buddha of the Bhadrakalpa. His tree was the Pippala, which is the Bodhi tree. The tree stood several hundred feet high, though it had been repeatedly cut down;
it still remained four or five *zhang* tall. Because the Buddha sat beneath it and attained Perfect Enlightenment, these aforementioned seven Buddhas were all—
One attains enlightenment beneath a tree; yet trees necessarily exist on mountains, and mountains and trees are all *āraṇyakas*.

Since these constitute the very foundation for the Buddhas’ attainment of the Way, I do not begrudge the prolixity of my words as I repeatedly elucidate this matter, striving to ensure that you gain true faith.
This is to manifest the single-minded compassionate heart of a Bodhisattva who delights in the practice of seclusion.
"You all should know that in the araṇya there are such immeasurable and boundless merits and benefits.
This verse summarizes these merits and benefits; the actual merits of the araṇya are truly immeasurable, and what has been set forth above is but a small portion. △ Second, the verse in praise.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Delighting in Solitary Practice spoke these verses for the great assembly:
"When a renunciant bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, what thoughts and what actions should they cultivate? All the terrors that exist in the world arise from the view of 'I' and 'mine.
If one can sever both 'I' and 'mine,' all terrors will have no basis to rely upon."
This verse concerns dwelling in an araṇya (hermitage) while maintaining contemplation to trace back to the source. The first two lines ask:
having already left the household life and residing in an araṇya, what should one contemplate in the mind, and what kind of meritorious deeds should one perform?

The third line provides the actual instruction for maintaining contemplation to trace back to the source: "all that is terrifying" refers to all afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and the retribution of suffering within the realm of outflows (*āsrava*).
Cause and effect can bind and oppress; ordinary beings, left to their own devices, neither perceive nor understand this.
When observed with noble wisdom, it is truly terrifying. This is merely an investigation; only through the fourth line can one return to the source.

"Self-view" refers to the conceptual grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*); "mine-ness" refers to the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), which is the false attachment that external phenomena exist because they belong to the self.

"Mine" (*mama*) refers to that which belongs to the self. "Arising" (*utpāda*) has the meaning of being brought forth. That is to say, fear originally does not exist; it exists only in dependence upon the self.

Therefore, it is said that all [fears] arise from the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) and the view of what belongs to the self (*mama-kāra*). "If one can... and so forth clarifies the meaning of extinguishing delusion and returning to the truth.
This means that since all fears arise from the self, they may likewise be severed by depending on the extinction of the self. If one can generate bodhicitta...
Gather the mind and uphold the resolve of a man of integrity; give rise to the illumination of wisdom, and naturally the five aggregates will all be empty and the two attachments will both cease.
Since the two views upon which they rely are thus empty, all terrors will crumble away and dissolve like ice. Therefore, there is nothing upon which to rely.
If there is a mind that can grasp at the view of a self, it will ultimately fail to accomplish the path to enlightenment. Nirvāṇa is eternally abiding and entirely without marks;
how much more so, then, regarding afflictions and non-dharmic characteristics?

This verse investigates, by way of inversion, that one should dwell in the state free from faults. The first two lines state that those who possess the view of a self will eternally fall into birth and death and be unable to achieve the Way.
The third line provides a contrastive clarification: the *nirvāṇa* realized by the Sages is, in its very essence, true and eternal;

because it is entirely devoid of arising and ceasing, it is called "permanently abiding" (*nitya*). That which is "all without marks" (*animitta*) is precisely the fundamental substance of *nirvāṇa*. It is without...

The characteristics of afflictions (*kleśa*). There is no characteristic of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), no characteristic of self (*ātman*), and no characteristic of dharmas (*dharma*). Furthermore, one must not cling to the characteristic of nirvāṇa.

If one knows that there is a nirvāṇa to be realized, this too constitutes a failure to forget the grasping at dharmas (*dharmagrāha*); such a thing is still not permissible, let alone anything inferior.

By using the superior to illustrate the inferior, it is known that afflictions are themselves the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, and are not merely the characteristic of dharmas. This encompasses [the entire meaning].
All the delusions of views and thoughts held by ordinary beings and externalists are ultimately false and utterly devoid of reality;

therefore, they are called "non-characteristics" (*alakṣaṇa*). This serves as a counter-illustration that only when all views of both the holy and the ordinary are forgotten can one hope to have a share in Bodhi.
Not clinging to any phenomena or sentient beings, with a mind free from contention, one cultivates right mindfulness. Within the four modes of deportment, one tames the mind;
one should enter the araṇya and remain ever tranquil. Able to sever the afflictions and be content in heart, one dwells in the empty and silent abode of the araṇya.
This correctly reveals that one should dwell having abandoned faults. The explanation is found in the long prose (*dīrgha-pada*).

Entering the three gates of liberation and the signless (*animitta*), dwelling in the forest hermitage (*araṇya*) free from dust and defilement, one is able to contemplate the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination, the Four Noble Truths, and the two kinds of emptiness—the true and wondrous principle. Unshaken by the eight worldly dharmas, such a Mahāsattva dwells.

"Āraṇya" (a forest hermitage). This clearly explains that one possessing virtue should dwell therein. Within an āraṇya, one is separated from all worldly defilements; the environment is naturally tranquil and the mind is empty.
Therefore, the three gates of liberation are easily entered. The "eight dharmas" are the eight winds, namely: gain, loss, defamation, [fame, praise, blame, pleasure, and pain].
Praise, fame, blame, and ill-repute; gain, loss, pleasure, and pain—these eight worldly dharmas are what the world loves and hates, and they are able to stir and agitate the human mind;

thus they are called the "eight winds. If the mind maintains its own integrity and dwells securely in the True Dharma, it will not be deluded or disturbed by love and hate, and these eight winds will be unable to shake or overturn it.
(As for the eight winds: first, the wind of gain. Whenever one obtains things that accord with one's wishes or that bring benefit to oneself, the body...)

The mind becomes joyful; this gives rise to craving. This is being fanned by the wind of gain and turned by gain. Second, the wind of loss: when one loses things that are pleasing, one feels wounded, saddened, and despondent, and is thus turned by them.

Third, the wind of disparagement: when one is slandered in secret, one becomes aware of it and gives rise to anger, and is thus turned by it. Fourth, the wind of praise: when one is praised in secret, one becomes aware of it and gives rise to joy, and is thus turned by it.

Fifth, the wind of renown: when one is praised openly, one feels joy without even realizing it, and is thus turned by it. Sixth, the wind of censure: when one is slandered openly, one feels anger without even realizing it, and is thus turned by it. Seventh, the wind of suffering: when confronted by adverse conditions, one is oppressed, and the body and mind become afflicted, and are thus turned by them.

The eight winds of pleasure refer to all favorable conditions and environments that delight the body and mind, by which one is turned. These aforementioned eight types are all things that ordinary people cannot control themselves; they unconsciously follow their movement. This constitutes the "eight winds.

Second, the two emptinesses refer to the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena. The "True and Sublime Principle" refers to the *tathatā* (Suchness) realized through these two emptinesses. Thus concludes the section below.
"Mahāsattva" is a specific title for a Bodhisattva, meaning one who is able to possess the various virtues mentioned above. This is [the definition].

For one who truly dwells in an araṇya, they are able to contemplate their own body as being like withered wood, or like foam upon water, or like an illusion or a dream. Without clinging to the two extremes, they abide in the mark of equanimity.
Such a sattva dwelling in an araṇya [contemplates] this impermanent body, bound by sinful karma, which is from the very beginning false and empty.
There is no reality to the dual grasping at self and dharmas, nor to the characteristics of faults; these cannot be found throughout the three periods of time.
One’s own body and the bodies of others are not two; all dharmas are likewise so. Contemplating the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) with precision, one finds neither coming nor going.
Thus does the Bodhisattva dwell in the araṇya: whether his body is anointed with sandalwood and praised, or cut and hacked with a blade and reviled, regarding these [he remains equanimous].
The two [opposites] are without love or hatred. Thus does a bodhisattva dwell in the araṇya.
This metaphor clarifies that there is no fear in the araṇya. The first two phrases constitute the contemplation of forgetting the body and the absence of self (*anātman*).

The third phrase provides the formal explanation: since there is no view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), there is also no view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); these two extremes refer to the two views of annihilationism and eternalism. Alternatively...
When phenomena, principle, self, dharmas, and so forth are each grasped as fixed positions and cannot be harmonized, they all belong to the two extremes.

Therefore, the two extremes are the disease, while non-attachment is the medicine. Since one does not cling to the two extremes, all phenomena and principles, self and dharmas, annihilation and permanence, and so on, are all fused into the single essence of True Suchness (Tathatā). Hence, it is called the "mark of equality. *Sattva* is...

This Bodhisattva, with this single phrase, points out the place of refuge for people. From the passage "sinful karma below" onward, it further explains that [phenomena] are like water bubbles, illusions, and dreams;
they are not only impermanent, but moreover false and without reality. Taking the two attachments as the cause, the characteristics of sin constitute the retribution.
That which cannot be apprehended in the three periods of time means that the past has already ceased, the present is not real, and the future has no form;
all are like dreams, illusions, or bubbles on water, and are therefore said to be unapprehendable. The four lines following "one's own body" explain the aforementioned characteristic of equality:
since there is no duality between self and others, this is indeed equality; by realizing that all phenomena are devoid of dualistic characteristics, [equality is established].
The clouds are also like this. "Observing with clarity" means examining according to the principle. "Dharmatā" (the nature of phenomena) refers to the essential nature of all dharmas.
"Without coming or going" means that all dharmas are suchness (*tathatā*). Now, coming and going are precisely birth and cessation;

this is because the nature of phenomena is without birth, yet sentient beings perceive it through delusion, like flowers in the sky seen by those with cataracts. To praise what exists as having an origin when it is fundamentally non-existent—how could this be?
Is there not the mark of coming and going? Thus concludes the section below. Regarding the four lines beginning with "sandalwood": this further explains the preceding meaning in depth.

Suppose there were a person who anointed the body of a Bodhisattva with sandalwood—this is a favorable condition—and though they praised him with beautiful words—this is affectionate speech—the Bodhisattva would still feel no joy. Furthermore, suppose there were an evil person who slaughtered him with a knife.
To revile and insult a bodhisattva—all such things are adverse conditions. Yet, the bodhisattva likewise does not give rise to anger.
Since they harbor neither hatred nor attachment toward these two types of people, this is because both self and phenomena are empty. This accords with the previous metaphor of the withered tree;
such a person is one who is entirely devoid of emotional sentiment. The following line concludes: a bodhisattva who is thus is a true [bodhisattva].

One who dwells in an araṇya (hermitage) should know that withered wood can serve only as a metaphor, intended merely to convey the quality of being insentient. If one were to insist that body and mind must be entirely identical to withered wood, then one would be like wood or stone, devoid of consciousness, which is termed a non-Buddhist (tīrthika).

Thus, it is known that for a great practitioner, stillness and illumination mutually guide one another, so as not to fall into one-sidedness. While on the side of stillness they may temporarily resemble withered wood, on the side of illumination, even withered wood is insufficient as a metaphor.
Having left the household life, one should dwell joyfully in an araṇya, contemplating thus day and night:

"The araṇya is the true site of practice (maṇḍala), for therein all Tathāgatas attain perfect enlightenment. The araṇya is the sublime emptiness of the True Dharma, the source from which the supramundane True Dharma arises.
The araṇya is honored by the noble ones, for it can give birth to the noble paths of the Three Vehicles. Thus is the araṇya.
The abode of the noble ones, for all sages and worthies dwell therein eternally; the palace of the Tathāgatas, for the Buddhas of the ten directions rely upon it;
the Vajrāsana, for the Buddhas of the three periods attain the Way there;
the palace of nirvāṇa, for the Tathāgatas of the three periods enter parinirvāṇa there.
The following verses extensively clarify the characteristics of phenomena as they emerge from the *araṇya*. The first two lines indicate abiding and the practice of contemplation;

the subsequent two lines reveal the fundamental source of all Buddhas. "Sublime Dharma" (*saddharma*) is precisely the mind of sentient beings, which is capable of encompassing all mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Supramundane phenomena are the unchanging essence of *tathatā* (suchness).
Worldly phenomena are precisely the functioning of True Suchness (tathatā) as it accords with conditions. Yet, while it accords with conditions, it does not change;

and while it remains unchanged, it accords with conditions. When it accords with conditions, the myriad realms are fully manifest; when it remains unchanged, not even a speck of dust can be established.
There is nothing to be praised, yet it is praised; it is forcibly praised as "wondrous. There is nothing to be named, yet it is named; it is forcibly named as "Dharma.
Therefore, it is called the "Wondrous Dharma" (*Saddharma*). As for "emptiness" (*śūnyatā*): because within the pure and true essence there is no delusion, it is called empty;
this is "true emptiness. As for "wondrous": that which responds when there is an invocation is the "great function. Such is the sublime Dharma that transcends the world.
"All that arises from the *araṇya* (forest hermitage)" means that all streams ultimately return to their source. While the *araṇya* below is the same, the benefits obtained therein differ.
Because it can bring about the Path of the Sages, it is honored by the Sages; because the Sages and Worthies dwell there constantly, it is likened to a "dwelling" (*gṛha*);
because it is the place where all Buddhas rely upon, it is called a "palace" (*kūṭāgāra*); and because all Buddhas attain the Way through it, [it is so designated].
It is like a seat; because the qualities attained therein possess the two meanings of firmness and sharpness, it is called "Vajra.
Furthermore, because all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa within it, it is also named "Nirvana."
The forest hermitage is the chamber of great loving-kindness, for bodhisattvas dwell here to cultivate loving-kindness.

The forest hermitage is the field of compassion, for the Buddhas of the three periods of time cultivated compassion there. The forest hermitage is the chamber of the six supernormal powers, for bodhisattvas sport therein.
The forest hermitage is great fearlessness, for it can sever all terrors. The forest hermitage...
The forest hermitage is samādhi, for those seeking the Way attain meditative concentration therein. The forest hermitage is a dhāraṇī, for those who uphold mantras possess spiritual power therein.
The forest hermitage is a hall of wholesome dharmas, for all wholesome dharmas increase therein.
The forest hermitage is the chamber of bodhi, for bodhisattvas practicing the Way attain patience therein.
There are sixteen phrases. In each case, the first phrase establishes the name based on its locus, while the second phrase explains the meaning based on that name.

That is to say: because one cultivates loving-kindness (*maitrī*) based upon this, it is called the "chamber of loving-kindness. Because one cultivates compassion (*karuṇā*) based upon this, it is also called the "field of compassion" (*karuṇā-kṣetra*).

Because one sports therein, it is called the "chamber of the six supernormal powers" (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); "sporting" means manifesting various modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*) without departing from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*). Because it can sever all terrors, it is called "great fearlessness" (*mahā-vaiśāradya*), which refers to the four grounds of self-confidence (*catur-vaiśāradya*).

It is called *samādhi* because practitioners rely upon it to attain meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). (Also termed "equanimous maintenance" (*samāhita*), meaning to maintain the mind with equanimity, remaining free from both dullness and agitation.

It is called *dhāraṇī* because by relying upon it, one can recite mantras and obtain supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*). (This means "total retention": to retain all phenomena and uphold immeasurable meanings. This refers to the fact that when one recites mantras in a quiet place, there will inevitably be a response;

one attains subtle mastery and spiritual penetration, such that its application is unfathomable—hence, "supernatural power. Furthermore, it is said that by relying upon it, wholesome qualities increase.
The Hall of Wholesome Dharmas (*kuśaladharma-śālā*). Furthermore, because one attains patience (*kṣānti*) by relying upon it, it is called the "Bodhi Chamber.

Indeed, a thousand merits and ten thousand virtues are all accomplished through cultivation in an araṇya; even praise cannot exhaust them. This is an explanation by way of reverse phrasing (*pratiloma-nirukti*).

If explained by way of direct phrasing (*anuloma-nirukti*), since an araṇya is like a chamber of loving-kindness (*maitrī-śālā*), one who dwells here is able to cultivate a mind of loving-kindness and so forth. It may be said thus.

One attains it through the mind (the character "attain" in "attaining patience" must ultimately signify being in accord with the Way). Now, since one takes bodhi as the chamber—bodhi meaning "awakening"—the practitioner relies upon original awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) to initiate initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*).

When initial awakening (ādi-bodhi) merges with original awakening (mūla-bodhi), one attains ultimate realization of the Way; this silent attainment within oneself is the meaning of "patience" (kṣānti).

If you wish to forever transcend the suffering of the triple world, you must cultivate and realize Bodhi and Nirvana. To benefit all sentient beings throughout the pervasive Dharma-realm, you should dwell in the Aranya, the chamber of Bodhi.
This is an exhortation to cultivate and realize [the truth] in an araṇya (hermitage). The two characters "if one desires" (*yù yù*) are words intended to alert people to arouse the bodhicitta.
As for the three realms being called "suffering," it is because they are oppressed by birth and death and the five turbidities converge therein.

If one is a courageous man of resolve, it is only logical that he should transcend them; thus, he will forever escape the cycle of suffering and no longer undergo birth and death. The following sentence...
This is the fruit for which one yearns; it is logically appropriate to cultivate and realize it. Bodhi is the virtue of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), and Nirvāṇa is the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

"Cultivation" (*xiū*) refers to investigation and inquiry; "realization" (*zhèng*) refers to actual practice. This phrase [refers to] self-benefit; "pervading everywhere" below refers to benefiting others.

The "Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*) encompasses the three lands (*tridhātu*), and "all sentient beings" encompasses both the holy and the ordinary. (The three lands exclude the *svabhāva-kṣetra*; these are all places where Buddhas benefit living beings. As the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "Just as..."

When one comes to a single place to attain enlightenment and preach the Dharma, it pervades the ten directions and the entire dharma-realm, even down to every atom and every buddha-field, where the Great Wheel of Dharma is turned.
All those of the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sainthood, as well as ordinary sentient beings, all partake in this compassionate transformation;
therefore, it is called "pervasive. The instruction to "reside below" means that if one wishes to transcend the three realms and realize bodhi—
To benefit sentient beings, it cannot be achieved through practice and realization in a *araṇya*—a place remote from dust and free from desire.
Therefore, the *araṇya* is honored as the chamber of Bodhi.
The six perfections and four means of integration that I have cultivated, I dedicate and bestow upon the three realms of existence and the four debts of gratitude,
so that both self and others may together enter the city of ambrosia and realize the true dharma-realm of suchness.

This verse refers to the dedication [of merit] toward the common realization of nirvāṇa. The six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) and the four means of integration (catvāri saṃgraha-vastūni) encompass the meaning of all myriad practices;

these dharma-gates are all the merits of a bodhisattva’s twofold benefit [of self and others]. Unable to bear merely perfecting one's own person, one further takes the dharma-gates one has cultivated and realized and dedicates them to others—this is called "giving" (dāna).
The "three realms of existence" (trai-dhātuka) refers to the causes and effects of sentient beings within the three worlds.
It does not perish; it encompasses the three realms of existence. There are two types of fourfold debts of gratitude (*catvāra upakārāḥ*). First, they are like a long journey:

namely, the debt of gratitude for the covering and supporting of Heaven and Earth, the debt of gratitude for the illuminating and presiding of the Sun and Moon, the debt of gratitude for the lands and waters provided by sovereigns and kings, and the debt of gratitude for the nurturing and raising by one's parents. Second, as stated in this very sutra:

namely, the debt of gratitude to one's parents, the debt of gratitude to sentient beings, the debt of gratitude to the king, and the debt of gratitude to the Triple Gem. This latter category comprehensively includes all others, both self and other.

The ten dharma realms and the city of ambrosia serve as metaphors for the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, wherein from the beginning there is neither birth nor extinction, just as one who drinks ambrosia does not die.

"One suchness" refers to the single, true *dharmadhātu*. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Beings of the four modes of birth and those in the nine realms of existence alike ascend the profound gate of the Flower Treasury;
those in the eight difficulties and the three miserable paths together enter the nature-ocean of Vairocana. This is what is meant.
...Indeed. △ Third, the Tathāgata’s Seal of Certification.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Who Delights in the Practice of Seclusion had expounded this Dharma for the great assembly, the Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, son of good family! For the sake of the great assembly and those who seek the Buddha-way in future ages..."

I shall analytically expound the sublime merits of the forest hermitage (āraṇyaka), which bring benefit, peace, and happiness to all sentient beings of the present and future, leading them toward the path of true and perfect awakening. You have accomplished immeasurable merit.
Even if a thousand Buddhas were to speak together, they could not exhaustively describe it.
At that time, the nineteen characters below [the phrase "the Buddha said"] are all explanatory prose added by the scribe.

Because the Bodhisattva proclaimed this on behalf of the Buddha and it perfectly accords with the Buddha’s meaning, the Buddha praised it most highly, exclaiming "Excellent! Excellent! The passage beginning with "You have... is the actual teaching.
Regarding the meaning of praise: below, it is explained in detail. This refers to the exposition of many benefits within a single *araṇya*.

First, it clarifies the nature of fear, wherein there are various states of entanglement. Next, it clarifies the *araṇya*, from the beginning to the end of attaining the fruit through freedom from fear.
Furthermore, it clarifies the practice of maintaining mindfulness to trace back to the source, by means of the self...

He saw that views are the root of terror. Furthermore, he subsequently elucidated the departure from faults and the manifestation of virtues; he took refuge in the bitter practice as the foundation for attaining Buddhahood.
He employed metaphors to reveal the Dharma and extensively explained the distinctions between the characteristics of phenomena.

He reiterated these points through verses, profoundly investigating the paths and realizations of both the holy and the ordinary, dedicating [merit] toward the three realms of existence to manifest his compassionate intent to rescue and aid others, and to repay the four debts of gratitude.
All enter the transformation of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Self and others both benefit, and all ascend together within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*);

thus it is called "extraordinary merit. To fulfill this is the Way of the True and Correct. Even if one were to write it with the ink of an ocean of volumes using a single character as the gateway to the Dharma, it could not be exhausted;
its merit is difficult to measure, for it is inexhaustible even if the realm of space were to end. Because of this virtue that assists in transformation, the merit returns to the Bodhisattva.
Therefore, even though all the Buddhas praise it together, they cannot exhaust its qualities.

△ At that time, when the multitudes throughout the four seas had obtained benefit, the Bodhisattva Jñānaprabha and the great assembly of immeasurable asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas, having heard of the most supreme merits of the araṇya, immediately attained the dhāraṇī-door of hearing and retaining. Immeasurable sentient beings gave rise to the incomparable [resolve for enlightenment].
