They resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attained non-retrogression. One thousand billion sentient beings distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Regarding those who attain the *dhāraṇī* gate of hearing and retaining: they awaken to a thousand meanings upon hearing a single word and obtain the great *saṃgraha*.

Other benefits are to be understood according to the preceding [section]. Thus concludes the first chapter, "Praise for Joyfully Departing from the World. II. Chapter Two: "Weariness with the Body," consisting of two parts:
Maitreya’s Inquiry and Contemplation. 1. Title of the Chapter.
Chapter Seven: On Loathing the Body.

This chapter is titled "Loathing the Body" because it contains the contemplation of the body’s impurity as something to be loathed, further elucidated through various metaphors that inspire profound revulsion.
Indeed, without loathing, there is no liberation; it is by means of loathing the body that one becomes detached.
The mind cultivates stainless conduct; this is also the foundation for the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*). △ Second, the scriptural text has two parts. First, the inquiry:
regarding one who correctly dwells in an araṇya, what contemplation is there concerning the body? Second, the narrative by the scribe.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground,
joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
△ Second, Maitreya’s formal inquiry:

"World-Honored One, we have now understood. There are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who, having renounced the world, dwell in *āraṇyakas*, subdue their minds, and cultivate stainless conduct. Yet, when these bodhisattvas dwell in such secluded places, they themselves [regard] this..."
Regarding the body: what contemplation should be practiced?
To regulate the three karmas and subdue the deluded mind is precisely the cultivation and realization of the araṇya;
to maintain pure conduct is precisely the gate of stainless practice. This merely restates the previous meaning. However, from here on below is the formal inquiry. This is not—
Maitreya did not know [the answer]. For the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings, he asked this question.
"A secluded place" (*śūnyāgāra*) is the elegant synonym for an *araṇya* (forest hermitage). "One's own body" refers to the present body of the practitioner.

"Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) is the wisdom that arises from meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to investigate and examine. The three characters "should be practiced" (*kartavyam*) mean that which ought to be done.

The author [asks]: "In which contemplation must one necessarily abide? What word serves as the interrogative? This is because the Tathāgata’s establishment of the teachings is skillfully adapted for beginners;

like administering medicine according to the illness, the various methods differ. Since there are many distinctions among the contemplative dharmas, such as the five *sthāpanā-citta* (five-stopping-mind) contemplations, he asks "in which contemplation.
II. The Tathāgata’s Approval and Admonition to Listen to the Explanation.
2. First, the praise and exhortation for listening with joy.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva, saying: "Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
Out of great compassion for sentient beings, you have asked the Tathāgata about the dharma-gate of the wondrous practice of entering the contemplation of noble wisdom. You should listen attentively."
"I shall now explain it for you. "Yes indeed, World-Honored One; we wish to hear it with joy.
The final two phrases, "entering the holy" (*ārya*) and so forth, describe the supreme benefit within meditative contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

"Holy" (*ārya*) means correctness. "Wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to awakening and illumination. Contemplation is that which enables entry; the holy is that which is entered; and wisdom is the function of thorough investigation within contemplation.

This is precisely initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*). "Sublime practice" (*miao-xing*) refers to the effort of cultivating contemplation; "Dharma-gate" (*dharma-mukha*) refers to the essential path for attaining realization.
This is because one achieves the Buddha-mind through the ordinary mind and reaches sagely wisdom by relying on fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
One must enter from this point; therefore, it is called the "Sublime Practice Dharma-gate. The following admonition regarding listening is easy to understand. II. The Tathāgata.
The correct exposition has five parts. First, the Buddha and his analysis have two sections.

The first is the heading for the various contemplations: "Good son, when a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya seeks anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he minutely observes within the four modes of deportment that this contaminated body consists of thirty-seven kinds of impurity."
"Filthy and loathsome; it is unlovely; it is not firm.
This serves as the general heading for all meditative contemplations. Following the four modes of deportment, it sets forth the method for seeking bodhi.
This means that during the activities of walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, movement is always appropriate and stillness is always governed by the Dharma.
Walking does not lead to negligence, and sitting does not lead to dullness or distraction. Thus, one possesses a majestic presence that inspires awe and a dignified demeanor that serves as a model;
hence, it is called "dignified deportment" (*īryāpatha*). Regarding "subtle observation," this refers precisely to the thirty-seven types of objects of contemplation that emerge from such practice.
"Thorough investigation" refers to observation; "profound" refers to subtlety. Regarding the thirty-seven types all being described as impure and foul, they are divided into three categories.
First, the twelve external characteristics, namely: hair, body hair, nails, teeth, eye discharge, tears, saliva, and spittle.

Excrement, urine, filth, and sweat constitute the first twelve [parts]. Second, the physical vessel has twelve parts, namely: skin, flesh, blood, sinews, vessels, bones, marrow, fat, grease, brain, and membranes.
Third, the internal contents have twelve parts; "contents" refers to what is contained and stored, namely: liver, gallbladder, intestines, and stomach.
The spleen, kidneys, heart, and lungs—both the raw and the cooked viscera; red phlegm and white phlegm:

these thirty-six types, together with the body as their collective characteristic, constitute the thirty-seven [impurities]. When explained through both their general and specific aspects, they total thirty-seven.

Furthermore, the nine orifices constantly flow with all manner of impurities, namely the foul substances within the internal sacs. The wise do not cherish them; they are like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows.
Therefore, it is not firm and falls into birth and death; hence it is called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*). By performing this contemplation, one gives rise to a profound sense of weary detachment.
II. The Separate Classification of Various Contemplations (29): 1. The Contemplation of the Defiled Vessel Containing Snakes.

One should contemplate this body as being like an unbaked clay vessel: though its exterior is skillfully adorned and decorated with various colors and the seven treasures of gold and silver, its interior is filled to overflowing with excrement and all manner of impurities. Carrying it upon one's shoulders, one proceeds according to the vessel.
All who see it feel love and delight, unaware that the vessel is filled with impurities and contains six black snakes constantly dwelling within it.
As soon as one snake moves, the vessel immediately breaks apart; its poisonous harm and foul stench are utterly unbearable.
This is the text of the primary analogy. "A broken vessel" refers to an earthenware pot; it serves to demonstrate its susceptibility to destruction, meaning its fundamental substance is clay.
"Adorned with the seven treasures, with gold inlaid and silver set upon the exterior" refers to its aesthetic beauty, which is a metaphor for the external ornaments of the human body.
"Filled within with filth and excrement" is a metaphor for the thirty-six kinds of impurities.
"Carrying it on both shoulders and walking according to the vessel" is a metaphor for not forgetting ego-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) and cherishing the body accordingly.
"All who see it give rise to love and joy" is a metaphor for honoring it because of its outward appearance.
"Not knowing what is inside the vessel" is a metaphor for people being deluded and failing to engage in self-examination. "The six snakes within" is a metaphor for the body and mind.
These are the six ailments. First, "a snake following its movements downward" serves as a metaphor for impermanence, which does not preserve one even from morning to evening.

"Poisonous harm, stench, and foulness" serve as metaphors for impermanence, suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impurity—things that the wise do not cherish (the six ailments of body and mind correspond naturally to these [Dharma] principles).
People of the world adorn their bodies like painted vessels filled with impurities. Greed, hatred, and delusion are called diseases of the mind;
wind, bile, and phlegm are called diseases of the body. These six internal and external diseases are capable of harming both body and mind.
Just as when those six snakes dwell within a vessel, if even one snake moves, the vessel is immediately destroyed;

so too, when even one ailment arises, the body is impermanent. Son of good family, when an ordained bodhisattva dwells in solitude and contemplates this body, it is called the first mark of the contemplation of impurity.
This applies the Dharma to the analogy. The first four lines correspond to the broken vessel; the six afflictions, such as greed, correspond to the snakes.

Thus it is said: "When the snakes move, the vessel breaks; when the disease erupts, the body perishes. The passage beginning with "Good son" concludes the name of this meditative visualization. △ Second, the contemplation on the impurity of the dead dog.
The renunciant bodhisattva, throughout the day and night, further contemplates his own body as foul, putrid, and impure, just like a dead dog. Why is this?
Because that body is likewise composed of the impurities of his parents, serving as the causal conditions for its birth.
Regarding the contemplation of the body as being like a dead dog: although human beings and other species differ in their categories, they are identical in their impurity and loathsomeness.
Why is this raised as a further inquiry and then explained? There are three meanings: first, it is foul and loathsome;
second, the dead dog is impermanent; third, that which arises through conditions is unreal. If one observes with subtle discernment, there is yet another profound meaning. If...
One develops revulsion toward the impure, arouses the mind with regard to impermanence, and realizes emptiness regarding the unreal. Then, one attains a vast and sudden awakening:
since all things arise through conditions, they lack intrinsic nature; in their very essence, they are the Truth. Thus, the impure is transformed into true purity.
Impermanence is itself true permanence. It is like when an eye disease is cured, the floating flowers [seen by the diseased eye] also vanish.
Question: What is the difference between this and the previous section? Answer: The previous section concerns contemplation of the present; this section also includes contemplation after death.

Therefore, each section is distinct. (Regarding "conditioned arising is unreal": this means that all sentient and insentient things do not arise of themselves, but are born from causes and conditions. Furthermore, taking the human realm as one example: it arises from the three factors of the father’s semen, the mother’s blood, and one’s own consciousness-seed.)

Through the conjunction of conditions, that which is illusory arises; if causes and conditions separate, what is illusorily termed "extinction" occurs. Since it arises and ceases from causes and conditions, one knows that its very substance is unreal. Yet after great awakening, true nature does not perish—this is my Dharma-body.
△ Third, the contemplation on the destruction of the anthill by an elephant.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like an anthill inhabited by many ants. At that time, there appears a white elephant.

He came to the edge of the platform and touched it with his body; the platform immediately collapsed and shattered. "Good son, this platform is what is called the body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The white elephant is the messenger of Yamarāja. The body returning to the next world is like the elephant destroying the platform."
This is the contemplation of impermanence (*anitya*). "Ants" refers to small insects; "mound" refers to an earthen mound that serves as the dwelling place for ants.
"The many ants dwell securely" means that as long as the mound exists, the ants remain secure. [The following] "Good son" and so forth applies the analogy to the Dharma.

The earthen platform is a metaphor for the body; the ants are a metaphor for life. The conjunction and mutual support of consciousness, breath, and warmth constitute the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) of a person, which dwells in dependence upon the body.
As long as the body exists, life exists, just as the ants remain on the platform. The white elephant is a metaphor for the demon of impermanence (*anityatā-māraka*).
Just as when the white elephant touches the platform, both the platform and the ants are destroyed, so too does the demon of death seize the person.
Both body and life shall perish. The final two lines conclude both the teaching and the metaphor together: "Alas!
If one contemplates this impermanence and gives rise to great awakening, one will suddenly manifest untainted right wisdom (*anāsrava-samyagjñāna*).

This wisdom will illuminate and penetrate through to the realization that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) are entirely empty, enabling one to cross beyond all suffering and calamity and transcend the realm where birth and death do not apply—realizing that which ghosts and spirits cannot even perceive."

The Hook: Controlling the Unpredictable Ghost of Death. This is like reaching out into empty space to seize a shadow; there is nowhere for the hand to grasp. △ Fourth, the Contemplation of the Banana Tree’s Lack of Substance.
A renunciant bodhisattva further contemplates his own body and forms this thought: "From the crown of my head to my feet, this body of mine..."
Skin, flesh, bone, and marrow combine together to form the body; it is like a plantain tree, for there is no core within.
This is the contemplation of non-self and also the contemplation of emptiness. First, one contemplates one's own body as being composed of the combination of various elements to form a single body:
when these are gathered, it exists, but when they are separated, it is empty. Since it has no substantial reality of its own, where can a sovereign self be found?

Ah! Therefore, it is compared to the plantain tree (*kadalī*). Because the plantain has no solid core, being wrapped by layers of leaves—solid on the outside but hollow within—one leaf remains after another is peeled away.
Thus, as long as the leaves remain, there is existence; when the leaves are exhausted, there is emptiness.
Nor is there any sovereign master. If one investigates this through both principle and analogy, one will attain sudden and great enlightenment;

then one will know that true emptiness follows conditions to form phenomena, and that the myriad phenomena are, in their very essence, the truth. Form and emptiness are mutually identical; principle and phenomena are harmoniously integrated.
When this fierce awakening becomes clear and manifest, one is counted among the thousand Buddhas. △ Fifth, the contemplation of earth adhering to a wall.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as having no strength; it is thinly covered by skin and flesh, like plaster adhering to a wall.
The hundreds of millions of hairs are like grass growing from the ground, and the subtle wind-element enters and exits the pores. What person of wisdom would [cherish such a thing]?
One should take pleasure in this body because it decays and changes moment by moment;
since it possesses no enduring power, one speaks of its lack of solidity, which is also the contemplation of impermanence. Thus, the body is not [regarded as] one's own self.
Because the skin and flesh thinly cover it, it resembles a body. Yet, since it is said to be "thinly covered," one already perceives its impermanence;
it is like plaster smeared upon a wall, which temporarily conceals gaps but ultimately lacks solidity or endurance.

Hair and fur grow from the skin and flesh just as grass grows from the earth—here, "earth" refers to the layer of soil on the wall. Thus, we know that when grass grows upon the surface of a wall, it will inevitably [fall away] after a long time.
It falls; its crevices open of their own accord, allowing wind to pass through in and out, until before long it collapses.

Wind entering the body in this manner is likewise [the case for the practitioner]. Who would not feel profound revulsion? "Moment by moment" refers to the shifting flux of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
"Decaying and turning" means that death is imminent. For one who practices contemplation, having thus realized impermanence:
Suddenly awakening, one asks: "Who is it that decays? To what does one return after death? When a single thought accords with reality, the great dream is awakened from;
only then does one know that fundamentally there is no arising or ceasing, and that the very substance of being is the Buddha. 6. The Contemplation of Raising a Snake to Suffer Harm.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like one who raises a venomous snake only to suffer its harm;
although I now sustain and nourish this body with food, drink, and clothing, it remains ungrateful and will ultimately cause me to fall into the evil realms.
This is the contemplation on suffering. The venomous snake is a metaphor for greed, hatred, and delusion; they repeatedly poison and harm one's innate virtuous qualities (*prakṛti-guṇa*).

Sentient beings indulge in these poisons as if raising a snake. Thus we know that if one indulges in greed, one’s desires will never be satisfied, and it will poison and harm the virtue of liberation.

If one indulges in hatred, one will become enraged and commit injury or killing, which poisons and harms the virtue of the *dharmakāya*. If one indulges in delusion, one will naturally fall into darkness.
Delusion poisons the virtue of *prajñā*. Once these three virtues are lost, the three types of karma increase profusely; thus one dies and falls into the evil realms.
Is this not taking harm upon oneself? Therefore, when a Bodhisattva has made this contemplation, they give rise to deep fear and dread, and develop great courage and vigor.
Like a great general breaking through a heavy siege, they exert their strength to break out, whereby the three poisons are transformed.
Thus, through these three virtues, suffering and affliction are suddenly transformed into the fruit of happiness. △ Seventh, the contemplation on enemies feigning friendship:
The renunciant bodhisattva further contemplates his own person as being like an enemy who feigns the role of a close friend, watching for an opportunity to strike.

Furthermore, one may administer poison to sever another's life-force; my body is likewise so—it is fundamentally not real and will ultimately lead to impermanence, for it is not something beloved by the Noble Ones.

This is the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*). A hostile enemy may feign friendship, and if one trusts them, they will surely destroy one's body and life; this serves as a metaphor for the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
To feign intimacy with it is to surely sever one's life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*).

Therefore, if a Bodhisattva of great capacity can, within this impermanent body, realize that which is truly eternal and indestructible, they will surely cause their enemies to surrender and their adversaries to take refuge.
8. The Contemplation on the Arising and Ceasing of Water Bubbles.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like a bubble upon the water;

though it may possess the exquisite color of a lapis lazuli gem, it arises and ceases through momentary causes and conditions without constancy, for all conditioned things do not endure for long from one moment to the next.
This is the contemplation of impermanence. A water bubble is but a floating froth; it appears like a pearl when viewed, yet it vanishes as soon as one tries to grasp it.
The body is likewise: it seems real when observed, yet it perishes in an instant. If a Bodhisattva can realize this at this point, [he has attained true understanding].
Thus, the entire bubble is water; the true nature is eternally abiding. To turn back and see one's own original face is no different from the Tathāgata’s perfect *saṃbhogakāya*.
△ Ninth: The Contemplation of the Unreality of the City of the Gandharvas.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like a city of the gandharvas:
although it manifests appearances, it does not truly exist. My present body is likewise so.
This is the contemplation of emptiness. A "city of the gandharvas" (gandharvanagara) is like a mirage; it is the vapor of sea monsters that coalesces into city walls, towers, and pavilions.
Though it appears real when observed, its substance is non-existent. Now, applying this principle to the lower method: my own body is likewise so.
What currently exists is non-existent. As the Sūtra says: "That which is born at the very beginning is simultaneously subject to extinction; this is not spoken for the sake of the ignorant.
If you can look through this with a cool, discerning eye, the city of Gandharvas will be transformed into the land of nature, and the illusory body will be the true body.
10. The Contemplation that Images are Not Real.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like a reflection: "My body is likewise; though it exists, it is not real.
This is also the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). A shadow beneath the sun or an image within a mirror—neither the shadow departs from its form, nor does the image depart from the mirror.
If one realizes that the shadow returns to its reality, then the entire image is but the mirror. Only then does one know that sentient beings are fundamentally Buddhas.
△ 11. Contemplation on Invasion by Powerful Enemies.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like a powerful foreign enemy;
likewise, my body is now also thus—afflictions, these enemies, invade and plunder my roots of goodness.

This is the contemplation of suffering. Nirvana is like one's own native land; birth-and-death is like a foreign land. One's native land has a sovereign lord, while the foreign land has hostile enemies.
The sovereign lord is a metaphor for the Dharmakāya; the hostile enemies are a metaphor for the afflictions (*kleśa*).

The Dharmakāya is fully endowed with myriad virtues, whereas the afflictions plunder and ravage the roots of goodness. When the Bodhisattva observes from this vantage point, he attains sudden enlightenment in a single thought-moment.
Afflictions are themselves bodhi; birth and death are themselves nirvana. It is like when an enemy becomes a capable general, or plunder turns into a marvelous achievement.
△ 12. Contemplation on the Collapse of the Decayed House.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like a dilapidated house; though it may be repaired and maintained, it is destined to collapse.
My body is likewise: though it receives my affection and care, it is inevitably impermanent.
This, too, is the contemplation of impermanence. Furthermore, observe the analogy below; "my body" is the application to the subject.
Indeed, when a wise person contemplates this, why would they repair a decaying house? They should quickly mount the elder’s carriage. One should likewise not be startled by impermanence.

One then beholds the longevity of distant years (the elder’s carriage). This is like the parable of the burning house in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The elder entices his children out of the house first with three carriages and later bestows upon them equally a single carriage.

These three things symbolize the provisional (*upāya*), while the single carriage symbolizes the real (*tattva*). Now, borrowing that metaphor: contemplations such as impermanence, suffering, and emptiness are the provisional; through these, one realizes the nature and attains Buddhahood, which is the real.

The provisional contemplations are like the three carriages—the goat, deer, and ox—while achieving the Way is like ascending the great white ox-cart. Entering the real from the provisional is identical [in both cases]; therefore, the metaphor is cited briefly. △ Thirteen: Contemplation of Fear Toward a Nearby Enemy.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like a neighboring hostile country, where the inhabitants of its cities and towns constantly harbor fear;
"Now my own body is likewise thus, for in every moment of thought I stand in dread of the enemy of impermanence."
This is also the contemplation of suffering. The hostile country is a metaphor for birth and death; the city is a metaphor for one's own body;

and the people are metaphors for the six sense faculties. Although the hostile country in the metaphor does not actually invade or plunder, the people within this city constantly harbor fear because of their proximity to it.
Likewise, although impermanence in the Dharma has not yet arrived, the practicing bodhisattva is nonetheless startled at every moment of thought.
The mind. However, one who is startled must necessarily apply the mind; one who applies the mind is necessarily able to exercise wisdom.

When wisdom is exercised, one will certainly transcend birth and death. This is like that neighboring enemy lord: he may cultivate benevolence and spread virtue, causing others to come as guests at his mere reputation;
or he may assemble generals and train troops, likewise causing their gallbladders to shatter upon hearing his name alone. △ Fourteen: Attachment.
The Contemplation of the Body Being Burned by Fire:
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like immeasurable fuel being consumed by fire;
yet this fierce fire is never satiated. My body is likewise: with the fire of craving, it burns the fuel of the five desires, and thus my mind increases [in affliction].
It is also like this. This is the contemplation of suffering. Craving for the five desires burns like fire consuming wood; the growth of craving is insatiable like a fire.
If a bodhisattva turns back to contemplate for even a single thought-moment, craving is transformed into wisdom, and the five desires are transformed into the True.

Thus, when wisdom and principle accord, one dwells in carefree ease at that very place. (Do not interpret the two characters "five desires" [wǔyù] as wealth and beauty; they refer to the body that undergoes the five desires.

Because craving resides in the mind, the body suffers toil; the more the mind craves, the more the body labors. It is like fire burning wood—the wood must surely be consumed. When the fire of affliction oppresses the body, the body is likewise impermanent. Therefore it is said: "The growth of the mind is also like this.")
△ Fifteenth: The Contemplation of a Compassionate Mother Cherishing Her Child.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like a newborn child, whom a compassionate mother cherishes and constantly protects with care.
My own body is likewise so. If I do not protect this body and mind from illness, I will be unable to achieve any cultivation or realization;
this is the contemplation of impermanence. Just as a child dies if it loses its mother, the body falls ill if it is not protected;

being ill, one cannot cultivate or realize. It is like a child who, having died, cannot continue the lineage. Therefore, the Bodhisattva contemplates this and applies himself with even greater vigilance.
Be cautious. Guard your body and cultivate the Way, as one would protect a child to ensure the continuity of the lineage.

However, regarding the phrase "the body and mind of illness," it is more appropriate to read the character *zhì* (之) as *hài* (害). This means that if one does not guard [the body], it will bring harm to the body and mind.
For when the body is ill and the mind is anxious, sorrow and affliction obstruct the Way; is this not indeed harm? △ Sixteen: Washing Charcoal. No [text].

Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being impure by nature. It is like a person who, loathing the color of charcoal, employs various skillful means to wash it with water;
though an immeasurable amount of time passes, its blackness remains as before until the charcoal is finally exhausted.

In the end, it provides no benefit whatsoever. My body is likewise: it is tainted and impure; even if one were to wash it with the waters of the ocean until the end of the future, it would be equally useless.
This is the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), which engenders revulsion and increases the aspiration for the Way. For indeed, the color of charcoal is inherently black;
even if it were washed for years, it could never become white. The body is inherently impure; even if one were to wash it with all the waters of the ocean, it could not be made pure.
The Bodhisattva contemplates and awakens to this, whereupon, in a single moment, he turns back from delusion to return to the truth. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth—[the roots...]
The dust-like consciousnesses and mind, through mindful recollection, are transformed into supreme awakening. Reaching this point, who can wash whom?
Who can defile whom? △ Seventeen: The Contemplation of Pouring Oil onto Fuel.
Furthermore, the renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like firewood drenched in oil and set ablaze by flames; moreover, it is met with a great wind that cannot be stopped.
This body is likewise: it is called the fuel of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), drenched with the oil of craving and affection, and set ablaze by the fire of hatred.
The power of the wind of ignorance never ceases;
this is the contemplation of impermanence (*anitya*). "To drench" means to pour. "Fuel" refers to firewood.

When oil is poured upon the fuel and it is consumed by fire, which then encounters a great wind and blazes intensely, it burns through the forests and wilds with a force that cannot be stopped. This serves as a metaphor for the moisture of greed.
When the body is incited by anger and driven by the winds of ignorance with great force, it can burn away one's inherent virtues; this becomes increasingly difficult to exhaust.
If a Bodhisattva casts their gaze and examines Avalokiteśvara, how would it be to perceive the emptiness of the five aggregates? △ Eighteenth:
Contemplation on Many Illnesses and Evil Ailments.
The renunciant bodhisattva contemplates his own body as being like a malignant disease, for it is the locus where four hundred and four ailments reside;
this is the contemplation of suffering. Regarding these four hundred and four ailments, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: there are one hundred and one wind-related ailments.
There are one hundred and one diseases of fire, one hundred and one diseases of water, and one hundred and one miscellaneous diseases.
It can be said that there is no greater affliction than having a body. Yet, disease is a burden to the body, just as the body is a burden to the Way.

When a Bodhisattva contemplates this, the dual attachments to self and phenomena are instantly emptied in a single thought-moment; thus, malignant illnesses are transformed into sublime functions. All diseases...

Exhaustively practice the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). (The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: "There are two kinds of illness: first, hunger and thirst as the primary illness; second, the four hundred and four illnesses as the secondary illness.

The conditions for all illnesses do not exceed three types, namely: wind, heat, and phlegm. These three types of illness can be eliminated by three medicines: oil eliminates wind; ghee and rock honey eliminate bile-fever (*pitta*); honey and aged granulated sugar eliminate phlegm.
For miscellaneous illnesses, one should employ all these medicines to treat them. 19. Contemplation on the Impermanence of the Nineteen Parasites.
It is also like the large intestine, for it is the dwelling place of eighty-four thousand worms; thus it is an impermanent location. Since the exhaled breath does not return, it is impermanent.
This contemplation of impurity is also a contemplation of impermanence. Some say that there are eighty-four thousand families of worms within the body.

It pervades the entire body; here, however, it is simply stated that it exists in the large intestine. Nevertheless, one should directly employ this as the practice of the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā) without needing to calculate its precise location.
Furthermore, contemplating that this body is a locus of impermanence and so forth is the contemplation of impermanence (anitya-saṃjñā).

Therefore, it concludes by stating that the non-returning of the exhaled breath is due to impermanence. Generally speaking, when a Bodhisattva performs such contemplation, it is also like [the practice of] dhyāna.

The Master investigates the *huatou* (critical phrase). At the point of doubt, there is much awakening. This contemplation of impermanence, suffering, and emptiness leads one to turn around at the point of greatest aversion.
Suppose you were to flip over your own skin; eighty thousand worms would transform into eyes and hands throughout your entire body.
Amidst this transient guest-folk, recognize the unmoving Lord of the House. Only then will you truly know that the contemplations of impermanence, impurity, and so forth are indeed [the path].
They serve as elixirs for transforming the bones and as "knocking-wood" tiles. △ Twenty: The Contemplation of Tiles, Stones, and River Water.

They are like insentient things because the spirit and consciousness can easily depart from them, just as with tiles and stones; they are also like river water because they do not abide for even a moment from one instant to the next.
The first three phrases concern the contemplation of non-self (*anātman*); the latter three phrases concern the contemplation of impermanence (*anitya*).
This is because that which is "not sentient" is precisely the insentient, and "spiritual consciousness" refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).

It means that although the body is originally sentient, it is compared to the insentient because the spiritual consciousness is easily detached and lacks inherent sovereignty. Furthermore, being "easily detached" is equivalent to being easily subject to death, for karma drags the consciousness along.
Once it departs, it immediately leaves the body; for even a brief moment, its absence is identical to that of insentient matter. Therefore, tiles and stones are used as a metaphor.

It should be understood that this passage can all be analyzed through the three-membered syllogism (*trirūpa-anumāna*). For example: The subject (*dharmin*) is the body. The thesis (*pakṣa*) is that it lacks an autonomous sovereign.
The reason (*hetu*) is that the conscious spirit (*vijñāna*) easily departs and is impermanent. The concordant example (*sapakṣa*) is like tiles and stones. This is truly because...
Clay and stones are easily detached and impermanent; clay and stones have no sovereign master.

By this analogy, one should know that the consciousness within the body is easily detached and impermanent, for it likewise lacks a sovereign master of its own. The subsequent phrase may also serve as a formal inference (*pramāṇa*):

the body is the subject (*dharmin*), its arising and ceasing is the thesis (*pakṣa*), and the reason (*hetu*) is that it does not abide even momentarily from one moment to the next. This is the same [as the previous case].
It is like a river; it merely establishes its thesis outside of the literal text, with slight inconsistencies. △ Twenty-one: The Contemplation of the Infant Pressing Oil.
It is also like pressing oil, for one undergoes toil and suffering in all matters; thus, being without anything to rely upon, one is like an infant.

Because one has lost one's parents, this is the contemplation of suffering. Pressing oil without taking [the essence] but creating evil, yet gaining only toil and hardship, is a metaphor for a human life:
rushing about after sensory objects is likewise thus. "Having no place of reliance" means turning one's back on awakening and uniting with the dust of defilement; it is like...
An infant, having lost its mother, has no one upon whom to rely. Herein, the infant is a metaphor for one's own body; the parents are a metaphor for Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
If a person relies on the sutras to practice contemplation, and suddenly turns away from defilements to unite with awakening, this is like the infant seeing its mother.
△ Twenty-second: The Contemplation of the Frog-like Burrow.
There is no protector, for one is like a frog swallowed by a snake. It is like a bottomless pit, because the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) cannot be known.
This is also the contemplation of impermanence and suffering. "Having no protector" means being lost regarding the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*); it is not [the case that] the world...
One may avoid death, yet when impermanence arrives, there is truly no means of salvation. In the analogy, a frog encountering a snake has no way to escape;
likewise, in the Dharma, a person encountered by the "killing ghost" (māra) has no means of salvation. A pit dug in the ground is a hole so deep it has no bottom;
once a person falls into it, they cannot emerge. This serves as the metaphor. The mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) correspond to this analogy.
Regarding the statement that "a person sinks into it such that it cannot be known," there are two meanings. First, the pit is revealed by heaven and is so deep as to be unfathomable;
this is a metaphor for the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), whose essence is itself delusion. They spontaneously create karma, yet the person does not know it themselves.

However, the two characters "can be known" (*jìng kě zhī*) in the sutra do not seem appropriate. Alternatively, it may be said that within the metaphor, the character "know" (*zhī*) should actually be the character "fathom" (*cè*). Thus it says:
The pit is deep and bottomless, such that people cannot fathom it. According to Fashang’s explanation, the character "ke" (可) should be read as "neng" (能).

This refers to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) which spontaneously create karma; human beings, in their delusion, are unable to know this themselves. Those who study the scriptures must not be like those who fix the strings of a zither—rigidity is not the way;
flexibility is most excellent. "Mind" refers to the mind-king (*cittarāja*), of which there are eight types; "mental factors" (*caitta*) are those associated with the mind.
There are fifty-one [mental factors] that are activated by these [consciousnesses]. As for the eight kings, they are:

eye-consciousness, ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the manas-consciousness, and the ālaya-consciousness. Regarding the fifty-one mental factors (*caitta*), they consist of:

five universal factors (*sarvatraga*), five object-specific factors (*viniyata*), eleven wholesome factors (*kuśala*), six primary afflictions (*kleśa*), twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), and [four] indeterminate factors.
There are four concentrations, totaling fifty-one. Just as the mind-king moves and acts, the mental factors follow it.

Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have been deluded regarding the truth and given rise to falsehood, falling into this state from which they cannot emerge of their own accord. It is no different from a person falling into a pit;
the circumstances are identical. When a Bodhisattva contemplates this, he suddenly steps out of the deep pit and brings [the beings] to peace and security.

The demon of killing is eliminated, and thus the world attains great peace; the four classes of people delight in their vocations (the eight consciousnesses are called "kings" because they exercise sovereign mastery over the objects they perceive). △ Twenty-third:
The Contemplation of Severing Attachment to Annihilation and Permanence.

They are constantly insatiable, for their minds never grow weary of the pleasures of the five desires. They are constantly lacking self-mastery, for they are bound by the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
The first three phrases describe greed and its lack of contentment, like the ocean receiving the hundred rivers. To afflict the body and exhaust the mind is the contemplation of suffering (*duḥkha*).
Furthermore, the five desires are the objects corresponding to the five sense faculties: form, sound, fragrance, taste, and touch. When these are adverse, they give rise to aversion;

when favorable, they give rise to attachment, such that there is never any satisfaction. The Bodhisattva observes this and realizes for himself that the nature-virtues and dharma-treasures within the Tathāgatagarbha fill the entire Dharma-realm.
Upon reaching this realization, he turns back to reflect upon his former greed for the five desires and the attachments of his own mind.

All pleasures can be dismissed with a single laugh; they never cease. Since it is said that they are eternally not under one's own control, this precisely refers to the transformation of the views of annihilationism and eternalism, wherein there is no sovereign self.

Thus, through the contemplation of non-self, the Bodhisattva awakens to this truth, turning away from the views of annihilationism and eternalism to realize true permanence, and transforming false views into right wisdom. 24. Contemplation on the Shameless Corpse.

They feel no shame or remorse; though they have been nurtured by their kin, they abandon the very life that sustained them, and thus they are like corpses, for day and night they draw near to destruction.

The first three phrases constitute the contemplation of mistaking a thief for one’s son; they are also a contemplation of suffering (*duḥkhānupaśyanā*). The text is incomplete and its meaning is not clear; it should read:
"For example, suppose there is a person who abandons his own biological son and recognizes a thief as his son. However, as for that thief-son...
Although one has received the profound kindness of being nurtured by one’s own father and close kin, one feels no shame or remorse;

instead, one commits various karmic deeds that bring hardship upon one’s father. Furthermore, one robs the family treasures. If we apply this to the Dharma: the true mind is like the legitimate son, yet one is deluded and abandons it;
the deluded mind is like a false son, yet one recognizes and identifies with it. The deluded mind runs wild and unrestrained, acting as if it were the legitimate son.
Lacking a sense of shame and remorse, one creates karma; thus, one’s own body receives retribution according to that karma.
This results in bringing disgrace upon one’s father and squandering the wealth of the Dharma, effectively plundering the family treasure.

However, if at some point one turns back from delusion to awaken to the truth—just as one recognizes a true son and captures a thief—then the family treasure will be restored and the ancestral lineage will continue. This is also like the section on "the corpse" below.
This is the contemplation of impermanence. One’s own body is unaware, like a corpse;
the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) flows on, moment by moment impermanent, ultimately ending in death, just like a corpse. Day and night, it draws near to destruction.
This merely means that it will not last long. However, when a Bodhisattva contemplates it, suddenly life is revived from within death, and thus he knows.
It is eternally abiding and indestructible. △ Twenty-fifth, the contemplation of the body as the basis for experiencing suffering:
It experiences only various sufferings because there is no true happiness in any place; it is the basis for suffering because all manner of suffering dwells in dependence upon this body.
All of these are contemplations on suffering (*duḥkha*). Sufferings do not merely consist of adverse objects; they do not merely pertain to the three realms (*tridhātu*).

One should know that the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles is like stopping at a conjured city (*parikalpita-nagara*); it is not yet true bliss. This is because the heavy sufferings of the three miserable paths (*apāya*) [are not yet extinguished].
Regarding the eight sufferings of human beings, everyone knows them to be suffering.

However, as for the joys and pleasures of the various devas, when they become attached in the mind and one is oppressed by them such that there is no freedom, these are experienced as pleasure by those in the heavens; yet viewed by the Buddha, they are likewise suffering.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The three realms have no peace; they are like a burning house. Thus, the various sufferings follow one another in succession.
It continues without interruption. How could it be that only objects of suffering are contrary to reality while objects of pleasure are not?
Yet when a Bodhisattva contemplates this, seeing that true happiness is absent in every place, one wonders: "Where, ultimately, does true happiness reside?
Suddenly, amidst a heap of suffering and affliction, through intense and urgent pressure, the delusions of one's own mind are instantly dispelled, and the sky of one's nature shines forth clearly.
By illuminating [this], one knows that the ultimate limit of all suffering is none other than the wondrous true suchness-nature of the original Tathāgatagarbha.
Next, in contemplation, one observes that the body is the basis upon which suffering relies; thus, all manifold sufferings abide in dependence upon the body.

When a Bodhisattva contemplates this, they realize that the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) is the root that summons suffering. Thereupon, they employ non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) to suddenly sever it.

If the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) does not exist, then the skin no longer remains, and the hair has nothing to which it may adhere. △ Twenty-sixth: The Contemplation of the Void Village as Empty and Quiescent.
Like an empty village, because there is no sovereign within this body, it is ultimately empty and quiescent; it is that which is grasped through pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*).
Because they are falsely constructed and imagined.
The first three phrases refer to the contemplation of non-self (*anātman-vipaśyanā*); the subsequent three phrases refer to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

A "village" (*grāma*) is like a marketplace, a horse-head [crossroads], and so forth; it refers to a place where residents are gathered and where travelers rest. However, since it is called a "gathering,"...
It falls. It is valued because there is someone [within it], yet because there is no person within it, it is called an "empty village.
This is a metaphor for the lack of a sovereign master within the body of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), just as a village may be devoid of people. Herein, the lower teaching is applied:

the bodies of sentient beings are a provisional conglomeration of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). They are transmuted by the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and driven by karmic conditions. Though they desire life, they inevitably die; though they prefer what is upright...
It is certainly false. Since it is not autonomous, how could there be a sovereign master? Yet, when a Bodhisattva contemplates in this way, seeing that there is no sovereign master, they ask:
"Who is it that is currently so lively and active? If one makes this inquiry here, the Master immediately responds.
The following phrase is yet another contemplation: that which is ultimately empty and still is the *dharmatā*. This is because of the *dharma*...
The nature is pure; it is swept clean of even the slightest speck of dust. It is like clear eyes facing a cloudless sky—pure, void, and profoundly still, truly without a single thing.

The latter two phrases concerning "pervasive conceptualization" (parikalpa) refer to the arising of delusion based upon the Truth. "Pervasive conceptualization" means universal calculation and deliberation; it refers to the deluded thoughts of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
In principle, these do not exist at all, yet they are established as existing through attachment. "Constructing" (*gou*) means creating through volitional activity.
Furthermore, "painting" refers to colored painting. It is like constructing a house within a dream, adorned with the five colors;

while dreaming, one grasps it as real, yet upon waking, it is entirely empty. Therefore, it is called a "false construction. How could it be that it is only empty after waking? Rather, even while dreaming, it is empty.
When a Bodhisattva observes this, they realize that the person in the dream is the very same person who is awake, thereby attaining full comprehension.
The objects within a dream are merely the mind’s own manifestation; one likewise realizes that the objects within the waking state are also manifested solely by the mind.

This is the sudden entry into the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), wherein the self-nature of all phenomena is primordial. △ Twenty-seventh: The Contemplation of the Ship in an Empty Valley.
They are like echoes in a valley, for they are all manifestations of the false and illusory. They are also like ships; if there is no helmsman, one will drift away and sink.

The first three phrases constitute the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), while the subsequent three phrases constitute the contemplation of non-self (*anātma-vipaśyanā*). An echo in an empty valley, though heard, is in reality [non-existent].
There is [an echo], yet it was originally non-existent within the valley; this also serves as a metaphor for the falsity of one's own body. It manifests falsely according to karmic conditions;

when observed, it seems to exist, yet in principle, it is non-existent. If a Bodhisattva realizes that the resonance returns to the sound itself, they will attain a great awakening in their very essence.
Furthermore, as follows: the small is called a boat (*kṣudra-nau*), and the large is called a ship (*mahā-nau*). Boat and ship are metaphors for the human body; the boatman is... [the mind].

This is a metaphor for the Buddha-nature. It means that if one has a boat but no pilot, the boat will drift and sink; this metaphorizes a body without Buddha-nature, wherein the body is merely a corpse.
The Buddha taught this contemplation precisely because he wished for the Bodhisattva to encounter the pilot within the boat.
If one meets with the pilot, then one will immediately reach the other shore. 28. The Contemplation of the Great Vehicle Reaching the Shore.

The Bodhisattva contemplates this: from that which appears useless, he selects out its great utility. The great vehicle is a metaphor for the body; the wealth and treasures are a metaphor for the Dharma.

Why? To provide an inquiry and explanation. The inquiry asks: "Since the body is an unsubstantial entity characterized by impermanence, suffering, and emptiness, how can it perform the function of transporting [one to liberation]?"
"Regarding 'the implements for entry,' the commentary states: because one rides upon the Mahāyāna to reach Bodhi.

Now, the term 'One Vehicle' (Ekayāna) above refers to the capacity of the body to receive the Dharma, just as a carriage can carry a load. The two characters 'Mahāyāna' correspond to the preceding 'wealth and treasures,' which is to say, the Mahāyāna Dharma.
If one does not personally encounter it with the body and hear it with the ears, nor grasp it with the mind and comprehend it with the spirit, by what means could one realize the Way? Therefore..."
The Buddhas of the three periods of time all attained Bodhi only after practicing and realizing it as ordinary beings.

This is because the various metaphors used previously have already caused people to feel weary and weary again; fearing that they might become even more terrified, I shall therefore demonstrate this once more, not sparing the prolixity.
Until the very end, with a sudden pull at the critical moment, those who were terrified and loathing are made to leap and reach the shore.
How great is the Sacred Scripture! It is the excellent medicine that accords with the ailment. △ Twenty-nine:
Summary of Reaching the Shore.

"Good son, an ordained bodhisattva observes day and night; it is not that they do not cherish such a body, but rather they do so because they desire to cause sentient beings to emerge from the ocean of birth and death and reach the other shore."
Regarding the various contemplations mentioned above, they are not intended for a single person to perform all of them universally.
Rather, the intent is for individuals to practice one or two of them day and night. This is not to say that people do not harbor doubts; indeed, I fear those who might object:

"Since the body is the vessel for the Dharma, it stands to reason that it should be cherished and protected. Why then must one dwell in mountain forests or perilous places? Furthermore, why must one observe day and night?"
It is better to overcome such toil. Could there ever be a gentleman who does not cherish his own person? Thus the Tathāgata explained it: It is not that he does not cherish [the body];

rather, it is that the body and the Way cannot both be fully preserved. If one compares the body with the Way, then by protecting the body, one neglects the Way and will forever undergo the cycle of saṃsāra.
If one values the Way and treats the body lightly, then one can reach the other shore. △
Second, the conclusion of the essential Dharma.
At that time, after the World-Honored One had spoken this Dharma, he addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying:
"Good son, one who cultivates such practices is called a renunciant son of the Buddha; this is the essential Dharma to be contemplated."

Such practice refers to all forms of contemplation. Because one seeks the Way through weariness with the body, practicing according to the teachings, one will surely reach the other shore without traversing detours;
therefore, it is called the "Essential Dharma" (Fayao). △ Third, the exhortation to circulate [the teaching].
If there are sons of the Buddha who have resolved their minds on Bodhicitta and, seeking Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, dwell in an araṇya and practice these thirty-seven contemplations,
as well as teaching others to practice them, explaining and transcribing these essential teachings,
receiving, upholding, reading, and reciting them, remaining far removed from all grasping at "I" and "mine," and forever severing attachment to the five [aggregates]— [they shall attain this].
One desires worldly happiness.
It is for the sake of realizing bodhi that a Buddha becomes a Buddha. Therefore, the Buddha said:

"If there is one who can give rise to the bodhicitta in order to seek the path of bodhi, they are called a son of the Buddha. Having already given rise to this mind and having already sought it, as mentioned above...
Regarding this path: one must dwell in an araṇya and cultivate the thirty-seven contemplations as described above for one’s own benefit.

Furthermore, one should teach others to practice them for the benefit of others. Moreover, with regard to such essential teachings, one may explain them by analyzing the text and elucidating the meaning;
or one may transcribe them by copying the words from one to another; or one may receive and uphold them by internalizing and maintaining them. Or...

Through reading and study, one understands the meaning and becomes proficient in the text. Furthermore, it is repeatedly emphasized that whether one is personally practicing contemplation or providing explanations and so forth, one must not cling to the mark of a self (*ātman*) nor cling to the mark of phenomena (*dharma*).

When one does not cling to the mark of a self, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is empty; when one does not cling to the mark of phenomena, the grasping at "mine" (*mamakāra*) is empty. Thus, since both types of grasping are empty, the mind...

Both subject and object are forgotten; hence it is said, "permanently severed," etc. (The capacity for craving is precisely the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*); the five desires are precisely that which belongs to the self (*ātmīya*). Just as the five desires are what belongs to me, they are likewise the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*)).
△ Fourth, the ultimate perfection of virtue.
One will swiftly bring to maturity an indestructible faith and seek great enlightenment, not sparing even one’s own body or life, much less any worldly treasures.
In this very lifetime, one will certainly attain the ultimate fulfillment of the vajra-jñāna-mudrā of all Tathāgatas.
They shall never regress from the unsurpassed path; they shall swiftly bring the six perfections and myriad practices to fulfillment, and quickly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

They are able to mature [the roots of virtue] swiftly because they practice the essentials of the Dharma; they do not let their faith be destroyed because they are firm in their resolve and do not waver;
they seek great enlightenment because their natural endowment is transcendent and penetrating;

they do not spare their own bodies or lives because they seek only the Way and are unaware of a self, let alone inferior things, for they understand liberation as the weighing of the heavy against the light and thus have no stinginess. Manifesting...
"One who will certainly attain it in this very body" means that the task of a single lifetime is accomplished without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
"One who reaches ultimate fulfillment" means that one's own realization is no less than the realization of a Buddha. "The Vajra Wisdom Seal" means that it is the very Dharma of the Buddha’s mind.

"One who does not regress from the Path" means that one’s diligence is further made manifest. "One for whom the practice of crossing over is swiftly perfected" means that realization is achieved through the sudden and perfect method (*yuan-dun*). Thus, one quickly attains accomplishment.
As for Bodhi: it is like a fine horse that, upon seeing the shadow of a whip, pursues the wind across a thousand *li*.

Thus, while the various contemplations and metaphors above may initially appear similar to the Small Beginning [teachings], they ultimately constitute the Perfect and Sudden. Entering the profound by relying on the shallow is precisely the subtle excellence of this sutra.
△ Fifth: Hearing the Chapter and Accomplishing Practice.
At that time, within the assembly, eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas who had newly resolved their minds became deeply weary of the world;

having attained the power of great patience (*kṣānti*), they no longer regressed from the unsurpassed path. One hundred thousand brahmins gave rise to the bodhicitta, matured their faculty of faith, and attained non-regression.
Thirty-six thousand sons and daughters of good family distanced themselves from and were freed from dust and defilement.
One attains the purity of the Dharma-eye.
World-weariness is an auxiliary condition for transcending the world. For if one does not feel weariness, one will delight in and become attached to the five desires;

how then could one accomplish the practice? Regarding those who have attained the power of great patience, another sutra states: "Bodhisattvas on the first stage primarily cultivate the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*)."

It is not that the other perfections are not cultivated; rather, they are practiced according to conditions and one's capacity. In the second stage (*bhūmi*), the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*) is primarily cultivated;

in the third stage, the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is primarily cultivated. If one uses that as proof for this, since it is said that the power of patience is already great, it cannot be achieved by anyone who has not realized the third stage.
Furthermore, regarding the unsurpassed path, there is no longer any regression in rank or practice, even for a single thought-moment.
All these belong to the stages above the ground (*bhūmi*). As for those who have resolved their minds on Bodhi: formerly they were Brahmins from families of pure conduct;
now, upon hearing once that all meditations on impurity are to be loathed, they immediately resolve their great mind and enter directly into the first *vihāra*.

Compared with the hundred parables of the *Avataṃsaka*, this is not inferior. The faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) is the root of all wholesome dharmas, yet it is through causes that the faculty of faith is established.
All myriad virtues are fully present therein. Regarding such phrases as "distant from dust and free from defilement," the explanation may be found in the preceding text.
(As for those who are inferior [to this], the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* contains one hundred parables comparing the arousal of the bodhicitta; yet even these hundred parables do not equal this mind.)

△ Third, Maitreya raises doubts regarding the Buddha’s previous discourse on the intensive questioning of cultivation and realization in the forest hermitage (*araṇya*).

Because the Buddha, within the *Araṇyavarga*, repeatedly elucidated the benefits of cultivation and realization for those of the three faculties, and furthermore, because the Bodhisattva Delighting in the Practice of Seclusion (*Pravivekacārī*) again proclaimed this on behalf of the Buddha, extensively demonstrating its supreme benefits, Maitreya consequently gave rise to his doubts. Furthermore—
This section is established because it represents the application of requests on behalf of the assembly. It is divided into two parts. First, the title:
*Pāramitā* Chapter, Number Eight. In the Sanskrit language, it is *pāramitā*;
here [in Chinese], it is translated as "Reaching the Other Shore. This name is derived metaphorically from the attainment of crossing over. Now, regarding that...

The one on this shore spoke to the one on the opposite shore, saying: "Just as there is suffering on this shore and happiness on the other shore, suppose there is a person who wishes to abandon suffering and seek happiness;
they must board a boat or raft to cross the great river before they can reach the other shore and experience all manner of joy.
This is because 'this shore' is a metaphor for birth and death, 'the other shore' is a metaphor for *nirvāṇa*, and the 'great river' is a metaphor for the afflictions (*kleśas*). (6)
The perfections (pāramitās) are like boats and rafts. For this reason, the Tathāgata extensively elucidated the six perfections and various dharma-gates within the sūtras.
This is because the karmic fruits of sentient beings continue in succession, preventing them from attaining liberation; thus they suffer while remaining on this shore.

Therefore, the Buddha commanded that one rely upon the six dharmas, such as giving, and practice according to the teachings. By doing so, one can eliminate the six corruptions and give birth to [the virtues].
Death enables one to reach *nirvāṇa*, just as one who boards a boat crosses a river and arrives at the other shore. Furthermore, each of the six perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*) has three types;
these may be seen for oneself in the text. △ Second, the main body of the sutra, which has two parts: first, Maitreya’s inquiry; second, the narrator’s introduction.

At that time, Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Matters arise from causes; teachings flourish by borrowing conditions. Had it not been for Maitreya’s inquiry, even though the Buddha possesses true compassion, by what means would he have provided this exposition?
II. The Actual Presentation of the Questions (in four parts). 1. Doubting the Buddha’s Present Teaching.
"Bhagavān, for what reason do you so earnestly praise those who dwell in an araṇya while practicing the bodhisattva path,
yet do not praise those who dwell in other places while practicing the bodhisattva path?"
"Other places" refers to locations outside of the *araṇya*, such as cities, villages, or areas inhabited by people.
Yet, the Buddha does not teach without cause; there must be a reason for his teaching. Therefore, he asks: "For what reason? △ Second, citing the past to corroborate the present.
At one time, the Tathāgata was on Vulture Peak Mountain, where he extensively expounded the essential teachings for the sake of the bodhisattvas, saying:
"A bodhisattva may at times stay in the house of a courtesan or associate with a butcher, using countless skillful means to instruct, benefit, and gladden them."
He benefits sentient beings by preaching the sublime Dharma, causing them to enter the Buddha-way.
"At one time" refers to the occasion when the preceding teacher and disciples were assembled, and the conditions for teaching and listening converged.
The mountain is called Gṛdhrakūṭa (Vulture Peak) based on its physical form; "vulture" is the name of a bird, and the shape of the mountain resembles that of a vulture.
It is also called Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa). It is not called "Vulture Peak" but rather "Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata" (the Vulture Peak Mountain); this is a term of honor.
For while the mountain itself was not originally sacred, that which is sacred is the Buddha and the sages.

Since the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas frequently preached the Dharma on this mountain, it is through the sanctity of these beings that the mountain’s sanctity is manifested. The various Bodhisattvas are those with the capacity for the Mahāyāna; [this is] the essential Dharma.
This refers to the Mahāyāna Dharma. For the Dharma is precisely the mind of sentient beings, and the mind encompasses all dharmas; therefore, it is called the "Essence of the Dharma" (*dharmoddāna*).

As for the "extensive explanation," it is as described in the passage: "Even if one were to write with the ink of the oceans using a single character as a gateway to the Dharma, it would not be exhausted.

On the contrary, courtesans and butchers are among the lowliest families of the Western Regions; if one associates with them, it is easy to be corrupted by their habits.
Yet, [the Buddha] instructs Bodhisattvas to associate with them and even approach them—how leisurely and unrestrained!
Even regarding lute-playing, singing, and wine shops, there is nothing he deems improper; all are Bodhisattva practices for the purpose of teaching, benefiting, and gladdening countless beings.
As for "expedient means" (*upāya*): whether acting in accordance with [the world] or transforming it through contrariety, there is nothing that does not benefit sentient beings.
Even worldly conventional speech is all wondrous Dharma, intended to cause people to rely upon it and turn toward it, leading them into the Buddha-way.

(What was previously explained was spoken for Bodhisattvas of profound rank who possess immeasurable supernatural powers and wisdom; what is there that would be improper? He knew that although the names of the bodhisattvas were the same, their spiritual powers and wisdom were not the same. Yet it was not that he did not know Maitreya; the reason he asked was simply to request clarification for the sake of those who were doubtful.

First, the prose section provides a detailed exposition in five parts. First, it identifies and defines two types of bodhisattvas:

At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: "Good son, there are two kinds of bodhisattvas who have resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and seek the path to enlightenment. The first is the householder; the second is the renunciant."
Regarding the "householder": those who are called bodhisattvas while remaining at home are sages of profound rank who manifest in the body of a layperson to practice the bodhisattva path;

One’s power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is insufficient; therefore, one must dwell in an aranya, distancing oneself from worldly affairs so that one may remain free from affliction.
As the saying goes: "A fledgling can only cling to a branch; an infant still ought to stay by its mother.
How could one possibly be compared on the same footing as a Bodhisattva of the profound stages? △ Second, a brief description of the two kinds of distinctions.
A lay bodhisattva, desiring to transform and guide others, may approach brothels and butcher shops; a renunciant bodhisattva does not do so.

In order to descend [to the level of those to be converted], he manifests in forms corresponding to their kind and employs the means of "common purpose" (*samānārthatā*) to gather and transform them—namely, first using the hook of desire to draw them in.

Later, they were led into the Buddha’s assembly; all of these are inconceivable matters. As for those who have left the household life, as soon as they emerge from worldly conditions, their power of the Way is not yet firm.
If they were to enter the marketplace again, I fear they might encounter the calamity of Dharmagandhā (the *Dengjia* difficulty).

Thus it is said: "It would not be like this" (the "calamity of Dharmagandhā" refers to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, where the Venerable Ānanda, because he practiced universal compassion without distinguishing between the lowly and the humble, was subjected to the seductive arts of the woman Mātangī, and consequently met with great peril).

This is the explanation. △ Fourth, following the preceding, an earnest exhortation to contemplate.
"You should observe this gateway of practice (*caryāmukha*) in this way.
These two characters—'this' (*iti*) and 'way' (*mukha*)—refer to the aforementioned three roots and nine grades of both householders and renunciants;

"practicing" (*caryā*) refers to their sustained application, and "gateway" (*mukha*) refers to the ability to enter [the path]. "You" refers to Maitreya, extending to the great assembly, and reaching far into all sentient beings of the future.
One should contemplate these three characters as words of exhortation, meaning: "Since the Buddha has already spoken them, you should practice them.

Furthermore, one observes that these characters have two meanings. If pronounced with the departing tone (qùshēng), they refer to the wisdom of non-discriminative initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), which belongs to cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanā-prajñā*).
If pronounced with the level tone (píngshēng), they refer to the mind with discrimination that dwells upon and deeply investigates mental images; therefore, it is called "contemplation" (*guān*).

"Examination" refers to the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). This is explained here with reference to a beginner. Since it is called "examination," it should indeed be the wisdom of reflection;

however, its meaning also encompasses cultivation (*bhāvanā*). △ Fifth, the extensive explanation of the superior dharma of renunciation has six parts. First, those in deep stages are not restricted by their location.
Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva who has gone forth and cultivated the path of the Buddha attains the untainted and true Dharma,
and according to conditions, brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings.
Having already clarified that one has attained the untainted [dharma] and so forth, such a person is one who has realized the principle; they differ from a beginner.

Therefore, in benefiting and bringing joy to others according to circumstances, the intention is not to restrict oneself to a particular location—why must it necessarily be a forest hermitage (araṇya)?
△ Second, those who have not yet attained must seek superior conditions.
If there is a son of the Buddha who has not yet attained true wisdom and dwells in an araṇya, he must seek to draw near to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
If he encounters a true spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), he will certainly never retreat from the bodhisattva practices. For these reasons:
"O sons of the Buddha, you should with a sincere mind seek to see one Buddha and one Bodhisattva.

Cultivating and realizing [the truth] within an araṇya is specifically taught for those of initial capacity. Since it is said that 'true wisdom has not yet been attained,' this means that the two attachments to self and phenomena have not yet perished;
one still remains within the outflows (*āsrava*). Without a quiet place, one cannot collect the mind; therefore, it is called 'dwelling'."
In an araṇya, it is difficult for one who is not a noble teacher to give rise to true wisdom; therefore, it is said that one must "approach" [a teacher].

Even if one does not encounter a noble teacher, one must certainly pay homage to a wise and truly virtuous spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who can point the way directly before one’s face, enabling one to practice so that the bodhicitta never regresses. For this reason, it follows from the preceding discussion on "encountering."

Regarding the causes and conditions for the Holy Masters and others, the passage beginning with "O sons of the Buddha" serves as a conclusion and an exhortation that one should seek [this realization].
Now, if one seeks it, it must be with a sincere heart; for unless one possesses a sincere heart, one cannot move [the Buddhas] to respond.

Since it is said that one seeks to see them with a sincere heart, the path of response and stimulus will intersect: either they will manifest their bodies and preach the Dharma within stillness, or they will bestow the truth within a dream.

The Essential Instruction: It is said that when the water of the sentient beings' minds is pure, the reflections of all Buddhas appear therein. △ Third, identifying the name and exhorting to practice:
"Good sons, this is called the essential dharma for transcending the world. You all should practice and study it with a single mind."
The mind for attaining Buddhahood is possessed by all sentient beings. Those who encounter the necessary conditions awaken and enter [the path] according to those conditions;
those who do not encounter them wander outwardly in pursuit. Since you all possess this mind, have heard this Dharma, and have met with superior conditions, how could you fail to practice?
Therefore, our World-Honored One exhorts us most earnestly: "Practice and study with a single mind. One...
As for the mind: it suddenly severs all affairs through the investigation of right mindfulness. This is what is meant by "focusing the mind on a single point;
there is no task that cannot be accomplished. △ Fourth, it is easy to realize Bodhi in an araṇya (hermitage).
Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva who has gone forth renounces the world and dwells in an araṇya. With little exertion of effort,
they attain the fulfillment of the eighty-four thousand practices of the pāramitās and swiftly realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The following is the direct answer to Maitreya’s question. Since the previous question asked why the araṇya is praised while other places are not, this is now answered.
The meaning is that other places are simply the mundane world, where the five desires disturb the mind.
It is difficult to advance on the Path; this is precisely why Bodhisattvas grow weary of desire and seek liberation. How could it be sufficient to praise [worldly life]?

Thus we know that world-weariness is the condition for leaving the home-life, while cultivation and realization are the foundation of leaving the home-life. One must have an araṇya as the place for practice;
since such a location is secluded and quiet, the fruits of the Path are easily accomplished. Therefore, it is said: "With few requirements, one's efforts are efficacious."
"Power. Regarding "attaining fulfillment," it means that sentient beings possess eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*).

Now, by observing them with concentration and wisdom, they suddenly and instantaneously become empty. Thus, afflictions are transformed into seeds of wisdom, and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is transmuted into nirvāṇa.

This *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is realized through direct confrontation; therefore, it is called "swift realization. △ Fifth, the inquiry and explanation regarding the ease of fulfilling the three perfections.
Why is this so? If one renounces fame and profit to dwell in mountain forests, one will certainly have no stinginess regarding body, life, or wealth.
Forever free from attachment, one naturally and easily fulfills the three types of *pāramitās*.
Why is this? It follows from what was stated previously: why is it that the word "only" (*kevalam*) serves as the indicator for the inquiry? The meaning is:

why must *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* necessarily depend upon dwelling in an *araṇya* before it can be swiftly realized? If we set aside the subsequent explanation, it means that once one has renounced the household life...
Regarding fame and profit: those who dwell in mountain forests must surely hold life lightly and value the Way, taking its realization as their goal.
They contemplate the body as frost upon the grass, life as a candle in the wind, and wealth as floating clouds in the sky;
therefore, it is said they will certainly have no stinginess. Thus, body, life, and wealth cannot bind or entangle their minds. This is why [they attain] Bodhi...

It is easily accomplished; hence it is said that they are "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*) and so forth. The three kinds of *pāramitās* refer to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) mentioned below, as well as the three kinds of "approaching the reality" (*tattva*).

One should understand that *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* (unsurpassed perfect enlightenment) is the general characteristic of the fruit of wisdom, while the three kinds of *pāramitās* are the specific characteristics of enlightenment. Furthermore, enlightenment constitutes self-benefit.
These three types [of giving] also benefit others; therefore, the intent of the inquiry lies there, while the intent of the answer lies here.
