Furthermore, as for the previous statement that one "perfects eighty-four thousand practices of the *pāramitās*," this mention of only three types is because the brief encompasses the extensive (the seclusion within mountains and forests is precisely the *araṇya*).
6. Regarding the question, the various *pāramitās* are further elucidated in two parts: 1. Maitreya’s question concerning giving (*dāna*).

Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how can a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya, who does not possess wealth or treasures, fulfill the perfection of dāna?"

This question is most pertinent. It is said that the Bodhisattva’s cultivation and realization take the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) as their cause, and among these six, the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā) is foremost.
Furthermore, giving can encompass all six. Now, following the Buddha’s teaching, you dwell in an araṇya and do not possess any wealth or goods.
As you wish to practice giving, what is there to bestow? If the perfection of giving is not practiced, then the six perfections [are incomplete].
[The Bodhisattva] was not satisfied. Since the cause—the practice—is insufficient, what fruit could possibly be realized? Therefore, he asks: "By what causes and conditions, etc.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s extensive demonstration has four parts. First, the direct answer regarding the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā).

The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Maitreya: "Good son, when a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya enters a village, whatever food he begs for, he first gives a small portion to sentient beings and gives another portion to those who desire it;
this is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). Furthermore, he offers his own body and life as an offering to the Triple Gem."
To bestow one’s head, eyes, marrow, and brain upon those who come seeking them is what is called the *upāya-pāramitā* (the perfection of skillful means).
To preach the supramundane Dharma for the sake of those who seek the Dharma, causing them to resolve upon unexcelled bodhicitta, is what is called the *bhūta-pāramitā* (the perfection of reality).
Son of good family, this is called a renunciant bodhisattva who has accomplished the *dāna-pāramitā* (the perfection of giving).
This section clarifies the Buddha’s intention: why must almsgiving necessarily consist of material wealth? It merely signifies that the mind is free from stinginess;
thus, the state of liberation itself is almsgiving. Although cultivation and realization take place in forest hermitages (araṇya), the practice of begging for food must be carried out in villages.
Regarding the food one has begged for: if one encounters a sentient being suffering from hunger, before eating it oneself, one should first give a small portion to them;

this is *dāna* (giving). (There are two explanations for this: first, having already obtained food, if one happens to encounter a person who is poor and hungry, out of compassion and an inability to bear their plight, one should first share some of the food to relieve them, even though one has not yet eaten.

This serves both to save the person and to establish a karmic connection (*kalyāṇamitra*). For a practitioner, compassion is the foundation, and this is also what is logically required. Second, since it specifies "a small portion," it refers to taking food out after the sequence of making offerings.)
"Give to the ghosts and spirits" (for ghosts and spirits are themselves sentient beings). The preceding section clarified what occurs before eating; this clarifies what occurs after eating.

"The remaining portion" refers to the leftovers of what was eaten. "Give to those who desire it" means that it is likewise appropriate for hungry people who wish to eat and thirsty people who wish to drink.
This concludes the names [of the recipients] below. The Chinese and Sanskrit terms correspond accordingly.
"Previously" refers to one of the three types of giving (dāna-pāramitā) categorized above.

It means that while one believes there is a path to be sought by means of one's own body and life, one fails to realize that these very things—body and so forth—are being offered as supreme sustenance to the Triple Gem and bestowed upon those who come seeking.
Among all forms of giving, the sacrifice of body and life is the most weighty. To "designate this as 'intimacy'" (*pratyāsatti*) is to speak of a mutual commitment; for indeed, there is...
Those whose resolve is to transcend the mundane world are intimate with the Way and not intimate with the body; they draw near to principle and distance themselves from phenomena.
Furthermore, it is not that the gentleman does not truly love his own body, but when weighed against the Way, he cannot preserve both;
he must simply be able to relinquish what is most difficult to relinquish, which is the practice of a Bodhisattva. This is the third point of the previous section.
This is the second [category]. Since one has already brought oneself close to the principle through kinship and drawn near to the Way, how could one not ascend high to the other shore?

Therefore, this concluding name is called the "Perfection of Intimacy" (*upaniṣad-pāramitā*). Regarding the phrase "for those who seek the Dharma," it means that one prioritizes one's own benefit before benefiting others;
this is the most excellent among the perfections of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). Truly, for one who seeks the Dharma, there must necessarily be transcendence.
Regarding the mind of the world, one must preach the supramundane Dharma to those who seek it, causing them to resolve upon Bodhicitta and ensuring they likewise achieve the Unsurpassed Way.
Thus, the merit of benefiting both self and others cannot be exceeded.
As for the title "The True Other Shore," it signifies that the name corresponds to its meaning; it refers to the realization of principle. This is precisely the three aforementioned types...
Third. Regarding the various *pāramitās* below, they are all fundamentally named as "one. Generally, not sparing one's body or life is called "intimacy" (*upaniṣad*);
generally, whatever benefits others is termed "reality" (*tattva*). All [subsequent items] follow this principle. △ Second, the clarification of the various *pāramitās* has nine parts.
First, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). Furthermore, son of good family, because an ordained bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, he practices the twelve dhūta ascetic virtues.
When walking, he looks at the ground two cubits ahead so as not to harm living beings; thus, he is said to possess the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).
The perfection of generosity. Firmly upholding the precepts without sparing even one's own body or life is called the perfection of proximity.
Seeking the transcendence of the world, preaching the Dharma to transform others, and causing them to resolve upon unsurpassed bodhicitta is called the perfection of reality.
Good son, these are called the perfections of ethical discipline achieved by a renunciant bodhisattva.
Many. The twelve *dhūta* practices are explained as in the section on the *vinaya* in five fascicles. Regarding "two *hasta*s of ground": one *hasta* of the Buddha is three feet six inches;
one *hasta* of a human is one foot eight inches. Here, it is calculated according to the human measure, meaning two [human *hasta*s].
An elbow measures three chi and six cun. A bhikṣu who maintains the full precepts does not look to the side when walking, nor does he gaze far ahead.
Whenever he takes a step, he looks only two elbows’ length of ground before him; this is because he dares not injure even the most minute insects.
This may be called the ultimate expression of compassion. Yet it is not merely a matter of compassion alone; rather, he focuses his mind exclusively so that no thoughts arise.

Free from deluded thoughts, one’s progress becomes serene and composed, further inspiring the hearts of others with reverence. This is what is meant by having a majestic presence that inspires awe and possessing virtue that commands respect;
thus, one attains the designation of a "venerable" (arhat). The above has been explained in terms of the *saṃvara-śīla* (precepts of restraint) among the three clusters of precepts (*tri-śīla*).
Those who uphold the firm prohibitory precepts possess the Bodhisattva precepts, as pure and bright as ice and frost.

Not only do they not transgress them with their bodies, but even when encountering objects and conditions, their minds remain unmoved. This is what is meant by one crossing the sea who cherishes their life-preserving float.
Therefore, it is called "firm and steadfast. Regarding "not sparing one's body or life," as stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*: for the sake of the Dharma, one may extinguish the body;

one requests the Dharma without weariness; and one burns the body, the arms, or the fingers. If one does not burn the body, arms, or fingers as an offering to the Buddhas, one is not a renunciant bodhisattva and so forth.
As for "immediately attaining the name of 'intimate' (親近) at the conclusion of the section below," this refers to being close to and honoring [the Buddha].

The Buddha’s precepts are close to and respectful of principle, for they enable one to reach the other shore; this is precisely the *śīla* of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of seeking" (*yǐ qiú xià*), the first sentence lacks the character "one" (*yī*); this refers to those who seek the Dharma, as it is also stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.

Seeing later students of the Dharma who have come from as far as a hundred or a thousand *li* to seek the Mahāyāna sūtras and vinaya, one should explain them to them according to the Dharma and so forth, causing those who hear it to generate the bodhicitta.
Because one attributes the merit of this altruistic virtue to oneself, it constitutes a true *pāramitā*. This is the precept of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings. Well done.
The conclusion for the men below can be understood accordingly (this is all explained in terms of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattva precepts). △ Second, the Perfection of Patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Furthermore, son of good family, when a renunciant bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, he is able to extinguish anger and attains the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta-samādhi*).
He also does not disparage or insult any sentient beings; this is then called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). If...
To speak a single phrase of Dharma for a single person, causing them to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
is what is called the true *pāramitā*. Son of good family, this is called a renunciant bodhisattva who has accomplished the *pāramitā* of patience (*kṣānti*).
"To be able to extinguish anger" means that when others inflict insults upon a bodhisattva, their mind remains unmoved;
this is called the extinction of anger. "Attaining the samādhi of loving-kindness" means not only being free from anger, but rather giving rise to compassion and pity in its place.
Pitying those who are ignorant, one should not disparage or humiliate them; that is, "what you do not desire for yourself, do not inflict upon others.
This concludes the title [of this section]. As for the practice: while practicing patience (*kṣānti*) benefits oneself alone, preaching the Dharma also benefits others.
However, preaching even a single verse to a single person is not restricted by the literal wording; for if it is so for one person, it is likewise for all.
The same applies to the multitude. It is simply that causing them to resolve upon Bodhicitta is what is paramount; they are bound together as practitioners of the true path.
This means that once one possesses the name of a Bodhisattva, there must truly be conduct that accords with that reality. (The section on "Sons of Good Family" below concludes their names.
[The minor section on "Cultivating Intimacy" was likely omitted during transcription; there is no need for forced interpretation]. △ Third, the Degree of Progress.)
Furthermore, good son, an ordained bodhisattva, in order to cause sentient beings to attain Buddhahood, cultivates the practice of vigor.
Although he has not yet attained Buddhahood and his merit and wisdom are still weak, he does not crave ease and comfort, nor does he commit various transgressions.
Regarding the ascetic practices performed by bodhisattvas in the past, he gives rise to deep joy, looking up with reverence and admiration, never ceasing for a moment. By these causes...

This condition is precisely what is called the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*). To cast aside body and life as if discarding mucus or spittle, never succumbing to indolence at any time, is precisely what is called the perfection of intimacy (*upaniṣad-pāramitā*).

When encountering those with the necessary conditions, to teach the supreme path and cause them to advance toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*) is precisely what is called the perfection of reality (*tattva-pāramitā*).
Through the mind of diligence, these ten practices are such that they do not regress in the past, are firm in the present, and will be swiftly fulfilled in the future.
Son of good family, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva who has gone forth and has accomplished the perfection of diligence (vīrya-pāramitā).
"Causing [them] to descend below" reveals the fundamental intent of his diligence; it is not for himself alone.
Because all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, yet are shrouded by ignorance and entangled in the net of karma, they are unable to achieve Buddhahood.

Therefore, he personally cultivates diligence so that he may first achieve Buddhahood himself and subsequently deliver them. "Not having attained [it] below" explains his prior achievement of Buddhahood.
The intention is this: thinking that as long as one has not yet attained Buddhahood, one's merit and wisdom are weak;

thus, fearing that sentient beings might remain deluded, fail to awaken, and be difficult to transform, one first attains Buddhahood for oneself. Possessing supernatural powers and wisdom, one is then able to subdue them and preach the Dharma.
By means of teachings suited to the occasion and the supernatural powers of transformation, sentient beings may attain liberation.
"Not being greedy for" [the lower realms] further explains the meaning of having already attained success; there are two interpretations. First, not being greedy for one's own peace and happiness;
second, also because one does not commit various transgressions, one has thus already attained success. "In the past," etc., refers to emulating the ancients and following their practice.
This means that one should give rise to profound joy regarding the ascetic practices performed by past Bodhisattvas; this is what is meant by "meeting the occasion.
However, without diligence, one cannot attain the fruit of Buddhahood, and without ascetic practice, one cannot manifest diligence.
Now, wishing to be able to perform ascetic practices so as to make diligence even firmer, and through the firmness of that diligence, one will certainly achieve Buddhahood.
Swiftly. This is why one uplifts oneself in reverent devotion and looks up to him with longing. "Uplifted" (qiao) also implies diligence, like a bird spreading its wings while looking for food.

"Reverent" (jing) refers to humble submission within the heart; "model" (zong) means honoring him to take his principles as a standard; and "looking up" (yang) expresses the sincerity of thirsty yearning.

Therefore, one must surely succeed in practicing it. This is why it is said that there is always no rest. This concludes the section on the name based on causes and conditions, which refers to the primary teaching of revering ascetic practice.
Regarding "discarding [the self]" below: this means holding life lightly and the Path as paramount, forgetting one's own body for the sake of the Dharma.
Because at all times one has never been indolent, one draws near to principle and approaches the Path. Thus, the conclusion states:

"Approaching [the teacher]" and so forth. "Encountering those of lower capacity": this means that while approaching [the teacher] can only benefit oneself, it is from this point onward that one is able to benefit others.

"The supreme path" refers to the teachings of the Perfect and Sudden (Yuan-dun) and the Ultimate Reality (Zhong-shi). "Causing them to proceed toward" means desiring to receive the teachings and realize the fruit.
However, in preaching the Dharma, one must encounter those with whom there is a karmic affinity, for they are easy to deliver. Thus, it is concluded by naming it "True Reality."
Because his teaching of the Dharma is called the discourse on the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), it causes others to advance toward Bodhi;
furthermore, he realizes it by conforming to the limit of reality. This is termed "correspondence with reality," and thus the name is established based on this reality.

From the passage beginning with "By means of diligence" onwards, it concerns the benefits accomplished through causal practice. As for the "ten practices," these are the practices performed by the ten perfections (*pāramitā*). [Past...]

Below, the text correctly clarifies the great benefits accomplished throughout the three periods of time. Regarding the past, since his diligence is described as "ascetic practice," its roots are deep and firm, and thus he does not retreat.
Regarding the present, his diligence is characterized by the vow to deliver sentient beings; because his resolve is free from cowardice, it is called "steadfast.
Regarding the future, enlightenment will not require a long duration, and thus it is said to be "swiftly fulfilled. This is excellent.
The man’s name is established based on his actual status. △ Fourth, the Dhyāna-pāramitā.

Furthermore, son of good family, a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya cultivates samādhi in order to gather all dharmas so they are not lost, to enter the various liberations, to forever sever extreme views, and to manifest supernatural powers to transform those multitudes.

To cause [beings] to give birth to right knowledge, sever the root of afflictions, enter the true Dharma-realm, awaken to the path of reality as it is, and proceed toward Bodhi— by these causes and conditions,
this is named the Perfection of Meditative Concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*). Desiring to cause sentient beings to be no different from oneself,
so that they may all attain fulfillment, one tames sentient beings, does not abandon samādhi, and cultivates this without sparing body or life.

Samādhi is thus named the Perfection of Intimacy (*upaniṣad-pāramitā*). To preach the profound and wondrous Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, causing them all to incline toward unsurpassed bodhi, is thus named the Perfection of Reality (*tattva-pāramitā*).
Noble son, this is called a renunciant bodhisattva who has accomplished the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi-pāramitā*).
"Samādhi" (三昧) is synonymous with "right reception" (正受) and is another term for meditative concentration (禪定).
"All dharmas" refers to the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and the latter five perfections. "Gathering" (攝) carries the meaning of grasping or holding;

"causing them not to be lost or scattered" precisely clarifies the power of samādhi to grasp and maintain these qualities. For instance, regarding the perfection of giving: if it were not held by samādhi, then...
Engaging in deluded conceptualization scatters one’s efforts into conditioned activities; even if one thereby gains merit, it remains entirely outflowing (sāsrava).
By being sustained by samādhi, one does not give rise to deluded thoughts and turns toward the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta);

thus all activities become non-outflowing (anāsrava), and that which is attained will necessarily be the wondrous fruit of Bodhi. This is the case for this one perfection; it is the same for all the perfections.
Therefore, it is said that one "enters all liberations. Here, "entry" means harmonious accord; "all" refers to the nine perfections as well as all phenomena.

By being sustained by samādhi, one does not turn according to objects or conditions when encountering them. This can be described as the myriad affairs being in turmoil while the single mind remains unmoved;
hence, it is called "liberation. Regarding the phrase "permanently severing extreme views," this refers not only to the severance [of views] by non-Buddhists.

They constantly fall into extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). This clearly demonstrates that regarding all dharmas through the various perfections (*pāramitā*), as long as one has not attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) to maintain them, one cannot avoid adhering to either the phenomenal or the noumenal aspect as a single extreme;
all such instances belong to extreme views. The above has been discussed primarily in terms of the essence of the virtues for one's own benefit.

"Manifesting below" refers to the arising of function based on the essence; that is, the manifestation of physical transformations and supernatural powers that permeate all beings, both noble and ordinary, as an unfathomable efficacy.
"Transforming those sentient beings so they may attain right wisdom" refers to the arising of compassion for the benefit of living beings.
Because one has personally abandoned extremes and heterodoxy to attain right wisdom oneself, one causes others to do likewise; because one has personally severed the afflictions...
It also causes others to sever [delusion]. The "Fundamental" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the root of all afflictions (*kleśa*).
"Entering the True Dharma-realm" refers to the wondrous principle of the single truth, the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) where all Buddhas realize the Way.

"Awakening to the Path of Suchness" means that awakening is the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*); "suchness" (*tathatā*) is true suchness; "reality" (*bhūtatā*) is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This is because true suchness is reality...
The *lakṣaṇa* (mark) is the fundamental substance of all phenomena (*dharmas*). If one awakens to it, then all phenomena merge into the single reality, and all become the true path.
That which leads toward *bodhi* is precisely the ultimate fruit of Buddhahood. All that precedes this constitutes first benefiting oneself and subsequently benefiting others;
thus, the following section is named by taking up the latter to conclude the former. Hereafter, the discussion shall be strictly limited to benefiting others.

This manifests the ultimate extent of compassion (*karuṇā*). However, while those who have already been transformed are led to attain right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), there remain those who have not yet been reached by transformation;
thus, he makes a vow, desiring that all sentient beings be no different from himself. This is also a dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) for the sake of sentient beings.
Regarding "taming" (*vinaya*) below: although the above possesses the compassion that benefits others and the vow of dedication, it seems as though [the taming] has not yet been fully realized.
To "appear in person" means that his current subduing of beings constitutes the manifestation of his body to preach the Dharma. "Not abandoning samādhi" signifies being still amidst movement.
"Not sparing one's own body or life" reveals the intensity of his altruistic resolve; he does not regard his own body or life as of primary importance.
Furthermore, within the gateway of benefiting others, he acts without acting; through transforming and benefiting the ten directions, he acts without action.
When the essence itself remains unmoved, one may be said to be intimately aligned with principle and near to the Way; thus, it concludes by stating "intimate approach to the pāramitās.

The phrase "for all those below" clarifies that the teaching is given while in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Since one is already within concentration, teaching without speaking is called the "wondrous Dharma," and speaking without speaking is called the "profound and wondrous Dharma.
The phrase "all cause [them] below" refers to enabling those sentient beings who are to be transformed.
This refers to progressing toward the fruit of Buddhahood. Regarding the phrase "is called" (*ming xia*), it concludes by designating it as "true reality" (*zhenshi*):

because the teaching expounded within meditative concentration accords with *tathatā* (suchness) and is real, it is named "true reality. Regarding the phrase "good son" (*shannan xia*), it summarizes the name of the concentration. △ Fifth, the Perfection of Wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Furthermore, son of good family, a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in seclusion should draw near to and make offerings to all Buddhas, bodhisattvas, and omniscient ones.
He should always delight in hearing the profound and wondrous Dharma, giving rise to a heart of yearning that is never satiated.

He should be skillful in discerning the truth of the two realities (*satyadvaya*), severing the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), and attaining mastery in the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), thereby expounding all dharmas.
Essential. Because it can resolve the doubts of the multitude, for these reasons it is named Prajñāpāramitā.
Regarding "dwelling in seclusion": "dwelling" (chu) refers to the place where one resides with the body; "seclusion" (kongxian) is precisely the araṇya.
"Approaching" (親近) refers to relying upon the essential nature of the aforementioned meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). This reveals that the great function is fully manifested.

Since it says "approaching and making offerings to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas," this means that without arising from the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samādhi*), one manifests various dignified postures (*īryāpatha*).
From being able to manifest a hundred thousand bodies from a single body, up to clouds of infinite bodies, one reaches everywhere throughout infinite Buddha-lands to make offerings.
They nurture immeasurable Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Regarding those of "all-encompassing wisdom" (sarvajña), there are two explanations:
first, that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas themselves are the persons of all-encompassing wisdom; second, that all sentient beings with the great resolve are wise ones.
The intention is not merely to make offerings to the Buddha, but also to make offerings to sentient beings. Thus, by drawing near and making offerings, one obtains merit;

by constantly delighting in hearing [the Dharma] and so forth, one plants the seeds of wisdom. However, regarding the Dharma that is heard: it is the "wondrous Dharma" when each type of being understands according to their own kind;

it is the "profound and wondrous Dharma" when those with great capacities truly enter into it; and it is the "most profound and wondrous Dharma" when it is perfect, sudden, and unsurpassed. This is because...
Because the mind seeking the Dharma is supreme, one gives rise to yearning and reverence; because one vows to study the gates of the Dharma, one is never weary or satisfied.
"Skillfully able to humble oneself" [refers to] further receiving the teaching of the Perfection of Wisdom, which is the vow to deliver all sentient beings. Regarding the "truth of the two truths":

the first is the True Truth (*satyadharma*), which is the principle of the reality of the single nature (*ekaprakṛti*). This is what is called the fundamental ground of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
There is no differentiation; both affirmation and negation are extinguished, and subject and object are simultaneously stilled.

Taking the myriad phenomena as True Suchness (*tathatā*) and unifying the Three Vehicles (the Vehicle of Śrāvakas, the Vehicle of Pratyekabuddhas, and the Vehicle of Bodhisattvas) as the Ultimate Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one speaks in accordance with the True Principle; therefore, it is called the "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*).
Second, regarding the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*): it reveals the phenomena of the single-natured dependent origination.
That is to say, within the gateway of the Buddha’s work, not a single dharma is abandoned; subjects are exhorted to loyalty, children to filial piety, nations to order, and families to harmony.

By promoting goodness, it reveals the bliss of heaven; by punishing evil, it manifests the suffering of hell; and it elucidates all causes, conditions, and karmic retributions according to worldly convention.
Therefore, it is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Yet, both truths are termed "ultimate reality" (*tattva*):
this means that while the ultimate truth is true in its own essence, the conventional truth is true in its phenomena. Both, without exception, are reality.

Regarding this ultimate principle: there are two obstructions, namely the afflictive obstruction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstruction (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). The afflictions can obstruct wholesome matters and are thus also called the "obstruction to matters" (*vastvāvaraṇa*).

The object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is the principle to be realized and is not itself an obstruction; however, because one clings to that principle of the object of knowledge, it becomes an obstruction.

Furthermore, because it can obstruct the principle, it is also called the "obstruction to the principle" (*tattvāvaraṇa*). The term "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*) carries the meaning of "to veil" or "to conceal. True...

Wisdom cannot penetrate or transcend [the conventional]; it derives its name from its function. A Bodhisattva employs the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) and eloquence (*pratibhāna*) to reveal the essential nature and characteristics [of phenomena], enabling people to sever [delusion].

Regarding the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), there are five types. Because they penetrate both phenomena and principle (*dharma* and *tattva*) without obstruction, they are called the "five sciences.

The first is the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*). "Sound" (*śabda*) refers to the teachings expressed through sound; "science" (*vidyā*) means clear understanding. This refers to worldly literature.
1. Calculation (*saṃkhyā-vidyā*): Because one has thoroughly understood and mastered the methods for establishing [numerical systems]. 2. Logic (*hetu-vidyā*):

"Cause" (*hetu*) refers to the fundamental basis from which all phenomena arise; because one has thoroughly understood the various worldly discourses, as well as diagrams, seals, and insignia—the causes of the myriad phenomena—along with the four great elements and the five phases (*pañca-mahābhūta*, *pañca-dhātu*). 3. Medical Science (*cikitsā-vidyā*): That is, the science of medical treatment.

It is also a method. This refers to the thorough understanding of the various ailments of the world, such as epilepsy, demonic poisons, the imbalance of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), curses by spirits and deities, and diseases of cold and heat.

Fourth is the science of arts and crafts (*śilpakarmasthāna-vidyā*), which refers to skill in the arts and crafts, including worldly rhetoric and verse composition, as well as the construction of cities and towns, agriculture, and irrigation.

[The fifth is] inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*). "Inner" refers to the internal teachings of the Buddha-dharma. This means that by means of ethical discipline one remedies the breaking of precepts; by means of meditative concentration one remedies distraction; and by means of wisdom one remedies ignorance. It extends to all varieties of defilement and purity, the false and the correct, and birth-and-death. As for the merchant class, various types of music, divination, and the calculation of celestial phenomena and terrestrial geography—all these are fully understood. Thus, there are five [sciences]. Inner science is the internal teaching of the Buddha-dharma. That is to say, one uses the observance of precepts to remedy the violation of precepts; meditative concentration to remedy mental scattering;
and wisdom to remedy delusion, even extending to all manner of defiled and pure, false and correct, and samsaric states.

Because one has clearly understood all the dharmas that serve as antidotes to *nirvāṇa*, and because one is clear and unimpeded regarding these five dharmas, it is said that one "has mastered the five sciences" (*pañcavidyāsthāna*).
Regarding the "essential points of all dharmas": "all dharmas" refers to the complete inclusion of all mundane and supramundane phenomena;
"essentials" means "sublime," referring to that which can encompass much within a little. As the *Avataṃsaka* says: "All..."
All is created by mind alone. Through wisdom and eloquence, one can realize that the myriad phenomena all return to the single mind;

the mind is the essential core of all dharmas. To resolve the doubts of others—doubt meaning hesitation and indecision, whether regarding persons, phenomena, or oneself—the Bodhisattva provides a single word in times of urgency, enabling them to reach a definitive conclusion and attain right faith. Below.
This is the textual conclusion. Because it is well able to discern causes and conditions, it is given the name *prajñāpāramitā*.
In the Sanskrit language, *prajñā* means "wisdom" (*hui zhi*); *pāramitā* is as explained previously.

For the sake of seeking even half a verse, one discards body and life, undaunted by manifold sufferings until reaching great enlightenment; thus, one immediately achieves the perfection of intimacy (*upaniṣad-pāramitā*).
To abandon one’s entire body for the sake of half a verse, as our World-Honored One did— sacrificing his body to a rākṣasa in order to seek half a verse because he knew only that the Dharma exists,
yet was unaware of the existence of the body— and likewise, to endure all manner of sufferings until reaching Great Bodhi,
as our World-Honored One did when, in a previous life as a king, he made a vow to diligently seek unsurpassed bodhi and struck [the gong].
He proclaimed his resolve and sought the Dharma in all four directions. He paid homage to the seer Asita, gathering fruits, drawing water, collecting firewood, and preparing food;

he even used his own body as a seat for him. Knowing only the existence of his teacher and being unaware of himself, he took those provisions at that time as the cause, which now results in the fruit of Buddhahood; thus it is said that he has reached great Bodhi, the state of all-enlightenment.

The practitioner should act in this way: by making the path their kin and the body distant, and by drawing near to the teacher while remaining remote from status, they shall achieve accomplishment through the very name of the bond (*saṃdhi*).
Within the great assembly, they shall preach the Dharma for others, never withholding or begrudging the profound and wondrous meanings, thereby enabling them to give rise [to realization].

Regarding the great bodhicitta, one attains non-retrogression in the bodhisattva practices and is constantly able to observe that one’s own body, the araṇya, the bodhicitta, and the true dharmakāya—these four—are without distinction. Thus it is, thus it is.

Because they contemplate the wondrous principle, they are named True Perfection (bhūta-pāramitā). Good son, this is called a renunciant bodhisattva who has accomplished the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
To preach the Dharma within a great assembly, one must necessarily possess fearless eloquence (*vaiśāradya*). That which is profound and subtle meaning is precisely the Buddha’s mind-dharma;
it is known only by those who have realized it. As it is said: "The path of language is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity ceases;

it is fundamentally beyond thought and deliberation. Therefore, it is called "subtle meaning. That I now nevertheless speak it for the sake of others is because I manifest the principle through words and employ words to reveal it.

This is because of the principle [of the Dharma]. If there were ultimately no teaching at all, then the Perfection of Wisdom would be useless. "That which is not hidden" means that one conceals it within one's own realization;

"that which is not cherished" means protecting it by not speaking of it. These are both faults of stinginess regarding the Dharma and constitute a great transgression for one who propagates the teachings.
When it is now said that "there is nothing hidden or cherished," this refers to the fact that for a beginner, [realization] must depend upon words.
Because he has seen the Path, he instructs others according to what he has studied and leads others to realization according to what he has realized himself.

He possesses a public-spirited mind and is free from the fault of stinginess regarding the Dharma. The phrase "is able to" [in the context of] the following four lines establishes the efficacy of benefiting others.

The phrase "constantly able to" [in the context of] the following [lines] directs one toward the practice of observing daily activities. This is intended so that principle and phenomena may be harmonized.

Pervasive. Because they are bound together as reality, one contemplates one's own body as the person who relies upon the *araṇya*, and further contemplates the *araṇya* as the place upon which one's body relies; both of these belong to the category of phenomenal phenomena (*vastu-dharma*).
Bodhicitta is the mind that desires to realize awakening, which is wisdom; it is the cause for attaining Buddhahood. Reality.
The *dharmakāya* refers to taking true suchness (*tathatā*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as the body; it is the fruit to be realized.

These two [the *svābhāvikakāya* and the *dharmakāya*] are both explained in terms of principle (*li*). Thus, these four types refer to the four dharmas of the aforementioned locus of the body, cause, and fruit.

That they are without distinction means that through the observation of sublime wisdom, phenomena are seen as true within their very occurrence; they are harmoniously integrated and non-dual. This is what is meant by "the three realms."
Sharing the same root with me, the myriad dharmas and I are of one essence; therefore it is said, "Thus, thus. The first "thus" is a term for pointing out the dharma;
the second "thus" is a term for certification. "Contemplating the Subtle" below concludes the preceding and initiates what follows.
"Immediately attaining" below concludes the name of reality. "Good son" below concludes the general heading of Prajñā. △ Six: Expedient Means.

[The Buddha] said, "Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva who has gone forth dwells in a secluded place and is constantly able to cultivate the pāramitā of superior wisdom through skillful means.
By means of the knowledge of others' minds, he is able to comprehend the inclinations, afflictions, and mental activities of sentient beings."

It is distinct. Administering medicine according to the illness, it causes all to be healed and cured. One freely sports in supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and samādhis, gives rise to the vow of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā-praṇidhāna*), and brings sentient beings to maturity. There is no dharma of the Buddhas that is not thoroughly mastered.
For these reasons, it is named the Perfection of Skillful Means (*upāyakauśalya-pāramitā*).

Regarding "expedient means" (*upāya*): "fang" (方) means "dharma," and "bian" (便) means "benefit. A bodhisattva employs superior wisdom to observe the capacities of sentient beings, utilizing skillful methods to benefit others.
This is also the ancient method of the Buddhas of the past; by studying and practicing it, one is said to "cultivate and practice.
Observing the task of delivering sentient beings in every thought-moment without ceasing, one is said to be "constantly able."
Because by means of this, both self and others reach the further shore (*pāra*), it is called *pāramitā*. Regarding the "knowledge of others' minds" (*paracittajñāna*):
the Bodhisattva, through the supernormal power of knowledge (*jñānābhijñā*), penetrates the mental thoughts of others and is able to understand them all;

therefore, it is said that he "is able to comprehend sentient beings (*sattva*) and so forth. "Sentient beings" is a general term for all living creatures, as they possess consciousness (*sacittaka*). Thus, based on...
"Deluded consciousness constitutes 'name. Regarding "intentions and desires," "intent" refers to the mental thoughts of others;

"desires" refers to the joy of others' minds; "afflictions" refers to the sorrow and suffering of the mind; and "distinctions in mental activity" refers to the various discursive thoughts of the mental faculty (*manas*).

All of these are spoken in reference to the sentient beings who are the objects of observation. As for "administering medicine according to the illness": "illness" refers to [the afflictions of] sentient beings.

The mental reflection is the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of the Bodhisattva. For example, causing sentient beings with excessive greed to practice the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), and causing those with excessive hatred to practice the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion (*maitrī-karuṇā-bhāvanā*), thereby enabling them all to be cured—that is, to practice the transcendence of suffering—is like a skilled physician administering medicine:

as soon as it reaches the ailment, the disease is eliminated. (The character *chā* is pronounced in the departing tone; it signifies the recovery from illness. This refers to such things as the "sovereign play" (*vibhutva-vikrīḍita*).
Responding to things without self-interest is like the moon descending upon the hundred rivers; this is called "sovereignty" (svatantra), manifesting transformations according to circumstances.
Like the wind passing through the great void, it is called "playful sport" (vikrīḍita). All these are profound, wondrous, and spiritually penetrating, never departing from their very locus;

therefore, they are called "supernormal powers" (abhijñā). Because movement is itself stillness, it is called "samādhi. Great Compassion and Vow are the foundation of skillful means (upāya). Thus it is perfected.

This is the ripening of the fruit of the compassionate vow for sentient beings. The two subsequent lines refer to all Buddhas. The Dharma does not transcend the provisional and the real, nor the Small and the Great Vehicles.
To "penetrate" means to have ultimate and clear understanding. The phrase "by these causes and conditions" and following serves to conclude the preceding section by establishing the title.
Because they desire to benefit all sentient beings, they do not cling to or begrudge their body, life, or wealth; this is what is called "approaching the pāramitās.
Because they treat enemies and kin with equanimity for the sake of all sentient beings, they preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma to lead them into the Buddha-wisdom;
this is what is called "the true pāramitā. Good son, these are called the renunciant bodhisattva...
"Sā. To have accomplished the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya-pāramitā*) such that one does not cling at all to body, life, or wealth, truly means to draw near to the Path.

Such a person does not even perceive the existence of body or life, let alone material possessions. "Gù" (固) means to hold fast; "xī" (惜) means to be stingy or parsimonious. Because the Bodhisattva possesses great compassion...
With such an urgent mind of compassion for the benefit of sentient beings, how could one be willing to stubbornly cling to one's own body and possessions, rather than acting for the sake of others?

Yet, among the benevolent men and righteous scholars of the world who seek to perfect their virtue—such as Jing Ke, Yu Rang, and others—they still did not spare their own lives and souls, let alone a Bodhisattva.
Thus, by relying on virtue, one attains renown; therefore it is said, "approaching [the teacher]," and so forth, regarding enemies and kin.
Equanimity is precisely where the Bodhisattva greatly forgets worldly affairs.

Since one contemplates the equality of the Buddha-nature, how could one treat enemies with distance while benefiting those who are kin? To preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma is the Mahāyāna teaching;
to cause others to enter the wisdom of the Buddha is the fruit of the Mahāyāna. Because it accords with true practice, it concludes with the seal of reality.
[This concludes] the name. "Good son," and so forth, summarizes the section below. △ Seven: The Vow to Deliver.

Furthermore, good son, when a renunciant bodhisattva enters the mountain forests, they are able to constantly practice the perfection of the vow (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) for the sake of all sentient beings.
Their minds constantly observe the true nature of all phenomena as being neither existent nor empty—the wondrous Middle Way.
Regarding principle, they are fully able to discern all conventional matters; for the sake of transforming sentient beings, they constantly cultivate loving-kindness and compassion.
By reason of these causes and conditions, this is termed the perfection of aspiration (praṇidhāna-pāramitā).
"Vow" (*praṇidhāna*) refers to that which the mind esteems; it is the aspiration for the dual benefit of both oneself and others. "The mind is ever... and the following two lines [refer to this].
All phenomena do not transcend the eighteen *dhātus*, as well as all causes and effects of defilement and purity. "True nature" (*tathatā*) is the true ontological essence of all phenomena.
When present in sentient beings, it is called *buddhadhātu* (Buddha-nature); when present in insentient things, it is called *dharmatā* (Dharma-nature). This is...

This is the object of contemplation. The passage beginning with "It is not existent" (非有) correctly clarifies the meaning of true nature (*tathatā*). That is to say, the true nature of all phenomena has no form when viewed, and is therefore not existent;
yet it responds according to conditions, and is therefore not empty. Existence is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while emptiness is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
However, since it is said to be "neither existent nor empty," then emptiness and existence do not entangle one another, and the ultimate and the conventional do not obstruct each other.
"Unfettered" (bujī) is termed the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). The two characters "subtle principle" (*miliǎo*) signify the meaning of the Middle Way as being neither entangled nor unfettered.
All that precedes is explained in terms of contemplating principle (*li*); from "in the mundane" (*yú shìsú*) onwards, all is explained in terms of contemplating phenomena (*shì*).
Mundane phenomena refer to the various dependent arisings of good and evil, heterodox and orthodox; the Bodhisattva employs wisdom to discern them clearly, such that there is nothing not understood.
Indeed, this is the foundation for the two benefits of a bodhisattva. The phrase "in order to transform sentient beings" refers specifically to the vow of benefiting others.
For without compassion, one can never benefit others; thus, the following concludes the definition [of the name].
(Question: How is compassion cultivated? Answer: To cultivate it is to maintain an unceasing mindfulness of the task of delivering sentient beings.)
By embracing sentient beings through the four great vows, and even sacrificing one’s body without breaking one’s compassionate vow, one is said to have attained the *pāramitā* of intimacy.
By preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma with unimpeded eloquence, such that those who hear it never ultimately regress, one is said to have attained the *pāramitā* of reality.
Good son, this is called the accomplishment of a renunciant bodhisattva.
Regarding the *pāramitā* of aspiration, there are the Four Great Vows:
"Sentient beings are boundless; I vow to deliver them," and so on, up to "The Buddha-way is unsurpassed; I vow to attain it.

Furthermore, as stated below, this means disregarding even one's own body and life, never abandoning compassionate vows, and binding oneself to those who are close through these compassionate vows. Compassionate vows.

This is the reality [of the teaching]. The following two phrases explain the subtle: it means that the Dharma does not consist in profound mystery to be considered wondrous; rather, its value lies in its accordance with the capacities [of beings].

What is called "wondrous" is the exercise of skillful means (*upāya*) based upon reality; when skillful means do not lose sight of reality, it is "subtle and wondrous. To discern between the true and the false is called "discernment" (*pratibhāna*);

to employ this so as to accord with principle is called "talent" (*pratibhāna*). Because he possesses clear discernment and talent, and mastery over both the provisional and the real, [he is so described]. Thus...
It is said: "Unobstructed. The passage beginning with "If there are those who hear" clarifies how sentient beings obtain benefit.

Since it is stated that they do not regress, this sufficiently demonstrates the truth of the wondrous Dharma and the reality of its eloquence. Thus, it is concluded by naming it the "True Other Shore."
This is also a name established based on actual reality. "Good son," and so forth, concludes the name of the vow. △ Eight: Power of the Forces.

Furthermore, good son, a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya, by means of the power of correct wisdom, thoroughly understands the black and white mental activities of sentient beings and is able to preach the appropriate Dharma for them, causing them to enter the profound and wondrous Mahāyāna.
This meaning is that one is able to abide securely in ultimate *nirvāṇa*. For this reason, it is called the *bala-pāramitā* (perfection of power).
"Power" refers to the practical application of wisdom. "Mental activity" refers to the deluded thoughts of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*). "Black and white" refers to good and evil.

These are alternative designations. Generally, white represents wholesome thoughts and black represents unwholesome thoughts. "To be able to act as the lower" means that when the teaching accords with the capacity of the recipient, it is called the "corresponding dharma.
For example, if sentient beings contemplate black karma in their minds, [the Buddha] explains for them the retributive fruits of the hells and the three miserable paths without fail.
If they contemplate white karma in their minds, he then explains that the causes and effects of precepts and goodness follow one another like shadows following forms. This causes [them to...]
Regarding "entering the Mahāyāna" and so forth: it is as taught that all conventional expressions accord with the Tathāgata’s ultimate path.
Regarding "being able to abide therein" and so forth: it is as taught that the minor assemblies of humans and devas ultimately converge in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
As for the term "ultimate" (*niṣṭhā*) in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it refers to the title of the Buddha-fruit; it does not mean death. This is because one skillfully observes the activities of the mind.

Teaching the Dharma in accordance with the capacity of the listener is the manifestation of the power of wisdom. Therefore, it is summarized by the phrase "for this cause and condition," and so forth (*Nirvāṇa*—here translated as "perfect quiescence"—refers to the True Principle;

it is inherently perfect and without deficiency, while delusive afflictions are inherently quiescent and originally non-existent. It is also called "extinction and liberation" (*nirvāṇa*), meaning the extinction and removal of the afflictions of the five abodes, and the transcendence of the two kinds of birth-and-death).

By means of the eye of right wisdom, one perceives the principle that the five aggregates are empty and quiescent; because one is able to sacrifice body and life for the benefit of sentient beings, this is termed the "perfection of intimacy.

By means of the power of wondrous wisdom, one transforms those with false views, causing them to sever the evil karma of saṃsāra and birth-and-death, and to proceed toward the ultimate nirvāṇa of eternal bliss; this is termed "true perfection."
Pāramitā. Good son, this is called the bodhisattva who has left the home life.

Having accomplished the perfection of power (*balapāramitā*) and taking wisdom as his eye, he is thus named "Wisdom-Eyed" (*jñānacakṣus*). The illumination that perceives these two characters is precisely the *prajñā* of contemplative observation (*vipaśyanā*).

The five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) do not refer merely to a single body; they encompass all phenomena of both form and mind. Regarding the principle of emptiness and quiescence (*śūnyatā-śānti*), there are two meanings.
The first is the meaning that dependent origination is empty of substantiality. The second is the meaning that phenomena themselves are the truth, returning to suchness.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When a Bodhisattva dwells in their own samādhi, they see the seeing, the objects of seeing, and all perceived appearances as being like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent. This is the meaning of non-substantiality. It further states: "This..."
Views and conditions are fundamentally the inherently pure and luminous essence of bodhi; this is precisely the meaning of returning to the truth. Regarding "capable of relinquishing" and below:
since the Bodhisattva uses right wisdom to illuminate the emptiness of the aggregates, they possess the freedom to either maintain or dissolve [phenomena] without being burdened by external objects.

Taking the benefit of sentient beings as one’s fundamental vow, one casts off the body as if shedding a garment; because this accords with the Way, the text concludes by stating "approaching [the Buddhas]" and so forth.

The phrase "with wondrous" and below clarifies the actual practice of benefiting sentient beings. "Wondrous wisdom" refers to the *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (wisdom of profound discernment), which is able to observe the various mental activities of sentient beings, whether they are deviant or correct.
Furthermore, by means of the power of wisdom, one preaches the Dharma to teach and transform them, causing those with deviant views...
Those who turn away from evil, those whose minds have committed misdeeds but subsequently follow what is good, and those who transmigrate through birth and death:
"birth and death" is spoken of in terms of their general characteristics, while "transmigration" is spoken of in terms of transformation.

This means that if one commits evil among human beings and dies to fall into the three miserable realms, once the retribution in those realms is exhausted, if one encounters favorable conditions, one will again be born as a human or a deva. This is like a wheel revolving, alternating between high and low positions.

Birth and death constitute the fruit, while evil karma constitutes the cause. As for "causing them to sever [these]," once they have heard the Bodhisattva’s instructions, they no longer create the karmic causes of birth and death and do not undergo the fruits of saṃsāra;
thus, they attribute their gratitude to the Bodhisattva. Therefore, it is said that he "causes them to sever."
"Proceeding downward" means transforming the ordinary into the holy. Nirvāṇa is the essential substance; permanence and bliss are its attributes.
"Permanence" means the eternal exhaustion of birth and death; "bliss" means the eternal disappearance of all suffering. Therefore, it is called "ultimate nirvāṇa.
"Immediately attaining" [the state below] is precisely the reality of the power of wisdom; thus, this phrase serves as the title. "Good sons," etc., is the concluding summary. △
The Ninth: The Perfection of Wisdom.

Furthermore, son of good family, when a renunciant bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, understands the wholesome and unwholesome regarding all phenomena, remains far removed from false views, embraces the true Dharma, neither loathes saṃsāra nor delights in nirvāṇa, he is then said to have attained [this perfection].
This constitutes the perfection of wisdom (*jñānapāramitā*).

Wisdom is of many kinds; briefly stated, there are two: first, the wisdom that accords with reality (*yathābhūta-jñāna*); second, the wisdom that accords with the measure of phenomena (*yāvadbhāvikatā-jñāna*).

Regarding the wisdom that accords with reality: it refers to the wisdom that perceives the principle of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as it truly is, which is supremely sublime, profoundly quiescent, and without increase.

There is no decrease; this is called knowledge as it truly is (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). Knowledge according to measure (*yathāmātra-jñāna*) refers to the ultimate penetration of all objects of experience:
seeing that if sentient beings deviate from the principle and its wisdom, they undergo birth and death;
seeing that if sentient beings accord with the principle and its wisdom, they attain nirvana. This is called knowledge according to measure. Now, the sutra says: "In one..."
To thoroughly understand all phenomena as being either wholesome or unwholesome means to observe and discern them without being deceived by external objects.

To remain far removed from inferior views and to possess clear right view is essential; for to repudiate cause and effect and to hold erroneous attachments to the extremes of nihilism or eternalism is called wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).

Because one does not succumb to depravity or delusion, it is called "distancing oneself. Because one turns back from falsehood to return to the true mind, thereby harmonizing all phenomena, it is called the "True Dharma" (*saddharma*).

Because one penetrates the nature of phenomena and maintains them, it is called "embracing" (*parigraha*). Thus, the distinctions between superior and inferior, evil and good, and the heterodox and the orthodox are clearly understood.

This refers precisely to the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). "Not wearying of the lower" means that on the ground of the principle of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), saṃsāra is fundamentally empty;
what, then, is there to weary of? Nirvāṇa is fundamentally inherent; what, then, is there to delight in? As it is said: "Nirvāṇa and saṃsāra are equal to flowers in the sky."

The single, ultimate *tathatā* (suchness) is precisely the wisdom of suchness (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). Because one reaches the other shore by means of this wisdom, it is called the *prajñāpāramitā* (perfection of wisdom).

Although what has been discussed above is termed "wisdom," it is presented here from the perspective of self-benefit; however, between "thoroughly knowing" (*parijñā*) and "removing" (*prahāṇa*), each is either implicit or explicit.

"Thoroughly knowing" refers to the initial arising of *ādikṣaya-bodhi* (initial awakening), wherein one clearly perceives and understands so as not to be turned by good or evil karma; hence it is called "thoroughly knowing. "Removing" refers to the functional activity of *ādikṣaya-bodhi*, wherein, through the application of the path of non-interruption (*anantarya-mārga*) in a single moment of correspondence, one is no longer deluded by false views.

Therefore, it is called "keeping far away. This is because false views comprehensively include all afflictions, while good and evil likewise comprehensively include karma and its fruits. When understood through comprehension (*vijñāna*), good and evil also comprehensively include false views; when kept far away through renunciation (*virati*), false views also comprehensively include good and evil.

Through comprehension, karma is manifest and afflictions are hidden; through renunciation, afflictions are manifest and karma is hidden. These two meanings mutually encompass one another; this is merely the skill of the translator. Furthermore, regarding "embracing the True Dharma" (*saddharma-parigraha*): "embrace" (*pari*) means to gather and collect, and "accept" (*graha*) means to contain and receive. That is to say, it refers to gathering and collecting [the teachings on] karma, its fruits, and so forth.

All are contained within the True Dharma. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states, the five aggregates and four categories are unified as the wondrous nature of True Suchness; this is entirely due to the power of wisdom.
Not cherishing one's own self, but feeling compassion for all sentient beings, one constantly practices great relinquishment of body, life, and wealth;
this is what is called being "near" to the pāramitās. By means of subtle and wondrous wisdom, one preaches the Dharma of the One Vehicle for all sentient beings, causing them to enter [the path].
Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For these reasons, it is called the true pāramitā.
Good son, this is what is meant by a renunciant bodhisattva who has accomplished the jñāna-pāramitā.
"Not loving the inferior" means that while ordinary people love their own bodies, benevolent people take pity on all beings; while commoners value wealth, the wise value the Way.
Now, because the Bodhisattva takes pity on beings and values the Way, he does not love his own body, nor does he value wealth or life.

This is what is meant by constantly practicing great relinquishment (*mahopekṣā*). Great relinquishment is the equality of enemies and kin; it is to abandon oneself for the sake of others. Because of this—
Because one cherishes benevolence and values the Way, it is termed the "perfection of intimacy" (*upaniṣad-pāramitā*). By means of subtle and wondrous wisdom, one brings forth the reality of wisdom;
because one is able to realize that the provisional and the real are of one essence, it is called "subtle and wondrous. This refers to the teaching of the One Vehicle Dharma.
This is the One Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*). The phrase "to cause [beings] to enter" below pertains to the two meanings of practice and fruit.

However, without wondrous wisdom (*jñāna*), one cannot expound the One Vehicle; without the One Vehicle, one cannot give rise to wondrous practice; and without wondrous practice, one cannot realize and enter the wondrous fruit of Bodhi.
The section beginning with "For this reason" concludes [the argument], meaning that by means of this [wisdom], one can expound the One Vehicle and cause [beings to enter it].

Because it enters into the causes and conditions for awakening (*bodhi*), it is designated as "true reality" (*tattva*) and so forth. [The passage beginning with] "Good son... concludes by establishing the name. [Question:

These perfections (*pāramitās*) and the previous two—the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) and the power of wisdom (*prajñā-bala*)—have different names, yet their textual meaning appears similar. I do not know how they are to be distinguished; I humbly beg you to instruct me. [Answer: Originally there were six perfections, which were expanded into ten.

One should know that the latter five perfections are all derived from the expansion of the perfection of wisdom. Therefore, the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*) is the expedient artifice of the perfection of wisdom; the perfection of vows (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*) is the aspiration of wisdom; the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*) is the thorough penetration of wisdom; and the perfection of knowledge (*jñāna-pāramitā*) is the ultimate consummation of wisdom. Thus [they are distinguished].

When analyzed, they form five; when synthesized, they are simply wisdom (*prajñā*). Now, speaking according to their analysis, they are largely the same with minor differences. "Largely the same" means that the phrasing and meaning are similar; "minor differences" means that some variations cannot be avoided. For instance, as for what is emphasized by the powers (*bala*):

Transforming the heterodox toward the orthodox, that which is emphasized in the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Perfection of Wisdom) is the direct teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Furthermore, while the *Bala-pāramitā* (Perfection of Power) illuminates the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha*) to benefit sentient beings, it has not yet revealed the state where both subject and object are forgotten.

In the *Prajñāpāramitā*, one does not loathe birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) nor delight in nirvana (*nirvāṇa*), but rather causes others to enter into *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. As previously stated, these perfections are mutually inclusive and perfectly integrated, such that there is nothing they do not penetrate; this is the principle of expansion and contraction, which students should understand.
△ Third, the extensive opening according to capacities, in eight parts. First, a further inquiry into the eighty-four thousand [teachings].
"Good son, for what reason are these pāramitās said to have eighty-four thousand distinctions?
One should know that this section [should have been placed] within the previous section on 'Easily Attaining Bodhi in an Araṇya. The Buddha said: 'The bodhisattva grows weary...'"
Dwelling in an araṇya apart from the world, one expends little effort yet attains the fulfillment of the eighty-four thousand practices of the pāramitās and swiftly realizes bodhi.
This, however, is merely a concise discourse that establishes the definitive points and provides their essential explanation.
Furthermore, regarding the three kinds of ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*): as these ten perfections have now been completed, this [text] raises a further inquiry, asking:

"For what reason are they said to be eighty-four thousand? This refers to "conduct" (*caryā*), while the former referred to "practices" (*carita*). However, "differentiation" (*vibhāga*) here refers precisely to the differentiation of conduct.
This is merely the introduction of the inquiry; the explanation follows in the subsequent text. △ Second, the detailed explanation.
"You should know that there are four kinds of distinctions. For those with excessive greed, I have analytically expounded two thousand one hundred perfections (*pāramitās*).
For those with excessive hatred, I have analytically expounded two thousand one hundred perfections. For those with excessive delusion,"

For those who possess equal proportions, he analytically expounds two thousand one hundred pāramitās; for those who possess equal proportions, he analytically expounds two thousand one hundred pāramitās.
"Greed" (*lobha*) refers to insatiable longing. "Much" (*bahu*) refers to the manifold nature of the objects of desire, such as wealth, sex, fame, food, and sleep;
or the five sensory objects—form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. Because greed arises in relation to every single desirable object, it is called "much.
Greed is a universal affliction common to all sentient beings. Regarding the phrase "analyzing and explaining," this refers to the remedial methods. For indeed, as...
He expounds the Dharma like a skilled physician treating an illness; with the appropriate medicine, a single dose brings recovery.

Since the disease of sentient beings' craving has many varieties, he preaches two thousand one hundred [teachings] to apply to their specific ailments and treat them. (Regarding these two thousand one hundred and so forth, as stated in the *Bhadrapāla-kalpika-sūtra*:

"The Bodhisattva cultivates and practices the Dharmas, from the first 'Radiance' up to the 'Distribution of Relics,' comprising three hundred and fifty *pāramitā* dharma-gates, each of which includes giving, ethical discipline, patience, and so on.")

The six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) of vigor, meditative concentration, and wisdom collectively constitute two thousand one hundred *pāramitās*. As for the term "perfection" (*pāramitā*), it means that when the practice of both phenomena and principle is fulfilled, one crosses the flow of birth and death and ascends to the shore of *nirvāṇa* without end.

Since greed is thus [to be understood], so too are hatred, delusion, and their equal distribution (*sabhāga*). "Equal distribution" refers to the state that is neither greedy, nor hateful, nor deluded;
it is the even-mindedness of non-conceptualization. Together with the preceding [categories of] hatred and delusion, each possesses two [aspects].
The one thousand and one hundred [teachings] are all called *pāramitās*. For example, regarding those who cross over craving:
taking birth and death as this shore and liberation as the other shore, one uses the two thousand and one hundred dharma-gates as a raft.
Craving is like a great river; that is to say, by boarding the vessel of the two thousand and one hundred dharma-gates, one leaves behind birth and death on this shore.

Reaching the shore, one crosses the great river of craving and reaches the further shore of liberation. The cases of hatred, delusion, and their equal proportions may be understood by analogy with this.
△ Third, the conclusion establishing the fundamental increase and multiplication.
"Good son, taking these two thousand one hundred pāramitās as the root,
they increase further by multiples until they become eighty-four thousand pāramitās."
Regarding "increasing further by multiples and so forth": one transforms into ten, thereby resulting in twenty-one thousand.
Those with much greed, much anger, and so on, each possess twenty-one thousand; together they total eighty-four thousand. △ Fourth, the conclusion as a Dharma-gate for the benefit of others.
Such dharmas as these are all practices for the benefit of others;
they are performed for the sake of benefiting others because they correspond to the ailments of others. △ Fifth, the practice of self-benefit through subduing:
"Good son, if there are sentient beings whose natures are difficult to subdue, and who, having heard this Dharma, have not yet tamed their minds, then..."
For them, he proclaims eighty-four thousand gateways to samādhi. Such sublime dharmas are all practices for self-benefit;
their nature is inferior, meaning that those whose fundamental nature is difficult to subdue are known by the Bodhisattva.
For their sake, the Bodhisattva teaches eighty-four thousand dharmas of the pāramitās to bring them under control. "Hearing this" refers to those sentient beings who, although...
Having heard it but not yet having faith, their nature is not yet harmonized and their minds are not yet subdued; this means the teaching has not met with their capacity.
To avoid leaving them in a separate category, he proceeds to proclaim what follows: namely, "changing the lead but not the medicine," with the sole purpose of ensuring they take it.
Therefore, the terminology is changed and termed the "Gate of Samādhi. *Samādhi* is translated as "Right Reception" (*samyak-samāpatti*). By means of the eighty-four thousand...
Each of the thousands has its own inherent principle, which is precisely right reception (*samyak-samādhi*). To harmonize skillfully with the capacities [of beings] constitutes the wondrous Dharma.

The final two phrases conclude [the section]; these all refer to those who benefit themselves. The name is not applied based on the one who preaches the Dharma, but rather based on the one who receives the Dharma.
Since they are able to subdue their own minds, this constitutes the self-benefit of those individuals. △ Six: Benefit.
This is his practice of taming others.

If there are sentient beings whose natures are difficult to tame, and whose minds remain unsubdued even after hearing this Dharma, he then proclaims for them the eighty-four thousand dharani-gates. Such sublime teachings are all practices for the benefit of others.

This Dharma refers to the aforementioned eighty-four thousand gates of samādhi. Furthermore, for those who do not yet possess the karmic affinity, it is explained as the *dhāraṇī* of esoteric speech (*madhura-vāk*).
Within this, there are distinctions between multi-syllabled, single-syllabled, and wordless forms.

The "wordless" refers to the ultimate mind-Dharma, which admits no verbal expression and can only be known through direct realization. As for the "single-syllabled" and other forms, these are divine mantras (*vidyā-mantra*).
For example, the single-syllable dhāraṇīs such as Oṃ and Hūṃ possess inconceivable, wondrous efficacy.

As for those consisting of many syllables, they are as extensive as the *Śūraṅgama*, the *Uṣṇīṣavijayā*, and so forth; next, there are those such as the *Svastyayana* for the elimination of calamities.
The term *dhāraṇī* is translated here as "total retention" (*zongchi*). It refers to that which collectively encompasses all phenomena and maintains immeasurable meanings;
it is the name for divine mantras that respond to the ailments of sentient beings. There are likewise eighty-four thousand such mantras, which constitute the secret intent of all Buddhas.

They awaken the spiritual consciousness of others, causing their minds to penetrate and pervade the Dharma, with the sole purpose of ensuring they receive the teachings. This constitutes the wondrous Dharma for the benefit of others.
This is the practice. The gate has the meaning of "passage," signifying entry into the Way by means of the Dharma, just as one enters a house through a door.

(The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma does not exceed the two categories of Exoteric and Esoteric. The Exoteric corresponds to the various teachings; the Esoteric refers to *dhāraṇīs*. Because there are differences according to the capacities of sentient beings, the Dharmas are of many kinds. Nevertheless, teachings enter through the three types of wisdom, and mantras become efficacious through recitation.

Upon reaching the point of clarifying the mind and realizing the Way, they are equal and without distinction. This is what is meant by the so-called "the source to which one returns is non-dual, while the expedient means have many gates. △ Seventh, a personal account of taming sentient beings.
"Good son, for the sake of taming all sentient beings, I have taught such dharmas and employed countless skillful means,
manifesting various forms to transform and guide living beings. Good son, for this reason,
all humans and devas universally praise the Tathāgata, calling him the 'Teacher'."
I shall now explain the lower, sharp practice of benefiting others. It is like a skilled charioteer taming a horse, or like a master carpenter working with wood.
"Taming" refers to regulating the three karmas; "subduing" refers to governing one's temperament and nature.
The Buddha is the teacher who is capable of taming, and sentient beings are the objects to be tamed. To teach such a Dharma constitutes the upper eight [precepts].
The fourteen thousand *pāramitās* and the gates of *samādhi* are all explained as the manifest teaching of perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
The eighty-four thousand *dhāraṇī* gates are all explained as the secret teaching of perfect penetration.

Furthermore, regarding the countless skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), which exceed eighty-four thousand and extend to immeasurable dharma-gates, they are all intended to meet the capacities of sentient beings.
The Dharma does not go beyond the four *siddhāntas*. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:

"By means of various causes and conditions, various parables, and the extensive exposition of verbal teachings, through countless skillful means, he guides sentient beings and causes them to leave behind all attachments.

This refers precisely to this. To manifest various forms means to respond to devas by appearing as a deva, to respond to humans by appearing as a human, and so forth; these are collectively termed [the manifestation of various forms].
Manifesting bodies according to their respective types and preaching the Dharma in accordance with their capacities, all for the purpose of teaching and transforming sentient beings.

Good son, this concludes [the section on] the Buddha as teacher. By means of this single phrase, it承接 (links back to) the aforementioned manifestations of body and preaching of the Dharma, which bring about various benefits and are able to move the hearts of people;
therefore, all humans and devas universally acclaim the Tathāgata, calling him the "Teacher" (*śāstṛ*), meaning that he is able to guide.
...the teacher. △ Eight: Cultivating Practice to Eliminate Obstacles in the Future and Present.

Good son, all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the future and the present, all cultivate the eighty-four thousand gates of the *pāramitās*, the eighty-four thousand gates of the various *samādhis*, and the eighty-four thousand gates of the *dhāraṇīs*. Forever...
They sever eighty-four thousand subtle afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and eighty-four thousand subtle cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
In the future, at the lower assembly, the three periods of time are identical; the paths of all Buddhas are the same, and they all descend.
Their names, numbers, and dharma-gates are all as previously explained. Regarding the permanent severance of the eighty-four thousand subtle afflictive hindrances: because...
The ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) serve as the root. Taking one underlying tendency as the head and nine underlying tendencies as its auxiliaries, they thus constitute one hundred.

Calculated across the three periods of time, there are one hundred for each, totaling three hundred. However, because the present period is brief, the assistance of the others is not considered when it is one hundred.
Furthermore, within each of the two periods of the past and future—making two hundred—the individual underlying tendencies are likewise treated one by one.

Taking these as the heads, with the nine *anuśayas* (latent proclivities) acting as their assistants, they together total two thousand. Adding the one hundred from the present life, they total two thousand one hundred.

Furthermore, if categorized according to the four types of sentient beings—those with much greed, much hatred, much delusion, and those who are "evenly distributed" (*sabhāga*)—each has two thousand one hundred, totaling eight thousand four hundred.
Moreover, if categorized according to the four great elements and the six sense-decays (*ṣaḍāyatana*), each has eight [thousand].

One thousand four hundred [times] one hundred, totaling eighty-four thousand. Because the number of afflictions (*kleśa*) is so vast, it is called the "subtle obstacle of afflictions" (*sūkṣma-kleśāvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*) correspond to that same number; for instance, as one abandons a portion of the afflictions, one realizes a portion of the true reality (*tattva*).
Regarding the realized reality, there is the cognition that "there is something realized," and thus it is called "the object of knowledge. To cling to this [cognition] is... [obstructive].

Because they are forgotten, they constitute obstacles. Since they follow those afflictions (*kleśa*), they likewise have their respective numbers (the four great elements are earth, water, fire, and wind;
