the six bases of decay [ṣadāyatana] are form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena; these can lead consciousness toward objects of cognition and cause the decline of wholesome dharmas). △ Fourth, the summary conclusion on the realization of the fruit.
They all proceeded to the *araṇya* beneath the Bodhi tree, sat upon the Vajrāsana, entered the Vajra-samādhi,
and having subdued all the Māras and hostile spirits, realized *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

This refers to all Buddhas of the future and present. Being able to cultivate various dharma-gates and sever various afflictions, when they approach the time of realizing the fruit, they all proceed to the site of enlightenment at the *āraṇya* (wilderness) Dharma, beneath the King of Trees, upon the Vajra Seat.
(Regarding the tree being called "bodhi": the tree is not bodhi; because one attains the path of bodhi beneath the tree, the tree is made manifest by that path, and is therefore named "bodhi").

Regarding the statement "seated as Vajra": it is also seated as non-Vajra. The Path is metaphorically called "Vajra" because the essence of the path realized by the Buddha is most firm; just as the substance of a diamond cannot be destroyed by other objects, its function is able to shatter delusions, just as the sharpness of a diamond can destroy myriad things.

That meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is also named "Vajra" because the concentration entered by the Buddha cannot be broken by any heavenly Māras or external paths (*tīrthika*); it is as firm as a diamond, capable of subduing heavenly Māras and restraining external paths, just like the sharpness of a diamond.
Regarding the phrase "subduing all" and below: it means that when each Buddha attains enlightenment, they cause the palaces of the Māras to tremble; therefore, the hosts...
The Māras compete to come and threaten him in various ways, desiring to shatter the Buddha’s meditative concentration; thus he is called the "Enemy Māra.

By means of his power of concentration, the Buddha causes them to flee in terror; hence the terms "subduing" and so forth. "Attaining realization" refers immediately to the ultimate attainment of Buddhahood.
△ Second, the verses in gāthā form restate this in two parts. First, the heading of the chapter.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
II. The Main Verses (eleven parts). I. Grand Praise of the Triple Gem:
The Great Dharma King who transcends the three realms appears in the world to transform all classes of beings. [Equal in number to] the sands of the Ganges are the various Bodhisattvas...
Sa. Entering the gate of the Buddha’s ambrosial wisdom.
The first phrase praises the Buddha: because the Buddha is able to transcend the triple world instantaneously, he is the Great Dharma King.

This means that he preaches the Dharma according to the capacities of beings, employing both provisional and ultimate teachings with mastery over all dharmas; therefore, he is called the Dharma King. The second phrase reveals the Buddha’s original intent.
Because the Buddha descends from the Dharma-body to manifest transformation-bodies, it is said that he appears in the world. "Transformation" (hua) refers to teaching and transforming (*śāsana*).
"The multitudes" refers to sentient beings of the five vehicles' spiritual lineages. Now, the reason the Buddha appears is precisely for the purpose of teaching and transforming.
These three phrases clarify the assembly to whom he addresses; as they all possess great capacity, they are called Bodhisattvas. Because...
Because the number of beings is so vast, they are referred to as "as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The four lines refer to the fruit that is accomplished.
Regarding "wisdom" (*prajñā*), there are two translations for this term: first, *dharmatā-prajñā* (the wisdom of ultimate reality), which is the principle realized;

second, *pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā* (the wisdom of contemplative observation), which is the cognition that realizes. "Gate" (*mukha*) has the sense of "passage," meaning that one enters [into reality] by means of this wisdom.
Principle (*tattva*) is that which is entered; wisdom (*prajñā*) is the means of entry. Because it is named after this means of entry, wisdom serves as the gateway for entering principle.
"Ambrosia" (*amṛta*) refers to the medicine of immortality; it is used as a metaphor for wisdom. Once realized, it is realized forever, just as one who drinks ambrosia does not die.
This is originally the Buddha-wisdom, but now, through transformation, Bodhisattvas are also able to enter it; hence it is called "entry."

The Buddhas and so forth: therein, the Buddha Jewel as the Dharma King, the Dharma Jewel as the gateway of wisdom, and the Sangha Jewel of the bodhisattvas constitute the Three Jewels of the Mahāyāna. △ Second, Maitreya’s inquiry.
The Honored One Maitreya, who attained the Way through kalpas past, inquired with a heart of great compassion: "Excellent, O Vimala Dharma Prince!
Your wisdom is able to open the true Buddha Vehicle."

Regarding those who attain the Way over successive kalpas, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "In the past, during the time of the Buddha Candrasūryapradīpa, [the Buddha] was the Bodhisattva named Seeking Fame.
From that time until his attainment of Buddhahood in the future, the number of kalpas he has traversed is exceedingly great."
Therefore, the statement that he attained the Way after passing through kalpas reveals the profundity of his practice. "Maitreya" is the elegant Chinese translation of [the original name];
because he takes compassion as his surname, he is called Maitreya. The second line praises the inquiry; the third line praises the Buddha’s eulogy.

"Stainless" (*vimala*) refers to the Honored One currently residing in the stage of "one more birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*). With afflictions exhausted and fruition perfected, he is provisionally assigned to the rank of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*);
because he stands above the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), he is "Honored. Because his afflictions are exhausted, he is called "Stainless. The Buddha is the Dharma King;
as Maitreya is able to succeed to and carry on the Buddha’s work, he is called a "Dharma Prince" (*dharmarājaputra*). The two characters "wisdom" (*jñāna*) are terms of praise, meaning wisdom.
Only then may one inquire on behalf of the assembly. The True Buddha Vehicle is precisely the One Buddha Vehicle; it is the teaching of perfect reality.
"Opening" means to initiate or inspire. This refers to how, through this single inquiry, the Buddha then expounds the teaching, attributing the merit to the requester.
Therefore, he praises [the teaching] as being able to open [the way]. △ Third, granting permission to speak and exhorting the listeners:
"With my lion-like fearless eloquence, I shall expound the path leading to awakening within the Mahāyāna. You all should listen with single-minded attention and great care;
transmit it to those in the future who are worthy to receive it. Even if the worlds of the ten directions were to become empty, do not allow this [teaching] to be severed or exhausted."
The Worldly Path: The lion is the king among beasts; its majesty subdues all other species. When it roars, the herds of animals hide their tracks and the winged birds fall to the ground.
Now the Buddha uses himself as a metaphor: wherever the Buddha goes, all the devas pay him reverent homage and the hundred spirits take refuge in him; therefore, he is compared [to the lion].

The Buddha is the lion among men. Regarding "fearless eloquence": because the Buddha is endowed with the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) and the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), he manifests the truth and refutes the heterodox;
thus, the celestial Māras' skulls split open and the heretics vanish from sight. This is likened to the roar of a lion, which is why it is called "fearless.
The second phrase takes verbal instruction in the Way as the act of speaking, and the Mahāyāna and so forth as that which is spoken.
All that is ultimately definitive in meaning is universally categorized as the Mahāyāna;

this sutra is like the path among all Mahāyāna teachings for proceeding toward wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Wondrous enlightenment is the fruit of Buddhahood. This sutra contains various methods of contemplation.
Because it enables one to advance toward wondrous enlightenment, it is called the "Path of Awakening. The first three phrases admonish the listener; the fourth phrase grants permission to speak.
"Transmitting and entrusting" refers to oral transmission, for one transmits the path realized by oneself to others. "Those of the future" refers to practitioners of later generations.
Regarding those who should be taught, there are two meanings: first, this is the Buddha’s original intention, as he ought to instruct them accordingly.
Therefore, it is said that one should bestow [the teaching]. Second, this refers to selecting the recipient who is fit to receive it.

The final two phrases explain the meaning of "should bestow": that while the world cannot remain empty and may even be made empty, the supramundane *Cittabhūmi-darśana* (Contemplation of the Mind-Ground) must not be allowed to be severed or exhausted. Yet, if there is no one to transmit it, the Buddha-Dharma will perish.
He exhorted and entrusted [the teaching] to them; therefore, it is said, "Do not allow... and so forth. △ Fourth, the classification of grades:
Those seeking the supramundane path to liberation do not exceed the three faculties and nine grades. Those of the superior faculty in the three grades dwell in various *araṇyas*;

those of middling and inferior faculties transform the world according to conditions. The fruits of the path they seek are equal and without difference; they all equally realize True Suchness (*tathatā*) and Buddhahood.

The "Ocean of Nature" (prakṛti-samudra). The phrase "those who seek" refers to future seekers of the Way. "Liberation" and so forth refer to the *Cittabhūmi-darśana-dharma* (The Dharma of Contemplating the Ground of the Mind).

This means that by being able to contemplate the ground of the mind, one can transcend the world and attain great liberation; thus, the ground of the mind constitutes the Way. The next three [verses]...

The phrasing follows the prose section. The final two lines mean that although there are three grades of root-nature and nine types of categories, these distinctions arise solely because of differences in the sharpness or dullness of individuals;

however, the path and fruit sought remain equal and without distinction, for they are like the thousand paths and nine avenues leading to the royal city, which are not two. This concludes the formal explanation of the preceding statement.

The meaning is as follows: that which is called "equality without distinction" refers to the fact that what the Buddha taught for persons of the three faculties and nine grades is the same single *tathatā* (suchness) of Buddha-nature.
It is like the great ocean, which is boundless and receives a hundred streams; because all these streams enter the sea, they become one salty taste.
This sutra is also like this, for it is able to bring together those of the three faculties and nine grades to enter [the truth] together.
Because of the Buddha-nature. △ Fifth, the benefits of true wisdom:
Having already attained the untainted state of a true Mahāsattva, they manifest according to what is appropriate to save all sentient beings.
They reveal the gate of the non-duality of existence and emptiness, benefiting themselves and others without interruption.

The first line of the verse praises Maitreya and others; since they possess the mind to seek instruction, they must surely have the resolve to propagate [the teaching], and thus they are praised as "True Mahāsattvas" (*bhūta-mahāsattva*).
"Having already attained the untainted" (*anāsrava*) praises their own perfected path, for they shall never again fall back.
The second line concerns benefiting others, which expresses the meaning of a "True Mahāsattva"; "according to what is appropriate" means acting in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
"Manifesting according to response" means appearing in a body in accordance with the karmic conditions of those who perceive it, such as the thirty-two manifestations of Avalokiteśvara.

Since all beings within the nine realms—both sages and ordinary people—possess dharmas they seek and each have their respective obstacles, there are instances of both hidden resonance and manifest seeking.

When there is a hidden resonance, he rescues them from suffering; when there is manifest seeking, he expounds the Dharma. Therefore, it is said that he "relieves all sentient beings and reveals [the truth]."

The lower part is broad and the upper part is manifest; this signifies salvation. One may explain them separately or interpret them as a synthesis. To explain them separately is like the four modes of existence (*bhava*) in the *Āgamas*, where cause and effect are distinct and orderly.

In the *Prajñāpāramitā*, one enters emptiness (*śūnyatā*), whereby phenomena are extinguished and attachments are eliminated. To interpret them as a synthesis means that emptiness is itself existence, which is the sense of following conditions (*pratyaya*);
existence is itself emptiness, which is the sense of non-alteration (*avikāra*). That neither emptiness nor existence is clung to is the Gate of Non-duality. Chapter [X].
The four lines conclude the virtue of the two benefits, transmitting the Buddha’s seal of mind in an uninterrupted succession that is infinite;
thus, there is no hiatus. △ Six: That which should be cultivated before attainment.

O sons of the Buddha who have not yet attained the outflow-free state, you should diligently cultivate the three trainings. Dedicate your roots of goodness to all sentient beings, and with single-minded devotion, focus your mindfulness on the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

The "Buddha-sons" are ordinary persons who have just resolved upon the Great Mind. Since it is said that they have not yet attained the untainted (*anāsrava*) state and are currently within the tainted (*sāsrava*), the subsequent phrase exhorts them to practice.
To accord with principle is called "should" (*yīng*); to be in harmony with the Way is called "correct" (*zhèng*); and to apply oneself with vigor is called "diligent" (*qín*).

"Cultivation" (*xiū*) means refining. Regarding the "three kinds of learners," referring to what precedes indicates the three faculties (*indriya*); referring to what follows indicates the three perfections (*pāramitā*).

The third phrase means that one does not merely cultivate for oneself, but further includes dedication (*pariṇāmana*). This means dedicating what one has attained toward all sentient beings, vowing that all sentient beings may equally obtain supreme benefit;
this is precisely giving (*dāna*). From the words "with a single mind" (*yīxīn*) below, there is concern that [the path] might be...

If one's power is not yet firm, one will fall when confronted by external objects; therefore, one must dwell single-mindedly and seek the protective empowerment of the spiritual powers of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
△ Seventh: Making Vows for Constant Intimacy.
May I always behold the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, with their bodies adorned by boundless merit and virtue.

May I always hear the sound of the rain of Dharma, so that all may equally receive its moisture and their resolve never regress. Even if my body were to dwell perpetually in hell, it would not be that I am not drawing near to the Greatly Compassionate Honored One;
even if my body were to dwell perpetually in saṃsāra, it would not be that I do not personally hear the subtle and wondrous Dharma. By these causes and conditions...
O Sons of the Buddha: Fixing the mind, one should constantly keep in mind the Teacher of Gods and Humans.

There is the dwelling of the eighteen stages of non-attachment, the dwelling of not being separated from the time of the Buddha’s presence, and also the dwelling of aspiring for the Buddha’s instruction.
However, since Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are holy masters who provide guidance and protection, how could one not make a vow to be constantly in their presence?

The next line praises the physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas; as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* regarding the "Ocean of Marks of the Ten Bodies of the Tathāgata," these are all accomplished through the adornment of boundless merit during the causal stage.
Regarding the following two lines: since one has vowed to constantly behold the Buddha-body, how could one...
They constantly hear the rain of the Dharma; because the Tathāgata speaks with a single voice yet each according to their kind understands it, it is said that all equally receive its moisture.
Now, as for this "rain of the Dharma," it is like when the heavens above send down a universal rain:
all grasses and trees thereby attain growth and flourish, eventually reaching the stage where flowers bloom and fruits ripen. Likewise, when people hear the Buddha-Dharma, it can cause them to...
The mind of the Way does not regress, ultimately reaching *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. With the four lines following "with this body," he further makes a profound vow:
"I would rather my own body dwell eternally in hell. Since hell is a place of extreme suffering, how could one possibly remain there?
This is merely a hyperbolic expression; his true wish is simply to always remain near the Compassionate Honored One. It is not that he does not desire intimacy [with the Buddha].
The word "recently" (*jin*) is a term used for contrast; it properly means "to be constantly near. "Saṃsāra" refers to birth and death;
it means that one would rather undergo birth and death than abandon hearing the Dharma. The final two lines summarize this constant proximity:

as a child of the Buddha, who through these causes and conditions constantly aspires to behold the Buddha and hear the Dharma, one must certainly bind the mind to constant mindfulness and must not forget it for even a moment. O Teacher of Gods and Humans!
He is also a Buddha. This means that through sincere cultivation one awakens resonance; he necessarily responds to that resonance, like the moon reflecting in a river.
△ Eighth, the extensive verses on the various perfections (pāramitās). First, the verse on the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā):

If there is a son of the Buddha who cultivates the Noble Path, having resolved upon the unsurpassed Bodhicitta, and out of world-weariness dwells in an araṇya, he may also be said to cultivate the three kinds of pāramitās.
Giving first from his own daily food, while simultaneously bestowing the Jewel of the Dharma upon sentient beings—with the three spheres being pure—this is dāna-pāramitā.
By cultivating this cause, his virtue becomes perfected; one should know that he shall realize and attain [the fruit].

The pāramitā [of giving] depends solely on the purity of the mind and not on material wealth. If one gives precious wealth with a defiled mind, it is not equal to giving even a small portion with a pure mind.
When the gift of wealth is thus characterized, it is called the perfection of dāna; this pāramitā is neither two nor three.

The first four lines are easy to understand. The "three kinds of *pāramitās*" refer to the three types of *pāramitās*—generosity (*dāna*), ethical discipline (*śīla*), and patience (*kṣānti*)—that were previously mentioned as being proximate to the true [perfection].
The phrase "also attains" (*yi de*) is an example of the prose-style terminology. From "Each day" onwards, it correctly elucidates the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*).

This verse summarizes the previous discussion on giving small portions of alms-food to hungry sentient beings and so forth. Since a śramaṇa does not possess wealth, this constitutes the gift of material wealth (*āmiṣadāna*).

Furthermore, it includes the gift of the Dharma (*dharmadāna*) mentioned below. Regarding the "three wheels" (*trimaṇḍala*) mentioned below, it refers to the self, the object, and the person who receives the gift;
these are called the three wheels. "Purity" refers to the mind, meaning that one is free from attachment to a self.

The marks [of subject, object, and action]—not clinging to the mark of the dharma, not clinging to the mark of the recipient of the gift—is called the emptiness of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-śūnyatā*).
*Dāna* is the Sanskrit term for giving. One who cultivates the cause by this means refers to taking this perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) as the causal practice of cultivation;
when it is further endowed with the virtue of the purity of the three spheres, the perfection of giving finally becomes complete. Therefore...
It is called "perfection" (*pūrṇa*). One should know that these two characters are words intended to awaken and cause understanding.
Because one realizes the essence and enters the Path, it is called "realization" (*sākṣātkriyā*). Because one attains the further shore, it is called "pāramitā.
The following section clarifies the actual nature of giving: although that which is able to reach the further shore is attained through the practice of giving, that which is reached is only...
Only through giving that is pure in its three spheres and free from signs can one truly realize [the fruit]; how could it be achieved by means of tainted material wealth?
Therefore, it is not by means of wealth. If there are the following two lines, they compare the merit of the two minds—the defiled and the pure.
The defiled mind hopes for karmic retribution; thus, the precious treasures and material goods offered by such a mind all belong to the realm of existence (*saṃsāra*).
Regarding the causes of outflows (āsrava), they are not as [superior] as when correctly compared with the pure mind. One whose mind is pure does not expect karmic retribution;

thus, even a minute fraction [of a gift] becomes an outflow-free (anāsrava) act of giving. The reality of its realization is such that the giving of jewels with a defiled mind, though copious, cannot equal it. This selects the latter two stages, stating that these constitute the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), rather than the second stage of "approaching" (*upasaṃkramaṇa*) or the third stage of "reality" (*tattva*).
Therefore, it says "not the second or third. This verse [describes] the long prose section on how one can attain the fulfillment of the perfection of giving.
To be able to give away one’s own body, life, wife, and children—this is called the "Approaching Paramita.
If there are good men or women who seek the Dharma, to preach all Mahayana sutras for them and cause them to resolve upon unsurpassed bodhicitta—this is called the "True Paramita.
Possessing compassion, pure faith, and a sense of shame and remorse, to gather in sentient beings while remaining free from greed, and to vow to become a Tathagata.
Unsurpassed wisdom. The two types of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—are called the first crossing (*pāramitā*).
The first phrase refers to the ultimate extent of giving within the category of generosity. Since one no longer cherishes the body, one becomes intimate with virtue and draws near to the Way;
therefore, the name is established in the second phrase. The final two lines of the verse praise the reality of the gift of Dharma. [The term] "male" (*puruṣa*)...
The woman’s reply, “Excellent,” indicates that her disposition is gentle and kind, making her a fit vessel for receiving the Way.

The Dharma’s response, “I seek you,” signifies the sincerity of her longing for the Way and the purity of her resolve. Since she possesses such great capacity, she is worthy of being taught the Mahāyāna sūtras so that she may cultivate and realize them;
this is because the person and the Dharma are well-suited to one another. "All" refers to all the Mahāyāna [teachings].
This is a general designation meaning that one teaches according to the capacity of the recipient; it is not a statement made for all cases indiscriminately.

It causes [the practitioner] to give rise to the lower [level], clearly manifesting the appropriate efficacy. Regarding the term "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*) in the word *bodhicitta*, it reveals that this is the Bodhi of the Buddha-way.
Therefore, the subsequent phrase concludes by naming it "true" (*tattva*): it is called "true" (*zhen*) because it is not false, and "real" (*shi*) because it is not empty. Thus it is.

Practicing giving leads to reaching the other shore. "Compassion" (the first character) below indicates the virtue of possessing shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*). "Gathering and bestowing" (the second character) below clarifies the practice of benefiting others.
This can be described as generating shame and remorse within oneself to leave behind greed, while also causing others to leave behind greed.

"Vowing for accomplishment" (the third character) below refers to the dedication toward the Buddha-way. "Wealth and Dharma" (the fourth character) below concludes the first perfection, which is the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). △ Second.
Verse on the Perfection of Ethics:
Firmly upholding the Bodhisattva’s threefold aggregate of precepts, one awakens the bodhicitta and departs from birth and death;
protecting the Buddha-dharma so it may abide in the world, one who can repent of transgressions truly maintains the precepts.

The three clusters (*triskandha*) are: the Mahāyāna *saṃvara-śīla* (precepts of restraint), which states, "Commit no evil"; the Mahāyāna *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (precepts of gathering virtuous dharmas), which states, "Cultivate all that is good";
and the Mahāyāna *sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla* (precepts of benefiting sentient beings), which states, "Do not fail to deliver any living being.

"Cluster" (*skandha*) means "complete. Briefly stated, there are ten grave and forty-eight light precepts; extensively stated, there are thirty thousand and eight hundred thousand. As for their limitlessness...

"Measuring" (liang) means to reveal and develop the merit of maintaining the precepts below. "Revealing" (kai) means to dispel delusion; "developing" (fa) means to give rise to right wisdom. Bodhi is the virtue of wisdom;
being free from birth and death is the virtue of cessation. Altogether, the two preceding phrases mean that the Way is accomplished through the precepts.
"Protecting and guarding" (yonghu) means to cause the Dharma to abide for a long time. Regarding those who have committed offenses through error, they originally had no intention [to transgress].

When an event occurs by chance and one is able to repent for the transgression, this is precisely what constitutes shame and remorse (*hrī-apatrāpya*). Therefore, they are collectively designated as those who truly uphold the precepts.
All disciples who receive the precepts should take this as their mirror. △ Third, the verse on the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
To subdue the mind of anger through the contemplation of compassion, to keep in mind past causes when confronted by enmity and harm, and to sacrifice one's own body and life to save sentient beings—
this is called the perfection of patience (kṣānti-pāramitā).

Patience can subdue one's own anger; compassion can pity the folly of others. "Contemplation" refers to examining their past causes; thus it says, "one should be mindful. These past causes are enmities and harms from previous lives; when encountering them in the present life, one cannot avoid being insulted. They are repaying old grievances, and I must accept this. This is because past causes are obscure and profound, such that foolish people cannot fathom them. When facing [such a situation], one should reflect: "This person is currently receiving the retribution for their own past offenses. If one thinks in this way, one will not harbor resentment toward them. Furthermore, if one contemplates the nature of all conditioned phenomena—that they are empty, impermanent, and subject to suffering—one will not give rise to anger even if insulted. Therefore, one should always maintain mindfulness. As the *Sūtra on the Ten Kinds of Dharma* states: "If one encounters an enemy who comes to harm, one should contemplate the causes and conditions of past lives. One should think: 'This person is now experiencing the fruit of their own past transgressions. If one reflects in this way, one will not give rise to anger. Thus, by contemplating the causes and conditions of past lives, one should remain mindful. If one does not contemplate past causes, one will fail to understand that the present is merely the maturation of past karma. Consequently, one will become angry and harbor resentment, which obstructs the path to liberation. Therefore, one must constantly practice mindfulness. Furthermore, if one contemplates the emptiness of the self, one realizes there is no "I" or "mine," and thus no basis for anger. If one contemplates the emptiness of phenomena, one realizes that all things arise from conditions and lack inherent existence; since there is nothing to grasp, how could anger arise? If one contemplates impermanence, one sees that both oneself and others are subject to birth and death, and that all things are fleeting and unstable; since there is no permanence, why should one be resentful? If one contemplates suffering, one sees that both oneself and others are submerged in the ocean of suffering, and that all things are inherently painful; since there is no joy to be found, how could one feel anger? Therefore, by contemplating these four truths—emptiness, impermanence, and suffering—one will not give rise to anger even when insulted. Moreover, if one contemplates the Buddha’s great compassion, one understands that the Tathāgata regards all sentient beings as his own children; if one thinks, "The Buddha would never wish me harm," one will naturally give rise to faith and respect. If one contemplates the Dharma’s true nature, one understands that the Dharma is free from affliction and is the source of peace and bliss; if one thinks, "The Dharma is my refuge," one will naturally give rise to reverence. If one contemplates the Sangha’s pure conduct, one understands that the assembly of the noble ones is the field of merit for all beings; if one thinks, "The Sangha is my guide," one will naturally give rise to devotion. By contemplating the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha in this way, one will not give rise to anger even when insulted. Furthermore, if one contemplates the equality of self and others, one realizes that there is no distinction between oneself and others; since there is no "other," how could there be resentment? If one contemplates the interdependence of causes and conditions, one understands that all things arise from the convergence of various factors; since there is no single agent, how could there be anger? If one contemplates the nature of karmic retribution, one understands that good and evil deeds inevitably produce their respective fruits; since this is the natural law of karma, one should accept it with equanimity. If one contemplates the benefits of patience, one understands that enduring insults is the gateway to the Bodhisattva path; since this is the practice of the sages, one should embrace it with joy. If one contemplates the faults of anger, one understands that harboring resentment leads to the three miserable realms; since this is the path of the foolish, one should abandon it immediately. By contemplating these six points—equality, interdependence, retribution, patience, faults, and benefits—one will not give rise to anger even when insulted. Furthermore, if one contemplates the ultimate truth, one understands that all dharmas are beyond conceptualization and free from arising and ceasing; since there is no duality, how could there be anger? If one contemplates conventional truth, one understands that all things are like illusions and dreams; since they are not real, why be resentful? If one contemplates the Middle Way, one understands that all things transcend extremes and are free from grasping; since there is no attachment, how could anger arise? By contemplating these three truths—ultimate, conventional, and middle—one will not give rise to anger even when insulted. When objects of perception provoke mutual hatred, enmity and harm deepen further; only the wise are not thus. Whenever adverse circumstances arise, they remain unmoved in voice or expression, maintaining their composure as if at ease.
They reflect: "I have done no wrong to this person; that they come to offend me must surely not be due to this life alone, but must stem from past lives.
Therefore, when encountering humiliation, they do not stir their thoughts, but instead turn back to reproach their own faults.
They come with harshness, but I respond with gentleness; they treat me with insult, but I welcome them with a smile.

Even if there were ancient grudges, they could do nothing against me. As for those who do not spare their own bodies or lives, it is because they have inherited the compassion of the past to save those foolish people.
Those sentient beings who inflict insults are said to be people who do not know compassion.
Compassion. When those who would certainly inflict harm do so to repay an old grievance, he does not spare his own life; instead, he vows to save them.
This demonstrates the reality of his patience and the intensity of his compassion. This is called the concluding summary of the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
△ Fourth, the verse on the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).

Capable of performing what is difficult to perform, they never abandon it for a moment; throughout three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, they constantly advance; with an unshared lack of defilement, they perpetually refine the mind;
for the sake of delivering sentient beings, they seek liberation.

"Difficult practices" refers to asceticism. This includes such acts as casting oneself from a height to end one's life, sacrificing one's body for the sake of the Dharma, or performing menial labor on land to serve as a bed or seat for others.
Generally, because Bodhisattvas seek the Way, they are unaware of their own bodies; they do not decline their suffering nor grow weary of their toil.
Therefore, it is said that "they are able to practice. Because they maintain this mindfulness at every moment, it is said that "they do not abandon it even for a moment. (3)
When the Sangha does not grow weary over a long period of time, they advance ever further. "Not common" means not identical;

that is to say, the diligence of a Bodhisattva is not the same as that of ordinary beings who are defiled by attachment to the five desires, nor is it the same as that of those of the Two Vehicles who are defiled by attachment to Nirvana.
Thus, constantly refining one's mind is precisely what manifests the perfection of vigor. However...

"Refining" does not refer to the refinement of elixirs in the Daoist tradition. Rather, it refers to one who is unattached to both emptiness and existence, purely refining the definitive meaning of the Middle Way within their own mind;
such a person is a true practitioner of cultivation. This is because they manifest a profuse altruistic intention to deliver those below [in the realms of suffering].

One must first seek liberation for oneself; only then can one cause others to attain liberation. This seems not difficult, yet it constitutes the merit of the two benefits (*dvayārtha*) and manifests the perfection of true reality (*bhūtapratipatti-pāramitā*).

(Question: The sutras often speak of "swift realization," yet here you again speak of three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*. This inevitably gives rise to doubt. Answer: For those of the sudden and perfect capacity (*yuan-dun-jī*), thoughts and eons are perfectly interfused.

Though they pass through three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*, they do not depart from the present thought-moment. How could ordinary sentiments possibly fathom this? △ Five: Verses on the Perfection of Meditation (*dhyāna-pāramitā*).
Entering and emerging from samādhi with mastery, they travel through the ten directions by means of transformative supernatural powers.
To sever the causes of sentient beings' afflictions, they seek liberation through the gateways of samādhi.

Samādhi is precisely meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Mastery (*vaśitā*) is precisely tranquility. Although one speaks of "entering" and "emerging," these are nothing other than manifestations of concentration.

Yet, because the nature of concentration is immovable, it truly does not exist within the interval of entering or emerging. One should know that walking, standing, sitting, and reclining are all none other than wondrous concentration.
Only when the celestial eye and the dragon’s gaze cannot perceive it can one attain true mastery.

Furthermore, within the concentration of transformation (*nirmāṇa-samādhi*), there is the great function of the Middle [Way]. This refers to manifesting all modes of deportment without departing from the fundamental nature.
Such transformations are like those of Avalokiteśvara appearing in accordance with circumstances; such spiritual powers (*abhijñā*) are like those of Viśuddhagarbha converting the heterodox.

Reaching the point of dividing forms and dispersing shadows, or manifesting bodies like the moon in water, one ascends without moving and pervades everywhere without thinking, throughout the lands of the ten directions.

There is no land where he does not manifest his body; therefore, it is said that he "traverses the ten directions. Regarding the phrase "in order to sever," this refers to the playful exercise of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-vikrīḍita*).
As for the term "afflictions" (*kleśa*) as the "cause," it means that afflictions are the cause of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) for sentient beings.

Since the primary aim within the gate of teaching and transforming is to deliver sentient beings, and since one must sever the causes of suffering if one wishes to lead them out of suffering, it is said, "in order to sever," and so forth. (3)
"Ma" (摩) means that once one possesses the altruistic mind, one also rescues others from within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) to bring them to liberation.

The Sanskrit term *samādhi* is translated here as "equilibrium-attainment" (*dengzhi*). "Equilibrium" (*deng*) refers to being free from both dullness (*laya*) and agitation (*auddhatya*); "attainment" (*zhi*) refers to reaching the Path by means of concentration.

It is also a specific designation for dhyāna-concentration, as one enters the Path through concentration; furthermore, it is metaphorically described as a "gate. (The single term *samādhi* has two meanings).

The explanation is as in the commentary, with the exception that the character "to seek" (求) is changed to "to save" (救). Second, because the original text contains the character "to seek" (求) in the phrase "seeking liberation" (求解脫), it seems to refer to the capacity of the practitioner (機). This means that the afflictions of sentient beings are themselves distracted and deluded thoughts;

now, wishing to sever them, although one relies upon the wisdom and supernatural powers of the Bodhisattvas, these serve nothing other than as superior conditions. To sever them, one must still do so oneself; liberation cannot be achieved without meditative concentration (禪定), and thus one "seeks" it—meaning one seeks meditative concentration in order to liberate oneself.

Thus, regarding the two characters "to sever" (為斷), the former meaning is correct; regarding the three characters "seeking, etc. (求等), the latter meaning is correct). △ Sixth: Verses on the Perfection of Wisdom (Prajñāpāramitā).

If one wishes to accomplish true wisdom, one should draw near to Bodhisattvas and Tathāgatas; delighting in hearing the sublime gateways of supramundane principles, one cultivates the attainment of the three insights and severs the two obstacles.

True wisdom is precisely *prajñā*. The first phrase establishes the definition; the subsequent phrase provides the formal explanation. Because one must encounter a superior teacher for guidance, it is called "intimate approach" (*upaniṣad*).
One who desires to transcend the world must rely on the wonderful Dharma as a guiding principle and gateway before being able to enter the Path.
Because one must listen to the teacher's instructions, it is called "delight in hearing. Thus, we know that a practitioner must encounter a true teacher.
It is difficult. It is difficult to hear the sublime Dharma. Without relying upon close association [with a teacher], how could that which is so joyfully sought be obtained?
Thus, as for the gateway of words to the sublime principle, the gateway serves as the thorough path to Buddhahood.
As Qingliang said: "To find its gateway is to equal the Buddhas in a single day; to lose its essential meaning is to labor in vain through kalpas of cultivation. If this is so...

To enter the gateway and comprehend the essential meaning, to cultivate and master the three insights (*trividyā*), and to be able to sever the two hindrances (*dvividhāvaraṇa*)—this will not be difficult.

(The three insights refer to the insight of the divine eye, the insight of recollecting past lives, and the insight of the exhaustion of outflows. The two hindrances are the hindrance of afflictions and the hindrance to the known. △ Seventh: Verses on the Perfection of Skillful Means (*upāyapāramitā*).
They are able to discern the differences in the minds of sentient beings; according to their ailments, they provide medicine for them to take and practice.
With compassion and skillful means, they respond to the suitability of their faculties, using expedient methods to benefit living beings and deliver the multitudes from existence.

The capacity for knowing necessarily involves observation, which belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*). The differentiation of the mind refers to the diverse mental intentions of sentient beings—such as what they are mindful of, what they contemplate, and what they cultivate—and it is through this that one knows their capacities.
The analogy of administering medicine according to the illness illustrates preaching the Dharma in accordance with those capacities.
The "illness" is a metaphor for the delusions and karma of sentient beings; the "medicine" is a metaphor for the Dharma-gates of the Bodhisattvas; and the "one who takes [the medicine]" is...
"This is taking medicine" means that the practitioner is one who follows and practices [the teaching]. In the analogy, the one who takes the medicine recovers from illness;
in the Dharma, the one who can practice exhausts all hindrances. "Compassionately providing medicine according to the illness" below explains that this refers to skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).
"Multitudes of beings" refers to sentient beings. Verse 8: The Power of Wisdom Combined with Vow.

He contemplates the true meaning of all phenomena; Unattached to the middle or the extremes, he is free from existence and non-existence. With pure wisdom uninterrupted, he realizes *tathatā* (suchness).
The two benefits are equalized, pervading the entire *dharmadhātu*. By the power of his wisdom, he understands the nature of sentient beings, And for their sake, he teaches the corresponding seeds.
The power of wisdom can enter the minds of sentient beings, causing them to sever the root of saṃsāric birth and death.

The power of wisdom can distinguish between black and white dharmas, discerning what to adopt and what to reject according to their needs. Birth and death and nirvāṇa are fundamentally equal; through this, one brings sentient beings to fulfillment, free from conceptual discrimination.
The first phrase refers to the wisdom that performs the contemplation; all phenomena constitute the teachings and principles that are the objects of contemplation.

The provisional teachings belong to the three vehicles, while the true meaning accords with the reality of the one vehicle. "Phrase" (句) refers to names and terminology, which pertain to that which expresses.
Ultimate reality (*tattvārtha*) is the intended meaning within the phrase; it is that which is to be explained. "Non-attachment" below refers to having realized the meaning within the phrase.

One must not attach to the two extremes, nor grasp at the middle way. One departs from the three characters "existence," "non-existence," and "middle. This explains the aforementioned "non-attachment":

for existence is the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*), while non-existence is the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); this explains the aforementioned character "extreme" (*anta*). However, since one has already departed from...
The two extremes do not exist, nor does a middle position. This is true wisdom illuminating the ultimate truth; its essence is all-pervasive—how could one discuss middle or extremes?
Therefore, it is said that "one does not cling," and so forth. The phrase "pure wisdom" below establishes the meaning of the two preceding lines.
Wisdom is called "pure" because it is non-conceptual. Thus, the subject of contemplation does not merely fail to cling to the meaning within the phrases, but does not cling to a middle either.

While remaining at the limit [of reality], one nevertheless observes all phenomena of the myriad existents as being harmoniously integrated without interval, all of which are the eternally abiding *tathatā*.

Regarding the "two benefits" (*dvayārtha*): it means that once a Bodhisattva has realized *tathatā* for their own benefit, they can further use this to benefit others, causing them all to realize *tathatā*;
only then do these constitute the true two benefits. Therefore, it is said to be "even and pervasive."
Regarding the *dharmadhātu*, there are two explanations. First, because both self and others have attained benefit, all realize the *tathatā* that pervades the *dharmadhātu*;
this is explained in terms of the realized principle (*prameya*). Second, once a bodhisattva has mastered this path, they are able to pervade the *dharmadhātu* and uniformly benefit sentient beings;
this is explained in terms of location (*deśa*). The power of wisdom can understand the lower [stages], clarifying that there is still conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*).

Regarding "wisdom": because it can illuminate the distinctions in the nature, characteristics, essence, and function of sentient beings' mental dispositions, it is said that [the Buddha] "preaches what is appropriate" and so forth.
This means that for those who are to be delivered by the Śrāvaka vehicle, he preaches the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and so on;

hence the term "various. Regarding "entering the minds of sentient beings": to accord with their capacities is called "entering. By the power of wisdom, he preaches the Dharma in accordance with their capacities, thereby being able to...
"Because the mental intentions of sentient beings coincide. Regarding "causing them to sever [delusion] below":

this means that once one knows that mental intentions are not uniform and are all merely false imaginings (*vikalpa*) capable of producing birth and death—the very root of saṃsāra—one preaches the Dharma for them so that they may abandon delusion and cut off its source;

hence it is said, "permanently severed. As for "being able to distinguish black and white dharmas," "distinguish" (*fen*) refers to discernment (*vibhajana*); "black and white" refers to the unwholesome and the wholesome (*kuśala*).
There are two types of evil karma; evil karma is black and brings about the three miserable realms, while virtuous karma is white and brings about rebirth as humans or devas.

Regarding what should be adopted or rejected according to circumstances, one selects those who can be saved. Those who individually understand this are all able to comprehend both the beginning and the end.
The final two lines concerning birth and death conclude the section on the excellence of the power of wisdom, meaning that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fundamentally equal.
There is no duality of essence. It is because sentient beings erroneously give rise to ignorance that it transforms into the consciousness of karma (*karmavijñāna*).
Yet the essence of this consciousness of karma is half-real and half-delusive: when deluded, there is birth and death; when awakened, it is itself nirvāṇa. Thus, two dharmas are established.
Now, when one illuminates this with the power of wisdom, even seeking a single nirvāṇa within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) cannot be found.
How much more so regarding birth and death! Therefore, it is said that they are fundamentally equal. Regarding the phrase "accomplishing the lower":

since it is said that equality is in reality without differentiation, yet differentiation arises spontaneously due to the deluded thoughts of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma for them.

Causing them to be separated from it is precisely the entire substance of true awakening (*bhūta-jñāna*). Because the Buddha attributes this merit to the Bodhisattva, he says "accomplishment" (*pariniṣpatti*) and so forth.
The two pāramitās of wisdom (*prajñā*) and power (*bala*) are originally one body; when opened, they become two, but when merged, they are one.
This is now their merging. However, regarding the ten pāramitās being deficient in *praṇidhāna* (vow), there is generally a sense of "tending toward" (*abhimukha*) within the text.

Aspiration: To resolve to deliver sentient beings is entirely for the sake of the vow of deliverance. That [the aspiration] remains hidden and unmanifest is because the Buddha is the Dharma King, possessing sovereign mastery over all dharmas;
thus, whether opening or closing [the teachings] as circumstances require, there is nothing that is not permissible. The above concludes the verses on the various *pāramitās*.
△ Ninth: Extensive Exposition According to Capabilities.
These ten kinds of sublime practices are subsumed within the eighty-four thousand [teachings];
according to their respective categories and superior dharma-gates, they are called the bodhisattva pāramitās.
The first phrase establishes the ten types. The second phrase means that if these are condensed, they constitute the ten pāramitās;
if expanded, they become eighty-four thousand. Now, because the expanded is subsumed within the condensed, it says "subsumed into" and so forth.

Regarding their respective categories, there are two explanations. The first is as stated in the prose: for those with excessive greed, [the teachings] are analyzed and expounded as two thousand one hundred.
The hundred [dharmas] are likewise for the latter three [categories], thus totaling eighty-four thousand. These are all sublime Dharma-gates serving as remedies.

Second, because the dispositions of sentient beings differ, their afflictions and karmas also vary. For those whose greed is heavy, one causes them to practice the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), using generosity to overcome stinginess.
For those whose evil karma is heavy, one causes them to practice the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*). Through ethical discipline...
It can cure evils and the like; extending to the eighty-four thousand [teachings], each according to its respective category, there is none that is not a medicine applied to a specific ailment.
Therefore, it is called a "superior dharma-gate. This concludes the section on the name, which leads back to the other shore. Whether extensive or concise, it is as such.

They cause all beings to leave birth and death behind, realize nirvana, and ascend high to the other shore. (This phrase is incorporated into the following sentence. Although the commentary states that the broad is subsumed by the concise, the phrasing is not smooth and the meaning remains obscure.

If one were to claim that the concise subsumes the broad—such as how the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) can subsume the six others—that would be plausible. However, as for the broad subsuming the concise, this has never been heard before; even with forced interpretation, it ultimately remains inconsistent.

If the text were amended to read "capable of subsuming eighty-four thousand gates"—meaning that the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*) can encompass many gates—then both the wording and the meaning would be consistent. Why? Because the prose section contains eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*, whereas these are absent from the verse. This is clearly a case of incorporation.

This is among the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*). If one does not dare to deviate from the scriptures, it is also acceptable to compose [this work] by expanding upon the concise; this is preferable to citing [passages] out of context or using them perversely. Furthermore, the principle of expanding the concise is more meritorious.
Should there be any errors in my exposition, I request those of superior insight to provide their own corrective vision. △ Ten: Extensive Benefit for Oneself and Others.

The eighty-four thousand samādhis can extinguish the distracted minds of sentient beings; the eighty-four thousand dhāraṇī-doors can eliminate the obstacles of delusion and dissolve the hosts of Māras.

*Samādhi* is the Sanskrit term for *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. The ancient masters state that "skillful means according with conditions" (*upāya-anu-pratyaya-śamatha*) is also an alternative name for meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*).
The phrase "capable of extinguishing [afflictions]" refers to the preeminent function of *samādhi*.
The distracted mind consists of the eighty-four thousand afflictions; *samādhi* remedies them accordingly, in that same number. This is *dhāraṇī*.
This refers to the literal meaning of the aforementioned *dhāraṇī*: because it protects the good and wards off evil, it is called "Total Retention" (*dhāraṇī*).
It can eliminate the obstacles of delusion and can dissolve the hosts of Māras; because of the divine efficacy of this total retention, it is said to be able to remove them.
The enumeration of its eighty-four thousand repetitions is as explained in the prose commentary. △ Eleven: Summary and Circulation.
By the power of skillful means of the Great Sage, the Dharma King, he transforms sentient beings through three essential teachings.
Casting the net of instruction into the ocean of birth and death, he establishes those people and devas in a place of peace and bliss.

Solely honored among the ten realms as the Great Sage, possessing mastery over both the provisional and the real as the Dharma King—though all are called Buddhas, one manifests as the Honored One among humans, while the other manifests as the Sovereign of the Dharma.

Through the power of skillful means, the aforementioned ten perfections, eighty thousand [dharmas], and so forth, are all skillful applications manifested according to the capacities of beings. Therefore, these three essential points of the Dharma clarify the true meaning.
"Expedient means" refers to the unequal opening and closing of the aforementioned *pāramitā*, *samādhi*, and *dhāraṇī* gates;

taking the adaptation to the capacity [of the recipient] as essential, it ensures that those who receive the teaching are numerous. Therefore, it is said "to transform sentient beings," all of which is the power and function of expedient means.
Regarding the "net of teaching": the Buddha gathers in sentient beings through the holy teachings of the five vehicles; thus, the sages and ordinary beings of the nine realms [are included].
It does not fall outside the scope of the Tathāgata; therefore, it is likened to a net. To "suspend downward" means to bestow from above upon those below.

All instances where the Buddha acts are considered "suspended teachings. Since the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) for sentient beings is as deep and vast as the great ocean, the Buddha preaches the Dharma within this ocean of birth and death to deliver sentient beings, just as one casts a net into the great ocean to catch fish.

It is like a fish; place it below. "Place" means to settle or install. The five characters "human beings, devas, etc. are interpreted in three ways. First, "human beings and devas" refers to the wholesome realms within the triple world (*tridhātu*).

Although they have not yet escaped birth and death (*saṃsāra*), they do not currently fall into the heavy sufferings of the three miserable destinies (*apāya*) and are temporarily prevented from losing their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
Subsequently, one again installs the sentient beings who have received transformation within these wholesome realms of humans and devas.
Regarding "the place of peace and bliss": the place of peace and bliss refers to *nirvāṇa* beyond the realms (*dhātu*).

Furthermore, it is only upon reaching ultimate, unsurpassed *bodhi* that one attains the great place of peace and bliss. One should understand that the three characters "transforming sentient beings" (*sattva-pariṇāmana*) apply universally;
that is, they apply to all nine realms, both noble and ordinary. When compared with the Buddha, all are called "sentient beings"; therefore, [this applies to] humans.
The term "two" (referring to the two vehicles) is restrictive. It is restricted merely to the two paths of humans and devas;

therefore, it is stated generally that within the realm (*dhātu*) there is birth-and-death with fixed limits (*paricchinna-vedanīya*), while outside the realm there is birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāma-vedanīya*).

For this reason, he manifests his body in the three lands—namely, the Land of Other-Enjoyment (*para-sambhoga-kṣetra*), the Land of Skillful Means with Remainder (*upāya-śeṣa-kṣetra*), and the Land of Common Dwelling of Ordinary and Holy Beings (*sādhāraṇa-kṣetra*)—and employs the four *siddhi*s (the four *siddhāntas*). Here, "all" (*siddha*) means "pervasive," and "*siddhānta*" means "bestowal. Thus, the Buddha universally bestows these four dharmas upon sentient beings.

The four types of *siddhānta* (doctrinal principles) are: first, the *loka-siddhānta*, which provides the benefit of joy; second, the *pudgala-siddhānta*, which provides the benefit of generating wholesome roots; third, the *pratipakṣa-siddhānta*, which provides the benefit of destroying evil; and fourth, the *paramārtha-siddhānta*, which provides the benefit of entering into principle.
These may be taught through the explicit exposition of the gates of *samādhi*, or through the esoteric meaning of *dhāraṇī*; thus, the manifest and the secret are perfectly integrated.
In the end, they all reached the other shore. △ Third, the benefits obtained upon hearing this chapter:
At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke this Dharma, eighty-four thousand sons of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven severed all obstructions of the realms.

They realized the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*). Countless hundreds of thousands of devaputras of the six desire realms awakened to the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and attained *dhāraṇīs*.

The sixteen great kings attained the *dhāraṇī* of hearing and retaining. The immeasurable fourfold assembly, upon hearing of the bodhisattva practices, some attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*), some attained gates of samādhi, some attained *dhāraṇīs*, and some attained great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Or...
There were bodhisattvas who had realized the third stage, up to and including the tenth stage, who leaped for joy with great exultation.
Immeasurable hundreds of thousands of humans and devas resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and became non-retrogressive.
Eight thousand humans and devas distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, attaining the pure Dharma-eye.

The obstruction of the various realms (*dhātu*) is precisely the obstruction of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva*). From within the stage of the three types of worthy ones (*tri-śukla-karma-patha*) and the preparatory practices (*prayoga*), upon first entering the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmi*), one abandons the obstruction of the nature of ordinary beings, realizes the all-pervading *tathatā*, and attains great joy (*mahā-pramuditā*).

Because this name was established from the moment of attaining the Path, it is called the Ground of Great Joy (*Pramuditā-bhūmi*). Regarding the realization of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), some say that one attains "Great" [Joy] at the First Dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*).

Dhāraṇī. Neither arising nor ceasing; these are accepted within the mind. Hereafter, each is explained according to the capacity of the audience; their modes of realization differ, all as stated in the original text.
"Distant from dust and free from defilement," etc., should also be interpreted according to the previous explanation. The above constitutes the correct explanation of the questions and doubts.
△ Second, the repeated answer to the further inquiry, in two parts: 1. The title of the chapter.
Chapter Nine: Adornments of Merit.
This chapter is titled as such because the Buddha answers Maitreya’s questions, extensively elucidating the four virtues that adorn one's own person.
△ Second, the text of the sūtra has four parts. First, Maitreya’s inquiry has three sections. First, the narration of receiving the Buddha’s words.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught, by dwelling in an araṇya and accomplishing its merits, one shall attain Buddhahood.”
These words spoken by the Buddha serve as the basis for the arising of doubt. Maitreya recounts them and subsequently presents his inquiry.
II. Raising the Inquiry:
How does a bodhisattva cultivate various merits and yet remain in this *āraṇya*?
The two characters "how" (*yú hé*) function as interrogative particles. Within this context, the character "all" (*zhū*) carries two meanings. First, "all" signifies "many.
This is because, following the preceding text where the Buddha spoke of three essential dharmas, each was expanded into eighty-four thousand [teachings], all of which constitute supreme merit.
The underlying intention is that in the *araṇya* (wilderness), the power of the human path is not yet sufficient and one's meritorious practices are not yet complete.
"How can one practice eighty-four thousand distinct Dharma-gates? This interpretation holds that he asks because he is following up on his previous doubts.
Alternatively, it may not follow from the previous [doubt], but rather he asks out of ignorance.

That is to say, the Buddha has stated that by accomplishing merit one shall attain Buddhahood, yet [the interlocutor] does not know how to cultivate these various merits. Here, the character "zhū" (various) is read lightly; it simply means "to act."

This is an auxiliary particle. It may be interpreted in two ways: either "By practicing what kind of merit can one dwell in this araṇya and attain Buddhahood? or "What kind of merit must one practice to be able to dwell in this araṇya and attain Buddhahood?
Both meanings are applicable as they correspond to the preceding and following contexts. However, according to the Buddha’s response, the latter meaning is correct.
△ Third, the request for instruction with a sense of urgency.
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me.
△ Second, the Tathāgata’s instruction has four parts. First, the general response concerning the single virtue of being worthy to abide.
At that time, the Buddha addressed Maitreya Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: "You, son of good family who are practicing and studying, should..."
There is, however, one virtue: such a person should dwell in an araṇya (forest hermitage) to seek the unsurpassed path.
This is the general response indicating the dwelling. △ Second, the investigation and explanation of the origin and details of this one virtue.
What is this one thing? It is the contemplation that the very source of all afflictions is one's own mind.
Having thoroughly realized this principle, one is able to dwell in a forest hermitage (*āraṇya*).
"Contemplation" refers to the wisdom of thorough investigation. All the delusions investigated below are collectively categorized as the five *vihāra-bhūmis* (stages of dwelling):
namely, the stage of views, the stage of the desire realm, the stage of the form realm, the stage of the formless realm, and the stage of ignorance. When expanded, these become eighty-four thousand.
To state that their root source is one's own mind is to point directly at it. There are two kinds of mind.
The one true mind is precisely the eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading nature of wondrous True Suchness (*tathatā*);

it is the substance shared by both sentient beings and Buddhas. Now, although it is called the "true mind," it is nonetheless the root of afflictions because, through a sudden lack of awareness, delusion arises in dependence upon the true, and various afflictions are produced based upon it. If one were to depart from this true [mind],...

How could there be affliction in the mind? It is like dust arising in dependence upon a mirror; apart from the mirror, there is no dust. Second is the deluded mind. Furthermore, this delusion is also twofold:
first is the *ālaya-vijñāna*, which serves as the root of all consciousnesses. Its substance is half-true and half-delusory.
The half-true is suchness (*tathatā*); the half-delusory is ignorance (*avidyā*). This refers to that which depends upon the *ālaya*.
It transforms into two parts: first, the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) which undergoes transformation; second, the object-part (nimitta-bhāga) which manifests as an appearance.

Together with the aforementioned ālayavijñāna, these constitute the three subtleties of ignorance. Because the seeing-part brings forth the objective realm of the object-part, the object-part is consequently able to manifest.
The seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) fails to realize that it is a manifestation of its own mind and, mistakenly believing external objects to truly exist, gives rise to grasping.

Consequently, subject and object stir the ocean of the mind, causing the waves of the various consciousnesses to arise and further generating the six coarse aspects: (1) the aspect of intellection (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*), which is the innate clinging to dharmas; (2) the aspect of continuity (*anubandha-lakṣaṇa*), which is the discriminative clinging to dharmas;

(3) the aspect of grasping (*parāmarśa-lakṣaṇa*), which is the innate clinging to a self (*ātman*); (4) the aspect of calculating names (*nāma-kalpanā-lakṣaṇa*), which is the discriminative clinging to a self; and (5) the aspect of initiating karma (*karma-samutthāna-lakṣaṇa*), which is the performance of all outflowing (*sāsrava*) actions.

Karma. The sixfold bondage of karma is the nature of suffering; it is precisely the retribution of the six realms of existence. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The ocean of the ālayavijñāna abides eternally, yet it is stirred by the winds of objective conditions."
The various waves of consciousness surge and arise in succession; because all afflictions originate from this, it is the root source of affliction.
Second is the sixth consciousness (manovijñāna); the various delusions of views and thoughts all arise because of this.
Thus, one knows that both the true mind and the deluded mind are roots of affliction. To thoroughly comprehend this—
As for "Dharma," it refers to that which is thoroughly realized through the wisdom that returns delusion to the True. This Dharma points to one's own mind as the object of realization.

Just as a person of great wisdom clearly perceives that delusive confusion is fundamentally empty, the manas-consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, and the ālayavijñāna is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. Returning to the original truth, its very substance is [the Dharma].

The Buddha said: "It is possible for those below [this level] to do so. This means that if there are individuals with such capacity who are able to dwell in an araṇya without failing their commitment, why must they necessarily cultivate all the *pāramitās*?
It is as the saying goes: "Once you know the One, ten thousand matters are finished. (Question: In the Dharma-character school [Faxiangzong], it is taught...)

The transformation of the mental states associated with the eight consciousnesses results in the Mirror-like Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*). The transformation of the mental states associated with the sixth consciousness results in the Wondrous Observing Wisdom (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*). While the substance of consciousness can only transform the defiled into the pure, this interpretation merely speaks of "transforming consciousness into wisdom.

Is this not contradictory? Answer: The School of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-yāna*) values discernment; the School of Nature (*dharmatā-yāna*) values integration. What is wrong with simply saying that consciousness is transformed into wisdom? Ancient masters have also made such statements. Do not use the School of Characteristics to challenge the School of Nature;

it is sufficient to understand the meaning. If you insist that discernment alone is correct, consider this: the Buddha taught that the three realms are "mind-only" (*citta-mātra*). Tell me, outside of this one mind, where do the various consciousnesses and their mental states reside? △ Third, a further inquiry.
This is an explanation by means of an analogy and its inverse.
Why is this so? It is like a rabid dog that, when driven and beaten by a person, pursues only the shards and stones but does not pursue the person.
In future ages, it shall be the same for those who have newly resolved to attain awakening and dwell in an araṇya.
If, upon encountering forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental objects, their minds become stained with attachment, such persons do not understand the root of affliction.

They fail to realize that these [afflictions] do not arise from the five sensory objects, but rather from one's own mind. This is precisely what is called "not yet being well-established in an araṇya."
"The rabid dog chasing stones" is a metaphor universally known to all people; it corresponds here to the inferior dharmas of the future.

"Those who have newly resolved their minds" refers to ordinary people who, having raised their resolve, abide in stillness and practice cultivation. "The future" refers to the period of the Final Dharma (*mofa*) following the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
"It is likewise so" generally follows the previous analogy. "If one sees the inferior [faculties]" refers to those capable of... [the root].

Regarding the objects [of perception]: this precisely corresponds to "chasing after stones. When the mind becomes stained and attached, it is like the eye encountering form, which gives rise to the visual consciousness and the simultaneous mental consciousness, whereby one subsequently discriminates various forms.
When the ear encounters sound, it gives rise to the auditory consciousness and the simultaneous mental consciousness, which rush outward and pursue the sounds.
The same applies to the other four [senses]. Because they chase after objects and grasp at conditions, they are—along with...
"The mad dog chasing stones" is no different [from this]. This person, below, explains the meaning of pursuing objects and grasping at conditions (*ālambana*).
He states that the root of their afflictions (*kleśa*) is precisely one's own mind; the five objects, such as form and sound, are also one's own mind.
Because they do not understand this, they falsely conceive of there being five real objects external to the mind, giving rise to deluded attachment—what is called "one's own mind grasping."
"One's own mind: that which is not illusion manifests as illusory phenomena. Regarding the phrase "that is to say" (*ji ci xia*) below:
this refers to such a person who, although possessing a mind that favors tranquility, does not recognize its fundamental source; they are called those who have not yet been able to dwell well.

One should know that the character "cause" (*yin*) in the phrase "not due to the cause of the five objects" is unstable; it is likely an error for the character "know" (*zhi*). If one insists on reading it as "cause," it lacks meaning.

This is extremely grave. Now, the character "zhī" (to know) is corrected to "zhèng" (correct). This states that these people do not know the root of afflictions (*kleśa*), which is precisely one's own mind.
This phrase merely rebukes their failure to recognize the mind; it further implies they do not know that the five sense objects (*viṣaya*) are also one's own mind.
(The five sense objects are form, sound, smell, taste, and touch. The reason the mental object (*dharmadhātu*) is not mentioned is because it is the outflowing condition of these five sense objects.
The reflection does not emerge apart from the five sense-objects; yet, one does not say that the five sense-objects are themselves one's own mind.

Rather, it is said that they arise from one's own mind, meaning that the true mind, following conditions, transforms into the appearance of objective aspects (nimitta-bhāga). However, since the object appears in dependence upon the mind, the entire object is identical to the mind.
It is like a reflection appearing in dependence upon a mirror: the entire reflection is identical to the mirror. Because of this ignorance, such is the case.

The subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of one's own mind grasps and clings to the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of one's own mind; yet, failing to realize that both are entirely nothing but mind, one merely conceives of them as existing separately outside the mind.

Because one holds such a view, this is not considered "abiding well. △ Fourth, the conclusion of the preceding section and the introduction of the subsequent section, consisting of a broad explanation in three parts: 1. Conclusion of the preceding section.
For these reasons, they delight in dwelling in tranquility and seek the unsurpassed path.
△ Second, opening the subsequent section: 5. Deeply investigating the root of delusion.
When all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas encounter the objects of the five desires appearing before them, they observe their own minds.
One should reflect thus: "From beginningless time until this day, I have transmigrated through the six realms of existence with no prospect of escape.

All this has arisen from my own deluded mind, which produces confusion and, regarding the objects of the five desires, gives rise to craving, attachment, and defilement. Thus it is for the Bodhisattva.
One who is capable of dwelling in an araṇya is so named.
Anyone who has merely resolved upon bodhicitta is called a bodhisattva. As for the term "mahāsattva," it refers to a great bodhisattva among bodhisattvas;
this is merely a title used to address a beginner, and does not refer to one of profound realization.
"Status" may be compared [to this]. As it is said, "great mind, great measure, great virtue, great person"—these are all titles of address.
If there are the five lower [objects], this is the method of contemplation taught by the Buddha. The objects of the five desires are the five sensory realms (*pañca-viṣaya*).
When these forms and so forth appear before one, they must necessarily confront the eyes and the other faculties. At the very moment of confrontation, one must suddenly observe for oneself.

"Mind. [The character] "should" should be read as "downward. This refers to the meaning of observation. "Beginningless," etc., refers to the deluded mind, which denotes the *karmic-consciousness* (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

That which "gives rise to confusion and inversion" refers to the transformation into the functioning consciousness (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and its discrimination. Because one does not recognize one's own mind, one is confused;

because one grasps at phenomena as being external to the mind, one is inverted. Thus, all instances of craving, attachment, and clinging toward the objects of the five desires are due to the deluded mind.
This is the fundamental point. As stated below, it concludes with the name "Able to Abide" (*kannju*). This is because the scriptural text must necessarily contain a hidden meaning.

The intended meaning is that once one recognizes the deluded mind and its grasping, one must not pursue objects or engage in discursive attachment. Thus, the mind does not follow after external objects.
Then the mind and its objects will naturally become empty, and the two types of grasping will naturally cease. Only those with sharp faculties can correspond with the *araṇya* (hermitage);
thus they are able to dwell there. If one does not reveal the underlying intention, the explicit text would be deficient and would contradict the following section.
Reflect on this. △ Second, such persons quickly realize Bodhi.
If someone asks, "Which sentient beings shall become Buddhas in future ages? one should point to these people, saying:
"In a future age, they shall emerge from the suffering of the triple world, shatter the armies of the four Māras, swiftly attain Bodhi, and enter the wisdom of the Buddha."
All those in the world—the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, asuras, and so forth—should all make offerings to him.
Because he has recognized his own deluded mind through the preceding section and does not pursue external conditions, he possesses the potential to attain the Way.

Fearing that those who doubt might remain undecided, [the Buddha] says, "If there should be someone who asks," and so forth. This was spoken by the Buddha to Maitreya; it is as if there were someone...
Question: You ask, "The Buddha delivers sentient beings, and all desire to become Buddhas; yet one does not know which sentient beings will attain Buddhahood in the future.
This is because the categories of sentient beings are vast, and while all possess Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), one simply does not know which category or which individual will achieve realization.
Such is the general doubt among worldly people. It should be pointed out below that this [doubt] was also intended by the Buddha himself.
Maitreya, in response to that questioner’s words: "This person" refers to the individual previously described who is capable of recognizing the deluded mind.
In a future life, such a person will swiftly achieve Bodhi. The underlying intent is that once the deluded mind is recognized, the deluded mind is empty;
when the deluded mind is empty, that is itself the True Mind, which is not obtained from without. This is why one becomes a Buddha. (End of Section 3, Part B). Narrative.

Regarding the meaning of "about to achieve": the suffering of the three realms is birth and death; the four demonic armies are the demon of afflictions, the demon of the five aggregates, the demon of death, and the celestial demon.
This means that whenever a Buddha achieves enlightenment, he must necessarily destroy these four demons. Once the four demons have been destroyed...
