Enlightenment is thus accomplished. "Entering the Buddha’s wisdom" means that "entering" is a state of union; it refers to the initial awakening (śikṣābodhi) uniting with the original awakening (mūlabodhi) to achieve ultimate awakening (atyantabodhi).
This constitutes entering the wisdom of the Buddha within one's own mind and returning to become the fundamental Buddha of one's own mind.

From the phrase "All [beings]" onwards, the merit of being worthy of offerings (arhat) is revealed; that is to say, having already attained Buddhahood, one acts for the sake of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.

As a field of merit, all those in the world should equally make offerings to them. Because one has realized through the aforementioned causes that one’s own mind is [the Buddha], one shall attain Buddhahood.
Since the efficacy of dwelling in an araṇya (hermitage) is such as this, it cannot be compared to those who delude the world for the sake of seeking ease under false pretenses.
△ Third, exhorting others to make offerings so as to obtain blessings.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family, with a pure mind, makes offerings to such a true and virtuous son of the Buddha dwelling in an araṇya,
the merit they obtain will be immeasurable and boundless.
The Buddha is one who has already become a Buddha; those who dwell in *araṇya* and recognize their own minds are the Buddhas of the future.

They are fields of merit for all sentient beings; even devas and nāgas should make offerings to them, let alone humans. Therefore, it is exhorted that by making offerings, one shall obtain immeasurable merit.
△ Fourth, an analogy is drawn to illustrate the merit of making offerings to one's mother.
Furthermore, if there were someone who made offerings of various precious jewels to their compassionate mother, the merit obtained would likewise be without distinction.

To briefly cite an example regarding the merit of honoring one’s mother: it should be understood that the World-Honored One, in order to repay the four debts of gratitude, extensively taught that the kindness of a compassionate mother is profound.
Since that time, the text has been extensive; fearing that readers might overlook this point, I have addressed it here.

Comparing their merits: suddenly, with a single exhortation, they provide a warning and encouragement to others. One’s body comes from the mother’s womb; one’s virtue comes from the mother’s instruction.
One should know that the compassionate mother is a living Buddha in the home; the father is likewise so. A child may offer precious jewels [to them].

The merit thus obtained is no different from that of one who makes offerings to the Buddha. That is to say, for a householder to be filial toward his parents—why must one go so far as to burn incense?
△ Fifth, the inquiry and explanation regarding the realization of Bodhi.

Why is this? Because such a person shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, turn the wheel of the true Dharma, deliver the multitudes of devas and humans, and continue the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it is never severed; for they shall act as a refuge for all sentient beings.
This section should have been moved to precede the section on "Making Offerings to One's Parents. The subsequent text states:
"The merit obtained from making offerings to such a true and virtuous son of the Buddha who dwells in an araṇya is immeasurable and boundless.
It then proceeds with: "Why is this? Because such a person shall attain... [and so forth]. The interrogation asks: "Although that person dwelling in the araṇya recognizes their own..."
The mind has nothing that does not benefit oneself. As for why one who is able to make offerings obtains merit that is immeasurable and boundless, the following passage explains this:

because such a person has already realized their own mind, they shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and will thus be counted among the Buddhas of the future. Any offering made to them is, in fact, an offering to the Buddha.
This is because their merit is superior. The section concerning the offering to one's mother should be moved to follow this; thus the text will flow smoothly and the meaning will also be appropriate.
If it were otherwise, although parents at home possess compassion, it would be nothing other than affection born of worldly attachment;
furthermore, they have not transcended birth and death—how could they reach Bodhi? This was likely done by a scribe after the translation, as he sought to [rearrange the order].
The omission of one section has been corrected by inserting it after the "Offering to the Mothers" (mātṛkā-pūjā). I request those with discerning eyes to examine this.

△ Third, the detailed explanation has two parts. First, those who are not suitable vessels must not dwell [here]. This has three parts. First, those with wrong views and greed for wealth must not dwell [here].
Furthermore, son of good family, there are two kinds of dharmas that bind a practitioner and render them incapable of dwelling in an araṇya:
first, delighting in the false dharma of nihilistic views; second, delighting in wealth, treasures, and objects of pleasure.
There are two lower headings for the section on abiding. First, the lower heading explains "delightful attachment," which refers to the desires of those with wrong dispositions.
"Denial" (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) refers to the repudiation of cause and effect. "Wrong teachings" refer to such practices as fire-worship and water-reverence.

This is because the seeds of these two views already exist within the mind, and the active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of these two views will inevitably emerge externally. Now, since it is said that one must sever these wrong views:

Taken together, these comprise the five sharp [afflictions], which are the delusions of view (*dṛṣ�-cravā-āsrava*). Second, the "lower" refers to the five dull [afflictions], specifically greed (*rāga*);

however, since "craving and delight" is synonymous with greed, this term encompasses all five dull afflictions, which are the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-āsrava*). Thus, they are collectively termed the delusions of view and thought.
Like a silkworm spinning its cocoon, one entangles and binds oneself; hence the expressions "bondage" and so forth. If this mind is not forgotten and this practice is constantly performed, even if...
To dwell in an araṇya under such circumstances is in vain and of no benefit. Therefore, it is said that one "is not fit to dwell" and so forth.
One should understand that the character *ling* (令) here is used as if the Buddha were speaking to Maitreya; whenever such instances occur, it means "let him not dwell. 2.
Not dwelling in the evil dharma of arrogance.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are two kinds of people who are unfit to dwell in an araṇya hermitage: first, those who are possessed of pride;
second, those who revile the Mahāyāna Dharma.
To despise others is called pride (*māna*); to esteem oneself is called arrogance (*mada*). One who is arrogant does not desire ascetic practice; one who is proud looks down upon right cultivation.
Pride can obstruct the Path, rendering even one’s dwelling therein useless; hence it is said that [such a person] is "incapable.

Under a single word of the Dharma-treasure of the Mahāyāna, the ground of the mind opens and through, and one may realize Bodhi immediately. Even if one seeks it, one fears not obtaining it—how much more so for one who hates it!

One will inevitably incur heavy suffering. Since such evil inevitably leads to slander, it becomes the karmic cause for the three miserable realms; even seeking a human rebirth, one fears it may not be obtained.
What benefit is there in dwelling in an araṇya? Therefore, it is said that one cannot endure living there. △ Third, do not dwell where wrong views prevail and precepts are broken.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are two kinds of persons who should not reside in an araṇya:
first, those with wrong views who do not believe the Buddha’s words; second, those who themselves break the precepts yet employ those who uphold them for their own labor.
Such persons as these should not reside in an araṇya seeking the unsurpassed path.

The first four lines present the heading; "First" and below provide the explanation; "In this way" and below provide the conclusion. This is because those of the four classes—scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants—all follow his teachings;
if they believe and are able to practice them, they will surely achieve their aspirations. How much more so for the disciples of the Buddha?

To disbelieve the Buddha’s words and instead form heterodox views is to share the same doctrine as the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas); what benefit is there in abiding by such a path? Second, it refers to the three trainings, beginning with the training in ethical discipline (śīla).

This constitutes the foundation. By upholding it, one can give rise to concentration and wisdom, and enlightenment may be expected. To destroy it is to lose one's foundation; it is merely a vain labor with no benefit.

Regarding "driving and employing those below": this refers to those who, having themselves broken the precepts, still feel no shame or remorse, and instead drive and employ those who uphold the precepts.
They are like criminals who wish to command their superiors—truly, such behavior is despicable.
[The author] laughs. Not only do they lack a sense of shame, but they have become even more arrogant. Therefore, the conclusion below states: "Such as these.
Since both have lost their fundamental basis, they should not reside [there]. If even residing is not permitted, how much less so seeking the Way? Alas!
It is only right that all *śramaṇas* who propagate the Dharma should reflect upon themselves. II. The Proper Object of the Teaching and Their Residence. Part One: Four [Points].
One should abide in eleven virtues. First, the four virtues beginning with dhāraṇī.
Furthermore, son of good family, one who possesses four kinds of virtues should dwell in an araṇya. What are these four?
First, possessing renown and dhāraṇī such that one does not forget; second, being able to clearly understand subtle meanings; third, correctly...
One should always maintain mindfulness and remain free from negligence. Fourth, one should act in accordance with the teachings.
Son of good family, if there is a son of the Buddha who accomplishes these four kinds of supreme virtues, he should dwell in an araṇya and cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.

Seeking the Unsurpassed Way. Furthermore, the following is the heading: "What is meant by 'investigation'? First, the following is the explanation. "Good son," and so forth, is the conclusion. Regarding "renown":

"name" refers to name-characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*), such as the nature and characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the six sense bases (*ṣad-āyatana*). "Hearing" (*śruta*) is the foremost of the three types of wisdom (*tri-prajñā*). As [it is said]:

When the faculty of hearing gives rise to consciousness, one surveys the meanings of the Buddha’s teachings and maintains them without forgetting; this is *dhāraṇī* (retention), which belongs to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*).

To be able to understand the subtle meanings is the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*). One must investigate what has been heard, exhaustively examine its ultimate point, and achieve a sudden, thorough penetration.
To comprehend the essential purport within hearing is what constitutes the ability to understand the subtle meaning.

"Right mindfulness" (*samyak-smṛti*) is precisely the bodhicitta, because it maintains an unceasing recollection of the *tathatā* dharma. Non-negligence (*apramāda*) is itself right mindfulness. The *Śata-dharmaka-śāstra* states:

"Diligence has the three roots (namely, non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion) as its basis; its nature consists of guarding and cultivating that which is to be practiced and abandoned, and it serves as the antidote to negligence."

Its function is to bring to completion all mundane and supramundane wholesome deeds. Regarding "prevention and cultivation": for the evil that is to be abandoned, one prevents it from arising; for the wholesome that is to be cultivated, one cultivates it so that it increases.
Regarding "conformity": to conform means not to oppose, and to conform means to follow; as the Buddha has instructed, one relies upon and acts according to them.
Together with the above, this constitutes the wisdom of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). "Good son" and below summarizes the four kinds of sublime virtues.

These are precisely the three types of wisdom—listening, reflection, and cultivation—as well as the bodhicitta; these constitute the great foundation for attaining Buddhahood and the excellent vessel for receiving the Way.
It may be said that the person and the ground are mutually suited; hence it is said, "one should," and so forth.

For those who practice the path of the Bodhisattva, let us first consider the contemplation of the mind. This is because the subtle and wondrous gates of the six perfections and myriad practices are indeed infinite.

However, how could a bodhisattva at the initial stage of practice be able to engage in extensive conduct? Therefore, for the time being, one should exclusively abide in right mindfulness and investigate the ground of the mind.
The wisdom capable of such investigation is the unsurpassed path, which is the very fruit sought. Thus, by employing wisdom to dispel consciousness, not a single thought arises;
it is seeking without seeking, for where there is seeking, there is no seeking. The unsurpassed, wondrous path is fundamentally one's own mind.

It is not that what is not realized is realized; even realization is without realization. This is not like the functioning of the deluded mind of ordinary people; therefore, it is called "supreme virtue" (*guṇa*).
△ Second, the four virtues beginning with compassion.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are four virtues by which a renunciant bodhisattva adorns his own person while dwelling in an araṇya, seeking the wisdom of a Buddha.
What are these four? First, great loving-kindness; second, great compassion; third, great sympathetic joy;
and fourth, great equanimity. Son of good family, these four dharmas can give rise to all merit and wisdom.
They bring benefit, peace, and happiness to immeasurable sentient beings, and swiftly realize the dharma of unsurpassed great bodhi.

The headings, indications, explanations, and conclusions are the same as before; all subsequent sections follow this pattern. Compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity are the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
This is purely an action for the benefit of others. "In this way," and so forth, clarifies that through such conduct one brings about merit. Regarding "able to produce [virtue]" and so forth:
by taking the four immeasurable minds as the means to benefit others, one is able to perfect one's own virtues; therefore, all merit and wisdom arise from this.
"Benefit and happiness," and so forth, correctly states the great benefit of benefiting others: compassion is able to extract suffering, which is precisely what constitutes salvation.

The benefit for others consists of: loving-kindness (*maitrī*) which bestows happiness, namely the benefit of peace and bliss; sympathetic joy (*muditā*) which enables the teaching of the Dharma, namely the benefit of instruction;

and equanimity (*upekṣā*) which observes with impartiality, namely the benefit of universal grace. Through these, one swiftly realizes the lower fetters and the qualities of Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
These are the two virtues of wisdom and abandonment. △ Third, the four virtues beginning with *dhūta*.
Furthermore, good son, there are another four virtues for a renunciant bodhisattva. By maintaining pure precepts, one can reach Bodhi. What are these four?
First, constantly abiding in the four stainless natures (*catur-vimala-dhātu*). Second, always practicing the twelve ascetic practices (*dvādaśa-dhūtaguṇa*). [The text continues...]
Tatha. Third, they remain far removed from both householders and renunciants. Fourth, they are forever free from flattery, deception, and envy.
Good son, all bodhisattvas rely on these four dharmas to forever leave behind birth and death and attain great bodhi.
Bodhi is the ultimate fruit; upholding the precepts is the foundation of all practices. When the conduct of the precepts is pure, then all practices are perfected.
Because one receives the fruit by means of the cause, it is said that one is able to reach Bodhi. These are the four stainless natures.
These are the four things: food and drink, clothing, bedding and seats, and medicine.
To be free from greed and anger toward these according to one's lot constitutes the nature of being stainless (*vimala*). Because greed and the like do not arise, its nature is inherently pure;

thus it is called "stainless. The twelve *dhūta* practices are all explained as before. Because they must not be interrupted, they are called "constant practice. "Far removed from the base," etc., refers to this.
One delights in the practice of seclusion. Those who remain at home are mostly defiled by the five desires; those who have left the home life may cling to the Hīnayāna.

If one practices the way of seclusion, one not only distances oneself from the five desires, but also does not draw near to the Hīnayāna. (The term "leaving the home life" is used as a general designation for both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.)

There are also those who have left the household life as non-Buddhist outsiders (this excludes the minor outsiders). Those who are sycophantic, deceitful, and envious all possess secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

To be "sycophantic" is to be fawning and flattering in speech; to be "deceitful" is to be guileful and fraudulent in conduct; to "envy" is to resent another's excellence; to "jealous" is to resent another's ability.
Once this mind is present, there is no need for further discussion. Therefore, it is said: "Permanently free from [these]. This concludes the section on the virtuous sons.
Furthermore, good son, there are four more dharmas for a renunciant bodhisattva that lead to eternal liberation from birth and death and the attainment of great bodhi.
This passage contains the heading but lacks the explanation; it is certainly an omission by the translator and need not be laboriously interpreted. △ Four: Upholding the Precepts.
These are the four virtues.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are four further dharmas for a renunciant bodhisattva that encompass all goodness. What are these four?
First, they purely uphold the prohibitive precepts and possess great learning. Second, they enter various samādhis and are able to be endowed with wisdom.
Wisdom. Third, attaining the six supernormal powers while concurrently cultivating the knowledge of all modes. Fourth, skillful means and being free from negligence.
Good son, these four dharmas are what the Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time have collectively practiced and studied. You, sons of the Buddha, [should likewise do so].
One should also practice this, so as to swiftly realize vast and unsurpassed bodhi.
"Precepts" (*śīla*) refers to restraint; "restraint" means maintaining [the prohibitions]. "Maintaining" refers to purity; "purity" means being immaculate. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"Purily maintain the prohibitive precepts, just as one protects a bright pearl. Regarding "much learning": because the nature of one who maintains the precepts is not clouded...
Because the turbidities [of the mind] have been purified, the Buddha-dharma enters the heart and is never again forgotten; this is what constitutes "extensive learning" (*bahuśruta*).

As for "samādhi," it is the essential nature of meditative concentration (*samāpatti*), which in reality has no manifold varieties. The term "various" used here is employed by manifesting the essence through its functions;

because these functions possess distinctions, various names are established. "Entering" (*praveśa*) refers to the gathering of functions; that is to say, gathering the functions back into the essence is called "entering the various concentrations."

One who is able to possess wisdom is one whose meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is characterized by clear observation. Thus, when concentration possesses wisdom, it is like a mirror possessing light;

it cannot be deceived by external objects. One who attains the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) realizes the great function of concentration. These six types are to be understood according to what was explained previously.

The "knowledge of all modes" (*sarvākārajñatā*) refers to both the knowledge of all modes and the knowledge of the paths (*mārgajñatā*), which are both the Buddha-knowledge. "Practicing them concurrently" distinguishes this from practicing them separately.

Although one may have attained the essence through the preceding causes and manifested their functions—possessing even the six supernormal powers—if one does not cultivate and infuse the knowledge of all modes, [the ultimate result will not be realized].
Fearing a fall into the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), one must practice both together.

However, while the wisdom of the two vehicles merely eliminates the grasping at a self (*ātman-grāha*), the wisdom of the Tathāgata must necessarily sever both the grasping at a self and the grasping at phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) before it is attained. Since severance is itself cultivation, it is called "practicing both together.
Skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) refers to benefiting sentient beings according to their needs. Heedfulness (*apramāda*) is as explained previously. O virtuous son...
The lower section on the joint cultivation across the three periods of time: this is the method universally practiced by all noble ones (ārya).

Therefore, without precepts one cannot achieve concentration (samādhi); without concentration one cannot give rise to wisdom (prajñā); and without supernormal powers (abhijñā) one cannot exercise the great function [of liberation].
Without extensive learning, one does not recognize the provisional and the ultimate; without skillful means, one cannot respond to the capacities of others.

Since both self-benefit and benefit for others, as well as the beginning and end of cause and effect, are all attained from this, it is called that which is "jointly practiced and studied. The following section encourages you to practice.
This refers to that which all Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time have collectively cultivated and studied. How could you, O Sons of the Buddha, be otherwise?
Therefore, it says, "you should also [practice] equally. △ Fifth, the four virtues beginning with giving.
Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva who has gone forth possesses four dharmas by which they do not regress from the bodhisattva practice.
What are these four? First, generosity; second, pleasant speech; third, beneficial conduct; and fourth, cooperation.
Son of good family, these four practices are the path leading to enlightenment and the root of benefiting sentient beings for all bodhisattvas.

All should practice and study these four, beginning with generosity (*dāna*). These are all dharmas for gathering and sustaining sentient beings; they are the skillful means (*upāya*) and provisional wisdom (*prajñā*) that are well able to gather and transform sentient beings, causing them to rely [upon the teacher].
Only then does one lead them by way of the right path of the Mahāyāna. (Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra)
It is said: "First, one uses the hook of desire to draw them in; afterwards, one causes them to enter the Buddha-wisdom. This refers to the first means of integration, *dāna* (giving).
It means that a bodhisattva employs two kinds of giving to integrate sentient beings. If sentient beings delight in material wealth, they are integrated by means of material giving;
if they delight in the Dharma, they are integrated by means of Dharma-giving. Once sentient beings have received the benefits of these two kinds of giving, because of this—
They give rise to affection and love, rely [on the teacher] to receive the Way, and attain abiding in the True Principle; therefore, this is called the inclusion through giving (*dāna-saṃgraha*).

As for kind speech (*priyavāditā*): it means that the Bodhisattva, in accordance with the faculties and natures of sentient beings, comforts and consoles them with skillful words, whereby all sentient beings—
One delights in hearing wholesome words; because of this, affection and love arise, leading one to rely [on the teacher] and receive the Path, thereby attaining abiding in the True Principle.

This is therefore called "gathering through kind speech. Third is "beneficial conduct," which refers to the Bodhisattva’s performance of wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind for the sake of benefiting others.
All sentient beings, by means of this, give rise to affection and love; they rely upon it to receive the Way and abide in the True Principle.

Therefore, it is called "gathering through beneficial conduct. Regarding the fourth, "commonality of purpose": this means that the Bodhisattva, with the clear vision of the Dharma-eye, perceives the faculties and natures of sentient beings.
According to their inclinations, he manifests various forms and acts in concert with them, causing each to partake in benefit.

Because of this, affectionate love arises; one relies upon and receives the Way, thereby attaining abiding in the True Principle. This is therefore called "gathering through common purpose" (*samānārthatā*).
[The text] concludes the section on the good sons below, stating: "These four practices are purely for the benefit of others; hence they are called the 'root'.
[The section] beginning with "All... below exhorts practice. △ Sixth, the observation of the four virtues, etc.
Furthermore, good son, a renunciant bodhisattva possesses four further virtues while dwelling in an araṇya, maintaining pure precepts, and adorning their own person.
What are these four? First, they observe that they themselves have no inherent nature, thereby subduing and severing the two types of grasping and realizing non-self.
Second, they observe that other persons likewise have no inherent nature, and thus remain free from hatred toward enemies and attachment toward kin.
Therefore, third, there is physical and mental bliss, because the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta-dharma*) are free from conceptual discrimination (*avikalpa*).
Fourth, one attains the wisdom of equality, because there is no distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. Noble son, these four dharmas are what all bodhisattvas should cultivate;
you, sons of the Buddha, should likewise cultivate them to proceed far toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).

"Maintaining pure precepts" means adorning one's own person; for through this, the mind becomes expansive and the body plump, virtue manifests in the facial complexion, and one is further protected by benevolent deities.
One’s dignified deportment becomes worthy of observation, serving as the foundation for cultivation and realization—this is what is meant by "virtue moistening the person.

As for "contemplation" and so forth, these refer to the specific practices performed by a bodhisattva. Regarding the phrase "having no inherent nature": [it refers to the realization that] there is no self-nature from the very beginning.

One should know one’s original nature. It is not the Buddha-nature that constitutes one's original nature, for sentient beings in their daily lives all take deluded consciousness to be their original nature;
yet this essence is unreal and manifests only in response to objects. Therefore, the Buddha commanded an investigation:
that which is solid is earth, moisture is water, warmth belongs to fire, and movement belongs to wind. In the midst of illness, these cannot function [as they appear].
Master, since death comes and one cannot remain, where is the inherent nature? Whenever deluded thoughts arise, observe in this manner;

then self-grasping will naturally subside, and the seeds and their manifestations will naturally be severed. (To "subside" means that active manifestations do not arise; to "sever" means that the seeds are also extinguished.
As for other bodies also lacking an inherent nature, one uses oneself as an analogy for others: if I have no self, how could they have a self?
Ah! Through this, the four marks of the person are suddenly and entirely empty. Thus, those who were previously objects of resentment are no longer hated, and those who were kin are no longer loved.
This is what it means for one’s observance of the precepts to be pure, thereby adorning one's own person.

Third, "below" refers to the fact that since the two aforementioned attachments are already empty, the body does not rush about and thus the body is autonomous; the mind does not pursue external objects and thus the mind [is autonomous].
Because it is sovereign, it is called "blissful. "Mind" refers to the eight consciousnesses as the mind-kings (*citta-rāja*); "factors" refers to the mental concomitants (*caitta*).

Since the fundamental nature is originally non-existent, how could there be any discrimination? Thus, the various phenomena of the kings and their factors should, upon a single thought, transform into supreme awakening.
The fourth section below clarifies the transformation of consciousness into wisdom. Regarding the attainment of the wisdom of equality: because the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is already empty.

When the seventh consciousness does not take the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eighth consciousness as its internal self, the seventh consciousness is transformed in that very place into the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*).
Regarding the subsequent phrase, "no distinction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa," this arises from the attainment of this wisdom.
Thus, one contemplates that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is not different from *nirvāṇa*, just as flowers in the sky (*ākāśapuṣpa*) are identical to emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
*Nirvāṇa* does not obstruct birth-and-death, just as emptiness is identical to flowers in the sky. Yet, the flower and emptiness are non-dual; they appear differently depending on the perceiver:
those with diseased eyes see the flowers, while those with healthy vision do not. If one seeks emptiness from the perspective of the Buddhas, [it is found to be thus].

The nature is unattainable; where, then, can the marks of the flower be found? It is universally one awakening, and thus there is no differentiation. These four virtues manifest self-benefit while concealing benefit for others.

[The passage from] "Good man" below concludes with an exhortation, which may be understood. [Question: Previously it was said that [enlightenment] is quickly realized, and again that it is swiftly realized;

yet here at the conclusion it is said that one "proceeds afar," and in later texts it is said that one "passes through a great ocean of kalpas. Since "swift" and "traversing a long distance" are contradictory, what is the meaning of this? [Answer: "Swift" refers to the fact that because the faculties are sharp and the contemplation is wondrous, one does not encounter detours.

One may perfect the fruits of vast kalpas within a single lifetime. Regarding the term "distant," this primarily reveals that what is realized is lofty and sublime, not situated in a lower station; it does not mean being physically remote. Furthermore, the phrase "passing through oceans of kalpas" refers to the fact that sentient beings are infinite and one’s altruistic resolve is so urgent that one does not shrink from a long duration, vowing to deliver them all.

This is what is meant by first awakening to the nature-ocean of Vairocana and subsequently entering the practice-gate of Samantabhadra. Although one passes through oceans of kalpas, because one is sustained by the power of one's vows, one is unaware that the time is long.
Since the contemplation of kalpas and their perfect fusion are thus unified, how could there be any contradiction? △ Seventh, the four virtues such as delivering sentient beings.

Furthermore, son of good family, all bodhisattvas have four vows by which they bring sentient beings to maturity and sustain the Three Jewels, never regressing throughout oceans of great eons. What are these four? First, the vow to deliver all sentient beings;
second, the vow to sever all afflictions; third, the vow to study all Dharma-gates; fourth, the vow...

They realize the fruit of all Buddhas. Good son, these four dharmas should be cultivated and studied by both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna bodhisattvas alike, for they are the locus of study for bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
This refers to the Four Great Vows. "Sentient beings" (*sattva*) refers to living beings;
because these beings possess consciousness, they are designated by that name based upon their deluded consciousness. "Maturation" refers to transformation and deliverance.

Yet all sentient beings are constantly intimate with the five desires and distant from pure conduct; they are well-versed in the cycle of birth and death, but remain ignorant of *nirvāṇa*. Now, by means of...

Regarding the four vows, because one intends to turn back [the cycle of suffering], it is said that they "bring sentient beings to maturity. "Abiding and maintaining" (*zhuchi*) has the meaning of succession and non-interruption.

The Three Jewels are the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. "Jewel" (*bao*) has the meaning of being precious. Among the four vows, attaining Buddhahood constitutes the abiding and maintenance of the Buddha Jewel;
studying the Dharma constitutes the abiding and maintenance of the Dharma Jewel; and the Bodhisattva’s own person, as well as the sentient beings to be saved, constitute the Sangha Jewel.
This refers to the Saṃgha-ratna. "Sūtra" means to traverse; "oceans of kalpas" refers to the length of time. Regarding those who are non-retrogressive:

they are sustained by their vows, such that even though they pass through a long duration, they do not perceive it as long. Regarding those who vow to deliver sentient beings: they make this vow based on the objective realm of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
This means that Bodhisattvas universally observe the various classes of sentient beings within the six realms of existence, all of whom are afflicted by birth and death.
Being oppressed by various sufferings, he therefore makes a vow, desiring to deliver them and cause them to transcend the three realms.

As for "vowing to sever all afflictions," this is a vow made based on the objective sphere of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*). That is to say, the Bodhisattva carefully examines that the delusions of affliction and karma are immeasurable and boundless;
they are capable of producing the bitter fruits of birth and death, causing one to transmigrate through the three realms without end.
Because they are inexhaustible, he makes a vow desiring to sever them, so as to cause all sentient beings to likewise sever them.

"Vowing to study all dharma-gates" means making a vow based on the objective realm of the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*). That is to say, the Bodhisattva thoroughly examines all dharmas of the path;
they are infinite and inexhaustible, yet all are capable of leading to Nirvana. Having himself completed this study, he also causes others to do so.

Because all sentient beings study together [in this]. (As for the "Dharma-gate" (*dharmaparyāya*): it refers to the precepts, meditative concentration, wisdom, and so forth. When opened out, they are immeasurable. "Dharma" (*dharma*) has the sense of being able to serve as a standard and support;

"gate" (*mukha*) has the sense of passage, meaning that by upholding these various path-dharmas, one passes through and enters the stage of Buddhahood. "Vowing to realize the fruit of all Buddhas" is a vow made based on the objective realm of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).
That is to say, the Bodhisattva carefully examines the fruit of Bodhi, which is supreme and unsurpassed; having personally accomplished it, he universally...

"May all sentient beings fully accomplish [this]"; thus it is said. (The term "all fruits of Buddhahood" (*sarva-buddhatva-phala*) refers to *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. Because these are the fruits realized by all Buddhas together, they are called "all fruits of Buddhahood.

From "Good son" onwards is the concluding exhortation. Regarding "great and small Bodhisattvas": those who have attained the profound stages of the path, such as the *bhūmi* levels up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), are "great";

those in the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kṣānti*) prior to the *bhūmis* are "small. Furthermore, among the three stages of worthiness, those who have entered into principle (*tattva*) and abide therein...
Dedication of merit (*pariṇāmanā*) is great; those at the stage of faith (*adhimukti-caryā*) and those who have first resolved their minds (*prathama-cittotpāda*) are small.

All should practice and study this; this is the formal exhortation. "That which is studied throughout the three periods of time" serves as the citation of proof. △ Eight: The Four Virtues, beginning with Joyful Delight (*ruci*).
Furthermore, son of good family, there are four further dharmas by which a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya maintains pure ethical discipline (*śīla*).
What are these four? First, delighting in emptiness (*śūnyatā*), because it is that which is revealed by emptiness. Second, attaining fearlessness, because of the realization of samādhi.
Third, giving rise to the vow of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) toward all sentient beings. Fourth, [abiding] in the two non-existences.
I have no wearying or turning-back mind. Good son, these four dharmas are the essential gateways for all bodhisattvas to enter the state of a noble one (*ārya*).
By relying on these four dharmas, they sever the two hindrances (*āvaraṇa*).

Regarding those who maintain pure ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*), as stated in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra*, there are four types of maintaining ethical discipline: 1. **The ethical discipline of aspiration** (*āśā-sthāpana-śīla*):

"Aspiration" (*āśā*) means seeking; "expectation" (*sthāpana*) means anticipating. This refers to firmly upholding the prohibitions and precepts with the aim of being reborn in the heavens or other auspicious realms.
2. **The ethical discipline of fear** (*bhaya-śīla*): This refers to firmly upholding [the precepts] out of dread of falling into the evil destinies or out of dread of an ill reputation.
1. The morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*): because it restrains [unwholesome conduct]. 2. The morality that accords with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣyānulomika-śīla*):

because it accords with the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), adorning the mind and firmly maintaining the prohibitive precepts. (The seven factors of enlightenment are as listed in the *Tripiṭaka-dharmasaṃkhyā*). 3. The morality of purity (*viśuddha-śīla*):

this refers to untainted morality (*anāsrava-śīla*), for it is able to leave behind the defilements of afflictions (*kleśa*). (This is precisely the morality produced by the untainted path-factors of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. Now, regarding the "renunciant Bodhisattva," although...
The initial arousal of the mind (prathamacittotpāda) is a resolve identical to that of the Great Awakened One; it is not yet the purity of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas.
[Question: Why is this so? [Answer: First, the explanation below: emptiness (śūnyatā) is the ultimate, true nature of reality (paramārtha-tattva).
This "delight" is not the attachment of emotional views, but rather the superior resolve for Bodhi. It is said that by virtue of having this mind, one will ultimately be able to...
It can be realized; therefore, it is said that it is "that which is revealed by emptiness. Indeed, the nature of emptiness is inherently possessed by all people.

However, worldly beings are deluded by the five desires and thus cannot manifest it. Now, by dwelling in an araṇya (hermitage), the mind-ground becomes pure, like the sky becoming clear when clouds disperse;
thus, true emptiness manifests. Yet, this true emptiness is immovable, which is itself the concentration of the nature (dharmatā-samādhi). The...
This refers to the statement that "precepts can give rise to meditative concentration. Regarding the phrase "attaining the state beyond inferiority":

there are many kinds of terrors, yet among them, the two types of birth and death are truly the greatest fears. Furthermore, while there are many kinds of samādhi, only the fundamental concentration (*prakṛti-samādhi*) constitutes the essential body.
Because one maintains pure precepts, emptiness manifests; this is precisely the fundamental concentration. Within this fundamental concentration...
Because there is no birth-and-death, there is no fear. Because it is accomplished through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is said that one "realizes samādhi.

Thus far, these two types [of practice] have been discussed primarily in terms of self-benefit. As for those who give rise to the vow of great compassion toward all sentient beings, they are further able to benefit others.
Once the fundamental nature of concentration is perfected and the sharp instruments are prepared, by giving rise to the vow of great compassion, one also causes others to achieve perfection.

The two kinds of selflessness are the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). Yet, within both persons and phenomena, there is fundamentally no self;

it is only because ordinary beings do not understand this that they conceive of a self with extreme intensity amidst what is selfless—namely, "my body," "my name," "my clothes," "my possessions," and so forth—even in the midst of walking, standing, sitting, reclining, speaking, and acting, they even think, "I am able."
"I can practice generosity, I can maintain the precepts," and so forth—through such inversions, one gives rise to all afflictions, the cycle of birth and death, and karmic actions.
Now, since the Bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya (forest hermitage), wisdom is generated from morality and meditative concentration. Thus, he perceives reality as it is:
the dharmas of the five aggregates are fundamentally empty; where is the person who exists as a mere designation? Therefore, both are devoid of self. There is no weariness [in this realization].

The term "wearing a vest" (bèi xīn) distinguishes the Bodhisattva from ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the Two Vehicles (*dvayayāna*). This means that ordinary beings are deluded regarding emptiness and attached to existence, while those of the Two Vehicles loathe existence and cling to emptiness.
Ordinary beings are bound to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and turn their backs on Nirvana; those of the Two Vehicles turn their backs on birth-and-death and head toward Nirvana.
Because both are attached to one extreme, they do not accord with the Middle Way. Now, for the Bodhisattva, self and non-self are one.

This is precisely the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). It does not loathe afflictions nor turn its back on birth and death; principle and phenomena are unimpeded, and emptiness and existence are mutually integrated.
Only this constitutes the Mahāyāna’s true two-fold non-self, which differs from that of ordinary beings and *śrāvakas*, who possess a mind of aversion and turning away.
"Good son," he concludes with the essential points for entering the noble path. Regarding what is called "the gateway to the essential points for entering the noble path":

to loathe existence and cling to emptiness is not the essential point for the noble ones; to be without loathing and without aversion is truly the essential gateway. Based on this conclusion below, those who sever the two obstacles [are so described].
Because it is manifested through emptiness, the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) are severed. Because great compassion is without weariness, the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are severed.

(As for the Śrāvakas who contemplate the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), they contemplate that within the five aggregates (*skandha*)—form and so forth—there is no internal sovereign; this is "selflessness within phenomena. This is not the same as the Bodhisattvas' realization that the five aggregates are also empty [in their very essence], which is the true reality (*dharmatā*).
△ Ninth: Abandoning views and the four virtues.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are four more dharmas by which a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya maintains the prohibitive precepts and adorns his body.
What are these four? First, the eternal relinquishing of the view of self; second, the relinquishing of the view of "mine";

third, the departure from the views of annihilationism and eternalism; and fourth, the profound ability to awaken to and understand the twelve links of dependent origination. Son of good family, [these are the four].
These four dharmas can eliminate the violation of precepts, guard pure morality, and adorn the body.
The view of "self" is the discrimination of self-grasping (*ātma-grāha*), while the view of "mine" is the discrimination of dharma-grasping (*dharma-grāha*).
Because these two views are not forgotten, one sinks forever into birth and death. Now, when a Bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, they do not discriminate within the body that there is a self.

I, moreover, do not conceptually differentiate "what belongs to me" outside of the body. Both the dualistic attachments to self and dharmas are empty; the two views of annihilationism and eternalism are likewise extinguished.

One can deeply awaken to and understand that, following the principle of dependent origination, one deeply penetrates the process of retrogressive contemplation back to its limit at ignorance (*avidyā*).
Thus, one is able to know the causes and effects of the three periods of time, with ignorance as the root. This meaning implies the severing of ignorance.
Realizing the True Principle. To observe in this manner is Right View. Good son, the lower fetters are severed and guarded.
△ Ten: Contemplating the Four Virtues of the Aggregates and so forth.

Furthermore, son of good family, a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya contemplates four dharmas that enable them to protect the prohibitions and precepts, cultivate sublime conduct, and strive for the wisdom of a Buddha.
What are these four? First, observing the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Second, observing the twelve sense bases (*dvādaśāyatana*) as being like an empty village. Third, observing the nature of the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) as being identical to the Dharma.
The realms. Fourth, to neither abandon nor cling to the phenomena of conventional truth. Son of good family, these four dharmas are what all bodhisattvas should cultivate and study.
Therefore, sons of the Buddha dwelling in an araṇya should single-mindedly practice them, seeking the unsurpassed path.
The five aggregates (*skandha*) of ordinary beings arise and perish from moment to moment; that is to say, nails grow, hair lengthens, breath wanes, and the face wrinkles.
Within a single *kṣaṇa*, there are nine hundred such arisings and perishing. The Bodhisattva observes in this way and knows that the body is impermanent.

Second, below, he observes the twelve bases (*āyatana*) of the sense faculties and their objects: they all arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and perish when those causes and conditions separate.
Then it ceases. Within this, there is no self, nor anything belonging to a self; its very substance is entirely empty, like an empty village.
This means that because there are no people within a village, it is empty; by analogy, there is no self within the sense faculties and their objects. These are the two aforementioned types.

The first is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). The second, "the lower," refers to the fusion of the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses, all of which return to the single true Dharma-realm;
this is the contemplation of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), which is purely true. The third, "the lower," is the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya*).

Because it does not depart from the conventional characteristics of worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is said that there is "nothing to be abandoned. Although one remains within worldly truth, one dwells amidst the dust of phenomena without being defiled, nor does one forget the ultimate truth.

Therefore, it is called "non-attachment. This is the transformation of the provisional into the real, which is also the contemplation of the Middle Way. From "Good son" downwards, the section concludes with an exhortation.
△ Eleven: Accomplishing the four virtues, etc.
Furthermore, son of good family, a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya fulfills four kinds of purity of ethical discipline (śīla) to adorn his own person.
What are these four? First, the accomplishment of the contemplation of not seeing the body; second, the accomplishment of the contemplation of not seeing speech;
third, the accomplishment of the contemplation of not seeing the mind; and fourth, the distancing from the sixty-two [wrong views].

He sees. He is well able to accomplish the contemplation of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Good son, if there is a son of the Buddha who accomplishes these four kinds of purity, he will realize and attain the state of right nature free from birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*) in this very body, and even swiftly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
For these reasons, you, sons of the Buddha, should contemplate these four kinds of Dharma-gates: sever the four evil realms, realize the four nirvāṇas,
and until the end of the future, deliver all sentient beings, causing them to realize anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

The first three types of causes allow precept (*śīla*) to give rise to concentration (*samādhi*). Within concentration, one observes that one’s own three karmas of body, speech, and mind are all accomplished through causes and conditions;
because they arise dependently and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), they are all ungraspable.

Yet, one does not perceive these three karmas, but realizes only the single reality (*ekasatya*). The sixty-two views (*dṛṣṭi-gata*) are collectively categorized as delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), with false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*) as their root.

"Detachment" refers to observing within meditative concentration (*samādhi*). One perceives that while it exists in dependence upon the physical body, one's own three types of karma are already empty.
Since there is nothing upon which to rely, where could various views (*dṛṣṭi*) possibly reside? They naturally dissolve like ice.

"Able to accomplish well" and so forth means that once false views are empty, correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) manifests of itself. As for the term "omniscience" (*sarvajña*), it is because by realizing this wisdom, one observes...
All phenomena are *tathatā* (suchness); this is precisely right gnosis (*samyag-jñāna*). "Good son" and below concludes the proof and exhorts practice.
"Manifesting the body" and below indicates that since all false views are empty, one personally realizes the true nature in its manifestation.

"Detached from birth" means not undergoing further rebirth, because one has personally attained the *dharmakāya*. The term "even unto" (*naiḥśreyasam*) is a word used for ellipsis; there must necessarily be...
Regarding the "stages of experience": furthermore, the phrase "swiftly realizing Bodhi" means that although one passes through the various stages, one does not dwell in or cling to them;
like a bird ascending a mountain, which reaches the summit in a single flight, it is therefore called "swift realization. This is precisely what is meant by "sudden accomplishment.

From "For this reason" onwards, the text concludes the preceding section with an exhortation. The "four evil paths" refer to the three realms of suffering plus the asuras. The "four nirvanas" refer to permanence, bliss, [self, and purity].
Self-purity. Before the stage of exhaustion has been reached, one immediately transcends birth and attains the Way, never wearying of the long duration [of practice].

All such various merits and adornments as described above arise from pure observance of the precepts; therefore, [the text] exhorts [this practice]. △ Second, the eight virtues regarding what one should abide in, part five:
first, the eight kinds of samādhi.
Furthermore, son of good family, a bodhisattva who has gone forth and dwells in an araṇya fulfills eight kinds of purity of samādhi to adorn his own person.
What are these eight? First, the purity of samādhi from sitting alone in an araṇya;
second, the purity of samādhi from being far removed from frivolous speech; third, the purity of samādhi from being far removed from the five desires; fourth...

First, by taming body and mind, samādhi is purified. Second, by being free from anger, samādhi is purified. Third, by subduing body and mind, samādhi is purified. Fourth, by being content with whatever clothing one receives, samādhi is purified.

Fifth, by being content with whatever food one receives, samādhi is purified. Sixth, by remaining far removed from improper seeking, samādhi is purified. Seventh, by remaining far removed from attachment arising due to sounds, samādhi is purified.
Eighth, by preaching the Dharma for the sake of the assembly without seeking profit or sustenance, samādhi is purified. Son of good family, you should...
By practicing thus, one will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
[This concludes] the summary provided below. What is it? [The following] interrogates. First, [the following] explains. "Good son," and so forth, concludes with an exhortation.

At the very beginning of renouncing the world, in order to distance oneself from the secular realm, one dwells in an araṇya (forest hermitage). One must dwell alone in quiet seclusion, withdrawing the gaze and reflecting inwardly.
This is precisely samādhi. To be unstained by even a speck of dust is precisely purity. Now, samādhi is concentration (samādhi), and purity is precept (śīla);
this is, therefore, the precept concomitant with concentration. As for "staying far away from frivolous speech," it is one of the four transgressions of verbal karma.
Sitting alone is the precept for the body; this is the precept for speech. Now, regarding the four transgressions of verbal karma, citing one encompasses all four.
This is also the precept of speech associated with meditative concentration; therefore, it is said that "samādhi is pure. As for the five desires, these are the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*).
To be "distant" from them means that the eye does not observe forms, but instead contemplates its own nature; the ear does not listen to sounds, but instead listens to its own nature. Thus...

When the body reaches the point of not perceiving touch and instead perceives its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this is also termed "concentration-concomitant" (*samādhi-sahaja*); thus it is said that "samādhi is pure.
Hereafter, all cases should be understood according to this principle. Regarding the "taming of body and mind": if the body does not transgress, the body is tamed;
if the mind is free from discursive thought (*vikalpa*), the mind is tamed, and so forth. "Contentment with food and drink" is one of the four stainless natures (*vimala-dharma*).

"Simply being able to act according to one's capacity without involving discursive thought (*vikalpa*), such that the very essence [of the mind] is itself the precept (*śīla*)—this is what is meant by 'remaining far removed from evil seeking.
To seek that which should not be sought is called 'evil seeking. Now, because one is pure within meditative concentration (*samādhi*), evil seeking is forever severed;

hence it is said 'to remain far removed. As for 'arousing attachment due to sound,' this refers to sounds that accord with one's inclinations, whereby the mind gives rise to defiled clinging; this is what is meant [by attachment]."
Love arises. Now, by returning to hear one's own nature, one is not turned by sounds; thus it is called "distancing.

To preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitude without seeking profit or sustenance is to benefit others through compassion. To preach while there is no preaching, without maintaining any reflected image or appearance, is itself samādhi.
Since one does not even know the existence of a body, how could one further seek profit? This is purity. [The passage continues with] "Good man," etc.
Concluding Exhortation. △ Second, the Eight Kinds of Wisdom.
Furthermore, son of good family, for a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya, there are further eight kinds of purity of wisdom.
What are the eight? First, the purity of wisdom through skillfulness regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Second, the twelve sense bases (*dvādaśāyatana*).

1. Purity of skillful wisdom regarding the aggregates (*skandha*). 2. Purity of skillful wisdom regarding the sense-bases (*āyatana*). 3. Purity of skillful wisdom regarding the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). 4.
Purity of skillful means and wisdom regarding the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*). 5. Purity of skillful means and wisdom regarding the three doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*).
6. Purity of skillful means and wisdom capable of extinguishing all afflictions (*kleśa*). 7. [The seventh...]
The eighth is the purity of wisdom through skillful means that can eliminate the sixty-two views.
Son of good family, these eight kinds of purity of wisdom are what you bodhisattvas should diligently cultivate,
so that you may swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

The five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)—namely, form (the five sense organs and six sense objects), sensation (the mind’s reception of external objects), perception (mental conceptualizations), formations (those that flow and fluctuate), and consciousness (the eighth [consciousness] which cognizes the three categories of objective realms)—are all termed "aggregates" because these five kinds conceal the Buddha-nature; they receive their name from this functional activity.

It is because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) are, in total, comprised of the two dharmas of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).
Within these three categories, there are three ways of classifying them—combining or expanding them—according to the capacities of sentient beings.

First, for those who are deluded regarding the mind but not regarding form, the categories are combined as to form and expanded as to mind, and thus taught as the five aggregates. (Regarding the combination of form: the five sense organs and six sense objects are combined into a single aggregate of form. Regarding the expansion of mind: the single dharma of mind is expanded.)

For the sake of those who are deluded regarding feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and for those who are deluded regarding form but not deluded regarding the mind, the mind is combined and form is expanded, and these are taught as the twelve bases (*āyatana*).

(To "combine the mind" means to combine feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness into a single faculty of mind. To "expand form" means to divide the single category of form into the five faculties and the six objects.

For those who are deluded regarding both form and mind, both form and mind are expanded, and these are taught as the eighteen elements (*dhātu*). (To "expand the mind" means to divide the single mind into...)

The six consciousnesses and the mental faculty (*manas*)—opening up form means dividing a single dharma of form into the five faculties and the six sense objects. All these are said to be "skillful wisdom and purity.

Wisdom is the spiritual function of one's own mind; when one had not yet dwelt in an araṇya (hermitage), one pursued delusions and was confused about the truth, becoming turbid and impure, and instead falling into discursive thought and discrimination. Now that one dwells in an araṇya, one is separated from all defilements and impurities.
Delusive thoughts are transformed into wisdom, and discrimination becomes skillful means (*upāya*). Now, this skillfulness is precisely expedient wisdom (*upāyakauśalyajñāna*).

Reaching this stage, one not only benefits oneself but also delivers sentient beings; that is to say, responding to others at the appropriate time and employing expedients according to their capacities.
It does not deviate from principle and remains in accord with reality. It is like a phantom person performing tasks, entirely devoid of conceptualization;
where both mind and mental factors are empty, this is called the purity of wisdom. As for the twenty-two faculties (*indriya*), they are simply twenty-two dharmas.

The five universal mental factors (*sarvatraga*) (namely: contact, attention, feeling, perception, and volition); the five object-specific mental factors (*viṣayapratiniyata*) (namely: desire, resolve, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom); and the eleven wholesome mental factors (*kuśala*) (namely: faith...).

Diligence, shame, remorse, non-attachment, non-hatred, non-delusion, pliancy, heedfulness, equanimity, and non-harming. (The "single mental consciousness" refers to the primary mind that arises simultaneously.

Regarding these twenty-two factors, they are called "roots" because they follow the precepts; since the precepts are the foundation for entering the state of a noble one (*ārya*), whenever the primary mind functions, these twenty-one factors are all able to assist it accordingly, ensuring that no evil is committed and all virtues are practiced.
To practice in this manner is called skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). That the mind remains free from attachment regarding all activities is called the purity of wisdom (*prajñā-viśuddhi*).
The three gates of liberation—namely, emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—are to be understood according to the previous explanation.

As for "all afflictions" (*kleśa*), they do not transcend the two delusions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi- and vitarka-kleśa*), as well as fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). Furthermore, these are also referred to as skillful means.
That is to say: when greed arises, it is countered by joy and equanimity; when anger arises, it is countered by gladness;
although delusion is a state of confusion, one should nonetheless advance in study from time to time so that wisdom may arise after a long period, thereby serving as its antidote;
when pride moves the mind, it is countered by reverence and carefulness; when doubt moves the mind, it is countered by resolute faith; and when wrong views arise—
At that time, one employs the causes and effects of the three periods of existence—the retributions for good and evil—as an antidote.

Through such antidotes, all afflictions (*kleśa*) are transformed into correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*). They naturally penetrate with clarity and illuminate with fusion, remaining far removed from conceptual discrimination;
therefore, it is said that they "can be extinguished. This constitutes the purity of wisdom. There are twenty secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), namely the ten minor secondary afflictions.

The middle [secondary afflictions] consist of two; the great secondary afflictions consist of eight. Because they follow and assist the sovereign mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and do not contradict the fundamental [afflictions], even what is now called "the skillful means capable of extinguishing" is none other than the application of the associated mental factors (*samprayukta-dharma*) as an antidote to cause their extinction.

Regarding the sixty-two views, the explanation is found in the preceding text; in general, they take the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as primary, based upon the emptiness of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

They engage in false conceptualization. Furthermore, by applying the categories of the three periods of time (*tri-kāla*) and the views of annihilationism and eternalism (*uccheda-śāśvata*), their [erroneous] numbers are increased and filled out. Now, by relying on ethical discipline (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*) arises; by relying on concentration, wisdom (*prajñā*) is produced.
This is able to cause those views to crumble like a wall and melt away like ice. [The phrase] "Good son" concludes the exhortation.
Regarding the names and meanings of the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), the explanation is found in the preceding text. △ The Eight Kinds of Supernormal Powers (*abhijñā*).
Furthermore, son of good family, when a renunciant bodhisattva dwells in an araṇya, there are eight kinds of pure supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) that adorn their own person.

What are these eight? First, regarding all material phenomena (*rūpadharma*), they attain the unobstructed divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which is purified through supernormal power and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*). Second, regarding all auditory objects (*śabdaviṣaya*), they attain the unobstructed divine [ear]...
1. Skillful means and the purity of supernormal power regarding the divine ear. 2. Skillful means and the purity of supernormal power regarding the purification of the [divine] eye. 3.
Regarding the minds and mental factors of all sentient beings, attaining unobstructed knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), skillful means, and the purity of supernormal power. 4.

Recollecting the places of birth and death in past lives, attaining unobstructed knowledge of past abodes (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*), skillful means, and the purity of supernormal power. 5. [The fifth...]
1. One who can travel to countless Buddha-fields in the ten directions, attaining unimpeded knowledge of the supernatural realm (*ṛddhividhi-jñāna*), with skillful means and pure supernormal powers.

2. One who can know whether the outflows (*āsrava*) of sentient beings have been exhausted or not, attaining unimpeded knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñāna*), with skillful means and pure supernormal powers. 3. One who can extinguish all afflictions (*kleśa*), attaining unimpeded...
The purity of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*) that unimpedes untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Eighth, the purity of supernormal powers through skillful means that manifests one’s own roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) to all beings and dedicates them for their benefit.
Noble son, these eight kinds of purity of supernormal powers are what Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions collectively study; you Bodhisattvas should also practice them.
Through practice, one swiftly realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
As for supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they are the wondrous functions inherently possessed by one's own nature; however, ordinary beings are obstructed by ignorance (*avidyā*).
Yet they were unable to attain penetration. Now, dwelling in an araṇya, one gives rise to concentration from precepts; relying on concentration, one brings forth its function.

This is numinous, subtle, and penetrates the divine, being unimpeded wherever it touches. Hence it is called "supernormal power" (abhijñā). Through mastery of supernormal powers, one ensures that the Dharma-body is not solitary.
This is called adorning the body. Although supernatural powers (abhijñā) arise from the essence of meditative concentration, they are fundamentally rooted in accomplishment within the araṇya;
these are all merits of the araṇya. First, the lower [category] is divided into eight kinds. The first is the supernormal power of the divine eye (divyacakṣur-abhijñā).
All material phenomena (rūpadharma) are objects (viṣaya) perceived by the visual faculty (cakṣur-indriya); this includes all mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
The myriad phenomena of the universe consist of two types: form and manifestation. To the fleshly eyes of ordinary beings, these appear as obstructions;
therefore, they do not function as a means of penetration. Now, the Bodhisattva, through the untainted power of precepts and meditative concentration, brings forth wondrous functioning.

Although this functioning is manifested through the eyes, it is in fact the numinous illumination that accords with the true nature. Thus, it can pervade the ten directions; wherever the eyes are turned, there is universal vision without any obstruction.
This is the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). Since it is brought forth by means of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).

Furthermore, seeing universally without obstruction is skillfulness; employing this for the benefit of others is expedient means (*upāya*). Being unobstructed and unhindered constitutes supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
It is like a mirror reflecting images, entirely free from defilement; therefore, it is called "pure. As it is with the divine eye, so it is with the [other] celestial faculties.

The same applies to the ear; one merely substitutes "sound" for "color," and all other details follow the previous pattern. Third is the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others (*paracittajñāna*).

This encompasses all sentient beings without exception; whatever thoughts arise in their minds, whether they be wholesome or unwholesome, and the distinctions between the heterodox and the orthodox—all these a Bodhisattva possessing this power can know.
Although "mind and mental factors" (*citta-caitta-dharma*) is a general term for all consciousnesses, for now—

This is explained in terms of the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. Because the seventh consciousness clings to a self and the sixth consciousness performs various conceptualizations and discriminations, it is so for the mental kings (the primary consciousnesses);

the same applies to their associated mental factors (caittas). As for the first five and the eighth consciousnesses, they all consist of recollective discrimination (*anusmaranavikalpa*) and do not engage in conceptualizing names and phrases;
therefore, they are not discussed here. Although we currently speak of the sixth and seventh, the conceptual discrimination (*abhinirūpaṇāvikalpa*) resides entirely [in the sixth].
Sixth, regarding the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*): this refers to the ability to know the mental states of others. It is named after its function alone.

Taking the arousal of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) through ethical discipline and meditative concentration as skillful means (*kauśalya*), and employing these powers to benefit sentient beings as the expedient (*upāya*), the ability to know others' minds is itself the supernormal power;
being unobstructed and unhindered is its purity. Fourth is the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). To recollect...
"Memory" refers to not forgetting. "The past" refers to successive lifetimes in previous births.

"Places of birth and death" does not exceed the realms of heavens and humans, nor the four modes of birth and six paths of existence; receiving a life-span is called "birth," and relinquishing that life-span is called "death.
As for "knowledge of former abodes," it is the wisdom capable of knowing one's dwelling in the world in the past. It is the attainment of non-obstruction.
This refers to being free from the delusion of the falling aggregates (*skandha*). By means of precepts and meditative concentration, one develops supernormal powers (*abhijñā*);

this is skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). Being able to know past lives is itself a supernormal power. Being free from the delusion of the falling aggregates is itself purity. Fifth is the supernormal power of the realm of psychic travel (*ṛddhi-viṣaya-abhijñā*):

one is able to go downward; though traveling to the ten directions, one arrives in a mere instant. Its significance encompasses both making offerings to the Buddhas and saving sentient beings. Furthermore...

Returning in an instant, unobstructed by clouds and mist and undivided by mountains and rivers—all of which are inconceivable—it is therefore called the "knowledge of the supernormal realm" (*ṛddhiviṣayajñāna*).

As for the two characters "supernormal realm" (*shenjing*), they refer to skillful artistry (*śilpa*); that is to say, emitting fire from the upper part of the body and water from the lower part of the body, and so forth.
Since these eighteen types are all unfathomable, the name is established based on this skillful artistry; it is also termed "supernormal" (*shen*).
The object is pervasive. Because it can exercise spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), it is skillful; exercising this pervasive power for the benefit of others is its skillful means.

To skillfully transcend thought and deliberation is called spiritual power (*abhijñā*). Being pervasive yet non-attached is purity. Sixth is the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*).
That which is able to know is the wisdom of the Bodhisattva. Whether sentient beings have exhausted their outflows or not is that which is known.

This is the objective realm (*viṣaya*). Generally, when the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is exhausted, it is called the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*); when the grasping at a self still persists, it is called not yet exhausted.
However, that which enables one to know sentient beings without obstruction is precisely the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows.

That meditative concentration (*samādhi*) can give rise to supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) is skillful means (*kauśalya*); employing these powers to benefit others is expedient means (*upāya*); and being able to know sentient beings is supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
Non-attachment to the characteristics of penetration is purity. Seventh is the penetration that extinguishes delusions.

All afflictions (*kleśa*) do not exceed the categories of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-vicikitsā*), the dust-like and sand-like [afflictions], and ignorance (*avidyā*); these constitute the delusions to be extinguished. When a Bodhisattva’s single thought-moment is empty, all delusions are suddenly exhausted and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is suddenly extinguished, just as light destroys darkness.
Having thoroughly understood and eradicated deep-seated habitual tendencies, it is therefore called untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*). By means of this—

To give rise to supernormal powers based on meditative concentration is skillfulness. To employ the swift movement of these powers for the benefit of others is expedient means. To suddenly extinguish afflictions is supernormal power.
For the mind to be empty and leave no trace is purity. Eighth is the supernormal power of dedication. As for "manifestly seeing one's own body":
This is precisely the path attained by oneself. Because there is no good that is not performed, it perfumes and forms untainted seeds;

therefore, it is called "roots of goodness" (*kuśalamūla*). Regarding "dedicating [merit] to sentient beings": the Bodhisattva, with a public-spirited mind, turns what belongs to oneself toward others, universally desiring that all sentient beings may together attain this path.
Because concentration can indeed give rise to supernormal powers, it is "skillful means. Turning oneself...
To act toward others is skillful means (*upāya*). To benefit beings without being perceived is supernormal power (*abhijñā*).
For the mind to have no attachments is purity. "Good son" and below conclude the exhortation. "In the ten directions" and below cite others to encourage practice.
Because the influence does not deviate from the cause, it says "swiftly realize," etc. △ Fourth: The Eight Kinds of Purity.
Furthermore, son of good family, a renunciant bodhisattva dwelling in an araṇya attains eight kinds of purity in this very life.
What are these eight? First, purity of bodily action; second, purity of verbal action;
third, purity of mental action; fourth, purity of right nature; fifth, purity of right mindfulness; sixth, purity of dhūta [ascetic practices]...
Purity. Seventh is purity through being free from flattery. Eighth is purity through never forgetting the bodhicitta for even a single thought-moment.

Son of good family, if there is a son of the Buddha who dwells in an araṇya and is fully endowed with these eight kinds of purity, he will, in his present body, accomplish boundless roots of goodness and shall no longer regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.

Its intrinsic nature is limpid and still, which is called "clarity" (*qing*). Its substance is pure and white, which is called "purity" (*jing*). It does not depart from the three karmas, yet it unfolds into eight types.
The first is bodily karma (*kāyakarman*). "Body" refers to the physical form; that is, what is produced by one's parents and composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Worldly people possess three kinds of evil karma regarding the body: the first is killing (*prāṇātipāta*), whether one kills oneself or instructs others to do so.
One kills a person, or hears of a killing and rejoices, or although the body has not yet moved, one raises the intention to kill.
By this karmic action of killing, one is able to obstruct the roots of goodness and turbidify one's own nature, so that it is no longer pure. The Bodhisattva precepts are like ice and frost.
Both internally and externally pure, not a single thought of any act of killing—whether light or grave—is produced, let alone physical movement;

therefore, it is called "pure. Second is stealing: taking any material wealth or possessions that have not been given, whether by forceful seizure or theft, which can obstruct liberation and turbidify one's own nature; therefore, it is not pure. The Bodhisattva...
The essence of the precepts is as bright and clear as ice and frost. When not a single thought of any act of stealing—whether light or grave—arises, this is called purity.

Regarding the three types of sexual misconduct: when not a single thought of committing adultery oneself or inciting others to commit adultery arises, how much less would one actually transgress with the body?
It is also like ice and frost; therefore, it is called "pure. The above constitutes the three types of bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
Second is verbal action (*vākkarman*). In all instances of speech, there are four kinds of faults; thus, it is not pure.

First is false speech (*mṛṣāvāda*), which means saying one has seen what one has not seen, or saying one has not seen what one has seen, and so forth. All speech that is untrue constitutes [the fault of] the mouth.
