those whose awakening is shallow are called "worthy ones" (*ārya*), while those whose awakening is thorough are called "sages" (*muni*). △ Fifth, the explanation of the equality of mind.

The nature of all worthy and holy ones is fundamentally empty and quiescent. Within unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), there is no observing or violating of precepts, nor is there any distinction between great and small.
There are no mental kings (*citta-rāja*) or mental factors (*caitta-dharma*). There is neither suffering nor pleasure. Thus, the self-nature of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is immaculate.
There is no distinction of superior, middling, or inferior. Why is this? Because the nature of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharmatā*) is equal.

"All worthies and sages" refers to those who have already attained realization—the ten stages of abiding (*vihāra*), the ten practices (*caryā*), and the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) constitute the worthies; the ten grounds (*bhūmi*) and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) constitute the sages.
This nature is fundamentally the truth of the unconditioned realized by these worthies and sages; nature itself is the Truth (*satya*).

This is the essence. As for "originally empty and quiescent," this merely establishes the premise; it means that it is originally empty and quiescent by nature, rather than becoming empty for the first time through some subsequent effort.
The section on "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) correctly explains the meaning of "quiescence": within the unconditioned dharmas of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), there is original equality.
The essence itself is unmoving and likewise unchanging; therefore, it is called the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which is the meaning of emptiness and quiescence.

Regarding the precepts, there is neither observance nor violation, for these are the precepts of inherent nature (*prakṛti-saṃvidyamāna-śīla*). Fundamentally, there is no observance through cessation or performance, nor is there any violation through breach or destruction.
Furthermore, there is no distinction between inferior and superior, because the unconditioned is equal; thus, there are no [distinctions between] the noble ones and the sages.
It is great, yet there is no smallness of the ignorant and deluded. The sovereign mind (citta-rāja) is accompanied by delusion, and its mental factors (caitta) are likewise so;
however, the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) ultimate truth is purely pure and free from delusion, and thus [these qualities] do not exist therein either.

Nevertheless, that ordinary beings have the suffering of birth and death while noble ones have the bliss of nirvāṇa involves all forms of duality. Now, the unconditioned mental dharma transcends all such dualities.
Therefore, even seeking for the holy or the ordinary is impossible to find; where, then, could suffering and pleasure exist? Thus, they are entirely non-existent.
That which is called the "Dharmadhātu" refers to the very substance abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); it is the One True Dharmadhātu.

From the phrase "self-nature" (*svabhāva*) downward, its essential nature and characteristics are revealed: namely, that the unconditioned mind-dharma takes self-nature free from defilement as its essence. This is the unsurpassed [middle].
The three lower grades are characterized by their distinctions (this collectively dispels emotional views and conceptual discrimination). Furthermore, it is questioned and explained:
why is it that within unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) there is absolutely nothing? The explanation states: because the nature of these unconditioned phenomena is equanimous (*samatā*).
If there were holding or violating, great or small, suffering or pleasure, and so forth, they would not be equanimous; they would lose what makes them unconditioned.
△ The sixty thousand dharmas return to one, just as the waters of many rivers flow into the ocean and become entirely of one flavor, for there are no distinct characteristics.

The metaphor of the many rivers represents the various differentiated dharmas previously mentioned; the ocean represents the unconditioned mind-dharma. That is to say, when the many waters enter [the ocean]...

The ocean has but one taste, which is salt; all phenomena return to the mind, which is likewise of one unconditioned nature (*asaṃskṛta*). Since the unconditioned mind and its dharmas are in reality without distinction, [the preceding point is established].
△ Seventh, further explaining that there is no difference.
This stainless nature is neither real nor unreal. This stainless nature is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), characterized by inexhaustibility and non-extinction;
its essence is fundamentally unarisen. This stainless nature is eternally abiding and immutable—the most supreme nirvāṇa—because it is pure of what belongs to a self (*ātman*).
This stainless nature (*vimalatva*) is far removed from all equality and inequality, because its essence is without differentiation.
"Stainless nature" means that its nature is free from defilement. This explains the meaning of the absence of distinct characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) following the previous section.
"Defilement" carries the sense of differentiation; because the nature is free from defilement, there are no distinct characteristics. However, this stainlessness is itself non-existence (*abhāva*).
This is merely a provisional designation; it is not the ultimate reality. It is "not real" because it lacks any fixed characteristic from the outset;

it is "not false" because it currently manifests functional activity. It is like the images appearing in a mirror: while the reflected images are distinct and clear, the substance of the mirror itself has no difference [between its states].

Regarding the subsequent four lines: the first line designates the essence, and the second line reconciles the meaning, stating that this stainless nature is precisely that which all Buddhas [realize].
This realizes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and also establishes its certainty. The following two lines further explain its profound meaning:
that within the ultimate truth, there is no characteristic of final exhaustion or annihilation; its essence is fundamentally unarisen. Because it is unarisen, it is therefore non-extinguished.
This absence of arising and extinguishing is the truly stainless nature (*vimala-dharmatā*). Next, the four lines mean not only this...
It is identical with the primary truth (*paramārtha*), eternally abiding and unchanging; it is the most supreme *nirvāṇa* realized by all Buddhas.
Now, there are three kinds of *nirvāṇa*, and this is the *nirvāṇa* of pure nature (*prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa*).

It is called "most supreme" because its self-nature is fundamentally pure, truly perfect and quiescent of delusion, and thus cannot be compared to that of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). This is what I [mean].
A single phrase expresses the virtues possessed by nirvāṇa. "Pure" refers to the virtue of purity. "Mine" refers to the two attachments to self and phenomena;
because both attachments are purified, it constitutes the virtue of purity. The first phrase, "eternally abiding and unchanging," constitutes the virtue of permanence.
Its meaning also encompasses primordial sovereignty, which constitutes the virtue of self. Its nature being free from all suffering constitutes the virtue of bliss. (4)
Because it is replete with virtues, it is called "supreme. The final four lines further eliminate attachment to equality.
Since the preceding text has eliminated all differentiated characteristics and taught the equality of nature, if one were to cling to this very equality, it would still constitute an obstruction;
therefore, it says: "This stainless nature is far removed from both equality and inequality. Yet, it is far removed from equality...
Thus, one is free from the obstacle of principle (*dharma-āvaraṇa*). By distancing oneself from inequality, one is free from the obstacle of phenomena (*vastu-āvaraṇa*).

Because there is no longer any opposition between phenomenon and principle, it is said that "one is far removed from all [such things]. As for "the essence being without difference," "difference" refers to differentiation;
this is because whatever involves opposition is necessarily differentiated. Since the true essence possesses no marks of difference, one is far removed from all such things. This...
Thus, the dispatching of emotions and the departure from attachment constitute the truly stainless nature (*vimala-dhātu*).

This is because the stainless is precisely the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and the unconditioned is the Dharma of the mind-ground (*citta-bhūmi*). The preceding section contains multiple explanations because it answers the questions posed by Mañjuśrī;
for the scope of the inquiry was profound, and thus the response was detailed. Mañjuśrī then raised a further objection, saying: "The fundamental source of the mind-Dharma is originally unstained."
Regarding "defilements": how is it that the mental factors (citta-dharma) are stained by greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth?
Therefore, the Buddha previously established various analogies to show that one knows the mental factors follow conditions, yet their myriad functions are fully manifested.

In response to the question, "How are the mental factors stained by greed and so forth?"—it is now, within this section of the profound discourse on mental factors, that the answer is given to the question of how the mental factors are fundamentally unstained from the very beginning. Thus, one should know [this].
The substance of the mind is unchanging, yet not even a speck of dust can be established therein.

This was precisely what the Tathāgata taught so that practitioners may know how to follow conditions to dispel attachments, and observe the unchanging to realize the truth; thus he made this statement.
△ Fourth, the conclusion and exhortation to practice contemplation.
If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
they should with single-mindedness practice this Dharma of Contemplating the Mind-Ground.

Virtuous sons and others are all those with the capacity for the Mahāyāna. Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is the fruit of the Mahāyāna. Cultivating practice with a single mind is the conduct of the Mahāyāna.
The *Cittabhūmi-darśana-dharma* is the teaching of the Mahāyāna. These constitute the four dharmas of principle, teaching, conduct, and fruit.
Nevertheless, the Buddha’s intention was for people to rely upon the teaching of the *cittabhūmi*; thus, one contemplates the mind.

Regarding the principle of the stages (*bhūmi*), if one must practice the cultivation of the contemplative mind, then the fruit of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* can be realized as if it were not difficult.

However, if one does not believe and does not practice, let alone being unable to accomplish the path to *bodhi* in this present life, even after thousands of births and ten thousand kalpas, there will be no time of escape from suffering. How tragic! △ Fourth, [the section] reiterating with verses:
The Verses, Part Two. First, the introduction of the chapter:
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse.
△ Second, the actual verses, seven parts. First, the verse on Mañjuśrī’s inquiry.
Mañjuśrī, the Mother of Awakening of the Three Times, inquires of the Tathāgata regarding the Dharma of the Ground of the Mind.
The Buddha is the Great Awakened One; thus, "Mother of Awakening" refers to the Mother of the Buddhas. "Mañjuśrī" is the Chinese transcription of the name of Mañjuśrī.

An explanation may be found in the first fascicle. The second phrase describes the inquiry: "to request" means to petition with earnest sincerity, and "to inquire" means to seek a definitive resolution.
△ Second, the verse summary of the Ground of Mind:
I now, within this great assembly, shall expound the gateway of contemplative practice for attaining Buddhahood. This Dharma is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower;
all in the world should look toward it with longing.
The first two lines provide a general heading; the following two lines exhort one to have faith. Third, the verse praises the profound merit of the twofold benefit:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions who realize Great Enlightenment have all accomplished it by practicing according to this Dharma. I am the Unsurpassed Teacher of Men."

He turns the wheel of the True Dharma throughout the world, transforming and delivering immeasurable sentient beings. One should know that this is due to awakening to the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground.

This verse is easy to understand; it refers to how all Buddhas, through their own realization, deliver sentient beings, all because they have equally awakened to the mind-ground and equally cultivated the contemplation of the mind.
△ Fourth, the verse on the extensive exposition of distinctions.
All sentient beings who hear this Dharma rejoice in their pursuit of Bodhi and receive predictions of enlightenment.

All those with the karmic affinity to receive the prediction shall become Buddhas by practicing this gate of contemplation. The Buddhas themselves enjoy the great bliss of the Dharma, dwelling in the wondrous jewel palace of the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground.
The Bodhisattvas who have received their office realize non-arising; they contemplate the gate of the Mind-Ground throughout the entire Dharma-realm. As for the Bodhisattvas in their final birth...
Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, one enters this contemplative practice to realize *bodhi*. This Dharma can rain down the seven treasures of the noble ones;
it is a *maṇi* jewel that fulfills the aspirations of sentient beings. This Dharma is named the "Mother of the Buddhas," giving birth to the bodies of the three Buddhas of the three periods of time.
This Dharma is named the "Vajra Armor," capable of resisting the armies of Māra from the four assemblies. This Dharma can act as a great ship, causing...
It ferries one across the middle stream to the place of treasure. This Dharma is the most supreme great Dharma-drum;
this Dharma is the lofty and eminent great Dharma-banner; this Dharma is the adamantine great Dharma-conch; this Dharma is the illuminating great Dharma-torch that lights the world.

This Dharma is like a great holy sovereign who rewards merit and punishes transgression in accordance with the human heart. This Dharma is like a fertile and moist field, providing sustenance, growth, and nourishment upon which all depend.
At that time, I used various analogies to clarify the meaning of emptiness.

The first phrase exhorts one to listen; the second phrase clarifies the benefit. Awakening (*bodhi*) is the fruit, and joyful aspiration is the resolve—meaning one joyfully accepts this resolve, desiring to advance toward awakening.
One who possesses such an aspiration will certainly receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*) from a Tathāgata.

Commentary: (The preceding text states: "If someone asks which sentient beings shall attain Buddhahood in future ages, one should point out that these people will certainly attain Buddhahood in future ages. These people are precisely those who practice contemplation; they will certainly attain Buddhahood. This is the bestowal of a prediction [vyākaraṇa].
The next two lines exhort one to cultivate the attainment of Buddhahood. The section beginning with "All Buddhas" below versifies the previous metaphors.)
The "Great Dharma-Bliss" (*mahā-dharma-sukha*) is the self-realization of all Buddhas.
That which is personally enjoyed by them—the bliss that accords with the *dharmatā*—is called Great Dharma-Bliss; this phrase refers to the fruit. The following phrase clarifies the practice:

it means dwelling single-mindedly and immovably like the great earth, and maintaining unwavering contemplation as if residing in a precious palace (the palace being a metaphor for the gate of contemplation). The "Bodhisattva who has received office" refers to one who has been consecrated.
One who has received the office upon the crown of the head is a bodhisattva who is about to succeed to the seat of the Buddha.

"Awakening to non-arising" means that "awakening" (*bodhi*) refers to the wisdom of realization, while "non-arising" (*anutpāda*)—a term that also implies non-extinction—refers to the principle realized therein.

"The gate of contemplating the mind-ground" means that this awakening is not achieved in vain; rather, it is through the Dharma-gate of contemplating the mind-ground that one suddenly attains illumination and penetrates the entire mind-ground.

"Awakening" (*wu*) refers to the principle of non-arising that is realized; because it penetrates vertically and pervades horizontally throughout the entire Dharma-realm, this is simply termed "awakening.
The two subsequent lines beginning with "the final body" clarify "realization," which refers to the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment attaining Buddhahood in a single lifetime.
It is called "the final body" in contrast to the previous state of boundless birth and death over vast eons; now, as one is about to realize the Way, [one takes] once more...
Because he does not undergo the two kinds of birth and death, he takes equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) as his final body.
The "Tree of Awakening" (*bodhi-vṛkṣa*) is the Bodhi tree. It is beneath this tree that the Bodhisattva sits, enters this contemplative practice, and realizes the fruit of awakening.
The "seven noble riches" (*sapta-ārya-dhana*) refer to the seven types beginning with faith; these constitute the supramundane wealth of the Dharma. All sentient beings should practice these.

There are seven dharmas that support and bring about the fruit of the Path; therefore, they are called the "Noble Wealths" (*ārya-dhana*). First, the wealth of faith (*śraddhā-dhana*). (Faith refers to the faculty of faith; it means the mind is able to resolutely accept and uphold the True Dharma as the requisite for attaining Buddhahood.

Hence, it is called the wealth of faith. Second, the wealth of exertion (*vīrya-dhana*). (This refers to diligence; it means that while the Truth has not yet been realized, one single-mindedly exerts effort to seek the path of liberation as the requisite for attaining Buddhahood.

Hence, it is called the wealth of exertion. Third, the wealth of ethical discipline (*śīla-dhana*). (Discipline refers to the precepts; it means that ethical discipline is the root of liberation, capable of preventing non-virtue in body, speech, and mind, and bringing to rest the evils of body, speech, and mind.)

These are considered the requisites for attaining Buddhahood; therefore, they are called the "wealth of precepts. Fourth is the wealth of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). (*Hrī* refers to shame before oneself; *apatrāpya* refers to shame before others. This means that if one possesses both shame and dread of blame, one will not commit unwholesome karma. Because these serve as the requisites for attaining Buddhahood, they are called the wealth of shame and dread of blame.

Fifth is the wealth of learning (*śruta*). (Learning is the foremost of the three types of wisdom. One who hears must be able to contemplate; one who contemplates must be able to practice. This means that if one can hear the Buddha’s teachings, one will develop sublime understanding and act according to what has been taught.

Because this serves as the requisite for attaining Buddhahood, it is called the wealth of learning. Sixth is the wealth of relinquishment (*tyāga*). (Relinquishment refers to giving. This means that if one can direct the mind with equanimity, the mind will be free from aversion...)

Generosity (*dāna*): To have no stinginess regarding one’s body, life, or wealth, offering them as the requisite for attaining Buddhahood; therefore, it is called the "wealth of giving. (7) Concentration and Wisdom (*samādhi-prajñā*):

Concentration and wisdom are *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Concentration gathers the mind so that it does not scatter and ceases all deluded thoughts. Wisdom illuminates and understands all phenomena, destroying all false views. These serve as the requisites for attaining Buddhahood; therefore, they are called the "wealth of concentration and wisdom.
Because the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground can produce these seven kinds of noble wealth and fulfill the bodhisattva’s heart-wishes, it is like a *maṇi* jewel that can rain down [all things].
The seven treasures also fulfill the heart's desires of sentient beings. (The seven treasures refer to gold, silver, lapis lazuli, tridacna shell, agate, coral, and amber.
The following metaphors each correspond to a specific merit, such as the Buddha-mother, the ship, and the armor; all are explained according to the prose commentary.
The two lines beginning with "Only like a well-irrigated field" constitute an independent verse (*gāthā*). "Well-irrigated" (*wo*) means to water;
"field" (*tian*) refers to ground where grain grows. This is because the field serves as a metaphor for the mind-ground of sentient beings.

When it is consistently scorched by afflictions (*kleśa*), it cannot produce the merits of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), just as parched land cannot produce sprouts. If one encounters this Dharma, it provides sustenance...

Because it opens the heart and enables the arising of wisdom, it is like a fertile and well-watered field. The metaphors for "arising" (*jeng*) and "accomplishing" (*cheng*) clarify both the literal and figurative meanings;

all depend upon their respective seasons. It is like the five grains in a field: the sprouting of the shoots is "arising," their daily growth is "increasing," and the ripening of the grain is "accomplishing"—all of which depend upon their proper time.
Just as arising must depend on spring, increasing must depend on summer, and accomplishing must [depend on autumn].
It depends on autumn; yet even with the moisture of untimely rain, it still cannot reach fruition. This is a metaphor for a practitioner encountering this sutra:
like a sprout receiving rain, it nourishes the seeds of outflow-free goodness and thus enables the arousal of the bodhicitta.

Just as growth must encounter spring, one again relies on the mind to cultivate contemplation, just as maturation must depend on summer. Relying on contemplation to realize the fruit is like reaching completion, which must depend on [autumn].
Autumn: all [seasons] ride upon their respective laws and rely upon their respective times. I conclude the meaning of emptiness with a single phrase:
emptiness is the unconditioned dharma of true emptiness; it is not a void of annihilation. △ Fifth: Verses on the True Teaching of the Ground of the Mind.
Thus one knows that the three realms are but a single mind. The mind possesses great power, and from it the world arises. It is sovereign and capable of acting as the master of transformations;
through evil thoughts and virtuous minds, it further accumulates karma. This is the cause of birth and death across the past, present, and future. Relying upon deluded karma, the world exists;
the fruits of the desirable and the undesirable perpetually succeed one another.
The two characters "is" (shi) and "knows" (zhi) refer to the words expressing clear understanding.
"The three realms are but one mind" refers to the preceding passage stating that within the three realms, the mind is the sovereign.

"The mind possesses great power" is a metaphor for how the true mind, following the conditions of ignorance, possesses inconceivable karmic power; because it can thus transform both the primary and secondary retributions, it is called "arising."

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Obscuration and darkness constitute space; within the obscurity of space, darkness coagulates to form matter. (Commentary: Ignorance (*avidyā*) takes obscuration as its characteristic. This means that True Suchness (*tathatā*) is unaware, and ignorance arises adventitiously.

Following the conditions of ignorance, the mind of the entire Dharma-realm manifests as the obscure and dull void of space. Regarding the phrase "within the obscurity of space": this refers to how, over a long period, this dull space and obscurity coalesce to form the insentient world.

"Matter" refers to the matter of mountains, rivers, and the great earth. There are two kinds of worlds: namely, the insentient world of the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*). There is... [text ends]
Sentient beings and their worlds constitute the primary retribution (*vipāka*). The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* further states: "Form is mixed with delusive thoughts;

the characteristics of thought constitute the body. This refers precisely to the primary retribution. (The commentary explains: "Form" refers to the forms of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind. "Delusive thoughts" refers to the mental states stirred by delusion, which lack any inherent substance. Since these delusive thoughts belong to the mind...)

Grasping the forms of the four great elements, form becomes intermingled with deluded thought. One falsely clings to the delusive appearances grasped by the conceptual mind and consequently identifies them as the body.
"Sovereign" (zìzài) below clarifies that the mind is the master of the three realms; because it possesses an unchanging essence while following conditions, it is called "sovereign.

Because it remains precisely unchanging while yet following conditions, it is called "capable of transformation" (néngbiàn). These are all the total essence and great function of the mind; therefore, it is called "self-... (zì...).
"Unequal," etc. Following the section on "unwholesome perceptions," this verse specifically explains the meaning of the continuity of the primary retribution (*vipāka*).

That is to say, since there is primary retribution, one is further able to initiate karma; therefore, wholesome and unwholesome states of mind are not equal. "Accumulation" (*cita*) means to gather and attract.

"Intention" (*cetanā*) means that because one can create wholesome and unwholesome karma, one then gathers and attracts wholesome and unwholesome fruits. This karma constitutes the cycle of birth and death throughout the three periods of time.
...the cause. Therefore, it says "past, present, and so forth. Under the heading "relying upon," it clarifies that results are produced by means of causes.
That is to say, since one relies on deluded karma as the cause to summon and produce the world as the result, one knows that deluded karma is the basis for the result.
However, a result must necessarily follow from a cause; thus, wholesome karma produces desirable results, while unwholesome karma produces...
It gives rise to fruits that are not desired. Because of this, cause and effect are uninterrupted, and the response is inexhaustible; therefore, it is said to be "constantly continuous.

This verse means that while the true mind is fundamentally neither good nor evil, its ability to produce the causes and effects of good and evil lies in its principle of "following conditions" (*anuparivartana*).
△ Sixth: Verses explaining through various metaphors.
The mind is like a flowing stream, never dwelling for even a moment; it is like a whirlwind passing over a land, or like a monkey playing among the trees.
It is like an illusion produced by magical means, or like a bird flying through the sky without obstruction; it is like people rushing about in an empty village.
Thus, the nature of the mind is fundamentally non-existent, yet ordinary beings cling to delusion, claiming it is not non-existent.
The first phrase means that the mind follows delusion and undergoes constant flux without abiding, like flowing water that never ceases.
The mind is able to perceive all objects universally, like a whirlwind sweeping across the earth. The mind is single-mindedly attached to the five desires, like a monkey frolicking in a tree.
It establishes all phenomena based on the condition of ignorance, just as various illusions are produced depending upon magical arts.
It also universally conditions [objects] without obstruction, like a bird flying through the sky. It appears to exist yet is non-existent, like an empty village.
It can engender birth and death, like a person running about. The final two lines conclude the discussion on deluded attachment;

"such as these" refers generally to the preceding verses. Regarding "mental phenomena" (*citta-dharma*): "mind" (*citta*) refers to deluded thought, and "phenomena" (*dharma*) refers to the five desires. "Non-existent" means...

Like dreams, illusions, bubbles, and shadows, they are fundamentally non-existent. This is...
Lao snapped his fingers; this was itself liberation. However, as for liberation, it is not merely the departure from suffering, but is in fact the realization of the Way.

At that time, the Tathāgata gave rise to great compassion for all sentient beings, like parents cherishing an only child.

This means that although the Dharma of the sutra remains in the world, there is concern that those with false views might misinterpret the Buddha’s meaning; therefore, he provides the mantra, for it is truly capable of destroying the false.

...and so forth. *Dhāraṇī* is here translated as "total retention" (*zongchi*). Because it protects the wholesome and obstructs the unwholesome, it is proclaimed to assist [the practitioner].

Oṃ (1) śitha (2) para (3) veda (4) kālu-mi (5) dhāraṇī. The Mahā-śāstra states: In the language of Qin, it means "capable of upholding.

Master Zhaol translated it as "Total Retention" (*zongchi*), meaning that it retains the wholesome so that it is not lost, and retains [the restraint against] the unwholesome so that it does not arise. Furthermore, it is said to be the secret meaning of all Buddhas;
by merely receiving and maintaining it, one obtains benefit according to conditions. This, too, does not go beyond the merit of obstructing evil and giving rise to the wholesome.

Now, following the secret meaning, I shall speak only of the efficacy of the Chinese and Sanskrit [mantras]. (For those who prefer extensive study, please consult the *Lengyan zhengmai* [The True Pulse of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra], where the explanation follows the mantra.

"Needle. This refers to all ten fingers being tucked inward. "Pressing the left against the right" means using the thumb of the left hand to press against the thumb of the right hand;

Its characteristic is called the Vajra-Bandha Seal (*vajrabandhamudrā*). "Vajra" signifies firmness and sharpness.

The preceding sections have already fully detailed the contemplative gates, mantras, mudrās, and so forth; it remains only for sentient beings to generate the bodhicitta.

Mind. Because it is named after the arousal of the mind, it is called the "Chapter on Arousing Bodhicitta. △ Second, the scriptural text has three parts.
First, the narrator describes the ritual setting:
At that time, the Bhagavān had already successfully attained the precious crown of consecration from all Tathāgatas and had transcended the three...

and whose omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) and knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) are exquisitely matured, is capable of manifesting the various distinctions among sentient beings.
Having thus proclaimed the sublime gateway of contemplating the mind for the sake of all living beings, the Bhagavat addressed Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva:

The term *sa-ma-ha-sa* refers to the six meanings of *bhagavat*, which have already been explained previously; it is an epithet for the Buddha. The phrase "already able" and so forth describes how the Buddha has excellently attained the supreme path of all Buddhas.
"Consecration" (*abhiṣeka*) signifies the Dharma, just as [it does] for a Golden Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*).
When the prince had grown up, the four oceans were drawn and placed in a golden vase. On the fifteenth day of the month, with the ministers assembled in order, incense was burned and music performed.
The old king personally held the vase and poured its contents over the crown of the prince’s head. At that moment, the prince ascended the throne and the old king retired.
This is used as a metaphor to mean that the Buddha has received the heart-seal (citta-mudrā) of all Buddhas, just like this.
"Consecration" refers to receiving office. The crown symbolizes the supreme; the jewels symbolize the most venerable. Therefore, it is said that he "transcends the three realms.
Regarding the phrase "having already attained," *dhāraṇī* means "total retention," signifying that it encompasses all phenomena and maintains immeasurable meanings.
It summarizes the inexhaustible Dharma-treasury of the Tathāgata, wherein the provisional and the ultimate proceed together. Therefore, it is called "sovereignty. *Samādhi* means... [text continues].

Samādhi means equal and impartial maintenance; it is the simultaneous departure from both laxity and agitation, the perfect integration of concentration and wisdom, and is also termed "mastery" and "sublime excellence.
This refers to the causal practice. Maturation refers to the perfection of the fruit: the knowledge of all things and the knowledge of all aspects.

"All are the Buddha’s wisdom. From "Able to act" below, the function of the Buddha’s wisdom is described; that is, he establishes teachings according to the capacities of beings, which vary in many ways, hence they are called "differentiated.
From "This is the Bhagavat" below, the conclusion of the description is given. From "Addressing Mañjuśrī" below, the Buddha’s speech is described.
II. The Bhagavat Shows the Assembly Five Parts: 1. The Tathāgata Grants Permission to Speak on the Arousing of the Mind.
"O Great Son of Good Family, for the sake of sentient beings, I have already expounded the Mind-Ground. I shall now further expound the Great Dharani for Arousing the Bodhicitta,
so that all sentient beings may arouse the mind of Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi and swiftly perfect the wondrous fruit."
The first three phrases conclude what preceded; "Furthermore" and below grant what follows. A "Great Dharani" refers to a divine mantra;

it is called "Great" because it possesses awesome power. If a person can uphold it, spiritual power will internally impel them, and they will inevitably resolve their mind for enlightenment and achieve the Way;

hence it says, "causing all [beings]," and so forth. When this sutra frequently speaks of "swift realization" and "swift perfection," there is no doubt that it belongs to the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao).
△ Second, Mañjuśrī’s statement of his request to resolve doubts.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Buddha has taught:
the past has already ceased; the future has not yet arrived; and the present does not abide. The nature of all mental phenomena throughout the three periods of time is entirely [thus]."

"Emptiness. As for that bodhicitta, what is meant by its 'arising'? Excellent, World-Honored One! We pray that you will explain this for us, so as to sever the web of all doubts and cause us to advance toward bodhi."

"Regarding what the Buddha has said": this recounts the words from the preceding passage by the Buddha concerning "that which has passed away and ceased," and so forth, meaning that the three periods of time are unattainable.

[The meaning of] this is unclear. It is like being caught in a net; if one were to resolve it with a single word, one would certainly advance upon the Path. Therefore it is said: "Severing all [views of] equality.
△ Third, the Buddha reveals the Dharma of emptiness to dispel views, in three parts: first, the teaching by means of the Dharma.
The Buddha told Mañjuśrī, "Good son, among all mental phenomena (*cittadharma*), various false views arise.

for such views have no basis."
Below the section on "All Minds," the Buddha said: "When I speak of the emptiness of mind, it is a provisional teaching for a specific occasion.

As for 'all mental phenomena' (*citta-dharma*), these refer to all mind-kings (*citta-rāja*) and mental factors (*caitta*). Those who give rise to various false views are all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Relying upon these mental phenomena, they falsely produce divergent views. Ordinary beings, by clinging to existence, give rise to the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); [non-Buddhists...]"
When the Way relies upon the mind, extreme views arise; all of these fail to accord with correct principle and collectively constitute false views.
Expanding further, there are sixty-two such views that confuse people’s true nature and harm their merit—all of which are the faults of relying on the mind.
The phrase "in order to sever and eliminate" [the mind] expresses the Buddha’s fundamental intent. Regarding the sixty-two views, the explanation is as given previously.

[The text] says: "Various views" refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth. Below the section on the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), it correctly explains the meaning of emptiness (*śūnyatā*):

namely, that the mind-king and mental factors exist when facing an object, but do not exist apart from the object; they arise and perish moment by moment and lack any intrinsic substance. Therefore, I say they are empty.
The phrase "In this way," etc., sets forth the efficacy of the emptiness of the mind: that is to say, since I have explained that all minds...
When it is empty, the various views and divergent calculations have no basis to rely upon; it is like hair having nothing to which it can attach once the skin no longer exists.
It is precisely to eliminate these divergent views that the emptiness of the mind is taught. △ Second, the explanation by means of analogy.
It is like a dense forest, thick and lush, where lions, white elephants, tigers, wolves, and other fierce beasts dwell in concealment.

When their venom erupts, they harm people, and all traces of human passage are utterly severed. At that time, a wise person sets fire to the forest; because the forest has been cleared away, [the beasts can no longer remain].
All the great and wicked beasts have been eliminated without remainder.
The dense forest is a metaphor for the mental factors (*citta-dharma*), and the wicked beasts are a metaphor for various views (*dṛṣṭi*).

This is because while wicked beasts harm the physical body of a single lifetime, evil views harm the Dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*) across successive lifetimes. The wise man is a metaphor for the Buddha; he burns the forest with fire.
If their dwelling place is cut off, the beasts will no longer exist; hence it is said that "nothing remains. This is a metaphor for the Buddha’s teaching on the emptiness of the mind:
when the basis for divergent views is severed, then all views of annihilationism and eternalism are spontaneously eliminated without needing to be severed, leaving nothing behind.
△ Third, the application to the Dharma.
The emptiness of the mind and the cessation of views are also like this.

The emptiness of the mind corresponds to the burning of the forest; the cessation of views corresponds to the extinction of the beasts. Since the dharma and the metaphor correspond, it is said, "are also like this.

[...afflictions].
Furthermore, son of good family, for what reason is the meaning of emptiness established? It is for the sake of extinguishing afflictions that arise from the deluded mind;

The illness of [clinging to] emptiness must also be eliminated. Why? If one holds the meaning of emptiness to be ultimate, then all phenomena would be without cause and without effect; what difference would there be from the Lokāyata?
By means of these two phrases, the meaning of establishing emptiness is raised as an inquiry; the subsequent section provides the explanation for its cessation.
Because the afflictions of sentient beings all arise from the deluded mind, a single moment of deluded movement gives rise to all delusions at once.
Therefore, one knows that the mind is the root of the disease of affliction. To eliminate this root of the disease, it is said that neither the internal nor the external can be apprehended.
Some say that the three periods of time are unobtainable; this is because one knows that when the mind ceases, afflictions have nothing upon which to rely.

Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] taught emptiness for the sake of cessation and so forth. "Good son," and so on—here, by means of "double emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), he dispels "single emptiness.
The Buddha said: "When I speak of emptiness, it is fundamentally for the purpose of dispelling afflictions. If sentient beings do not understand the Buddha..."

[The Master] said: "If one clings to emptiness as being ultimately existent—meaning that while afflictions are truly non-existent, the principle of emptiness is taken to be truly existent—one must know that the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) likewise cannot be retained and must itself be emptied.
Therefore, it is said that 'the nature of emptiness is also empty. (The upper character 'empty' refers to the emptiness that dispels afflictions;

the lower character 'empty' is the 'repeated emptiness' (*śūnya-śūnyatā*), which dispels the aforementioned emptiness of nature. Thus, one uses emptiness to dispel emptiness. The two subsequent lines regarding clinging to emptiness express the meaning of 'dispelling and removing,' namely:"
Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) can eliminate afflictions; emptiness is fundamentally the medicine. If one becomes attached to emptiness itself, then emptiness also becomes a malady.
Since it has thus become a malady of emptiness, it too must be eliminated. Why? This is a further inquiry followed by a reiterated explanation.

That is to say, for what reason does the Buddha judge the grasping at emptiness as a reality to be a malady? The explanation states: if a person is deluded and lacks understanding, [they grasp at it].
If emptiness were taken as the ultimate meaning, then all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane realms would be without cause and without effect;
one would thus become a non-Buddhist who negates cause and effect, no different from the Lokāyata materialists.
Therefore it is asked: "What is the distinction? Fearing that this might result in the malady of nihilism (*śūnyatā-roga*), how could one not dispel it? (Lokāyata;
here translated as "evil sophistry," refers to the non-Buddhist outsiders who negate cause and effect. △ Second, the analogy of medicine according to the illness.
Good son, it is like the agada medicine, which can cure all diseases. If there is a sick person who takes it, they will certainly recover.
Once the illness has been cured, the medicine departs along with the disease; if one who is not ill takes the medicine, the medicine itself turns back into a disease.
*Agada*. This is a name for a medicine from the Western Regions; here it is translated as "that which can remove all illnesses.

"When the illness has been cured, the medicine is removed" is the correct principle. This means that once the disease has been healed, the medicine should cease accordingly and must not be taken again.

The final two lines mean that although the medicine may be most excellent, it can be taken by one who is ill; however, if one takes it when there is no illness, the medicine will instead become a disease.
The Dharma taught by the Tathāgata is likewise. How does the gāthā-medicine remove the [afflictions] of the multitude?
The arising of afflictions, delusive thoughts, inverted views, and various mental illnesses—when sentient beings practice according to these teachings, it is like taking medicine for an illness;

Furthermore, when delusion is removed and wisdom ceases, so that no residual traces remain, then both person and phenomena are empty, and one accords with the Way, just as an illness [is cured].

When the medicine removes the illness, there is no difference [between the two states]. If one were to eliminate delusion by clinging to emptiness, it would merely increase the "sickness of emptiness.

What wise person would take medicine and contract an illness?

"Good son, if one gives rise to the view of existence, it is better than giving rise to the view of emptiness. Emptiness serves as the medicine for the disease of existence, whereas there is no medicine to treat emptiness itself.

Therefore, it is said, "If one gives rise to... and so forth. The following two lines explain the meaning of this superiority over the view of emptiness.

It is simply because ordinary beings cling to existence that they still recognize the existence of cause and effect, the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox, as well as good and evil, the noble and the ordinary.
Although they cannot yet directly realize the wondrous mind in which existence and emptiness are non-dual before their very eyes, they nevertheless do not dare to repudiate cause and effect.
Thus, the medicine of the Prajñā-wisdom of emptiness can be applied to treat them; therefore, it is called "emptiness."
This is for the purpose of curing illness. Suppose that although views have been eliminated, one ultimately clings to emptiness and regards emptiness as being correct;

"Delighting in [emptiness] is precisely the affliction of being attached to emptiness. Thus we know that ordinary beings fall into the state of *icchantika*, while those of the Two Vehicles fall into fixed natures;

"There is no medicine to cure emptiness" (meaning one cannot cure the affliction of attachment to emptiness). From "Good son" onwards, the text directly answers the previous question, stating that for this reason—

This means that once those views have been eliminated, one suddenly awakens from oneself and attains great penetration and great enlightenment.

"Bodhi. The final two phrases point to the name of the aforementioned samādhi; thus it is said: "This awakened mind is itself the bodhicitta.

It does not abide. All mental phenomena throughout the three periods of time are empty by their very nature. Regarding that bodhicitta, what can be said of its "arising"? Now the Buddha answers: "The mind of self-awakening is able to give rise to bodhicitta.
(5) Self-awakening has four meanings, divided into two parts: first, the heading that indicates and enumerates these four meanings.
Good son, the mind that awakens to itself has four meanings. What are these four? Part Two:
The Two Explanations of the Ordinary and the Sage. One: Establishing the Distinction Between the Two.
That is to say, ordinary beings have two kinds of mind; Buddhas and Bodhisattvas also have two kinds of mind.
Part Two: Distinguishing between Ordinary Beings and Sages (Three Sections). Section One: The Two Minds of Ordinary Beings.

"Good son, what are the characteristics of the two minds of ordinary beings? First, from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness, when they perceive their respective objects through causes and conditions, it is called the 'mind of self-awakening.
Second, when the mind and mental factors, apart from the five sense organs, combine to perceive an object, it is called the 'mind of self-awakening.
Good son, these two minds are capable of giving rise to bodhicitta."

"Consciousness" (*vijñāna*) refers to the meaning of discrimination. The first five [consciousnesses] are "discrimination by recollection," while the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is "discrimination by deliberation.

This is because when the eye-faculty encounters a visual object, it gives rise to a thought of discrimination; at its initial arising, before it yet relies upon names and words, it is called "eye-consciousness.
Furthermore, it can give rise to simultaneous attention (*manasikāra*) and deliberative discrimination, which is called...
"Consciousness. The phrase "up to and including" (*yāvat*) is an elliptical expression. That which is induced by the object of sound is auditory consciousness;
that induced by the object of odor is olfactory consciousness; that induced by the object of taste is gustatory consciousness; and that induced by the object of tangibility is tactile consciousness.
Since these arise from the five sense objects, they each take their own respective domains as their objects. The first five are all [preceded by] recollection.

Regarding the nature of objects as conditions: only the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) engages in subtle discrimination of mental objects (*dharmaviṣaya*), which is termed "conceptualization" (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*).

All three types of objects are taken as conditions—namely, the object of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvālambana*), the object with a shared substance (*sadravyālambana*), and the object of solitary images (*pratibimbālambana*). That which takes its own object through causal conditions is called the "mind of self-awakening."
This refers to the awakening of the mind by ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*). "Cause" (*hetu*) means the source; "condition" (*pratyaya*) means discernment. Regarding "one's own object":

visual consciousness takes the dust of form as its own specific object, and so on up to mental consciousness, which takes the dharma-dust—the shadow of the five dusts after they have ceased—as its own specific object.
By virtue of these conditions, one suddenly awakens and becomes aware of one's own objects; this is what constitutes an ordinary person.
This is the mind that awakens by itself. Second, below, it clarifies the common conditions for self-awakening. "Roots" refers to the eyes and so forth;

because they possess the capacity to generate consciousness, they are called roots. "Being apart from the five roots" means that the eye does not confront form, and so on, up to the body not confronting touch;
it is by not employing the five roots that one is said to be "apart. As for the mind and mental factors (citta-caitta-dharma) harmonizing to take objects as conditions, this is...
The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) also takes internal objects as its conditions. "Mind" refers to the mind-king (*cittarāja*), which is the mental consciousness;

"mental factors" (*caitta*) refer to the universal, object-specific, and other categories, totaling fifty-one that are fully present. This means that when the mental consciousness, the king, initiates movement, all the mental factors follow it.

When the king and the factors are in union, they together take internal objects as their conditions. However, these internal objects are not uniform, being either wholesome or unwholesome. As for the act of taking them as conditions, it is as follows:
Investigate and realize the realms of good and evil until you suddenly awaken; when the innate illumination is realized, that is the self-awakening of the mind.
"Good son" and below is the summary. In Sanskrit, *bodhi*; here it is translated as the "Path of Awakening. This refers to the self-awakening of the mind.
This is precisely the path of awakening; therefore, it is said that one can "give rise to bodhi. Question: Both employ consciousness (*vijñāna*); what is the distinction between these two? Answer:

Since the former refers to "eye-consciousness" and so forth, the eye is the faculty (*indriya*). This means that when the eye-faculty encounters the object-field of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*), [consciousness arises].

This is the function of the faculties (*indriya*). When they are suddenly aroused, the subsequent conceptualization (*vikalpa*) in accordance with that recollection is called the visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) taking an object.
This constitutes the function of both the faculty and the consciousness. As it is with the eye, so it is with the other five. As for the second [category], which is separate from the five faculties:
This does not employ the five sense faculties. Since it does not employ the five sense faculties, it likewise does not employ the five consciousnesses;

it employs solely the domain of the sovereign mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), internally taking dharmas as its object. This is what is meant by "commonly shared objects. (My private comment: In the teaching of the Patriarchal Chan, students are instructed to transcend mind, intellect, and consciousness to investigate.

Now, in the Tathāgata Chan, one must indeed employ mind, intellect, and consciousness to investigate. This is like a clever worldly thief whom the entire family loathes and all wish to expel—just as the Patriarchal school teaches one to distance oneself from them. Nevertheless, those who employ [the faculties] in the manner of the Tathāgata...)

It is like a clever thief whom the entire family refuses to employ. Yet, those within the family who possess discernment cherish his cleverness; they offer various exhortations to make him reform and start anew, so that he may be employed once more. Although this thief can ruin matters, he can also accomplish them. If he leads with fierce courage, he may attain the nobility of a marquis.

For this reason, this sutra employs the discerning mind to engage with objects, and one can likewise achieve self-awakening through it. Although the Chan school commands one to remain detached and insists that one must not rely on it, nor can one do without it.

Is the one who currently investigates the *huatou* (critical phrase) not using the discerning mind? Is the one who gives rise to doubt not using the discerning mind? It is simply that one must not be attached to it. When Lingyun saw the peach blossoms and awakened to the Way, was that not the visual consciousness?

When Xiangyan heard the bamboo strike and thereby clarified his mind, was this not because his auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*) was superior? Thus, these two individuals seem similar to the first type [of practitioner]. When one is engaged in formal practice within the hall and raises a doubt by holding the *huatou*, if they suddenly awaken to the Way, this seems similar to the second type.

Even if they do not entirely coincide, the present intent of the Buddha is that the conscious mind (*vijñāna-citta*) has utility and can likewise realize the Way. As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, when the twenty-five sages presented their accounts of *pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna* (perfect penetration), it was shown that the sense organs (*indriya*), the objects (*viṣaya*), and the conscious mind (*vijñāna-citta*) are all capable of realizing the Way.
Therefore, there is this discernment. To grasp or to relinquish depends solely on each individual’s own realization. △ Second, the two minds of the sages and worthies.
Good son, as for the characteristics of these two minds of the sages and worthies: first is the wisdom that contemplates true reality;
second is the wisdom that contemplates all objective realms.

Regarding "Contemplating Reality" (觀真) and below: ordinary beings employ consciousness (*vijñāna*), and thus it is called "conditioning" (*ālambana*); sages and worthies employ wisdom (*jñāna*), and thus it is called "contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*).
Contemplation does not give rise to discrimination; it is like a mirror reflecting an image. Wisdom is that which contemplates, and principle is that which is contemplated.

True reality is the principle of *tathatā* and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). This means that while wisdom accords with principle, it does not obstruct the distinct functioning of wisdom and principle.

However, this is precisely the wisdom that contemplates ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). The second [wisdom] below is the wisdom that contemplates phenomena (*saṃvṛti-satya*), for all objects are phenomena.

Thus, the former is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), while this is the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*). Nevertheless, when phenomena are brought back to principle, the provisional is itself emptiness;
since principle does not obstruct phenomena, emptiness is itself the provisional. When emptiness is the provisional, one does not cling to emptiness; when the provisional...
That which is emptiness is non-attachment to the provisional; it is non-attachment to the two extremes. This is precisely the contemplation of the Middle Way.
This is the gate of awakening for the worthy and the sages. △ Third, the conclusion establishing the four minds.
"Good son, these four kinds are called the mind realized through self-awakening.
Ordinary beings realize it through the objects they perceive; noble ones realize it through contemplative observation. Each has two types;
therefore, it is concluded with the words 'such as these. △ Fifth, a detailed explanation of the seal of contemplation, in six parts: 1. Mañjuśrī’s inquiry regarding contemplation."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the mind has no form or characteristics, nor does it have a place of abiding.
When an ordinary practitioner first gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, upon what basis do they rely, and what characteristics do they contemplate?"
"Mind has no form or appearance" means that the true mind is vast and boundless, empty, penetrating, and spiritually responsive;
it truly cannot be seen as large or small, square or round, and thus has no form or appearance. Since it cannot be apprehended internally, externally, or in between, it has no place of abiding.
These two phrases establish the fundamental meaning. "Ordinary people," etc., is the actual inquiry; its intent is to say that the worthy...
The Sage employs wisdom; it naturally has a point of entry. However, the ordinary person employs the consciousness-mind (*vijñāna-citta*) in their activities.
The Buddha’s teaching is to contemplate the mind (*citta-vipaśyanā*). Yet, since the mind has no place of abiding, upon what can one rely?

Therefore, it is asked: "Upon what basis? Since it has no form or appearance, what is there to contemplate? Therefore, it is asked: "What appearance is contemplated? (One should know that this question still proceeds from the "Chapter on Contemplating the Mind" [Guanxin pin], concerning the one who is able to contemplate the mind.)

This was investigated and understood from within liberation; it is not that one lacks knowledge of the text, but rather that this is for the sake of inquiry by the assembly). △ Second, the Tathāgata’s explanation.
The Buddha said: "Good son, the characteristic of the bodhicitta as observed by ordinary beings is like a pure, full moon-disk, abiding brilliantly upon the chest.
If one wishes to swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression, [one should dwell] in an araṇya..."
Whether in a secluded and empty chamber, one should sit with the body upright and right mindfulness established.
Binding the aforementioned Tathāgata-vajra-bandha mudrā, close the eyes and contemplate the bright moon within the chest. One should reflect thus: "This full moon disc is fifty *yojanas* in diameter;
it is stainless, luminous, and pure, transparent both inside and out, and supremely cool. The moon is the mind, and the mind is the moon; there is no dust or obscuration."
Free from defilement and with the non-arising of false conceptualization, it can cause the bodies and minds of sentient beings to be pure.

It causes the great bodhicitta to be firm and non-retrogressive. Forming this mudrā and maintaining mindfulness while observing the subtle and wondrous phrases of the great bodhicitta—the pure mantra that is the initial arousal of the mind of all Bodhisattvas—[one attains these benefits].
"Ordinary beings, below": this means that bodhi is the mind itself. The mind is in reality without marks (*animitta*).

Now, to produce marks from within this marklessness is also a skillful means (*upāya*) of the Buddha, serving as a representation for ordinary sentient beings to contemplate the mind. Therefore, it is said:
"It is like a pure and perfect lunar disc, dwelling with brilliant clarity upon the breast. This is because ordinary beings employ consciousness (*vijñāna*).

This is the method of meditation for teaching and binding the mind. In response to Mañjuśrī’s question—“Since the mind has no form or appearance, what kind of appearance should one contemplate?”—the Buddha said that one uses the moon as a metaphor for the mind; thus, it is said to be “like the lunar disc.
Regarding the phrase “abiding radiantly upon the breast,” this also answers the question of where the mind dwells when it has no dwelling place; the Buddha said: [it abides] there.
This is borrowed from the depths of my own heart to express the point of contemplating the mind. If one wishes to proceed further, I shall explain the preparatory practices (*prayoga*):

namely, if ordinary sentient beings desire to swiftly attain the stage of non-retrogression (which is the direct realization of the eighth bhūmi), they should fear that the five desires within the mundane world will disturb them such that the mind cannot remain pure; they must therefore dwell in an *āraṇya*, a secluded and tranquil place.

This refers to the location (the *āraṇya*, which indicates the mountains and beneath the trees; it is the place where one is separated from all clamor and confusion). As for the empty and silent chamber:
even if one cannot find the mountains or beneath the trees, it is also permissible to stay within an empty, quiet room. To sit with the body upright signifies meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Right mindfulness gives rise to wisdom. Furthermore, regarding the instruction to form mudrās:

it is because when one maintains an upright body and right mindfulness, there may be disturbances caused by malevolent spirits or obstructions resulting from past karma that hinder the attainment of meditative concentration. Therefore, one forms mudrās to protect against these;
they can cause malevolent spirits to flee afar and past karma to be extinguished, whereby right mindfulness will certainly be accomplished.
As for "closing the eyes," it means half-opening and half-closing them. As for "observing," it means maintaining mental visualization and focused mindfulness.

The "bright moon within the breast" refers to the mind-dharma that is being symbolized. "Engaging in such contemplation" refers to the mental application of visualizing according to the orthodox teachings.
Regarding the "moon disc of fifty *yojanas*," this is the measurement of the disc; one *yojana* equals forty *li*.
It is fifty *yojanas*, or two thousand *li*, in size. Regarding the three lines beginning with "Stainless" (*vimala*): "Moon-purity" (*candraprabhā*) symbolizes the purity of the mind.

That "the moon is the mind" and "the mind is the moon" is the sign of perfected contemplation; one is not aware of a mind existing, nor is one aware of a moon existing—they merge into a single entity.
The two lines concerning "dust and obscurations" are the signs of the exhaustion of delusions and the disappearance of emotional attachments. This is able to...

The following four lines describe the successful accomplishment of the visualization. Regarding the mudrā: it is the previously mentioned Vajrabandha mudrā, which symbolizes the wheel of body (*kāyacakra*);
the recitation is entrusted to the mouth; and the observation resides in the mind. These collectively encompass the power of the correspondence of the three wheels.
"Great Bodhicitta" and "sublime phrases" are the names of the mantra. From the words "All Bodhisattvas" onwards...
The Manifested Meaning: This means that those who uphold this mantra are able to give rise to the Great Mind (mahācitta), and their delusions and demons cannot disturb them;
therefore, it is called the "Pure Mantra," which is an elegant appellation for a divine spell. △ Third, the Transmission of the Mantra.
Oṃ (1) bodhi (2) śita (3) mucīpa (4) tāye (5) me (6). The meaning of the mantra is the same as before.
△ Fourth, the declaration of the mantra’s majestic power.
This dhāraṇī possesses great majesty and power; it enables the practitioner never again to regress.
All bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present, while on the stage of the causal ground at the time of their first resolve, all single-mindedly recollect and uphold this mantra.
Entering the stage of non-retrogression, one swiftly perfects right enlightenment.

The first four lines clarify the efficacy manifested in the present life; the subsequent sections clarify how [the practice] assists in accomplishing the efficacy of swiftly attaining realization throughout the three periods of time.
△ Fifth, a detailed exposition of the ritual for contemplation.
"Good son, at that time, the practitioner sits with body upright and right mindfulness, remaining entirely unmoving. Binding the mind upon the lunar disc, he matures his observation;
this is called the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Contemplating the Bodhicitta to Attain Buddhahood."
△ Section Six: Comparing and Revealing Superiority (in two parts). First, the merit of extinguishing transgressions:

If there are ordinary persons who cultivate this contemplation, [it shall extinguish] the five heinous crimes they have committed, the four types of ten evil deeds, and the state of being an icchantika.
All such sins as these shall be completely extinguished.

As for the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*): namely, killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an *arhat*, shedding the blood of a Buddha, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha that turns back the wheel of Dharma.

Regarding the four types of ten non-virtuous actions (*daśākuśala*): there are not actually four types of ten non-virtuous actions; the character "zhong" (seed/type) is certainly used here to denote their gravity.

[The character] "字" (zi) was erroneously added with the "grain" radical by the transcriber. These are the four kinds of grave offenses (*pārājika*) for a bhikṣu: namely, sexual misconduct, killing, stealing, and lying.

One who commits these is not permitted to dwell together with the community of monks; this constitutes a *parājika* offense. These are those which the Buddhas do not allow to be purified through repentance.
Regarding the ten evil deeds (*daśākuśala*), there are two [categories]: first, the commission of the ten *pārājika* offenses that violate the Bodhisattva precepts.
The ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*) are: first, killing; second, stealing; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech; fifth, selling intoxicants;

sixth, speaking of the faults of the fourfold assembly; seventh, praising oneself and disparaging others; eighth, being stingy and adding to one's disparagement [of others]; ninth, harboring anger and refusing instruction; tenth, slandering the Triple Gem (*triratna*).
The second category consists of the bodily actions of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct, and the vocal actions of lying and frivolous speech (*sambhinnapralāpa*).
Divisive speech, harsh speech, and the mental karma of covetousness, malice, and wrong views—these constitute the ten types of unwholesome karma.

Those who are *icchantikas*—which means "lacking faith"—namely those who slander the Buddha-dharma or follow external paths, will certainly fall into the Avīci Hell for these aforementioned most grievous offenses. However, if they turn their minds for even a single moment and cultivate this contemplation...
Section on the Gate. Furthermore, through mantras and mudrās, such offenses as these shall all be completely extinguished. △ Second, obtaining the merit of dhyāna, in two parts:
first, indicating the heading, posing the inquiry, and listing the names.
He immediately attains five kinds of samādhi gates. What are the five? First, the kṣaṇa-samādhi;
second, the paramāṇu-samādhi; third, the sitasūtra-samādhi; fourth, the uccanīca-samādhi; and fifth, the supratiṣṭhita-samādhi.
*Samādhi* is another name for *samāpatti*. "Gate" (*mukha*) has the meaning of "passage. This means that one enters through the gate of *samādhi* to reach the stage of Buddhahood.
△ Second, the detailed explanation of each term, which has six parts. First, *kṣaṇa-samādhi*.
What is called the *kṣaṇa-samādhi*? It refers to dwelling for a brief moment while contemplating a full moon.
It is like a monkey whose body is bound; it cannot go far, nor can it stop nearby, but remains still for only a short while, exhausted by hunger and thirst.
The ordinary person’s contemplation of the mind is also like this. To briefly attain samādhi is called a "kṣaṇa.
Since beginningless time, the consciousness and deluded thoughts of sentient beings have pursued objects and clung to conditions, not remaining still for even a kṣaṇa;
thus, they are like monkeys. Now, wishing to restrain the mind, one says: "Contemplate the full moon and abide therein. (Contemplation)

This is the method of binding the mind. "Full moon" refers to the lunar disc upon the chest, which represents the mind. If one practices contemplation according to mindfulness, deluded thoughts will not move; thus it is called "abiding. "Briefly" means for a short duration.
Because one has long been distracted and cannot maintain constant restraint, one uses the power of samādhi to temporarily halt those thoughts.
Therefore, parables such as the monkey’s body being bound are used to instruct and clarify this. One should simply endure hunger and thirst.
This is a metaphor for being unable to universally take all objects as one's focus. "Dwelling for a brief moment" is a metaphor for the temporary cessation of deluded thoughts.

The section beginning with "Ordinary persons" (Fànfū) below combines the teaching with the actual phenomenon to conclude the name [of the samādhi]. △ Second, the *Microdust Samādhi* (*Mìchén sānmèi*).
What is called the "Dust-like Samādhi"? It refers to a slight correspondence with samādhi.
For example, it is like a person who constantly eats bitter food and has never tasted sweetness; at one time, they obtain a single drop of honey that reaches the root of their tongue.
His superior joy increases and his exultation redoubles as he seeks even more honey.

In this way, the practitioner, having passed through long kalpas while consuming various bitter flavors, now attains a slight correspondence with the sweet flavor of samādhi; this is termed a "particle of dust" (rajas).
Regarding the designation established by "a mote of dust," this merely clarifies that through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one has attained but a small portion [of the truth].
Therefore, it is said that there is "partial correspondence. The analogy follows: the person represents the practitioner of contemplation; suffering represents the worldly afflictions (*kleśa*);

sweetness represents the tranquil state of *samādhi*. When the person eats the sweet food at once and, filled with joy, seeks even more honey, it means that person has experienced the flavor of honey.

Only upon tasting its sweetness does one realize the bitterness of what was eaten previously, and thus desires to obtain more of it. This is a metaphor for the ordinary person who has newly begun practice:
when they momentarily attain a partial correspondence with samādhi, they perceive the suffering of their former mental distraction through the bliss found within stillness;
consequently, they seek deeper concentration even further, just as that person seeks the honey. Thus proceeds the practitioner below.
Although this is a combined textual passage, it actually expresses both the dharma and its metaphor simultaneously; thus it says, "the sweet and delicious samādhi.

The phrase "with a small portion" below concludes the name [of the samādhi]. (Though it is called a "small portion," one has already felt the effort enter the path and is unwilling to let go, which is why one seeks much more. △ Third, the White Thread Samādhi.
What is called the "White Thread Samādhi"? It refers to an ordinary person who, from time immemorial until the end of the future, now attains this concentration.
It is like seeing a single white thread within a great mass of black dye; such is the practitioner.
Within the dark night of many births and deaths, one has now finally attained the pure and white samādhi;

this is termed "the thread. The "white thread" serves as a metaphor, referring specifically to a strand of white silk. By means of this, the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is revealed; hence the term *samādhi*.

The passage beginning with "Ordinary persons" clarifies the length of time in the past. The passage beginning with "Exhausting the future" clarifies the length of time yet to come. Now, [one] has attained it.

Regarding this meditative concentration (*samādhi*): it means that if ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), from time immemorial, had not encountered this contemplation, they would inevitably remain forever within the darkness of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) even until the end of the future. How fortunate to have now attained this concentration;
this constitutes having a share in *bodhi*. To illustrate this, the following parable is given: "Seeing white within the black."
What is this supreme joy and good fortune? It is because that which had never been seen before is now finally seen; thus one rejoices.
The passage beginning with "In this way, the practitioner" below provides the correspondence of the Dharma to the analogy:

the long night of the darkness of birth and death corresponds to the black dye in the analogy, while the fact that one has now attained the pure white samādhi corresponds to seeing a single white thread within the analogy.
This means that after having long remained in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one suddenly attains *samādhi* and is no longer disturbed in mind by afflictions (*kleśa*).
How could this not be a cause for supreme joy? However, since it says "seeing white within the black," this seems to carry the meaning of first seeing the Path (*darśanamārga*).
To name it "a single thread" (*yī lǚ*) is an unstable rendering by the translator; it should correctly be stated as "like a white thread. △ Fourth, the three stages of rising and falling.
Dullness.
What is called the "rising and falling" samādhi? It refers to when a practitioner observes that the mind is not yet mature;
it may be well-established or not well-established. Such a samādhi, which fluctuates like a scale rising and falling, is called "rising and falling."
"Those whose contemplation of the mind is not yet mature" means they have not attained full proficiency. This merely indicates abiding; alternatively, it is explained as "sometimes skillful.

This is because when one's practice is not yet mature, the arising and subsiding [of thoughts] are unstable. At times, concentration and wisdom are balanced, hence it is said "sometimes skillfully established.
At other times, they are lopsided and uneven, hence it is said "not yet skillfully established. Thus it continues below.
Designate the names of the knots: if they are successfully formed, they rise; if not yet formed, they sink. Rising is "arising" (qi); sinking is "subsiding" (fu).

These are named according to the practice (*gongfu*), hence they are called the Samādhi of Arising and Subsiding. [Question: Previously it was said that seeing white within black is explained as the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Now, again, you speak of arising and subsiding. Is this not the case where one has seen the Path and subsequently becomes deluded? [Answer: The previous explanation of the Path of Seeing refers to what resembles the Path of Seeing. It has not yet reached the state of pure truth; there is still a sense of vagueness. Generally speaking, it is not yet pure, and was only provisionally permitted as such.
△ Fifth, the samādhi of abiding.
What is called the samādhi of abiding? By practicing the preceding four concentrations, the mind attains abiding and is well able to guard itself.
It is unstained by any defilements. It is like a person in the summer who travels far across sandy deserts, enduring the full intensity of scorching heat;

his mind is parched with thirst and he is nearly unable to endure it. Suddenly, he obtains the sweet, pure water of the Snowy Mountains or celestial *sudhā* nectar, and his burning afflictions are instantly dispelled.
The body and mind are tranquil and composed; therefore, this samādhi is called "abiding securely.

By cultivating the first two lines below, one means that from the initial stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana) who resolves to cultivate meditative concentration, one proceeds from the shallow to the deep.

This can be described as becoming increasingly mature with each subsequent stage until it is forged into a single whole, such that it does not dissipate or scatter. Hence, it is said that "the mind attains peace."
"Abiding. "Well able to descend" refers to the characteristic of emerging into peaceful abiding (*anurakṣaṇā*). "Dusts" (*rajas*) are the objects of perception;

"defilement" (*saṃkleśa*) is the perceiving mind. Now, being undefiled is "guarding"; this may be called the profound stillness of mind and object, where concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are in suchness (*tathatā*).
This is the characteristic of peaceful abiding. "Like a person," etc., further illustrates the blissful characteristic of samādhi.
"During the summer months" refers to the time of the scorching heat. "People" refers to those traveling along distant roads.
"Sandy deserts" means that the path has no soil, consisting entirely of hot sand; above, one is scorched by the sun, and below, one is steamed by the sand.

Therefore, it is said that he "suffers the full brunt of fiery poison. That his mind is parched and exhausted, such that he can hardly endure it, means that his thirst has reached its limit with no hope of relief, at the moment when he awaits death.
When he suddenly obtains [the water] below, it immediately relieves his thirst and eases his exhaustion.
Once the thirst and exhaustion are relieved, he attains great peace and happiness; thus, it is said that "his body and mind are composed. One should understand that this passage contains...
The analogy lacks a point of correspondence. If one were to establish such a correspondence: "a person among people" represents the practitioner who cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

"The intense heat of summer" represents being possessed of all afflictions (*kleśa*) within the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). "Traveling far across sandy deserts" represents enduring birth and death for a long duration.
"Fully experiencing the heat of the poison" represents the five desires (*pañca-kāma-guṇa*) assailing the mind, whereby through afflictions and grasping, one constantly undergoes manifold sufferings.

The two lines following "Its mind" (*qí xīn*) serve as a metaphor for how the causes and effects of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) cannot rescue one another. "Suddenly obtaining" (*hū dé*) below serves as a metaphor for encountering [the Dharma] unexpectedly;

it signifies the good fortune of obtaining this sutra and practicing this samādhi accordingly. "Divine *sudhā*" (*tiān sūtuó*) serves as a metaphor for the supreme flavor of the Dharma within this sutra.
"Instantly eliminating feverish affliction" (*dùn chú rè nǎo*) serves as a metaphor for instantly eliminating birth-and-death; it clearly indicates that this is sudden [enlightenment].
