This teaches the Mahāyāna. That "body and mind are serene" is a metaphor for experiencing the bliss of the Dharma within meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
△ Sixth, the fruition of the qualities of concentration:
Having entered this concentration, one distances oneself from the obstacles of afflictions and gives rise to the sprout of unsurpassed Bodhi, swiftly ascending to the stage of a Bodhisattva.
Regarding the ten stages of merit (*guṇa-bhūmi*):

the first phrase refers to abiding in *samādhi*, which is the accomplishment of the power of meditative concentration. As for the "obstructions of affliction" (*kleśāvaraṇa*), they do not exceed the two types—those of affliction and those of the cognizable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because these are extinguished through concentration, it is said that one is "far removed" from them. The phrase "giving rise to" below refers to the initial arising of bodhi.
This is their characteristic; hence it is called the "Sprout. "Swiftly ascending" refers below to the virtue of attaining definitive, sudden realization.
Since one has already ascended to the Ten Stages (bhūmis), one will inevitably seek to attain Buddhahood. The *Awakening of Faith* states:

"Bodhisattvas of the Ten Stages manifest the highest and most vast body in the Heaven of Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha) and ultimately achieve Buddhahood. Now, having ascended to the Ten Stages, it is further said that these are "merits" (*guṇa*). This means:
For a Bodhisattva of the Ten Grounds, through the path of uninterrupted realization (*ānantarya-mārga*), they take spontaneous correspondence as their practice;

when the ignorance of the arising-phase (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa-avidyā*) is exhausted in a single thought-moment, they immediately enter wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*) and attain Buddhahood—this is called "Virtue.
Thus concludes the major section above on the Bhagavat’s manifestation to the assembly. △ Third, the benefits obtained upon hearing this chapter.
At that time, within the assembly, immeasurable humans and devas, having heard this profound mother of all bodhisattvas,
the inconceivable great dhāraṇī, ninety-eight thousand bodhisattvas and others realized the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi),
and immeasurable sentient beings resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
"Immeasurable humans and devas" is the general heading. "Hear" refers to the sutra they hear, as well as the dharanis and mantras.
"Ninety thousand," etc., distinguishes their merits. "Realize the Stage of Joy" refers to the first bhumi.
"Immeasurable," etc., refers to the initial generation of the great mind (bodhicitta). Since it is called "Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi," it surpasses the two vehicles by multiples. △ Seven.
II. Ultimate Attainment of Buddhahood. Chapter Title:

Chapter Twelve, "Attaining Buddhahood," which extensively explains the seals, mantras, and aids for contemplation that lead to the ultimate attainment of Buddhahood; thus it is titled "Attaining Buddhahood. II. The Scriptural Text.
8. First, the narrative introduction by the sūtra compiler:

At that time, the Bhagavat was well-established in the pure *dharmadhātu*, which is equal throughout the three periods of time, without beginning or end, immovable and serene, eternally uninterrupted and inexhaustible. The radiance of his great wisdom universally illumines the worlds with skillful means.
Then, manifesting supernatural powers, he transformed the lands of the ten directions so that there was nowhere they did not pervade.
This Bhagavat addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, saying:
This passage by the sūtra’s compiler describes the Buddha’s three bodies manifesting in their perfection, which is the virtue of responding to sentient beings.

The six lines beginning with "capable of skillfully" describe the nature and land of the Buddha’s Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Because the body and the land are merged in an inconceivable manner, it is said that he is "capable of skillfully."
That which is able to abide is the body; that which is abided in is the land. Since both the subject (the abider) and the object (the abode) are quiescent, it is called "abiding in peace.

As for the "Dharmadhātu," it is the land of the single true nature. "Dharma" refers to the Dharma-nature; "dhātu" is the land. Furthermore, although it is called "dhātu," it is not a realm in the conventional sense.

"Purity" refers to the characteristic attributes of the nature-land (*dharmatā-kṣetra*). It is called "clear" (*qing*) because its essence is limpid and tranquil; it is called "pure" (*jing*) because it is free from even the slightest speck of dust.

Regarding "equality throughout the three periods of time," this is stated in terms of the vertical dimension (*ūrdhva*) to indicate abiding. The phrase "without beginning and without end" below explains the meaning:
it signifies that the Dharmakāya Tathāgata is fundamentally without birth or extinction, and therefore has neither beginning nor end, persisting through all time.

There is nothing that can be transmigrated; therefore, it is called "immovable. It is eternally constant and independent; therefore, it is called "serene stillness. It is forever free from the two kinds of death;
therefore, it is called "ever-constant, without cessation or exhaustion. This describes the Buddha’s Dharma-body: its essence does not migrate or move;
body and land are in profound harmony, existing at all times and pervading all places. The light of great wisdom shines universally upon the world.
"Realm" (*dhātu*) refers to the description of the Buddha’s reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*). This means that the Reward Body Tathāgata takes wisdom as its essence:

internally, he illuminates the true *dharmadhātu* with the light of wisdom; externally, he illuminates those with great capacities through the light of his physical form. Such is his skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

"Manifesting supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) and so forth" describes the Buddha’s response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and transformation-body (*upapattikāya*). Because he responds to things according to the capacities of beings, it is called "skillful means" (*upāyakauśalya*).

Because he shares the same category as the ten realms of existence, it is called "manifesting supernatural powers. Like the moon reflected in water, his divided bodies respond inevitably to those who perceive them;
thus, it is said that he transforms the lands of the ten directions, pervading everywhere without exception. The above has described the three bodies of the Buddha. Response.
The discussion of the objects has concluded. Hereafter, [the text] addresses Mañjuśrī. Second, the enumeration of the three secrets:
After the yoga practitioner has visualized the moon disc, they should visualize the three kinds of great secret dharmas. What are these three?
First is the secret of mind; second is the secret of speech; third is the secret of body.
Yoga means "correspondence," referring to the mutual correspondence of the three—mudrās, mantras, and visualization. Therefore, it is called yoga.
"Practitioner" refers to the person who cultivates the visualization. Regarding the visualization of the lunar disc, as stated in the preceding text: "The moon is the mind."

The mind is itself the moon. "Has already" refers to the accomplishment of visualization. "One should visualize below" further instructs on the secret methods of correspondence to assist [the practice].
△ Third, the detailed classification of each [aspect] has eight parts; first, the secret of the mind.

What is called the secret dharma of the mind? The practitioner of yoga contemplates within the full moon the emergence of a five-pronged golden vajra, its radiance brilliant like molten gold, emitting countless great white rays of light.
Observing in this manner is called the "secret of the mind. The full moon symbolizes the mind, which is principle (*li*);
the five prongs symbolize the five sense objects, which are phenomena (*shi*). This thus represents the contemplation of how phenomena are established based upon principle.

(The term *guǒ* [prong] refers to a branch or component; for example, one speaks of "how many prongs" in the case of a golden vessel. That they are all golden in color—gold being yellow—signifies that they are all of the same nature as the mind.
It represents the Middle Way: since phenomena are established based on principle, one does not cling to principle;
yet, as all phenomena are entirely principle, one does not cling to phenomena—this is the contemplation of the Middle Way. "Vajra" signifies firmness and sharpness; "radiance" signifies *prajñā*.
The excellence of its brilliantly manifest light is the five-pronged [vajra] with each prong distinct. "Just like molten gold" refers to their being unified into a single essence.
The emission of countless great white radiances signifies that the pure dharmas transcend all numerical limits.
This is because ordinary beings grasp at the five sensory objects, creating various karmas; according to their karma they receive retribution, remaining forever immersed in the cycle of suffering.
It is always defiled and turbid; therefore, the Buddha instructed practitioners to cultivate contemplation by visualizing a lunar disc emerging from the chest.
Because the mind is signless (*animitta*), the moon is used to represent it. Its emergence below represents the fusion of the five sensory objects;
this is the Dharma-body, whose essence is as firm as a diamond (*vajra*). The radiance below represents the wisdom of that very essence, which is able to shatter all delusions.

The sharpness of the vajra’s function is such that the five-pronged radiance shines brilliantly; this symbolizes the complete realization of principle within phenomena (*dharma*), wherein the one is many.
"Like molten gold" symbolizes that every phenomenon is fundamentally principle, wherein the many are one.
Its downward extension symbolizes the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, all arising from the pure dharmas that are universally pervasive, perfectly interfused, and unrestricted.
This is also regarding the number. From "By this" onwards, the mental visualization is concluded.
△ Second, the secret of speech. What is called the secret of language? Oṃ (1) dharmatā-vilāsa (2).
This dhāraṇī possesses great majestic power; it is the mantra for all bodhisattvas to attain buddhahood. For this reason, it is called the "Secret of Speech.

"Secret" (mi) means that which is not transmitted by the mouth; "mysterious" (mi) means that which cannot be fathomed by the mind. Nevertheless, although it is not transmitted by the mouth, it nevertheless manifests.
To speak of it now is to speak with non-speech; speech itself is non-speech. To borrow speech to manifest the mantra is what is called a "true word" (mantra).
From "this dharma" (*tada*) onwards, it explains the majestic power of the mantra. Because it can subdue demons and restrain external forces, it is said to "possess great majesty and power.
Because the Buddhas of the three periods of time rely on the assistance of the mantra to achieve enlightenment, it is called the "True Word for Attaining Buddhahood. This is so.
Therefore, below is the conclusion of the names. △ The Secret of the Body.

What is called the secret dharma of the body? Within the *maṇḍala*, with the body upright and mindfulness correct, one forms with the hands the foremost seal for guiding one toward unsurpassed *bodhi*.
This is placed within the moon-disc at the heart, upon the breast.

The hands belong to the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*). By forming mudrās, one is able to protect against external conditions so they do not enter, and one is able to draw forth true wisdom to realize the principle;
all of this is inconceivable, and is therefore called "secret" (*guhya*). As for the "place of practice" (*maṇḍala*):

whether in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*) or beneath trees, with the body upright and right mindfulness, this is the mark of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Forming mudrās with the hands below clearly elucidates the secret of the body. Supreme Bodhi...
"Ti. This is the foremost seal of the Buddha-fruit; it is the secret dharma. "Placed below" indicates the location where the seal is to be positioned.
"Within the lunar disc of the mind" signifies that the Dharma is not separate from the mind. △ Fourth, the characteristics of the teachings and the seals.
"Good son, I shall now explain its seal-form (*mudrā*) for you. First, place both thumbs of the left and right hands respectively inside the palms of each hand.
Then, with the index, middle, and fourth fingers of each hand, firmly grasp the thumbs to form the hand."
The fist is the firm and stable Vajra Fist Mudrā. Next, without changing the fists, extend the left index finger, holding it straight up toward the void. Place the right fist at the heart.
With the little finger of the right fist, firmly grasp the first joint of the left index finger. Next, with the tip of the right fist...
"Pointing with the finger-head" refers to the first joint of the thumb of the right fist; it is likewise placed before the heart.
The scriptural text is very clear, so there is no need for further explanation; I have merely provided the illustration. △ Fifth, the names of the mudrās are set forth.
This is called the Supreme Wisdom Seal that Guides One to Unsurpassed Bodhi; it is also called the Great Radiance Seal that Can Extinguish the Darkness of Ignorance.
By forming this seal, through its power of empowerment, the Buddhas of the ten directions will touch the crown of the practitioner’s head.
He has received the supreme and definitive prediction of great bodhi. This is the Great Vairocana Tathāgata, the immeasurable mass of merit, the seal of great wondrous wisdom, and unsurpassed bodhi.
It is inherently present within every person, yet through delusion and ignorance they turn their backs upon it and are unable to return. Now that...

Having resolved to attain realization through cultivation, one fears there may be obstacles; therefore, one relies on this seal to assist them, ensuring the mind does not regress and proceeds directly toward Bodhi.
This serves as a guide, providing the benefit of being directed toward the Path; hence it is called the "First Seal of Wisdom.
The phrase "is able to extinguish" and below further clarifies the benefit of destroying delusions. This is because once the mind is already directed toward the Path...
The light of wisdom becomes increasingly bright, and all ignorance and the darkness of delusion naturally vanish; therefore, it is called the "Seal of Great Radiance.

The phrase "to bind below" refers to empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is equivalent to the recitation of mantras. The power (*bala*) refers to the crushing and manifesting of the divine efficacy of these mantras.
Therefore, the mudrā can induce contemplation, and the mantra can assist the mudrā. When the three karmas are thus rectified, they act as the cause that evokes a response;

the Buddhas of the ten directions are the objects of that response. It is like the moon appearing when the water is clear; as the path of resonance and response intersects, the Buddhas touch one's head and bestow a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Since this is called a "superior and definitive prediction," it is known that the attainment of Buddhahood is certain. This concludes the section on "The Great [Bodhisattvas]."
The summary of the Wisdom Seal (*jñānamudrā*). In Sanskrit, it is *Vairocana*, which here means "pervading all places"; this is the name of the Dharmakāya Tathāgata.

From "Immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) onwards, it reveals that the Wisdom Seal accords with the immeasurability of the Dharmakāya. Since merit (*puṇya*) is likewise immeasurable, it is called a "mass of merit" (*puṇyarāśi*).
Regarding the "Great and Sublime Wisdom Seal": the seal itself is the mass of merit, because it accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
It is called "Great" because it is immeasurable; it is called "Wondrous" because it transcends conceptual thought; it is called the "Seal of Wisdom" because it leads to the realization of Bodhi.
△ Sixth, the characteristics of the teaching and contemplation.
At that time, once the practitioner has bound this mudrā, they should immediately perform this visualization: all sentient beings together bind this mudrā and maintain the recitation of the mantra.
Throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there shall be no three evil realms or the bitter fruits of the eight difficulties; all shall together experience the foremost [state].
The bliss of the pure Dharma. Upon my head now is a great jewel crown; within that celestial crown, the five Tathāgatas sit in the full lotus posture.
I am the Tathāgata Vairocana, fully endowed with the thirty-two marks of perfection.
Possessing the eighty secondary marks, he emits great radiance that illuminates the worlds of the ten directions, benefiting and bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings.
To observe in this manner is called entering the most supreme samādhi of the Tathāgata Vairocana.
"Below all [is] this: the Tathāgata’s teaching to give rise to the mind that regards things as public property. One cannot bear to achieve [enlightenment] for oneself alone;

rather, one desires that the sentient beings of the entire *dharmadhātu* achieve it together. For the practitioner of visualization, while remaining unmoved by all conditions, they should direct their thoughts with right mindfulness:
'Since I have formed this mudrā, I visualize that all sentient beings together form this mudrā. Furthermore, it is said that one should recite the mantra."
At that time, one should also visualize all sentient beings as each holding the mantra; if one’s own visualization is perfected, then all are perfected.
Regarding "the ten directions" and below: one further visualizes the extraction of suffering and the bestowal of happiness.
"The ten directions" means pervading all places, and must necessarily include the exhaustion of all times. As for "there being no three evil realms," it means the hells are transformed into heavens.

The hall [of the Buddha] causes ghosts and animals to immediately attain the wholesome paths; those in the eight difficulties all achieve liberation, and the fruits of suffering are transformed into fruits of bliss.

Because these [sufferings] originally do not exist within the nature [of reality], sentient beings delusively undergo them; now, by causing them to turn back from delusion and return to the truth, all sufferings are suddenly extinguished.
The above describes the time when one is personally freed from suffering; at that moment, all [others] are likewise freed. This is the Great Compassion that uproots suffering.
This is the seal-visualization of [the Buddhas] receiving [joy] together. Regarding "receiving together" and below: it means that when one receives joy oneself, all beings likewise receive joy;
because this is a joy that accords with the nature (*dharmatā*), it is called "Dharma-joy. Because one rejoices without attachment, it is called "pure.

Because it is identical to what the Buddha has realized, it is called "supreme. Furthermore, this reveals the seal-visualization of great compassion bestowing joy. Regarding "I now" and below: visualize oneself...
The physical form is identical to the form of Vairocana, just like the Vairocana Buddha currently being fashioned, who wears a crown of five Buddhas upon his head.

As for "I am below," one observes one's own body: the entire body is Vairocana himself. His marks and signs, as well as his radiance, which illuminate the realms and benefit sentient beings, are all the functioning of my Dharma.
This, moreover, is the contemplation of the seal that the entire body is the Buddha. Thus it is.

The lower section explains the name (*Vairocana*). This refers to the Dharmakāya Buddha; the thirty-two marks and so forth refer to the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha; and the light illuminating the realms refers to the Saṃbhogakāya Buddha. Now, when the practitioner attains realization for themselves, it may be said that they are "saintly within the ordinary" and "three within the one.

To say that the three are the one is to realize that at the moment of one's own perfection, all sentient beings are likewise perfected. This may be called the non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*śaśva-arvārthāpratihata*), where the one and the many are mutually identical—a great, inconceivable realm. Therefore, it is called the "Supreme Samādhi."
△ 7. Analogical Contemplation by Borrowing a Simile.
For example, suppose there is a person who awakens to the subtle contemplation-gate of Kālu and performs this contemplation for themselves:
"My body is that of the King of the Garuḍas; my mind and speech are likewise so. By the power of this contemplation, one can neutralize poisons and medicines. (1)
All evil poisons will be unable to cause harm.

For example, suppose there is a person practicing this visualization. Although the term *kaluṣa* (迦盧華) is not clearly defined in the Sanskrit, since it states, "My body is itself the King of the Garuḍas," it follows by principle that the visualization should be understood in the same way. That is to say, when a person performs this visualization:
"One's entire body is the King of the Garuḍas. From this point downward, it clarifies the benefits of the perfected visualization.
Because the Garuḍa can dispel all poisons, one cannot be harmed by any evil toxins. △ This is the eighth: the benefit of the visualization combined with the dharmas.

The practitioner who is still an ordinary person is likewise so. Adopting the posture of subjugation, with the body unmoving and the hands forming the wisdom-mudrā, they silently recite the mantra while the mind enters this contemplation;
thus they can extinguish the three poisons, eliminate karmic obstructions, and increase merit and wisdom.
May all mundane and supramundane aspirations be swiftly fulfilled. May the eighty-four thousand afflictive obscurations no longer manifest.
May the heavy cognitive obscurations, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, gradually be extinguished.
May the stainless great wisdom—the Diamond Prajñāpāramitā capable of severing all—manifest in its full perfection. May one swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The practitioner is like the person in the combined analogy; it is also thus. To summarize the preceding analogies:

regarding the term "subduing," because the three karmas are in accord and Māra cannot enter, this name is established. As for the four lines beginning with "the body does not sink": [they refer to the practitioner who, by means of the three karmas, remains steadfast].

This corresponds to the previously mentioned "Awakening to the Kāra-Contemplation Gate. "Able to extinguish the three poisons," etc., corresponds to the previously mentioned "able to neutralize poisons and medicines.

The three phrases beginning with "increasing merit and wisdom," as well as the section following "immaculate great wisdom," correspond to the previously mentioned "my body is that of the King of the Garuḍas;
my mind, intentions, and speech are likewise so. Thus, afflictions do not manifest.
Regarding the extinction of the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*): combined with the aforementioned [extinction of] all evil poisons, they can no longer cause harm.
This is because it can extinguish the obscuration of afflictions, increase merit and wisdom, and bring forth the great wisdom that severs [delusion] as the Prajñāpāramitā manifests.
Since it is said that one swiftly attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, this refers to the ultimate attainment of Buddhahood; all of this is due to the power of the seal of the mantra.
It is accomplished; it is truly a vast, efficacious, and inconceivable Dharma-gate.
△ Fourth, Mañjuśrī’s Praise:
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "How rare, World-Honored One! How rare, Sugata! As...
He has appeared in the world. Rarer than the udumbara flower, even if he were to appear in the world, it would be difficult for him to preach this Dharma.

Such is the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma of the three secrets of the mind-ground, which truly brings benefit and happiness to all sentient beings and serves as the true, correct path for entering the stage of the Tathāgata and the stage of the Bodhisattva.
If there are sentient beings who do not spare their own bodies or lives to practice this Dharma, they will swiftly [attain realization].
"Attaining Bodhi.
"Sugata" is the title for the Buddha, meaning "One who has gone well to Bodhi. Although this praises the Buddha with words of rarity, it is in fact a praise of this Dharma;
for by means of the visualization and the seal-mantra, evil is destroyed and wisdom increased, whereby one may swiftly accomplish Bodhi. May [it be so].
This refers to those who have skillfully proceeded toward Bodhi. It is truly difficult for a Tathāgata to appear in the world;

it is even more difficult to teach these dharmas of mind, such as the seals of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-mudrā*). Why? Because they are taught only at such a time and place, and all are likened to the rarity of encountering the *udumbara* flower.
Therefore, it says, "Even if," and so forth. Below this, the three kinds of secrets are praised, meaning that by attaining these, one becomes a Buddha. Thus.
It is called "unsurpassed" because its merit is never in vain; thus it is called "real. It is the thorough path to attaining Buddhahood;
therefore, it is called the "right way. The passage beginning with "If there is... clarifies that although this Dharma-gate is supreme, one must encounter the right person.

If one truly meets a righteous person who encounters this Dharma-gate, they will feel profound joy and庆幸 (*qìngxìng*, lit. "joyful fortune"), thinking: "The Way can now be realized; I am no longer conscious of my own body. Thus it is said.
Regarding the phrase "not sparing one's body or life," etc.: suppose one harbors even a slight concern for personal gain or loss and thus cherishes one’s body and life;
then one will inevitably fail to persevere from beginning to end, and success will likely not be swift. Is it that the Dharma-gate is ineffective?
It is rather that one does not practice with sufficient vigor. May students take this to heart. △ Five: The Sublime Contemplation of Armor. Part One: A Brief Indication of Name and Meaning.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to practice the three kinds of secrets—the wondrous gateway to attaining Buddhahood—and desire to swiftly obtain the merit-body of a Tathāgata, they should don the thirty-two kinds of great adamantine armor of a bodhisattva and cultivate this sublime contemplation; they will certainly realize the purity of a Tathāgata."
The Pure Dharmakāya.
"Desiring to attain" means "desiring" as in "necessity. This refers to the essential point of raising the mind to engage in cultivation and study.
Since these are all the mental dharmas of the Buddhas, they are called "secret. Because one attains Buddhahood by practicing this, it is called a "Dharma-gate. This is merely...

"Raising up" refers to the contemplation that realizes [enlightenment]. "Early attainment" below refers to the Buddha-fruit that is realized. "When donning" below clarifies the superior practices that assist the Way.
This means that one who wishes to cultivate subtle contemplation to achieve Buddhahood first gives rise to the four great vows and the six perfections as great aspirations.
Through these aspirations, one protects and sustains their practice, just as armor protects the body. However, armor can...
It protects the body and can also defeat enemies; it is an analogy for the four vows and the six perfections. It can benefit oneself and also benefit others.
Because the armor has been completed, when one practices contemplation, delusions cannot obstruct and demons cannot invade;
therefore, it is said that "one will certainly realize [enlightenment]," and so forth. II. Investigation of the Name and Extensive Explanation.
What are called the thirty-two great armors? First, the great armor of not wearying of suffering within birth and death for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas.
Second, the great armor of vowing to deliver immeasurable sentient beings, never abandoning them even down to the smallest ants.

These two take great compassion and universal salvation as their armor. Although there are many types of armor, they do not go beyond the Bodhisattva’s four great vows and the dharma of the six perfections.
That is to say, since one desires to attain the dharma and achieve the Way, one must first give rise to the great vows to deliver sentient beings;
this is simply the natural principle within the Bodhisattva practice. Regarding the phrase "in the immeasurable" and below: although the attainment of the Way—though...
Regarding "desiring swift realization": when one does not grow weary of saving sentient beings, the elder attains the power of unimpeded mastery over prolonging or abbreviating time.

Regarding "not being weary of undergoing suffering in birth and death": this is because one is able to realize that birth and death do not obstruct nirvana. "Vowing to save those below," and so forth.
This clearly elucidates the universal salvation of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). However, the deliverance of sentient beings does not pertain solely to the single category of the human realm;
even down to the most minute creatures such as ants, their Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is identical. Unable to bear abandoning them, he thus says, "I vow to deliver them.
These two [vows] correspond to the vow: "To deliver boundless sentient beings. The reason one must borrow armor as a metaphor is that armor protects the body.
Not being intimidated by powerful adversaries is a metaphor for the mind protected by great vows; not fearing difficult tasks is the inclusion of the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).
Third, awakening sentient beings from the long dream of birth and death and establishing them in the three kinds of secret great armor. Fourth, [the fourth point].
To protect the Buddha-dharma at all times, like an echo responding to a sound, one dons the great armor of protecting the Dharma.

Third, one dons the armor of compassion and wisdom; fourth, one dons the armor of protecting the Dharma because sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance and entangled in birth and death, undergoing suffering within what is non-existent, as if in a long dream, unaware that it is fundamentally nothing.
Therefore, when Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma, they exhort and awaken others, further establishing them in the three kinds of secret dharmas.
Possessing such compassion and wisdom, they do not fear toil or difficulty; thus, like great armor, they vow to deliver and gather in all sentient beings.

(The three secrets are: the secret of mind, which is meditative contemplation; the secret of speech, which is the recitation of mantras; and the secret of body, which is the binding of mudrās. Fourth, "protecting the Dharma like an echo" refers to those who...
"Response is immediate. "Extensive protection is like armor. One should know that there are two kinds of protection. The first is as follows:

in places where the Dharma is being propagated, if heavenly Māras or non-Buddhists cause disturbance and destroy the Dharma, as soon as the Bodhisattva raises their mind to respond, they subdue all Māras and restrain all non-Buddhists;
this constitutes protection. The second is to observe the capacities [of sentient beings].

The transmission of the Dharma: generally, it is not bestowed upon those who are not suitable vessels, and this is also for the sake of protecting the Dharma. These two aspects are both subsumed within the two paramitas of meditation and wisdom, as well as within the vow to study all dharma-gates.
For responding to others according to their capacities through adaptive transformation, one cannot do so without study.
Fifth, the adamantine great armor that eternally extinguishes all afflictions capable of giving rise to the two views of existence and non-existence.

This takes meditative concentration and wisdom as its armor. "Capable of giving rise to" refers to the seeds of the various delusions, because they can give rise to active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
The "two views of existence and non-existence" are the two views of annihilationism and eternalism. "All afflictions" encompasses those of all five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*).
Regarding the various afflictions, both coarse and subtle: the initial statement of "perpetual severance" represents the great resolve of the practitioner.

It is truly like donning armor to defeat a powerful enemy; thus, it is called the "Vajra Great Armor," which signifies the vow to sever the afflictions and is subsumed within the three perfections of diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

Sixth, when those who come to seek them approach, one is able to relinquish one’s head, eyes, marrow, and brain, as well as one’s wife, children, and precious treasures; this is the great armor of renunciation.
Seventh, regarding all objects of pleasure enjoyed within one’s home, one never feels greedy attachment and is able to give them away; this is the great armor of generosity.

This takes the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) as its armor. As for the perfection of giving’s lack of惜惜 (reluctance) toward even marrow and brain, it is intended to sever the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*).
To be able to give without craving any objects of pleasure is likewise a difficult task; it is the armor that shatters stinginess and assists valor.
These two [aspects] are also subsumed under the vow to sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
Eighth, one is able to uphold the Bodhisattva’s three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) and does not abandon the great armor of *dhūta* practices;

this constitutes the armor of ethical conduct. The three clusters are: the precept of restraining misconduct (*saṃvara-śīla*), the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattvārtha-kriyā-śīla*).
With body and mind free from transgression, as clear and bright as ice and frost, they are called "pure precepts. This is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).

Furthermore, *dhūta* means "to shake off," which signifies the spirit of diligence (*vīrya*). It refers to shaking off one's mental energy so as to be able to destroy the dust of worldly toil (*kleśa*);

thus, it is a specific designation for destroying delusions. It also encompasses saving sentient beings and benefiting all things; this vow is subsumed under the vow to sever afflictions and the vow to study the Buddha-dharma.
Ninth: Donning the robe of patience. When encountering adverse conditions such as being reviled, abused, or beaten, one does not retaliate;
this constitutes the great armor. Taking the ability to endure as one's armor—gentle, flexible, and patient—is capable of resisting violence and is truly a suit of mail.
For it is precisely because one cannot endure that anger arises, manifesting various ugly forms. Patience can obstruct these uglinesses, just as clothing covers the body.
This is the most difficult task for a practitioner; therefore, it is likened to armor. This is the perfection of patience (kṣāntipāramitā).
Furthermore, it includes the vow to sever all afflictions;
tenth, to teach and transform all pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas, causing them to turn their minds toward the One Vehicle—the great armor.
This is taking wisdom as one's armor. Those Śrāvakas of fixed nature are indeed difficult to transform.
To cause them to advance toward the One Vehicle requires nothing other than skillful means and *prajñā*; this is precisely the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

"Turning the mind" refers to shifting from the provisional to the real, turning back from the Lesser Vehicle to the Great Vehicle; it is the act of generating the bodhicitta, which is comprised within the vow to deliver all sentient beings.
Eleventh: For example, it is like a great wind that does not cease day or night. This "great armor of diligence" takes diligence itself as its armor.
However, the metaphor of the wind is questionable; there has never been a great wind in antiquity or the present that did not eventually cease.
Is it not rather the case that it refers to the Vairambha wind, which arises and does not cease until destruction? If this were so, then the "great wind" would be the Vairambha wind.

Wind. The translator’s explanation is insufficiently detailed. It serves as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva benefiting sentient beings and delivering them from rebirth, being diligent and tireless like the wind that never ceases.
It can destroy the afflictions and the cycle of birth and death of sentient beings, just as the wind destroys the world.
It is also included within the vow to deliver all sentient beings.
Twelfth: The body and mind are tranquil; the mouth commits no transgression. One practices the great armor of liberation-samādhi; this takes meditative concentration as its armor.
The body is not agitated and is thus tranquil; the mind is not distracted and is thus tranquil;
the mouth commits no transgression and is thus tranquil. When the three karmas are all tranquil, one is unstained by even the slightest speck of dust. This is precisely...
It is the three liberations within the course of practice. Samādhi is meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). It is also comprised within the vow to sever the afflictions. Thirteenth:
regarding birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, there are no dualistic views; to benefit sentient beings with equanimity is the great armor.
This takes meditative concentration and wisdom as its armor. Birth-and-death and nirvana originally possess no dual characteristics; their essence is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).
Because ordinary beings are deluded, they falsely perceive birth-and-death, and they claim that sages sever afflictions and loftily realize nirvana.

They give rise to false discrimination; hence they are called "two views. Now, the Buddha instructs practitioners to perform contemplative observation so that they may realize that all phenomena are mind-only and that birth-and-death is fundamentally empty, which is itself nirvana. When these two views are suddenly eliminated, one can achieve the Way;
this constitutes self-benefit. Furthermore, by benefiting sentient beings, one can also benefit others through the true mind.
It is equal and common to all sentient beings. Since I have been able to realize it, how could they not do so?

Therefore, with a mind toward the public good, whether acting in accordance with their nature or transforming them through adversity, I further cause others to realize it as well; this is what constitutes abundant benefit for sentient beings.
All of these are difficult practices that can be performed, like donning armor without fear of the enemy; thus, this metaphor is employed. Sentient beings...
The vow to deliver [beings], the vow to achieve the Buddha-way, and their inclusion within the two perfections of dhyāna and prajñā.
Fourteenth: Unconditioned great compassion, which benefits all classes of beings without ever becoming weary or abandoning them; it is the great armor for bestowing happiness.
This is taking compassion as one's armor. One universally observes that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature; one does not wait for the presence of conditions before delivering them.

Taking the bonds of affectionate pity as "having conditions" and ordinary strangers on the road as "lacking conditions," if one can still bestow happiness even upon those lacking conditions, how much more so for those who do have conditions?
Therefore, this is called "great compassion for those without conditions. [It applies to] the multitudes of living beings.
This is not merely for the sake of ordinary beings; its meaning extends to those of the Hīnayāna as well. To never grow weary or abandon them is the tirelessness of compassion.
To "bestow happiness" means simply to grant the Buddha-dharma so that their minds may open and they may perceive the Path, thereby enjoying the bliss of the Dharma.

Alternatively, as in the case of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, bestowing the prediction of Buddhahood (buddhatva-vyākaraṇa) also constitutes bestowing happiness. This is the foremost form of Great Compassion that bestows happiness.
And the vow to deliver all sentient beings; the perfection of giving through the gift of Dharma; and its inclusion within the perfection of vigor.
Fifteenth: unimpeded great compassion that rescues and gathers all beings without limit, acting as the great armor for uprooting suffering.
This takes great compassion as its armor. When there is a stimulus, there is a response, never missing the proper time; hence it is called "unimpeded great compassion.

Regarding "rescuing and gathering all beings": "rescue" means to extract them from suffering, such as when Avalokiteśvara rescues those in the eight difficulties and frees them from the three poisons.
"Gathering" means to receive and sustain them, as when Avalokiteśvara responded to the two requests and accepted the jeweled necklace.

Because its location is not fixed and it has no temporal limit, it is immeasurable. This constitutes the armor of great compassion for uprooting suffering, as well as the vow to deliver sentient beings, and is subsumed within the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
Sixteenth: toward all sentient beings, one harbors no enmity or resentment, but constantly acts for their benefit.
This "great armor of great joy" takes great joy as its armor. One necessarily resolves past grudges, does not harbor resentments toward present enemies, and receives others with joyful acceptance.

Keeping this constantly in mind, it is said that one "constantly performs benefit" and also vows to "deliver sentient beings. This is subsumed under the two perfections of wisdom (*prajñā*) and diligence (*vīrya*).
Seventeenth: although practicing asceticism, one does not dread toil and labor, remaining forever without regression; this is the great armor of great relinquishment (*mahopekṣā*).
This takes great equanimity (*upekṣā*) as its armor. "Dà" (憚) means fear; "qú" (劬) means diligence.

Because of compassion, sympathetic joy, and delight, although one exerts oneself diligently to deliver sentient beings, one does not dread the weariness of the task, nor is one aware of having a body, nor is one aware of suffering.
Not knowing the distinction between self and other, and not knowing the discrimination of kin and stranger, one regards all with impartiality;
this is great equanimity (*upekṣā*). This dharma-gate is the vow to study, the vow to deliver sentient beings, and it is subsumed within the perfection of vigor (*vīryapāramitā*).
Eighteenth: When sentient beings suffering from afflictions come to the Bodhisattva, he does not weary of taking upon himself their suffering;

this is likewise the armor of great compassion that rescues them from suffering. While others cannot take upon themselves the sufferings of old age, illness, and death, and while shackles, fetters, and stocks do not bind the innocent—how could one possibly take their place? Thus we know that through the Bodhisattva’s great compassion, he may dispatch emanations.
One may transform oneself into a substitute, or employ supernormal powers to transform into a substitute, or manifest one's own body in the likeness of that person to replace them in the afterlife.
Even while undergoing manifold sufferings, one must never feel weary or disenchanted.
Since all phenomena are realized to be nothing but one’s own mind, one does not perceive suffering; how could one then become weary? Thus one vows.
It delivers sentient beings. Furthermore, it is subsumed under the two perfections of diligence and meditative concentration.
Nineteenth: one is able to see [it] as clearly as an āmalaka fruit held in the palm of one's hand; such is the great armor of liberation.
This takes the divine eye as one's armor. Observing the fruit within the palm illustrates the ease of direct perception (*pramāṇa*).

Being able to perceive both the distant and the near, just like a fruit in the palm, without any internal obstruction, is therefore called "liberation" (*vimukti*); it is the supernormal power of the divine eye.
Since such vision is unobstructed, saving sentient beings will surely not be difficult. This, too, is a dharma-gate that I vow to study; this is my vow to deliver all sentient beings.
And it is encompassed by the perfection of meditation.
The twentieth [point] is: seeing the body of the five aggregates as being like a *caṇḍāla* that harms wholesome deeds, one dons the great armor of non-attachment;
this takes non-attachment as the armor. Since there are the five aggregates constituting a body, there will necessarily be the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) that creates karma.
This causes untainted wholesome deeds not to be accomplished; thus, it is likened to a *caṇḍāla*, serving as a metaphor for that which harms wholesome deeds.
Because the Bodhisattva’s dual attachments to self and dharmas are entirely empty, they are said to be "unattached. Being unattached, they attain the wondrous while following the worldly flow;

there is nothing that is not Buddha-work. This constitutes the vow to sever afflictions, as well as being subsumed within the two perfections of ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Twenty-first: To see the twelve *āyatanas* as an empty village, to constantly harbor fear, and to wear the great armor of weary detachment—this too has concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as its armor.
The six sense faculties and the six sense objects constitute the twelve bases (*āyatana*).

As for the term "entrance" (*āya*), it is because the faculty can illuminate the object, while the object can enter the faculty; the object can draw in the faculty, while the faculty likewise enters the object. There is...
This is the function of mutual entry. Since it is so for one faculty (*indriya*), it is so for every faculty; hence they are called the twelve bases (*āyatana*).
Regarding the statement that a village is empty, it means there is no person within it. Yet, a village is valued for having people; when there is no person within its gates, fear arises.
The Bodhisattva contemplates these faculties and their objects (*viṣaya*) as all being dependently originated and lacking intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); in their very essence...
Because they cannot be apprehended, one conceives fear and gives rise to revulsion, desiring necessarily to abandon them.
Yet, since there is not a single place within the entirety of the Dharma-realm that is not comprised of sense organs and objects, if one intends to abandon them, where could one go?

Thus, one knows that the Bodhisattva, through the wondrous contemplation of True Suchness (tathatā), realizes that the myriad dharmas of the sense organs and objects are solely mind—that there is no dharma outside of the mind. This itself is abandonment.
Furthermore, one vows to study the Dharma-gates, which are subsumed within the two perfections of meditative concentration and wisdom.
Regarding the twenty-second [vow]: viewing the eighteen realms as being like illusions and transformations, devoid of any reality, constitutes the great armor of great wisdom.

This, too, takes wisdom as its armor. Regarding the eighteen *dhātus*—namely, the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses—they are called "realms" (*dhātu*) because each possesses its own distinct category and limitations. These, too, are observed through non-conceptual wisdom;

one realizes they lack any substantial reality and are like illusions or transformations. Their appearance is false, yet at the very locus where appearance is false, the nature (*svabhāva*) is itself the truth.
Then, attachment to phenomena is suddenly emptied; one ceases to create various karmas, encounters no obstacles wherever one goes, and attains liberation in the very essence of reality.
This is also what is encompassed by the vow to study the Dharma-gates, as well as by meditative concentration and wisdom.
Twenty-third: Practicing all dharmas as identical to the *dharmadhātu*, one perceives no manifold characteristics. This is the realization of the true great armor;

it is also the taking of *prajñā* as armor. This differs from the preceding section. The former, based on the falsity of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), exclusively manifested the wisdom that destroys delusion;
this, however, integrates characteristics back into their nature (*dharmatā*), enabling one to realize that the myriad dharmas of the triple world are identical to true suchness (*tathatā*).

Because it is the dharma-realm, it is said that one does not perceive manifold characteristics; this is the great wisdom capable of realizing *tathatā* (suchness). (Once *tathatā* is realized, one is a Buddha.
This constitutes the vow to study all dharma-gates and the aspiration to accomplish the Buddha-way, as well as being subsumed within the two gates of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Twenty-fourth: To conceal the evils of others, not to harbor one’s own faults, and to cultivate weary detachment from the triple world—this is the great armor for transcending the world.
This takes weary detachment from the world as its armor. Being able to conceal evil, one will surely be able to promote goodness;

this is the virtue of a gentleman. Not harboring one's faults, one must certainly rely on repentance; this is the sincerity of mind and speech. Having become weary of the triple world, one will surely...

Seeking deliverance is the vessel for attaining the Way; it is also the vow to accomplish the Buddha-way and is subsumed within the Perfection of Wisdom. (Question: This sutra belongs to the Mahāyāna, and its capacity must therefore be that of great roots.

Since [the practitioner] already feels weary of and seeks to escape [suffering], how does this differ from the Two Vehicles? (Answer: Although ordinary beings on the broad ground may give rise to the Great Mind, if they do not feel weary of and seek to escape [samsara], how could they transcend the world? Furthermore, this is explained in terms of ordinary beings; as for Bodhisattvas at deep stages, they should be discussed separately.
Twenty-fifth: Like a great king of physicians who prescribes medicine according to the disease, the bodhisattva’s great armor consists of evolving the teaching as appropriate to the occasion;
this, too, takes wisdom as its armor. To prescribe medicine according to the disease means that when the medicine and the ailment meet, a single dose brings the illness to an end.

Because the hand reaches the patient and the disease is eliminated, he is called a "King of Physicians. This serves as a metaphor for the bodhisattva evolving the teaching as appropriate to the occasion.
Transformation. A single word that strikes the vital point brings sentient beings to deliverance; yet this cannot be achieved by those who are not bodhisattvas of deep rank.

It is not comparable to the beginners mentioned previously. Rather, it belongs to the stage where one vows to perfect the Buddha-way, vows to deliver all sentient beings, and is encompassed by the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
The twenty-sixth is this: seeing that the essence of those three vehicles is fundamentally no different, one ultimately turns the mind back to return to the single great armor;
this takes wisdom and eloquence as the armor. The three vehicles are namely the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.
The One Buddha Vehicle: although their grades and characteristics differ, their Buddha-nature is identical; thus it is said that their essence is fundamentally not distinct.

Nevertheless, the Three Vehicles are provisional while the One Vehicle is the reality. By means of unimpeded eloquence, the Bodhisattva brings them to realize the convergence of the three into the one, so that they may all enter the Buddha Vehicle without any distinction between the provisional and the real, causing them to turn their minds and return to the path of the Buddha.
One shall attain Buddhahood; furthermore, there is the vow to deliver sentient beings, as well as its inclusion within the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā).
Twenty-seventh: to continue the lineage of the Triple Gem so that it is never severed, and to turn the wondrous wheel of Dharma as a great armor for delivering beings.

This, moreover, takes wisdom and eloquence as its armor. Those who wish to perpetuate the Three Jewels and ensure that the lineage of the Buddha remains unbroken must act as the Buddha’s representative to propagate the transformation [of others], transmitting the Dharma and delivering sentient beings through teachings suited to their capacities;

thus, those who receive this transformation are vast in number, which is why it is called the "Wondrous Wheel of Dharma. To deliver others in this way, it cannot be accomplished without wisdom, eloquence, patience, and gentleness.
Although saving sentient beings constitutes the armor, it is in fact patience (*kṣānti*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) that constitute the armor.
This refers to the vows to accomplish the Buddha-way and to save all sentient beings, which are subsumed within these two perfections of patience and wisdom.
Twenty-eighth: The Buddha possesses great benevolence and virtue toward sentient beings. To repay this debt of gratitude to the Buddha, one dons the great armor of cultivating the Path.
Since it is said that one cultivates the Path, it cannot be accomplished without taking concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) as one's armor.

From the very beginning, the Buddha has manifested traces for the sake of sentient beings, establishing Dharma gates and vowing to deliver all beings so that they may together attain the Buddha-way; this constitutes the Buddha’s great benevolence.
Furthermore, although sentient beings might cast away their bodies and sacrifice their lives, they could not repay even a ten-thousandth part of [the Buddha’s] grace.
To speak of practicing the Way in order to repay the Buddha’s kindness means that by practicing the Way one will surely attain the Way; by attaining the Way one will surely deliver sentient beings.
Thus, by not contradicting the Buddha’s command and not failing one's own spiritual nature, benefiting both self and others, one finally repays the Buddha’s kindness.
I vow to study this dharma-gate and vow to accomplish the Buddha-way. It is subsumed under the three perfections of diligence, patience, and wisdom.
Twenty-ninth: contemplating that all dharmas are by nature empty and quiescent, neither arising nor ceasing—this is the stainless great armor.

This, too, takes wisdom as its armor. By means of non-conceptual wisdom, one contemplates all phenomena as entirely pure and transparently luminous, such that not a single phenomenon is found to accord with the mind;
hence it is said that their fundamental nature is empty and quiescent. The following two lines explain this meaning.
Because it is immovable and steadfast, it is neither born nor extinguished; because it is vast and free from even the slightest speck of dust, it is called "stainless.
Taking contemplative wisdom as its armor, one vows to accomplish the Buddha-way, encompassed by the two gates of concentration and wisdom.
The thirtieth is: awakening to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), attaining *dhāraṇī*, possessing the eloquence of joyful speech, and the great armor of non-obstruction.
This, too, takes wisdom and eloquence as its armor. By nature, things are fundamentally unarisen and likewise unceasing; to suddenly realize this is called "awakening.
To reach a silent, intuitive realization within the mind is called "patience" (*kṣānti*). *Dhāraṇī* is the seal of the Buddha-mind.
To attain this is to become a Buddha; it is what is meant by the realization of the Way through true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

Eloquence in joyful exposition refers to the use of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) to deliver sentient beings. Because one attains the real through the expedient, it is called "unimpeded. Thus, one protects sentient beings and realizes the Way.

Therefore, it is called the Great Armor (*mahā-kavaca*). This refers to the vow to accomplish the Buddha-way, the vow to deliver all sentient beings, and its inclusion within the two perfections of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Thirty-first: extensively transforming sentient beings, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, and causing them to realize the fruit of Buddhahood—this is the single-flavor Great Armor.

This constitutes the armor of the perfection of giving through the gift of Dharma. As for the previous section on awakening to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), this refers to the wisdom of self-benefit, by which one personally attains the fruit of Buddhahood.
Furthermore, extensively transforming sentient beings so that they sit beneath the Bodhi tree and realize the fruit of Buddhahood belongs entirely to the benefit of others.
"Of a single flavor" refers to the Dharma of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). Since it is capable of being extensive...
He transforms them so that they may realize the fruit of Buddhahood; there will certainly be no distinction between the three vehicles or the five natures. Therefore, it is called "one flavor.
This also constitutes the perfection of giving through the practice of dharma-giving, as well as the means of attracting beings by means of the path and their deliverance.
The thirty-second is as follows: A single moment of mind (*kṣaṇacitta*), conjoined with *prajñā*, awakens to the phenomena of the three periods of time;
there is no other great armor. This takes *prajñā* as its armor. "A moment" refers to the brevity of time. "*Prajñā*" refers to the wisdom of contemplative insight.
"A single moment of mind," and so forth, means that even if one generates the resolve [for awakening] for only a brief duration, it immediately becomes conjoined with *prajñā*.
If they correspond, then by means of this prajñā, one illuminates the myriad dharmas of the three periods of time as the single prajñā of one’s own mind;

that is to say, there are no dharmas outside the mind. Therefore, it is called "without remainder. This is the vow to accomplish the Buddha-way, and it is subsumed within the two paramitas of meditative concentration (samādhi) and wisdom (prajñā).
This is called the thirty-two kinds of adamantine great armor of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;
the summary may be understood thus. △ Third, the conclusion on the benefits and merit:
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, if there be good sons or good daughters who wear such adamantine [armor] upon their bodies...

Wearing this armor, you should diligently cultivate the three secrets; in this very life, endowed with great merit and wisdom, you will swiftly realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The first phrase is the Buddha calling [the disciple] by name. The two characters "bodhisattva" (*púsà*) appear to have been erroneously added by the translator;

when the Buddha addresses his disciples, he calls them only by their names and does not use "bodhisattva" as a title of honor. The passage beginning with "If there is... introduces the person capable of cultivation.
The passage beginning with "The body is clothed in... clarifies the requisites for practice. A Confucian classic states: "A craftsman who wishes to excel in his work..."
In any undertaking, one must first sharpen one's tools; this is likewise the case here.

Taking the adamantine armor as the sharp tool and cultivating the three secrets as the virtuous practice, the following section precisely reveals their efficacy. Now, since it is said to pertain to the "present life,"...
Thus, it does not require a long period of time. Since he is said to be endowed with great merit and wisdom, he becomes the Honored One of Two Feet who has perfected the path of awakening;

hence, it is called *bodhi*. Because it is the definitive meaning of the Middle Way, it is called "Right and Equal" (*samyak-saṃbuddha*). Because he is the peerless sovereign who has transcended the world, it is called "Unsurpassed.
Because the task of a single lifetime has been accomplished, it is called "Swift Realization. △ Sixth, Mañjuśrī’s expression of gratitude.
At that time, the Great Sage Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, together with the great assembly,
having heard the Buddha’s teaching on the three kinds of secret and wondrous Dharma of the mind-ground, as well as the thirty-two adamantine armors—
the points of training for all bodhisattvas— each removed priceless necklaces and precious robes to offer them to Vairocana Tathāgata.
They came, together with the Honored Ones of the ten directions, and praised the Buddha, saying: "Excellent, excellent, Bhagavān!

You have expounded the boundless practices and vows of bodhisattvas, which benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, causing them to cast off the bodies of ordinary persons and enter the stage of Buddhahood."
"Excellent! and the preceding phrases are all introductory remarks by the compiler (*jingjia*). "At that time" and below describe the person who offers the praise;
"having heard the Buddha" and below describe the Dharma that was heard; "each removed" and below describe the articles of offering.

That one must offer worship upon hearing the Dharma is an expression of gratitude toward the Dharma. That one must remove their necklaces (*vibhūṣaṇa*) when making offerings is to signify the value placed upon them.
Furthermore, as for offering robes: since one must be naked when divested of clothing, it symbolizes that through liberation, one attains the vision of the fundamental body (*dharmakāya*).
As for making offerings to Vairocana Buddha: it symbolizes that the cause of wisdom must ultimately reach the *dharmakāya*. As for [making offerings to] the Honored Ones of the ten directions:
it symbolizes that the path of all Buddhas is identical. As for praising the Buddha: since gratitude must necessarily be expressed through words, it serves as such a manifestation.
"Excellent! and below this are Mañjuśrī’s words of praise. "Expounding... and below this describe the Buddha’s intention.
"The boundless practices and vows of the bodhisattvas" refers to the great capacities of those for whom [the teaching] is intended, as well as the aspirations regarding the Great Path they practice.
Thus, practice (*caryā*) is the three secret and wondrous contemplations, while aspiration (*praṇidhāna*) is the adamantine armor.
Yet, without aspiration one cannot induce practice, and without practice one cannot fulfill aspiration. Because practice and aspiration guide one another, this constitutes true benefit.
It enables all ordinary sentient beings to enter the stage of Buddhahood; it can be called the Great Peace.
This is the place of bliss. △ Seventh, the vow for circulation:
"Now, we, the great assembly gathered here from the ocean-like multitudes, in order to repay the Buddha's kindness, shall not spare our bodies or lives for the sake of all sentient beings."
Pervading all Buddha-fields, they shall analyze and expound this subtle and wondrous Dharma, receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, and disseminate it so that it shall never be interrupted.
We pray only that the Tathāgata will look down upon us from afar with protective mindfulness.
To repay the Buddha’s kindness and to deliver sentient beings, one must certainly take the vow not to spare one's own body or life.
For when entering the five turbidities of this evil world, the turbidity of hatred is difficult to transform; one must rely on patience to deal with it.
If one were to regard even once the value of body and life as paramount, the Buddha-dharma could certainly not be practiced, and sentient beings could certainly not be delivered.
Thus, even the Buddha’s grace cannot be fully repaid. For this reason, a bodhisattva can endure even malicious abuse and physical blows;
although one may not be able to follow the transformation immediately, it is possible to plan for it over the long term.
As for "pervading all buddha-fields," their propagation of the Dharma does not stop at a single location. This is for the sake of all sentient beings.
Regarding "beings": the saving of beings does not stop at a single category; their differentiation does not stop at a single dharma;
and the exposition of the teaching is not fixed solely upon either the provisional or the ultimate. By means of the provisional being identical with the ultimate, differentiation is not hindered;

by means of the ultimate being identical with the provisional, the subtle and wondrous is not lost. Since the salvation of beings takes exposition as its primary focus, it is placed first. As for cultivation...
Practice takes upholding as its primary focus; therefore, it follows next. Those who read should master the text and understand its meaning; those who recite should chant to nourish the spirit.

To take up the brush and transcribe it, and to distribute it for wide circulation—vertically pervading all times and horizontally pervading all places—one causes the Wheel of Dharma to turn perpetually and the Three Jewels to abide forever. Hence it is said: "To ensure that they are never interrupted."

Furthermore, I only pray that you will look down upon me with compassion and grant the Buddha’s empowerment. To say that he "grants protection and mindfulness from afar" means that while our Original Teacher resides in this Sahā world, his teachings are being circulated throughout other lands;
were it not for the Buddha’s distant empowerment, I fear my own power would be insufficient.
"Protector," so that they may not fall back; "one who is mindful," meaning one who must surely bestow compassion. △ Eighth, the benefits realized upon hearing this chapter.
At that time, the great assembly, having heard this wondrous Dharma, attained immense benefit. There were incalculable and countless bodhisattvas.
Each shall realize the stage of non-retrogression. All humans and devas shall obtain supreme benefit.
Even all sentient beings of the five destinies shall sever their heavy obscurations, attain immeasurable happiness, and all shall eventually attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
What is heard is the same, yet the assemblies where it was taught differ; thus, there are variations in the depth of realization and the gradations of the stages.
There are none, however, who do not take *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* as the fruit of their realization. This concludes the major section on the "Correct Main Body" (*zhengzongfen*).
△ Third, the *pariṇāmanā* (circulation) section. The preceding section on the making of vows constitutes the circulation according to the principles of textual analysis;
however, it is separated by the section on the benefits gained from hearing this chapter, which was misplaced by the many translators who failed to provide a detailed arrangement.
Now, following the error with the error, I shall temporarily entrust this to them; let it be circulated merely as an entrustment.
It is divided into two parts, with the title of Chapter Thirteen: Entrustment.
To exhort and entrust is called a "bequest" (*zhù*). It is a burden that you must propagate it. This is because when the Buddha dwelt in the world, he himself preached the teachings;
however, for their propagation in future generations, it is vital to find the right person. For if one finds such a person, the Dharma flourishes; if one loses them, it declines.
Thus, there is the bequest so that it may circulate to distant lands for all eternity. It is titled as such and derives its name from being relied upon and put into practice.
△ Second, the scriptural text has thirteen sections. First, the Tathāgata addresses the assembly:
At that time, Śākyamuni Tathāgata addressed the great assembly of the ocean-like gathering of asaṃkhyeya bodhisattvas, including Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva, saying:
The Great Being Mañjuśrī, being already the Mother of Buddhas, assists the Buddha and propagates his transformation out of his own fundamental resolve;
why then would he wait for an entrustment before acting? It is because one who is not an ancient Buddha cannot realize it, and one who is not a wise person cannot bear it.
Therefore, he entrusts it to Mañjuśrī alone to announce universally to the assembly; the intent lies in providing proof and inspiring confidence. (Sanskrit: *Mañjuśrī*)

*Asaṃkhyeya*. This is translated as "incalculable. Because the number is immeasurably vast, it is called the "Ocean Assembly. △ Second, the account of what has already been cultivated and accomplished:
For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nayutas of great kalpas, I have not begrudged my body or life, nor my head, eyes, hands, feet, or blood.
Flesh, marrow, and bones; wife, children, and kingdom; cities and all manner of rare treasures—whenever anyone came to seek them, he gave them all away as alms.
He practiced hundreds of thousands of difficult and painful austerities and attained the realization of the Mahāyāna *Cittabhūmi-darśana-mukha* (The Gateway to the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground).
*Nayuta* is simply a different Sanskrit term for *nayuta*; here it is translated as "thousands, tens of thousands, and millions.

The phrase "up to hundreds of thousands of great kalpas" merely indicates the length of time. "Not sparing one's body or life," and so forth, collectively refers to ascetic practices, which are the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
This refers to the statement that one gives everything to those who come seeking; however, while such a thing is easy to speak of, it is difficult to practice.
To practice this is truly difficult; the Buddha was able to do so, and thus he recounted his own experience to admonish the assembly. Regarding the section "Cultivation":

although the difficult practices and ascetic austerities are said to number in the hundreds of thousands, they are all subsumed within the Six Perfections (*ṣaṭpāramitā*), representing the perfect cultivation of the myriad practices.
Regarding the section "Attainment and Realization": this refers to the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground; it is not obtained in vain, but is realized through the midst of ascetic practices.
This is because, before the formal entrustment [of the teachings] had even occurred, he first showed this in order to inspire a sense of preciousness.
Thus, if even the Great Sage Tathāgata is not easily encountered, how could the great assembly at this Dharma-gathering be treated as ordinary?

One should know that while the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) can only cultivate merit, the remaining five perfections can all lead to the realization of the Way. Without precepts, one cannot give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Without...
Concentration alone cannot give rise to wisdom; without diligence and patience, one cannot bring the practice to completion; and without wisdom, one cannot realize the fruit.

Although the path is accomplished through the five perfections, if one does not practice the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), then within the fruit there will be no possession of the physical marks and signs or various virtues, nor will there be offerings from humans and devas. Therefore, among all the perfections, the perfection of giving is the foremost. Thus it is said.
The Buddha summarizes and thus exhorts the assembly. III. Entrustment and Circulation:
"I now entrust this Dharma to you all. You should know that this profound sutra was proclaimed by the unsurpassed Ten-Powered Ones of the ten directions and the three periods of time."
The first two lines constitute the formal entrustment. To "entrust" (*fu*) means to commit the Dharma; to "instruct" (*zhù*) means to exhort with words.

The phrase "You should know" and below serves as testimony that this was spoken by all Buddhas in common, and is not the private discourse of a single individual. This is because the triple world is nothing but mind.
The mind itself is the ground. Those who are able to contemplate it achieve ultimate liberation; those who cannot achieve ultimate sinking and wandering.
Because of this, humans and devas cannot fathom it, calling it "profound"; even those of provisional and lesser vehicles remain deluded by it, calling it "extremely profound.

Furthermore, it comprehensively explains the beginning and end of the orthodox teaching; therefore, it is called a *sūtra*. The unsurpassed ten powers are the Buddha, meaning that all Buddhas possess them.
The ten powers of knowledge (*daśa-bala*) enable one to know all things; only the Buddha is supreme, and there is no one above him.
Because he views through the eye of wisdom, he is called "Supreme. As for the ten powers: the first is the power of the possible and the impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*).

(This is because he knows the fixed nature of all causes, conditions, and karmic retributions—knowing that from such causes and conditions such retributions arise, and that such retributions do not arise. The second is the power of karma (*karma-bala*). (This is because he knows the various [actions] of all sentient beings across the past, present, and future...)

3. The power of karma (because one knows all sensations); 4. The power of concentration (because one knows all dhyānas and samādhis); 5. The power of faculties (because one knows the superior and inferior faculties of other sentient beings); 6.

The power of aspirations (because one knows the various desires and inclinations of other sentient beings); 7. The power of the path leading to all destinations (because one knows the characteristics of all paths and their respective destinations); 8.
The power of recollecting past lives (because one knows the names, joys and sorrows, and the length of lifespans of one life up to hundreds of thousands of lives); 9. The power of the divine eye.

1. The power of the eye (because one sees sentient beings at the time of birth and death, as well as their rebirth in good and evil realms). 10. The power of the exhaustion of outflows (because one knows for oneself that birth has been exhausted and one will not undergo further existence).
△ Fourth, the sublime benefit of proclaiming this sutra:
Such a jewel of a sutra as this is most supremely subtle and wondrous; it is capable of bringing all benefit and happiness to sentient beings.
Within this trichiliocosm and throughout the buddha-fields of the ten directions, for all the infinite classes of sentient beings that exist therein—

May beings in the animal realm, hungry ghosts, and those in the hells, through the extraordinary merit and the majestic power of this *Mahāyāna Citta-bhūmi-parīkṣā Sūtra*, be freed from all suffering and attain peace and happiness. The power of such a sūtra and its merit are inconceivable.
It can cause the lands where it resides to be abundant and joyful, free from all enemies and adversaries.

The term "Jewel" (*ratna*) used for the Sūtra signifies its preciousness; that is, the Dharma of the mind-ground. Because one becomes a Buddha through contemplation of it, it is as noble and precious as a jewel.

The Sūtra belongs to the category of the expressive (the *vācaka*), and because it is valued for its capacity to express what is noble, it is called a "Jewel Sūtra. The second phrase indicates [this].

"Exquisite. This provides the correct explanation for the meaning of "exquisite" below. "In this [world] below," filling the Dharma-realm and encompassing all sentient beings, refers to those who are the types of beings benefited by this sutra.
"From this," below, reveals the divine power of the sutra. "Causing them to depart from," below, reveals the efficacy of that divine power.
"In this manner," below, clarifies that the excellence transcends the realm of thought. "It can cause," below...
This clarifies the benefits of the land. Because its borders are peaceful and quiet, there is no resentment; because rain and sunshine accord with the seasons, there is abundance and joy.
△ Fifth, the analogy of being like a wish-fulfilling gem.
For example, suppose there is a person who obtains a wish-fulfilling jewel and places it within their home; it can produce all manner of exquisite articles of enjoyment.
This precious sutra is just like this: it can bestow inexhaustible peace and happiness upon the realm.
Regarding the jewel named "Wish-Fulfilling" (*cintāmaṇi*): it is so called because the jewel can produce treasures according to one's wishes.
This serves as a metaphor for the treasure of this sutra; if a person attains wondrous realization, their inexhaustible wealth of Dharma is likewise like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
Just as placing such a jewel in one's home can produce all articles of enjoyment, so too does the presence of this sutra bring forth auspiciousness. Therefore, it is called "wondrous."
The Jewel of the Sūtras is likewise so. The Dharma is the very life-force of the wisdom of all Buddhas and the field of merit for both ordinary beings and sages.
For this reason, devas and nāgas provide protection and aid, winds and rains follow their proper seasons, and one naturally enjoys the bliss of peace, tranquility, and abundance.
Furthermore, it causes those who practice contemplation to swiftly awaken spiritual understanding and enjoy the bliss of the *dharmatā*-nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is said that there is no...
All shall be at peace and happy. △ Sixth, the analogy of the celestial drum:

Just as the mani-jewel celestial drum of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven can produce hundreds of thousands of various sounds, causing the celestial hosts therein to experience all manner of bliss, so too is the Dharma-drum of this sutra; it can cause the realm to be most excellent.
Peace and happiness. For this reason, you great assembly should abide in the power of great patience and circulate this sutra.
"The Heaven of the Thirty-three" (Trāyastriṃśa) is the Chinese translation for the name of the Tuṣita heaven; it is situated atop Mount Sumeru.
There are eight heavens on each of the four sides, totaling thirty-two, with Śakra ruling from the center; collectively, they are called the Heaven of the Thirty-three. The drum is located there.
Because it belongs to those devas, it is called the "Deva Drum. *Maṇi* is translated here as "wishing-fulfilling" (*yìrú*).
It is named a "wishing-fulfilling drum" because it produces sound spontaneously without being struck by anyone; it accords with the intentions of those devas, and is thus called "wishing-fulfilling.

Furthermore, it can proclaim and expound such dharmas as the causes and effects of the ten wholesome paths of action; therefore, it is said to be "various. It serves as an admonition to the devas, so that they do not dare [to be negligent].
