It is unrestrained. It causes those celestial hosts to enjoy natural heavenly blessings; therefore, it is called "happiness. Below this in the sutra, the dharma corresponds [to the drum].
Since the sutra corresponds to the celestial drum, it says: "The Dharma-drum is likewise so. "Able to cause" and below clarifies the benefits of the Dharma-drum.
Because the sutra explains the provisional and the real, as well as various contemplations and meanings, it skillfully accords with the capacities of all beings. Relying on the teaching...
By practicing this, one attains the realization of the wondrous fruit and is forever freed from the two deaths; therefore, it is called the "Supreme Peace and Bliss.

From the words "For this reason" onwards, he reiterates his previous injunctions. Now, the reason why he specifically entrusts the propagation of the teaching to those with the power of patience is that, in the Dharma-ending age, sentient beings hold evil views and lack faith;
one must therefore apply gentleness and endurance, waiting for them through skillful means, so that over time they may eventually follow.
This is a transformation. △ Section Seven: Comparing and Revealing Superiority, Part Two. First, Mañjuśrī asks about merit.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how rare! How rare!

It is the Tathāgata, it is the Sugata, who has preached this profound Mahāyāna *Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Subtle Mind-Ground*, which is able to bring vast benefit to those practicing the Mahāyāna."

"Yes, indeed, World-Honored One; it is truly profound and subtle. If there are good sons or good daughters who are able to uphold this sutra, even just a single four-line verse—how much merit will such persons obtain?"
"Tathāgata" and "Sugata" are two of the ten titles [of a Buddha]. These two rare epithets serve as words of praise. What follows explains the true praise for this rarity:
because of the excellence of his mind-ground and the vastness of his benefit, no one but a Buddha could fully detail them;
that he is now able to speak of them is seldom encountered in the world, and is therefore called "rare. "Evam" (Thus) means to believe with deep conviction.
These words are truly intended for those of lower capacity to clarify the meaning of faith.

If there were those of lower capacity who pointed to others and asked about blessings, it would be because practitioners of the Mahāyāna, upon encountering such an opportunity even once, experience a joy and fortune as great as that of a carp leaping through the Dragon Gate;

they certainly do not need to wait for a question, for they naturally possess supreme merit. It is just as if among the scholar, farmer, artisan, and merchant, each has their own duties and may be busy.
Finding leisure amidst one's duties, one upholds even a single verse. Such a person has never lacked merit. I pray that you will now explain this so as to inspire faith in them;
hence it is asked, "How much merit is obtained? △ Second, the Buddha’s comparison of merits, which has four parts. First, the merit of making offerings of the seven treasures to the Buddha.

At that time, the Bhagavān addressed the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, saying: "If there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with the seven precious jewels filling as many trichiliocosm world-systems as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, used them to make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions;
and for each and every Buddha, constructed a vihāra adorned with the seven precious jewels and established it as a place of offering for the Buddha."
And as for the Bodhisattvas— for a full period of *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* kalpas— he shall likewise provide all their necessities to all those Tathāgatas’ immeasurable śrāvaka disciples,
making offerings to them without distinction, just as he offers to the Buddhas. Furthermore,
after these Buddhas and their śrāvakas have entered parinirvāṇa, he shall erect great jeweled stūpas and make offerings to their relics.
"If there are those below" refers generally to men and women in the world who, seeking to obtain merit through desire, must make offerings to the Buddha.
Regarding "the Ganges River," this indicates the place where the greatest heaps of jewels for offering emerge;
for indeed, the magnitude of a single trichiliocosm is immeasurable, let alone when compared to the sands of the Ganges. "Filled with the seven treasures" means:
One might fill the sands of the world-system with the seven treasures to offer as an act of worship;
yet, even by thus making offerings to a single Buddha, one’s sincerity would still not be exhausted, and so one makes offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions.

Furthermore, for each and every Buddha, one constructs a vihāra to house them, adorning it with the seven treasures. Not only does one make offerings to the Buddhas, but also to the Bodhisattvas—thus one offers in this manner.

Regarding "nurturing": it is not only universal across all places, but also exhaustive throughout all times; hence it says, "throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. The phrase "those various...
and so forth indicates that they not only make offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, but also to the Śrāvakas, who are no different from the Buddhas.
The above constitutes offerings made during one's present life. The section beginning with "In this way... further clarifies the offerings made after [the Buddha’s] passing.
This is "nurturing. *Parinirvāṇa*—here translated as "entering extinction"—is when one builds a stupa with jewels and further makes offerings to the *śarīra*.
This manifests the sincerity from beginning to end. As for *śarīra*, it refers to the sacred relics. Now, among the sentient beings of the world, such a thing truly does not exist;
this is merely a hypothetical analogy used to compare their merit. However, at the conclusion, there is a lack of evidence.
Regarding the passage on "Examining the Response of Merit," the intent is that by making offerings, one brings about merit that is spontaneously immeasurable. 2.
Four Verses on the Circulation of Merit:
If a good man or a good woman, even for a moment, hears, believes, and understands a single four-line verse of this *Cittabhūmi Sūtra*, they shall generate...
Regarding the bodhicitta: to uphold, recite, read, explain, or transcribe it—even to the smallest extent—such as explaining it to but a single person;
or if one is of inferior capacity, to hear it even briefly rather than having long-standing practice;

and to have faith and understanding rather than doubt or dullness—this refers to this Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground. Even if one cannot hear the full and universal exposition, [hearing] but a single verse or four lines [is sufficient].
Although its essence is subtle, it flows forth solely from the mind of bodhi. When one attains correct faith through silent realization within oneself, one understands that objects are but the mind.
Whether one takes up this practice as a daily recitation, or reads and chants it until the text is mastered, or explains it to expound its meaning—each approach leads to the same goal.
Or they may transcribe it for circulation, even if it consists of only four lines or a single phrase;

though the wording is extremely brief and the text is not extensive, this merely describes the practice, which will be compared in the following section. △ Third, a comparison showing that the merit of making offerings does not equal [the merit of upholding the text].
Compared to the merit obtained from this exposition of the sutra, the merit of those various offerings does not equal even one-sixteenth part;
it cannot be reached even by calculation or analogy. How much more so for the immeasurable benefit gained by one who fully receives, maintains, reads, recites, and extensively explains it to others.
The first two lines refer to the merit of making offerings to the Buddhas mentioned previously; from this point downward, there is a formal comparison.
The reason for speaking specifically of "expounding the sutra" is that although the upholding of the sutra possesses six aspects, expounding it is the most superior.
Compared to the merit obtained from the aforementioned offerings to the various Buddhas and so forth, the latter does not equal even one-sixteenth part of the merit of expounding the sutra.

This extends even to that which cannot be reached by calculation or analogy; it is merely due to the difference between being attached to signs and not being attached to signs, and between being with outflows and being without outflows.
Truly, such persons have never failed to be sincere in their offerings, never failed to be numerous in their dwellings, and never failed to be expansive in their conditions.
Thus, the Buddhas have never failed to be supreme, and they exhaustively fulfill all that is long.
As for the duration of time, although his merit was exceedingly vast, he nevertheless did not surpass those who possessed but a small amount.

This is because the former merely obtained blessings, whereas the latter possessed both wisdom and blessings. Blessings can assist the body, while wisdom can assist the nature. When the body is assisted, it attains glory;
when the nature is assisted, it attains integration. Thus one knows that through the integration of one's own nature, one ascends loftily to Buddhahood.
One’s status may be anticipated; though one’s person may be glorious, one still cannot escape the cycle of birth and death.
Yet even this does not equal the merit of a single word, let alone that of an entire scripture. Thus it is said, "How much less could they be complete," and so forth.
This is more than a mere comparison of a ladle of water to the great ocean, or the wings of a firefly to Mount Sumeru; it is utterly insufficient, like lips compared to teeth. As for the former...
When a person makes offerings to the Buddha, they see neither the Buddha nor the objects [of offering]. Subject and object are suddenly severed, and both image and reflection are forgotten.
This is because Prajñā guides them, not allowing them to dwell in signs; this is precisely what constitutes the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).

How could it be that this [text] alone can penetrate the truth while that [other] cannot? Now, in order to weigh them and manifest its superiority, I shall first speak of those who abide in the marks of phenomena.
△ Fourth, the circulation of the merit among the assembly of women has two parts: first, the formal narration of the six modes of dissemination.

If there are women who resolve their minds toward Bodhicitta and receive, uphold, read, recite, transcribe, or explain this *Cittabhūmi Sūtra*—as there have already been virtuous women mentioned in the preceding section—the reason this section specifically clarifies them is that those with correct faith among women are still few, let alone those who possess the Bodhicitta.
Out of the Buddha’s compassionate exhortation, he speaks of them specifically. Regarding "receive and uphold," etc.:
This is the merit of the six types [of practice] (whether this or that, not necessarily all six). △ Second, further clarification of the blessings of the present and future, in two parts.
First, in one's final body, one does not fall into the eight difficulties.
Such a woman is in her final body and shall not receive another; she will not fall into the evil realms or the eight difficult conditions.
This clarifies that through the power of merit, one is liberated from suffering. As for "final body," it refers to all sentient beings who, since beginningless time...
Having long endured birth and death, one was unable to attain a final existence. Now, having encountered superior conditions, one joyfully attains the merit of upholding [the Dharma] and so forth;
by virtue of this, one shall never again undergo suffering or sink into the realms of rebirth, and will certainly realize the holy aspiration. Thus, it is called the "final body.
The eight difficulties of the evil paths are to be understood as before. △ Second, the ten kinds of superior blessings manifested in the present life.
In this very life, one shall experience ten kinds of meritorious benefits: first, an increase in lifespan; second, the removal of various illnesses and afflictions;
third, the ability to extinguish karmic obstructions; fourth, the doubling of merit and wisdom; fifth, an absence of lack in material resources;
sixth, supple and radiant skin; seventh, being loved and respected by others; and eighth, obtaining filial and supportive children.
Ninth, one’s retinue is harmonious; tenth, one’s wholesome mind is firm and stable.

These clarify that blessings are obtained through merit. The Sūtra elucidates the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena). Since the *dharmatā* does not perish, one receives the retribution of increased longevity.
Since the *dharmatā* is free from illness, it can eliminate disease. Since the *dharmatā* is free from obstacles, it can eliminate hindrances. This is the nature.
Because they possess both merit and wisdom, those who uphold [this sutra] increase manifold. Since the sutra is endowed with meritorious virtues, one will not lack material resources.
Because its inherent virtues moisten the body, the skin becomes lustrous. Because the nature of the Dharma is most sublime and distinguished, it inspires love and respect in others.

One who upholds this sutra is filial toward the Buddha; therefore, they attract children who provide them with filial support. Because the mind and temperament of one who upholds the sutra are warm and gentle, they attract...
The retinue is harmonious. Tenth, regarding the firmness of the virtuous mind:

because of the urgency of mindfulness toward the Path and the constancy of progress upon the Path, one perfumes the mind until it becomes the noble diamond-seed (vajra-gotra). How could there not be the principle of firmness? △ Eighth, being worthy of offerings wherever one dwells.
Mañjuśrī, wherever this sūtra may be—whether being read, recited, explained, or transcribed—that place where the scroll resides is itself a stūpa of the Buddha.
All devas, humans, and non-humans should offer it the most exquisite and precious jewels of the human and celestial realms. Why is this? Because wherever this scripture is located...
In that place, there are Buddhas, as well as bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvakas. Why is this?
Because all Tathāgatas, having practiced this sutra and abandoned the state of ordinary beings, have attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
and because all worthy and holy ones have attained liberation through this sutra.

"Wherever it may be" means it is present throughout all directions; hence the phrase "in every place. "Whether reading or reciting" below refers to each of the six types of practitioners being dedicated to one of them.
Since the sutra expounds the Dharma-body and is itself a śarīra, any place where the sutra exists is equivalent to a stūpa of the Buddha.
"All" and so forth clarify those who are worthy of making offerings—namely, those who possess the sutra.
Since this place is like a Buddha-stūpa, all devas and humans should offer it worship. "Devas" refers to those from the Four Heavenly Kings upward;

"humans" refers to those from the sun and moon downward; and "non-humans" refers to the seven classes of spirits (the seven classes being the eight classes excluding the devas, namely the gandharvas and so forth), as well as various birds and beasts. Although their karmic retributions differ, their buddha-nature is the same.
The same applies to those who offer [these things] to the Buddha; they shall all attain Buddhahood.

Therefore, it is said that one should make offerings with precious objects from among humans and devas. The following section interrogates and explains the meaning of "should offer. The phrase "If this...
means that wherever this scripture resides is itself the Three Jewels abiding in the world. The phrase "Why is this... is a further interrogation. The phrase "All... is repeated...

Explanation: This means that when all Tathāgatas were practicing, they all relied upon this scripture’s "Mind-Ground" (cittabhūmi) to cultivate the three secrets of the contemplative gate (*vipaśyanā-mukha*).

Thus, having abandoned the state of ordinary beings, they clarified the attainment of benefits through cultivation. "That which has already been attained" refers to the eternal exhaustion of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

"Attaining Anuttara... and so forth, refers to the certain realization of the Buddha-fruit (*buddhaphala*). The section beginning with "All... is the final summary, which returns [the teaching] to the scripture and brings it to completion.
All worthies and sages attain liberation by relying on this sutra. This is because the gateway of contemplation is vast, and thus it encompasses a profound range of capacities.
Therefore, it says, "all," and so forth. △ Ninth, the benefits after the extinction [of the Buddha], in four parts: First, the Dharma Master is equal to the Buddha.
Mañjuśrī, after my parinirvāṇa, during the final five hundred years when the Dharma is about to perish, if there should be a Dharma master who receives,
upholds, recites, studies, explains, and transcribes this *Cittabhūmi Sūtra*, the king among all sūtras— such a Dharma master as this...
He is no different from me.

In the final five hundred years—that period when strife is entrenched, when people are full of arrogance, and when the True Dharma is difficult to practice—furthermore, as false paths flourish and the Buddha-dharma is on the verge of being swept away, it is said: "When the Dharma is about to perish," although...
This sutra is recorded in fascicles; however, its widespread propagation depends primarily on finding the right person. Therefore, it says, "If there should be... and so forth.
Regarding the section "When receiving [it]," this clarifies that Dharma masters are not of a single kind, all of whom act for the purpose of circulating the holy path.

Now, as for erecting the great banner of the Dharma, exposition and interpretation are supreme. Why is this? Because the way of benefiting others values opening up and revealing [the truth], and the intent lies therein.

"Those among sentient beings who follow through transformation are many. Regarding "the various sutras descend": this means that the sutras elucidate the mind-ground; since the mind governs all phenomena, it is honored as the King.
Regarding "in this way," the Dharma Master refers to one who is capable of both upholding and expounding [the teachings].

"I" refers to the Tathāgata speaking of himself. "Those equal to me" indicates that because the Dharma is supreme, the person is thereby manifested as venerable. Furthermore, it enables the preservation of the whole body.
He bears the burden [of the Dharma] and acts entirely for the sake of others. Holding the precious torch of wisdom, he dispels the profound darkness and remains ever-illuminated.
Possessing unimpeded eloquence, he transforms the wicked and the heterodox so they may return to the Right Path. Therefore it is said: "Such a Dharma Master is no different from me.
△ Second, the merit obtained by making offerings to the teacher.

If there are good men or good women who honor and revere this Dharma teacher, they thereby make offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time; the merit obtained is equal and non-dual.
This is called making a true Dharma offering to the Tathāgata. Such is called the offering of correct practice.

The Dharma is supreme and the person is honored; therefore, they should be venerated. This is explained as follows: although the transformation bodies of all Buddhas differ, their Dharma-bodies are identical.

Although those who propagate the Dharma may possess the ordinary physical forms of commoners in the final age, their original aspiration and resolve are the same as those of all Buddhas, and their life of wisdom is no different.
Therefore, to make offerings to a single teacher is equivalent to making offerings to all Buddhas. This is the result obtained [from such practice]. As for the cause:
To offer is to bring forth merit. Since the Dharma Master is identical to the Buddha, the merit obtained from such an offering is equal and non-dual with the merit of offering to the Buddha.
This is called "inferior" [in terms of object], yet at the time of making the offering, to treat the person with utmost sincerity and reverence is itself to revere the Dharma;
thus, when the mind and the Dharma are in accord, this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata. Thus it is said.
The following verse clarifies this: at the time of making offerings, the mind is in union with the Path; this is itself right practice.
Therefore, the mudrā constitutes the offering of right practice. △ Third, the inquiry and explanation of its meaning.

Why is this? Because this great Dharma Master, during a time when no Buddha is present, shall expound for sentient beings of the turbid and evil age who hold false views this profound King of Sutras on the Ground of the Mind, causing them to abandon evil views and proceed upon the path to Bodhi, widely proclaiming and disseminating it.
To cause the Dharma to abide for a long time—this is what is meant by a "Buddha without the primary and secondary marks. Such a person is worthy of being honored by all humans and devas.
The first phrase poses the question: "What is the reason that honoring a Dharma teacher is equal in merit to honoring all Buddhas?
The passage beginning with "This is" provides the explanation; it means that when a Buddha is in the world, the Buddha is able to...

Regarding his teaching and transformation: although the Buddha was not in the world, the Dharma Master taught and transformed others. For those who were turbid and base, he manifested the ability to practice what is difficult to practice;
thus, his Way was identical to that of all Buddhas. As for the time, it was turbid; as for the faculties, they were evil; their views were heterodox.

Yet this Dharma Master, amidst a world of turbid times and sentient beings of evil conduct and false views, did not fear their corruption nor grow weary of their delusions; he expounded the King of Sutras on the Profound Mind-Ground.
He may truly be called a bridge across the turbid and evil age, and a bright torch within a dark chamber. Thus, he led others away from evil views toward Bodhi. To—
Because it spreads extensively throughout the ten directions, it is said that it is "widely proclaimed and disseminated.

Because it causes the lineage of the Buddha to endure forever, it is said that it "causes the Dharma to abide for a long time. The phrase "one such as this" refers to a person; the term "inferior" is used to honor their title.
Although they lack the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, because their Way is identical to that of the Buddha, they are called "Buddhas without marks or characteristics. Why?
How venerable he is! [The text] below all [the preceding sections] concludes with an exhortation to offer support. △ Fourth, the Buddha’s prophecy regarding those who provide support:

"If there are good sons or good daughters who join their palms in reverent devotion toward this Dharma-preacher, I shall bestow upon them the prophecy of supreme, great Bodhi. Such persons shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"Palms joined" below refers to the sincerity of reverence. "I bestow" below refers to the appropriateness of the recompense. "Unsurpassed," etc., refers to the fruit of Buddhahood. "Bestowing" means to speak and give;
"causing one to remember" means to ensure that the recipient does not forget. This refers to speaking of the giving within the causal stage.

To prophesy the fruit in the future is called "bestowing a prediction" (vyākaraṇa). This person is one who has received such a prediction. Because the fruit is attained through causes, it is said that they "shall attain [it]" and so forth.
△ Ten: The Benefits of Repaying Kindness, in four parts. First: Clarifying the Reading and Recitation as Repayment of Kindness.
If a person hears this *Cittabhūmi Sūtra* and, in order to repay the four debts of gratitude, resolves upon the bodhicitta— whether by writing it themselves, having others write it,
or reading and reciting it until they have mastered it.
The *Cittabhūmi Sūtra* is the collective title for this single work. Its purpose is to repay the four debts of gratitude and so forth, which constitute the very act of generating the bodhicitta.
These four debts of gratitude consist of four types: parents, sentient beings, sovereigns, and the Three Jewels.

Originally, when the five hundred elders, including Wondrous Virtue (*Miaode*), heard the Dharma of the Ground of Mind, they were unwilling to listen with joy; therefore, the Buddha acted to lead them toward the generation of the bodhicitta.

It is taught that the four debts of gratitude must be repaid; yet, without the bodhicitta, one cannot repay them. When Wondrous Virtue and others heard this, they were subsequently able to resolve their minds toward enlightenment.
Although the Buddha does not explicitly name those individuals here, his intention is to lead them and exhort the assembly.
Now that they have heard this sutra and resolved upon the Great Mind, they must ensure its circulation; therefore, he exhorts them, saying: "Whether by writing it oneself, or..."

One causes others to transcribe [the text], and also engraves seals upon it. Furthermore, one must become proficient in the text; thus, there is reading and recitation (recitation being synonymous with chanting).

Once the text is mastered, wisdom arises, and one will surely attain a profound realization of the Buddha’s intent; hence, it is called "thorough mastery" (*tōri*). Although transcribing, upholding, reading, and reciting all bring benefit, thorough mastery is the most important.
"Thorough" (*tō*) means that the words and their meanings are mutually integrated; "mastery" (*ri*) means that one is unimpeded whether moving forward or backward.
Obstruction. △ Second, explaining that the merit obtained is boundless:
The amount of merit obtained by such persons as these cannot be measured to its limit, even by employing the power of a Buddha’s wisdom to calculate its quantity.
"Chou" (籌) means to calculate; "liang" (量) means to measure. That which the Buddha’s wisdom cannot calculate or measure refers to merit that accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*);
it is beyond comparison. △ Third, the protection of the various devas.
Such a person is called a true son of all Buddhas. All the devas, including Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Great Heavenly Kings;
Hārītī with her five hundred retinues; the great ghost-king Virūḍhaka; and the eight classes of nāgas and spirits—all [revere them].
All the various spirits and deities who listen to the Dharma shall never depart for day or night, but shall always provide protection.
Since they have mastered the intent of the Buddha and possess the merit of succession and exposition, they are truly the sons of all Buddhas.
The phrase "all [the spirits]" below correctly clarifies their guardianship. Brahmā is the Lord of the Form Realm; Śakra is the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
When each Buddha attains enlightenment, these two deities are the ones who request him to preach the Dharma.
The Four Great Heavenly Kings and their peers all serve as external protectors. Hārītī is the Sanskrit name for Guizimū (the Mother of Ghosts).
Nairātmā is the name of the son of the Mother of Ghosts; he is a great ghost king who governs a retinue of five hundred.
Regarding "not departing day or night": one is for the sake of hearing the Dharma, and the other is for the sake of providing protection. Hearing the Dharma is for oneself;
providing protection is undertaken through the power of vows. △ Fourth, clarifying the increase of wisdom and eloquence.
Thus, O Son of the Buddha, one increases mindfulness and wisdom and bestows unimpeded eloquence to teach and transform sentient beings, causing them to plant the seeds for Buddhahood.

Increasing [mindfulness and wisdom] constitutes self-benefit, while teaching and transforming others constitutes benefit for others. Now, as for benefiting others, it necessarily relies upon unimpeded eloquence.
This means that in the final age, those who propagate the sutras and receive the Way will be few; it is necessary to rely upon eloquence to awaken the multitude.

As for the purpose of causing others to plant the seeds of Buddhahood, there is an underlying intention within this: it is because faculties vary between sharp and dull, wisdom varies between shallow and deep, delusions vary between heavy and light, and spiritual effort varies between diligent and indolent.
There may be those whose faculties are sharp, whose wisdom is deep, whose delusions are light, and who are diligent; such individuals are able to...
To those who attain sudden enlightenment before words are even spoken, there is no need for prolixity; a single phrase or a solitary word is sufficient to cause them to take up the burden.

Next, for those whose faculties are sharp and wisdom deep, yet whose delusions are heavy and who are prone to indolence, one provides detailed explanations and instructions to inspire them to resolve their minds upon the Way and practice it.
Although they cannot achieve perfection instantaneously, after a long time they will be able to perceive the Way.

Furthermore, as for those of the next lower grade—those of dull faculties and lacking wisdom, whose obstructions are heavy and who are prone to many forms of indolence—one employs unimpeded talent and skill, resorting to causes, conditions, and parables to cause them to give rise to faith and know that the Three Jewels exist.

Although they cannot realize the realization themselves at present, this serves to perfume their minds and establish the seeds, acting as the direct cause for their future attainment of Buddhahood. Therefore...
This means it causes one to plant the seeds for Buddhahood. △ Eleven: Seeing the Buddha at the Time of Death. Part One: Clarifying that the Three Karmas are Unconfused when Seeing the Buddha.
"Mañjuśrī, in this way, when such good sons and good daughters approach the end of their lives, they will, before them, obtain a vision of [the Buddha]."
The Buddhas of the ten directions have their three karmas undisturbed.
Good sons and daughters are those who have mastered the sutras through hearing them; as for "beholding the Buddha at the moment of death," this refers to the body born of one's parents.
Since this form is constituted by semen and blood, it must inevitably perish; therefore, it is called "the moment of death. Nevertheless—

The merit of having mastered and upheld [the teachings] throughout one’s entire life, as well as the state of sainthood yet to come—which is invisible to others—is manifested through the signs and circumstances at the moment of death;
thus, one knows that cause and effect are clearly evident. For seeing the Buddha without distraction is precisely concentration (*samādhi*).
Since concentration can give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*), the subsequent text describes thirty kinds of purity. △ Second, explaining the three [aspects].
Each karma has ten benefits, three of which clarify the ten kinds of purity of bodily action (*kāyakarman*).
First, one attains ten kinds of purity of bodily action. What are these ten? First, the body does not experience suffering.
Second, the pupils of the eyes do not protrude. Third, the hands do not tremble. Fourth, the feet do not extend or contract. Fifth, [the discharge of] excrement and urine...
Sixth, the body does not perspire. Seventh, one does not externally rub or scratch oneself. Eighth, the hands and fists are fully extended.
Ninth, the facial expression remains unchanged. Tenth, one turns over as one pleases. Due to the power of the sutra, such signs appear.
This bodily karma is undisturbed; as one who has attained the Dharma through purification, they enjoy the bliss of the Dharma.

Although this is a body of karmic retribution, at the time of death, they do not suffer the pain of the limbs and joints breaking apart. As for "the pupils of the eyes not being exposed": [this refers to...]
Half-open and half-closed: this is the sign of entering meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Seeing the external, one knows the internal; such is the nature of his self-attainment.
The third and fourth [stages] are likewise signs of concentration. This refers to those who previously lacked cultivation;

at the time of death, they are like a crab being dropped into a boiling pot—unable to avoid frantic movement of hands and feet. To be neither agitated nor withdrawn, however, is the sign of passing away while seated.

The fifth and sixth [limbs] are also signs of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). If ordinary people of the world were all subject to the turning of karma, they would soil their bodies with excrement and urine, and saliva would flow down their faces;
yet here, there is no such leakage or flow—this is sustained by the power of concentration. The seventh and eighth are also signs of concentration.
Ordinary people, in their panic and helplessness, reach out toward external objects and clench their empty hands into fists, only to regret it in vain.
However, for a single lifetime, this means that externally one does not grasp at things; rather, being able to extend and relax with natural ease is the manifestation of the enjoyment of samādhi.
Even the "ninety-day" period is a sign of fixedness. If an ordinary person manifests the signs of death, their body becomes heavy and difficult to move.
In this state, the face does not change its expression, and the body remains still even while turning over; these are all signs of being naturally at ease within samādhi.
Following the two subsequent lines of the sutra, the conclusion is drawn back to the power of the scripture. △ Second, clarifying the ten kinds of purity in verbal karma.
Next, one attains ten kinds of purity in vocal action. What are these ten? First, uttering sublime speech;
second, uttering gentle speech; third, uttering auspicious speech; fourth, uttering speech that is pleasant to hear;
fifth, uttering compliant speech; sixth, uttering beneficial speech; seventh, uttering speech of majestic power; eighth, not turning one's back on one's retinue.

Ninth, one will be respected and loved by humans and devas. Tenth, one will praise what the Buddha has spoken. Such virtuous speech all arises from this sutra. Words are the manifestation of the mind;
whether they are false or correct, nothing can escape them. Thus, when words are uttered, the Way is revealed. Subtle and wondrous speech conceals its mechanism within the phrasing;
gentle and soft speech expresses sincerity as a skillful means. Auspicious speech is a favorable omen for the stream of the sages; it is speech that people delight to hear.

The words and meanings accord with the capacities [of beings]. It is speech that is compliant; skillful means; speech that benefits; speech that dispels the delusions of the audience; speech of majestic power;

speech in which the provisional and the ultimate are both revealed; speech that is not contradictory; speech that is upright and impartial; speech for which humans and devas hold reverence and affection—this is identical to the Buddha and no different from it.
To praise what the Buddha has spoken is to attribute the grace to the Buddha. "Thus" and below concludes by returning [the merit] to the sutra.
Power. △ Third, the ten kinds of purity of mental action (*manas-karman*).
Next, there are again ten kinds of purity of mental action. What are the ten? First, not giving rise to anger; second, not harboring resentment;
third, not giving rise to a mind of stinginess; fourth, not giving rise to a mind of envy; fifth, not speaking...
1. Transcending faults and evils; 2. Not giving rise to resentment; 3. Having no perverted mind; 4. Not coveting various objects; 5.
Remaining far removed from the seven types of pride; 6. Swiftly desiring to realize all Buddha-dharmas; 7. Perfecting samādhi.
Mañjuśrī, such merits as these all arise from the inconceivable power of receiving, upholding, reading, reciting, mastering, explaining,
and transcribing this profound and wondrous sūtra.
Because one has attained the joy of the Dharma, one is free from anger. Because one realizes the equality of enemies and kin, one harbors no resentment.
Because one has attained great liberation, the mind is free from stinginess. Because the nature of phenomena is harmonious, the mind is free from envy.

Because the nature of phenomena is all-encompassing, one does not speak of faults or evils (fixing the mind upon the mouth). Because one brings others into accord with oneself, one does not give rise to a heart of enmity; thus, one turns back from delusion.
Returning to the truth, there is thus no inversion. Since the Jewel of the Dharma is inherently possessed, one does not covet external things.

Realizing that the holy and the ordinary share the same essence, one remains far removed from the seven types of pride. Having awakened to the fact that Buddhahood is attained within this very mind, one swiftly desires to realize [this state] and so forth.
"All inferior [states]" refers to the fact that once realized, the myriad virtues are already fully present. "Mañjuśrī" and below conclude by returning to the power of the sutra.
△ Twelfth: Entrusting the Teaching to Inspire Faith.
This *Cittabhūmi Sūtra* cannot be heard in immeasurable places or at immeasurable times; how much less can it be seen and fully practiced?
You, the great assembly, should uphold this with single-minded devotion. Quickly cast off the state of ordinary beings and you shall attain the Buddha-way.
All phenomena are mind-only; the mind itself is the ground. All Buddhas are born from this, and for this reason it is called the *Sutra on the Ground of the Mind*.
Regarding the phrase "not in a low [place]" and so forth, it clarifies that it is not the proper place or time, and that one should not transmit it lightly.

This is because ordinary people and outsiders are obstructed by false delusions, and were the teaching to be spoken to them, they would likely give rise to slander. Furthermore, those of the Two Vehicles are bound by *nirvāṇa*, and were it to be spoken to them...
I still fear that you may harbor doubts. This is why the assembly for the Dharma must select its location, and instruction of others must await the proper time;

it is no more frequent than the appearance of the udumbara flower once in a great while. How much less so for those of inferior capacity—using the light to illustrate the heavy—since it is said that even at immeasurable places and times, one cannot even obtain the name of this teaching, let alone behold it. Yet, as for those who do behold it...
This means to behold the entire text with one's own eyes. "To practice fully" means to follow and carry out the teachings according to the instructions.

"You all," and so forth, concludes with an exhortation. In this great assembly, there is no distinction made between the holy and the ordinary. With a single mind, one lets go of all external conditions. To uphold [the teaching] means to cultivate contemplation and investigate the truth.
By swiftly abandoning the state of an ordinary person, birth and death are forever severed, and one shall attain the Buddha-way. Thus it is said:

The fruit of Bodhi is perfected; indeed, the affairs of this single lifetime are now concluded. Furthermore, he has been able to provide these exhortations for us to uphold [the teachings], which is the final expression of his true compassion—truly difficult to repay.
This is because it was personally spoken from the Golden Mouth and cannot be heard in countless other places.

How fortunate we are to have been born in the Central Land and to have personally encountered the Sacred Scriptures! It is further said that even in immeasurable time, such an opportunity may not be found.
I have heard that from beginningless time until now, we have passed through countless thousands of millions of births, yet it is only now that we have first heard this.

Thus, we know that the Buddha’s words are truly not established in vain. Nevertheless, although we have been able to see and hear them, they are nothing more than texts and scrolls; when we seek to penetrate their profound meaning, we are instead left in utter bewilderment.
Why is this? It is because since the teachings were transmitted to the Middle Kingdom during the reign of Emperor Xianzong of the Tang dynasty, they have been translated [into Chinese].

It has been nearly a thousand years since [the scripture’s arrival], yet no commentaries or sub-commentaries have appeared, making it difficult to lecture upon. Consequently, virtuous men and faithful women have remained unable to hear its meaning.
I, [Zhou], having fortunately received the power of the Buddha, have erroneously drafted this commentary on the True Exposition (*Zhēnquán*), providing a mere single thread for future generations.
Considering my own meager virtue, I am filled with shame and perspiration. △ Thirteenth: The Assembly in the Sea Accepts and Practices.
At that time, the great bodhisattvas in immeasurable numbers, such as Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta; bodhisattvas of newly awakened resolve, such as Jñānaprabha;
the great śrāvakas, such as Ājñātakauṇḍinya; and the eight classes of devas, nāgas, humans, and non-humans—each with single-minded devotion, received and upheld the Buddha’s words.
They were all filled with great joy, and having accepted them with faith, they put them into practice.

This is also a narrative arrangement by the compiler of the sutra. Mañjuśrī represents the class of bodhisattvas in the profound stages; Jñānaprabha represents the class of bodhisattvas at the initial stage;
Ājñātakauṇḍinya and others represent the class of disciples who are the Buddha’s shadow-like attendants; and the devas, nāgas, and so forth represent the class of protectors of the Dharma.
Thus, ordinary beings and sages intermingle, gathered together in a single assembly through a common affinity, hearing the teaching and each understanding it according to their own capacity.
To uphold and maintain [the teachings] is what is meant by "each and every one. To experience joy and well-being in both body and mind is what is meant by "all were greatly delighted.
To practice and realize in this manner is what is meant by "faithfully accepting and practicing."
By the merit of this exegesis of the sutra,
I pray that the imperial domain may remain eternally secure, the Emperor’s Way may flourish far and wide,
the sun of the Buddha may increase in brilliance, and the Wheel of Dharma may turn forever.
May the ruler be sagacious and the ministers worthy; may fathers be compassionate and sons filial. May the five grains ripen in abundance and the myriad people delight in their vocations.
Furthermore, I pray that my biological parents, ancestral kin, and the six classes of relatives shall be liberated from suffering and transcend this life to be reborn in the Pure Land.

Moreover, I pray that my preceptor who granted me the tonsure, the *upādhyāya* who transmitted the Dharma to me, and the ten masters who conferred the precepts upon me, shall all attain the Great Samādhi and advance to the highest rank.
I also pray that I myself, as well as my deceased disciples Zixuan and Zixuan, along with the deceased monks and fellow practitioners who were my dharma-sons at this temple—
both those who passed away previously and those who have since departed— may, by virtue of the merit of this scripture, swiftly ascend to the shore of enlightenment. Furthermore,

may all the monastics and lay patrons who assisted in the carving of these blocks see their blessings and longevity increased in this life, and together realize Bodhi in the future, repaying the four debts of gratitude.
All beings within the three realms of existence are equally sustained; may all sentient beings contained within the Dharma-realm together realize the Perfect Wisdom.
The *Shallow Commentary on the Mahāyāna Sūtra of the Original Life and Mind-Ground Contemplation*, Scroll Eight (End).
